DEATH RIDDLE Woman found dead in pond as cops seal off park amid ‘unexplained death’ probe and fire crews flood scene

A WOMAN has been found dead in a pond in a public park amid an unexplained death investigation.

Officers were called to Lowther Gardens in Lytham, Lancashire, at around 9am today following reports of a body in the water.

Emergency services rushed to the scene, where the body of a woman was found.

Police have not yet established her identity and are treating the death as unexplained while enquiries continue.

News.title: Is the hot weather over? Met Office UK weather forecast for September – and if there will be another heatwave
News.content:
sun & done? Is the hot weather over? Met Office UK weather forecast for September – and if there will be another heatwave

BRITS hoping for another blast of sensational summer heat may have to keep the suncream in the cupboard for now.

The latest Met Office outlook points to a much more changeable spell across the UK, with temperatures closer to the September norm.



It comes after an exceptionally hot and dry July, which contributed to drought conditions in all of Wales and almost three-quarters of England.

August remained warmer than average across the UK, and drier than average in most regions.



A fifth heatwave hit parts of England and Wales in the middle of the month, with the hottest day of the year recorded on the 13th, when the mercury reached 38.1C in Kew Gardens.

But more unsettled weather, heavy downpours and thunderstorms arrived later in August.

Is the hot weather over?

For the immediate future, the intense summer heat appears to have passed.

The Met Office says southern and central parts of the UK will be largely dry and bright today, while conditions turn more unsettled further north with wind and gales in areas.

Sunny spells will make it feel warm in southern England, with the London and South East forecast giving highs of 25C, and showers and strong winds in the north.

A band of rain is expected to sweep south across England and Wales overnight, becoming heavy in places.



Tuesday will feel noticeably fresher for many once the rain clears from the southeast, while showers continue further north but winds gradually ease.

Wednesday should bring a brighter and generally drier interlude before another band of rain arrives from the west on Thursday.

Drier and brighter weather is then forecast to return on Friday, with temperatures likely to be around average for the time of year.

What is the Met Office’s long-range forecast for September?

The unsettled theme is expected to continue into the middle of the month.

For September 11 to 20, the Met Office predicts a mixture of dry intervals and spells of rain or showers moving in from the west.



Strong winds could also develop at times, while some nights may turn cooler.

There could be longer dry breaks as mid-September approaches, but forecasters say “a return of prolonged dry, settled weather looks unlikely”.

Temperatures are expected to remain close to average overall during this period.

From September 21 to October 5, the Met Office says: “High pressure initially close to the UK, with a continuation of more settled conditions at times, may eventually start to weaken its influence on the weather towards the end of September.

“As a result, it may become more changeable with a greater chance of rain or showers in places, and perhaps some strong winds at times too.



“Temperatures will likely be a little above average overall, with relatively cool nights possible at first tending to reduce in frequency later in the period.”

So while temperatures could be above average, that doesn’t amount to a heatwave.

What is a heatwave?

The Met Office defines an official heatwave as when temperatures in a certain area meet or exceed a specific threshold for three consecutive days.

Because the climate varies across the UK, these are divided by counties and regions.

25C: Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales, northern England, and parts of the South West.

Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales, northern England, and parts of the South West. 26C to 27C: Central, eastern, and southern counties.

Central, eastern, and southern counties. 28C: Greater London and surrounding Home Counties.

If temperatures reach or exceed these daily limits for three full days in a row, an official heatwave is declared for that area.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Long-range predictions become less certain the further ahead they look, and the latest Met Office outlook does not currently signal a prolonged spell of exceptional September heat.

So while summer-like warmth could still make a comeback on individual days as we head into autumn, anyone hoping for another full-blown heatwave will have to wait and see.

News.title: Woman and man found stabbed to death inside house as suspect in his 40s arrested over ‘murder’
News.content:
DOUBLE STABBING Woman and man found stabbed to death inside house as suspect in his 40s arrested over ‘murder’

A MAN and a woman have been found stabbed to death in a house as a man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Cops have launched a murder probe after the two victims were discovered at a property in Blackburn, Lancashire at 8.22am today.

Emergency services raced to the scene this morning where paramedics from the North-West Ambulance Service sadly declared the pair deceased.

The man and woman have not yet been formally identified, with a post mortem examination due to take place.





Enquiries have led officers to arrest a man in his 40s on suspicion of murder and he currently remains in custody.

Police are now appealing for anyone with relevant information to come forward.

Officers will remain in the area as they continue to probe the incident.

A Lancashire Constabulary spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with their loved ones at this distressing time.



“We have a dedicated team of officers assigned to this case, carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic enquires in the area.

“There is currently a scene on at the property and will remain in place over the coming days.

“You will continue to see an increased police presence in the area, as we conduct enquiries and provide reassurance.

“If you have any information or concerns, please stop one of our officers for a chat.”



Anyone who saw or heard anything suspicious in the area over the last 24 hours, or captured any CCTV, dashcam, mobile phone or doorbell footage has been urged to contact the force.

You can email forcecontrolroom@lancashire.police.uk or call 101 – quoting log 0252 of September 7, 2026.

News.title: Outrage as French armada of FIVE boats and two choppers escorts migrant mega-dinghy 70 miles to UK beach
News.content:
FRENCH rescue boats and two helicopters helped a mega-dinghy carrying 140 migrants cross the Channel to a UK beach yesterday.

Five rescue boats escorted the inflatable as it completed the unprecedented 70-mile English Channel crossing on Sunday.



The “safety operation” involved handing out lifejackets to everyone on board, including 20 women and eight “very young children”.

The flimsy inflatable reached Eastney beach, in Portsmouth, intact on Sunday afternoon, with nobody being injured after 14 hours at sea.



The departure point was more than 200 miles from the usual beach which dinghies leave from at Gravelines in France.

Fuming social media users slammed the authorities for “facilitating” the crossing and called for cops to “do your job”.



One said: “It’s clear the boats can’t be stopped by paying the French police to stop the invaders in Calais and Dunkirk, as the migrants will just launch from another part of France.”

Leader of Portsmouth City Council Steve Pitt also hit out at “poor judgment” by the Home Office following anti-migration protests.



He said Portsmouth was “a completely unsuitable location” to land lifeboats.

“The Government needs to take more action to prevent small boat crossings. Clearly people are not happy with the situation and we respect everyone’s right to protest but it should be done peacefully and within the law.

“We are pleased the coaches were eventually able to leave Portsmouth early this morning to take people outside of Hampshire for processing in the normal way.

“The council wasn’t asked about the decision to land the lifeboats in Portsmouth. This was entirely a decision taken by UK Border Force, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency and the Home Office.

“It was a completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore, this entire situation was avoidable and has brought needless disruption to our city.



“I would like to thank the emergency services for their professionalism under very challenging circumstances.

“However, the Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement. They put people at risk. This cannot happen again.”

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp added: “The last 24 hours have seen multiple violations of the UK border by mega-dinghies full of illegal immigrants which the French authorities have allowed to depart.



“Andy Burnham and Shabana Mahmood have been boasting about French action, but hundreds of illegal immigrants arriving in just a few hours shows this is not working.

“Their weak approach is leaving our border wide open, with almost 20,000 illegal immigrants crossing so far this year. Only rough seas have prevented even more crossings.”

Fears are now growing the first-of-its-kind crossing could mean the opening up of new routes across the South Coast.

And a much wider crossing zone – rather than the narrow, predictable and well supported Dover route – could put major pressure on services.

Scores of British anti-migrant demonstrators waded into the sea to meet them in Portsmouth, Hampshire – a city known as the home of the Royal Navy.



Roughly 500 protesters descended on the port city overnight in a tense standoff with riot police as they vowed to prevent migrants leaving.

Grandfather Barry John-Williams, 69, said he had to deflate his own dinghy to stop protesters taking it.

He estimated three coaches were parked up waiting for the migrants.



Details of the extraordinary crossing emerged today, when a senior search and rescue operative in France described how the mega-dinghy left an isolated Normandy beach near Jobourg on Sunday morning.

“It was in the very early hours of Sunday morning then it pushed off from the beach, with everyone on board,” he said.

“Jobourg is not patrolled by police, because nobody would expect a boat to leave from such an isolated, rocky spot.

“Within an hour or so the boat was in serious difficulty, and passengers on board made Mayday calls on their mobile phones.”

The outboard motor on the 46ft boat had failed, meaning it was drifting dangerously around 14 miles off the coast.



It was then that five French vessels were dispatched. With them was a French Navy H-160 helicopter, and a Dragon 50 civil security chopper.

The Abeille Liberté got closest to the stricken boat, and found “all on board packed closely together, and clearly in some distress,” said the search and rescue source.

“We asked them who wanted to be rescued, and the answer was no-one,” they added.

“There were twenty women and eight children among them, and they clearly caused the most concern.

“Only a few migrants were wearing life jackets, so we handed out jackets to all of them. It seemed incomprehensible that they were risking their lives without life jackets.”



The source continued: “A second out-board motor was made to work, so the boat could continue on its voyage to Britain.”

By 1.30pm on Sunday, the craft was 38 miles from France, and heading towards British water, where it finally joined by an RNLI boat from Yarmouth, on the Isle of Wight, and a British aircraft.

“The British boats finally saw the inflatable safely to England,” said the source, who added that he and his colleagues were not legally entitled to stop the mega-dinghy at sea.



The French authorities confirmed it was the first time that an immigrant boat has attempted to reach the UK from such a distance.

Last night’s protests in Pompey echoed scenes at an anti-illegal migration protest which blocked the Port of Dover on Saturday.

Cars were stuck in huge queues after the balaclava-clad group blocked off roads from 7am.

It comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed a crackdown on crossings.

A spokesman for the Maritime Prefecture for the English Channel and the North Sea said the escort operation had been essential “for safety reasons.”



He said: “The situation had to be monitored, in preparation for rescues if necessary. Those on board were determined to reach the UK.

“Given the structural fragility of these consistently overloaded vessels, the decision was made not to force migrants onto state rescue boats, so as to avoid endangering their lives in the event of a shipwreck.”

Hampshire Police said: “On Sunday evening (6 September) Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary officers worked alongside and assisted our partners from Border Force, Maritime & Coastguard Agency and Portsmouth City Council at Eastney Marina following the arrival of a small boat crossing the channel.



“Our officers were deployed to the area to ensure the safety of the public and to prevent disorder.

“The crowd of approximately 200 people dispersed at around 04:00 this morning. A number of police, Coastguard and Border Force vehicles were damaged during the evening.

“A small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance from any agency or the public was seriously injured.

“Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles, or other criminal offences has been launched.



“We can also confirm that Border Force has advised us that individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing as part of the normal process after they were safely disembarked.”

News.title: My son, 12, was IMPALED on door handle during game of tag – seeing it inside his arm made me sick
News.content:
FREAK ACCIDENT My son, 12, was IMPALED on door handle during game of tag – seeing it inside his arm made me sick

A SCHOOLBOY became impaled on a door handle after a game of tag went horribly wrong.

Ollie Davey, 12, had been at a friend’s house in Cwmbran, south Wales, when a door handle became stuck under the skin on his left arm for an hour.



Natalie, Ollie’s mum, had been at work when she received several missed calls from him.

The 35-year-old hairdresser assumed her son was asking for a lift or wanted some money, but soon found out that an ambulance was racing over to the friend’s house following the traumatic accident.



Natalie initially thought they were being “dramatic”, but after being sent a picture of her son’s arm, she said she felt physically “sick”.

She rushed over to the house and found paramedics and firefighters trying to work out how to free the lad safely.

Ollie explained that the “freak accident” occurred during a game of tag when someone tried to slam a door on him – but when he put his arm out to stop it, the handle got caught on his skin.

Gruesome images show how the metal door handle pierced Ollie’s skin, with the outline of the object clearly visible.



Natalie said: “He sent me a photo and I could see his arm was actually stuck on the door handle.

“He was grey and sweaty when I got there, I think he was in shock. He was in pain [but] he wasn’t crying. He was really brave.”

After being stuck for an hour, emergency crews decided to call an air ambulance so medics could sedate Ollie to make sure he didn’t feel any pain when they removed the door handle from his skin.



“When they sedated him and when he had gone to sleep, they managed to take him off the door handle, just by pulling him out. I couldn’t look,” said Natalie.

There were initial concerns that Ollie had sustained severe tendon damage.

But the kid was taken to The Grange University Hospital where doctors were pleased to see that he only needed minor surgery to clean and stitch up the wound.



Ollie was sent home that day and received the surgery the next morning.

After having a bit of weakness in his arm, Ollie has since recovered and is back to his usual self.

Brave Ollie said that he was in a bit of pain during the horrifying ordeal but was more worried about the state of his arm.

Natalie said that his friends were “amazing” and helped look after him.

She added: “He gets a bit sore around the wound but he’s back to being his normal self and on his bike and playing football.”



Thankful the accident didn’t result in more serious injuries, Natalie is now sharing Ollie’s story to highlight the potential dangers of playing indoors.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Natalie said: “I thought maybe he would damage his bones or have more serious injuries, he was really lucky.

“It’s the running and the doors. You don’t think it’s going to happen, but it can happen to anyone really.”

News.title: Flight instructor mum and two sons, 10 & 13, killed in horror plane crash as dad fights for his life
News.content:
A MUM and her two young sons have died in a plane crash that left her husband severely injured.

Flight instructor Danna Eady, 41, was the pilot of a small aircraft that crashed near Fresno, California, killing her and her two youngest children, Pavel, 10, and Remus, 13.



Her husband Craig, who was also on the plane, was the sole survivor of the crash.

On September 5, their aircraft crashed and burst into flames when it went down on a hilltop near Sierra Sky Park Airport in California.



The two boys were tragically found dead inside the plane.

Danna was rescued from the wreckage in critical condition and rushed to hospital.

She later died after succumbing to her injuries.

Craig survived and remains in hospital with severe injured and third-degree burns.

A SupportNow page says: “Craig is grieving the loss of his wife and two children while beginning a challenging recovery of his own.

“[He] now faces a long and difficult road of surgeries, rehabilitation, medical care, and recovery.



“His care is expected to continue for at least the next six months and likely well beyond that.“

Danna leaves behind two older children, Lucien, 17, and Felicity, 18, who are dealing with the “devastating loss of their mother and brothers.”

The family support campaign says donations will help to pay for Craig’s medical treatment and other family expenses.



As an experienced certified flight instructor at Reedley College, Danna dreamed of becoming a commercial airline pilot.

Friend and fellow flight instructor Nick Wilcox described her as a veteran instructor who had helped numerous students become pilots.

He said: “Danna was always just up for an adventure.

“She loved flying. She died doing what she loved.”

Emergency services found the plane ablaze on a hill overlooking the San Joaquin River.



Firefighters managed to contain and extinguish the fire before it could spread to nearby homes.

There was also a brief power outage, according to PG&E’s.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The cause of the crash has not yet been established, but the National Transportation Safety Board is investigating.

The agency said the victims were in a Grumman American Avn. Corp. AA-5 airplane, a four-seat, single-engine aircraft.

News.title: Zoo worker is killed by crocodile in front of horrified visitors after beast dragged him into water in ‘death roll’
News.content:
A ZOO worker has been killed by a crocodile after it unleashed a “death roll” in front of horrified punters.

Shocking footage has emerged showing the moment the croc trapped the worker in its enclosure at Adventure Park in Papua New Guinea.



The terrifying incident on Saturday afternoon horrified park-goers when the beast suddenly locked its powerful jaw on its caretaker’s legs.

Eyewitnesses at the Port Moresby park say the man was dragged into the murky water during a feeding session.



It is understood the park attraction regularly holds crocodile feeding demonstrations for visitors to watch where zoo workers routinely come into close contact with the animals.

Footage taken a few months before the deadly attack chillingly shows zoo staff getting dangerously close to the crocodiles with one clip showing a worker sitting on a croc’s back.

Bystanders desperately scrambled to free the man from the enclosure – including one who used a pole to beat the beast – but they were unsuccessful.

He was reportedly held captive for an hour until the cops were finally able to kill the animal.



Within that time the croc thrashed and rolled with the man in its jaws.

Police used a total of eleven bullets to down the killer croc.

The worker was rescued and rushed to 3 Mile General Hospital for treatment but sadly died from his injuries on Sunday morning.



Bystander, Koibuga Remdi, said the crocodile was extremely difficult to stop, causing the man to lose a significant amount of blood.

He said: “Many of us witnessed the incident, but unfortunately, there was very little we could do to help.

“Our only option was to call the police for assistance.

“When the police arrived, Adventure Park employees began pumping water out of the pond to make the rescue easier.

“‘Some workers said the crocodile had been living there since before Papua New Guinea’s independence and had never attacked the people who fed and cared for it.



“Sadly, today it unexpectedly turned on its caretaker.”

Park visitor Gibson John told ABC: “He brought the chicken to the fence and the crocodile attacked the person and tried to bring him into the pool.

“He was in severe pain but he couldn’t scream.”

Mr John said he could see the pain in the mans eyes.

He continued: “The only thing I could hear him say was, ‘I haven’t done anything wrong.”



In the wild a death roll is used to subdue, drown and then tear prey apart.

It is understood the worker had been at the park for around two years.

The park remains closed until further notice.

Authorities and park officials have yet to provide further details about the circumstances that led to the attack or whether any additional safety measures will be introduced before the attraction eventually reopens.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It comes as a crocodile mauled a tourist to death at Mexican holiday hotspot in June.



The 28-year-old holidaymaker was dragged underwater by the beast in the Mexican resort town of Puerto Vallarta.

News.title: Two festivalgoers dead at Burning Man – a year after unsolved bloody tent murder stunned popular Nevada desert event
News.content:
TWO festivalgoers have died at Burning Man within days of each other as thousands descended on the Nevada desert for the famous event.

The deaths come just a year after a reveller was found stabbed to death inside a tent at the festival – a killing that remains unsolved.



Craig Mann, 60 was found dead by his campmates at Black Rock City on Saturday afternoon, according to organizers.

His cause of death has not yet been revealed.





Burning Man said in a statement: “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with the participant’s family, friends, campmates, and all those affected by this loss.”

Mann’s death came just days after another festivalgoer, a man in his mid-50s, suffered a medical emergency on Thursday.

Read more on Burning Man FESTIVAL 'MURDER' Burning Man 'murder' victim found in a pool of blood is pictured

According to the New York Post, organizers said lifesaving measures were immediately carried out before he was rushed to the festival’s onsite emergency care center.

He was later pronounced dead.



Burning Man Project said: “It is with heavy hearts that Burning Man Project confirms a Black Rock City participant in his mid-50s experienced a medical emergency, immediately received lifesaving measures, and was transported to the onsite center for emergency care where he was pronounced deceased.”

The two deaths came during a turbulent edition of the nine-day desert gathering, which began on August 30.

Heavy rain also forced organizers to temporarily close the festival’s main entrance and exit in the Black Rock Desert.

People heading to Burning Man were told on Friday to delay their journeys, while those already on the playa were urged not to drive.

The tragedies come against the chilling backdrop of an unsolved homicide that rocked the festival just a year ago.



Russian festivalgoer Vadim Kruglov, 37, was discovered dead inside a tent on August 30, 2025.

His body was reportedly found in a “pool of blood” as crowds gathered for the traditional burning of “The Man” – the giant wooden effigy at the heart of the event.

Kruglov had reportedly been fatally stabbed in the neck, the New York Post reported.

His death marked the first homicide in Burning Man’s history and his killer has still not been identified.

Detectives are working with state and federal partners to verify the findings, but authorities have stressed they still do not have verified information identifying a suspect.



Officers are also continuing to sift through tips and other evidence, while remaining in contact with Kruglov’s family.

Burning Man organisers previously pledged to cooperate with the investigation.

They said following Kruglov’s death: “Our hearts go out to Vadim’s family and friends, and we grieve the loss of a community member.

“Burning Man Project is doing everything we can to assist the sheriff’s investigation so the perpetrator can be caught and brought to justice.”

The Pershing County Sheriff’s Office also condemned the killing and appealed for information that could lead to the arrest of “any person who would commit such a heinous crime against another human being”.



Ahead of this year’s gathering, cops warned revellers to “stay vigilant” while investigators continue their hunt for whoever was responsible.

The Pershing County Sheriff’s Office believes Kruglov’s killing was an isolated incident but urged festivalgoers to remain aware of their surroundings, travel with others where possible and report suspicious or erratic behaviour.

Burning Man began as a small gathering on San Francisco‘s Baker Beach in 1986 before evolving into a sprawling annual celebration of art, music and self-expression in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Attendance peaked at close to 80,000 people in 2019 before falling in subsequent years.

Around 70,000 revellers from 102 countries attended last year’s gathering, which was also hit by fierce dust storms that reportedly left some attendees injured.

News.title: What we know about anti-migrant protests and organiser Danny Thomas
News.content:
Saturday's protest in Dover saw men in black clothing and balaclavas block the town's main roads for several hours.

It was organised by Thomas - seemingly after weeks of plotting over the summer - who comes from Hayling Island near Portsmouth.

When Border Force then had to decide where to ask the RNLI to bring a boatful of migrants ashore on Sunday after an unusual longer English Channel crossing from Baie de Seine, it opted for the Eastney landing stage.

The very place where the passenger ferry departs Portsmouth for Hayling Island.

Whether this decision was made through ignorance or incompetence, it made it very easy for Thomas to mobilise his local support late on Sunday using social media.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
News.content:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save Â£1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to Â£22.9bn from Â£29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party in terms of producing their first electric car which is just about to go into production".

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

The prime minister's official spokesman said: "We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities."

The spokesman added that Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds "is in close contact with JLR and he will be meeting them early this week", but ruled out "any form of bailout".

Business and trade committee chair Liam Byrne called the cuts a "body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands".

"Whether or not these redundancies are voluntary, we now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work," he added.

News.title: Chancellor John Healey refuses to rule out tax hikes in October Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has refused to rule out tax increases in next month's Budget after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

In an interview with the BBC, Healey said he wants people to feel "confident about Britain and our future".

But he said "times are tough", with Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) on Monday announcing 4,000 planned job cuts, mostly in the UK.

And he refused to comment on any decisions about tax ahead of his first Budget on 28 October, promising only to "balance the books" and "control public spending".

Asked about the impact of higher borrowing costs, which have surged in the last few days, the Chancellor said that the government was responding to "extreme pressures in the wider market," and reiterated that he wanted to "bring down welfare costs."

Earlier, in his first major speech as chancellor, Healey said his mission was to "make Great Britain growth Britain" again.

Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, he said,

"My defining mission as chancellor is growth, good growth in every postcode. And I've set out today the way this government will set about it: more devolution, more public leadership and control, more investment, more innovation, more jobs."

Healey said he is in "lockstep" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the need for fiscal discipline and having a buffer in the government's spending plans "against the sort of uncertainty that the JLR decision locally has shown".

It came as Healey offered an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of the Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

Speaking in Coventry, he set out a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

With seven weeks until the Budget, Healey said the government will stick to Labour's manifesto pledge, made under Sir Keir Starmer and former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, to not "increase taxes on working people".

He repeatedly refused to comment on possible tax rises or spending cuts ahead of 28 October, stating only: "Staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending."

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, said: "Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises."

He added that Healey "sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves".

In his speech from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in the Midlands, Healey described the UK as "turning the corner" and said greater devolution would spread economic growth more evenly across the UK.

But recent ructions in government debt markets have piled fresh pressure on already-stretched public finances, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs and the need to fund higher defence spending.

News.title: Murder arrests over baby girl's death in woodland
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a baby was found dead while camping with her family in Staffordshire.

The three-month-old girl died after emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest in woodland off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, at 08:45 BST on Saturday.

The people arrested were a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

All four were detained at the scene and have since been bailed while inquiries continue, Staffordshire Police said.

Det Insp Josh Lee said officers were working to gather further evidence around the circumstances of the girl's death and were "keeping an open mind".

He said it was being treated as an isolated incident and urged people not to share "unconfirmed and speculative" claims online.

News.title: 'I have chronic cancer but I'm not going to die' - BBC presenter Maryam Moshiri
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has shared more detail about her two years living with cancer, and the way the chronic disease will affect the rest of her life.

She was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

Speaking to her colleague Lucy Hockings, Moshiri said she was lucky her GP caught the cancer early and reflected on how she felt in the aftermath of her diagnosis.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
News.content:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner will announce the review in Parliament later.

She is expected to tell MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

"And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations," she will add.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The 14 areas where local government reorganisation is being paused while a review is carried out are:

Derby and Derbyshire

Devon, Plymouth and Torbay

East Sussex and Brighton

Gloucestershire

Hertfordshire

Kent and Medway

Lancashire, Blackburn with Darwen and Blackpool

Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland

Lincolnshire, North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire

Nottingham and Nottinghamshire

Oxfordshire and West Berkshire

Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent

Warwickshire

Worcestershire

The government said decisions had not yet been taken on Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, and West Sussex, with these areas being considered alongside the wider review.

News.title: OpenAI chief scientist warns no one is prepared for consequences of AI
News.content:
OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has called for "extreme caution" over AI's runaway progress and warned more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".

"I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," he wrote in a blog post entitled "An Alien Mind, external".

The post comes only a few days after the ChatGPT-maker released its latest model GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

OpenAI and other AI firms like Anthropic shared reports of their AI agents acting autonomously and carrying out real-world cyber-attacks on other companies.

In July, OpenAI called an incident in which its AI agents - AI systems which can operate alone after human instruction - hacked the tech platform Hugging Face "unprecedented".

Meanwhile in September a report claimed months earlier AI agents from the firm had also hijacked a German website.

"We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity," Pachocki wrote in the latest blog post.

He said OpenAI would continue to "build defensive systems" and seek technical solutions to alignment - a term used to describe ensuring a machine's actions and goals perfectly match human intent and safety guardrails.

Pachocki added one of the firm's main priorities moving forward would be to build an "automated AI researcher" to keep pace with AI progress while ensuring ways that human researchers could remain part of the process.

"Instead of better AI guardrails, regulations, or assurance to keep people safe, they propose developing internal AI agents to research these problems," said Professor Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge.

"Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough."

Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agreed with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI model development - but he claimed OpenAI was unwilling to be transparent, and said this meant warnings risked being dismissed as "just self-interested hype".

"If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," he wrote on X, external.

News.title: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
News.content:
Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.

Tributes to the late country legend have appeared online and at locations including the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, after Parton died on 25 August at the age of 80.

Writing on Instagram, Stella Parton thanked those who had shown "genuine support" for the star and her family - but said a "tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted" had been "challenging to absorb".

Her request for people to show "more compassion" in how they respond to Parton's death follows similar pleas from families of late celebrities over AI tributes.

In October, Robin Williams' daughter asked fans to stop sending fake AI-generated videos of her father.

Zelda Williams' plea was shared by Dr Martin Luther King Jr's daughter Bernice A King, who asked fans to "please stop" in a post on Instagram.

Little over a month later, Robert Redford's daughter Amy spoke out over AI content created, external to pay tribute to the American actor following his death last September.

"Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different," wrote Parton in her Instagram post on Friday, external.

"Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."

She said there had been a tide of AI and "garbage" posts, adding: "As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move onto the next stampede of endless misinformation."

Parton also asked that people look to her sister's life as "an example for tolerance" and mutual respect.

"It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she said.

News.title: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, The World Today presenter was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

News.title: Rapist serving life may face more assault charges
News.content:
A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations involving seven more women were passed to prosecutors.

Chinese national Zhenhao Zou is serving a life sentence with a minimum term of 24 years after he was found guilty of drugging and raping 10 women in London and China between September 2019 and May 2023.

Believing Zou had committed further crimes, police appealed for more potential victim-survivors to come forward.

The Metropolitan Police has sent a file containing the new allegations of sexual crimes to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which will decide whether to bring further charges.

According to the Met Police, the file contains evidence relating to several alleged offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.

It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as the alleged rape of two women who remain unidentified, the force said.

A total of 23 women contacted police following the appeal, but most of them did not want to pursue criminal charges, the force added.

The Met said separate inquiries were ongoing into allegations involving women who were allegedly assaulted by Zou in China, with officers working to obtain evidence from the Chinese authorities.

News.title: Money offered by SoS does not go far enough, parties say
News.content:
Money being offered by the secretary of state to resolve Stormont's budget deadlock does not go far enough, Sinn FÃ©in and the DUP have said.

The parties were speaking after the executive met Sir Chris Bryant, who arrived on Monday for talks about the issue.

BBC News NI understands that the initial offer to the executive was Â£350m a year over the next three years. But the executive is believed to have said it needs Â£450m annually to meet its pressures, leaving a gap of Â£100m each year.

The executive has said it cannot agree a budget for this financial year without additional support from the Westminster government.

Following the passing of a deadline in August, Stormont officials were given legal powers to spend up to 95% of last year's funding in the absence of ministers agreeing the budget.

Last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to get the Stormont government functioning properly with a budget, but it is unclear how much money London could provide.

Sir Chris held talks with the executive on that issue, as well as seeking the parties' views on potential reform of the institutions.

He held talks with the executive before meeting party leaders and holding one-to-one bilaterals with the five largest parties.

News.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
News.content:
Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.

Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson .Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.

Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.

The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

The recordings will go out throughout October on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at midday on the pair's new show.

A performance from Stockport-formed band Blossoms on 5 October will kick off the run.

Rock band Nothing But Thieves, US rising star Stella Lefty, Brit-nominated singer Beabadoobee and London-based artist Odeal are also among the artists on the line-up.

Brighton duo Royal Blood will close out this year's sessions on 30 October, but a surprise artist, who will perform just before them, is still to be announced.

West Midlands superstar Jorja Smith will be performing following on from the release of her third album, What Are The Odds.

News.title: 'Super-university' created amid funding squeeze
News.content:
The universities of Kent and Greenwich have merged to form the UK's first "super-university" amid sector-wide financial pressures.

The new London and South East University Group (LASE) becomes the UK's third largest, with more than 50,000 students across four campuses in south-east London and Kent.

Leaders say the institutions are "much stronger" together as higher education providers face mounting economic strain, but the University and College Union previously raised concerns that the merger signalled a "broader problem for the sector".

The two universities, which legally merged last month, will still operate as distinct academic divisions within the group, retaining their current names.

Students will still apply to the institution they choose and degrees will be awarded in the name of Kent or Greenwich.

But the group will now be able to offer subjects that they could not before when they were separate entities, and students will be able to use libraries and access wellbeing services across the campuses in Greenwich, Medway and Canterbury.

Chief executive Prof Jane Harrington said the merger had made the universities financially stronger.

She said the combined group would also be better placed to help tackle regional youth unemployment.

"If I was to look through south-east London going out we've got areas of urban deprivation, then you go out into Medway and Kent you've got areas of rural deprivation and then we've got areas of coastal deprivation," she said.

"It's a real opportunity for us to address the very people that the government's worried about."

News.title: Schools close early again for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
A number of schools will again close early on the day of the funeral for one of the men who died in a crash which killed seven, including two police officers.

Theo Rae, 17, was among the five in a car which went the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough in the early hours of 22 August and hit an oncoming Cleveland Police vehicle.

Middlesbrough Council said some schools had chosen to close ahead of Monday's funeral, including a primary school which claimed the move would "ensure safe transit home for all our families".

Schools in neighbouring South Bank closed early on Friday for Jakub Matusiak's funeral, which police said "passed without issue" and with "very minimal traffic disruption".

Rae's funeral is to take place at Teesside Crematorium, Acklam, Middlesbrough, on Monday afternoon.

The funeral cortege is expected to travel around Middlesbrough before going to St Bede's Chapel on Acklam Road.

Cleveland Police said Ladgate Lane, Ormesby Road, Cargo Fleet Lane and Acklam Road will all be affected.

News.title: 'The man who drugged and raped me was freed from prison and went on to kill'
News.content:
A man who drugged multiple women over a 40-year period and eventually killed his partner should never have been released from prison, according to one of his victims.

Richard Scatchard was jailed twice but released from prison on licence in 2013.

He went on to kill Kelly Faiers in 2023, by coercing her into taking sleeping tablets after drinking alcohol.

Some experts and a former police detective believe he should not have been free to kill her, having shown signs he was a danger to women.

Krystyna, 70, has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak publicly for the first time about her abuse by Scatchard.

He went on the run after Kelly's death, and was found dead in a caravan park six months later.

The National Crime Agency has said there is an "urgent need" to deal with what it said is a growing international issue of men drugging and raping women - sometimes filming the assaults and posting them online.

News.title: Pioneering fossil hunter recognised with blue plaque
News.content:
A pioneering fossil hunter who was one of the first women to be employed by the Natural History Museum has been recognised with a national blue plaque.

Dorothea Bate, who died in 1951 aged 72, "transformed our understanding of prehistoric animals and ancient environments" through her research, Historic England said.

She has been recognised with a plaque at the Natural History Museum, in Tring, Hertfordshire, which notes in its inscription that the palaeontologist was the "Officer-in-Charge of this museum from 1948".

Bate was born in Carmarthen, Wales, in 1878 and developed a fascination with the natural world from an early age.

She moved with her family to rural Gloucestershire as a young woman and spent hours exploring the surrounding countryside and caves, collecting fossils.

She had little formal education, instead largely teaching herself, and in 1900 asked for work behind the scenes at the Natural History Museum in London.

Her determination impressed museum staff, earning her a position as an assistant and beginning an association with the institution that would last more than 50 years.

She published her first scientific paper, A Short Account Of A Bone Cave In The Carboniferous Limestone Of The Wye Valley, in 1901.

Bate went on to undertake expeditions across the Mediterranean, often travelling alone to remote caves in search of evidence of ancient life.

In Cyprus, she discovered a previously unknown species of dwarf elephant and in 1909, while in the Balearics, she discovered the myotragus - an extinct goat-like antelope.

She achieved more than 80 published scientific papers, despite spending most of her career without a permanent paid position.

In 2017, a blue plaque was dedicated to Bate at Napier House in Carmarthen where she was born.

As schools reopen and people head back to work, the autumn shoulder season is an ideal time to explore some of Europe’s most beautiful cities at a gentler pace.

During September and October, visitor numbers tend to fall, allowing travellers to secure significant savings during a much quieter time of year.

“The prices of flights and hotels can drop quite significantly this time of year,” says Laura Carden-Lovell, travel expert and head of operations at travel resale marketplace Transfer Travel.

Nonetheless, she encourages off-peak holidaymakers to factor in additional costs that can quickly mount up.

“It’s important to also think about transportation within the city you want to visit and to find out how much this might cost,” recommends Carden-Lovell. “Walkable cities are great if you're planning on going on a quick city break, as you will be able to see a lot of places for free on foot.

“Car rental prices also typically fall during shoulder season periods compared to peak summer seasons.”

Many hidden gems in Europe, particularly in the Balkans, have seen a surge in interest driven by social media.

“Social media provides travellers with a snapshot of what to see and do in a particular destination, so platforms like TikTok and Instagram can be a great source of inspiration for holiday planning,” says Carden-Lovell.

For anyone who has been patiently waiting for the perfect last-minute city getaway, here are five budget-friendly destinations to consider:

1. Tirana in Albania

“Tirana in Albania is bright, colourful, and is full of history,” says Carden-Lovell.

“Albania is one of the largest, fastest-growing tourism markets in Europe, so its capital Tirana has become increasingly popular.”

The city encompasses many distinct and interesting areas to explore that blend a vibrant modern culture with a unique communist and Ottoman history.

“I would recommend starting exploring at Skanderbeg Square [the main plaza in the centre of Tirana], which costs nothing to explore,” advises Carden-Lovell. “Then head into Blloku, a lively neighbourhood where you can go café hopping.”

open image in gallery Tirana has become increasingly popular ( Alamy/PA )

To get the best picturesque views of Tirana, hop on the Dajti Ekspres, a cable car that takes you directly from the edge of Tirana up to the edge of Dajti Mountain National Park.

“It’s the longest leisure cable car in the Balkans and costs around £15 for a return trip,” says Carden-Lovell. “The national park itself is also completely free to explore.”

You can get flights to Tirana for incredible prices. For example, Wizz Air offers return flights from London Gatwick and London Luton to Tirana from around £34.

2. Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina

“Sarajevo is something a little bit different and is a great affordable option for an autumnal city break,” says Carden-Lovell.

It’s also regarded as an incredibly good city for mooching.

“In the Old Town there are lots of traditional market stalls, lots of local crafts, some really good food shops and some historic mosques to look around,” says Carden-Lovell.

open image in gallery A walking tour can be a great way to explore Sarajevo ( Alamy/PA )

“It has also got the famous Pigeon Square [officially known as Baščaršija Square], which is centred around the iconic wooden Sebilj fountain, so there’s a lot of history packed into this small city.”

A walking tour can be a great way to explore the highlights of the city.

“Most walking tours are free and are a great way to learn about what the city has to offer. You can book a lot of these online,” says Carden-Lovell.

Wizz Air offers return flights from London Luton to Sarajevo from around £78.98.

3. Sofia in Bulgaria

“Bulgaria is another great place to visit on a budget,” says Carden-Lovell. “Its capital, Sofia, has got some really nice cathedrals which are very pretty both inside and out.”

The capital of Bulgaria is filled with reminders of its extensive history.

open image in gallery You may get some real steals on flights to Sofia ( Alamy/PA )

“You could join a walking tour to look around some of the Roman ruins or churches, and the historic Roman thermal baths are also worth seeing if you have time,” says Carden-Lovell.

This delightful city has an efficient, affordable public transport network, so it’s very easy to get around.

“Sofia has a really cheap tram system, so you don’t necessarily have to walk everywhere if you don’t want to,” says Carden-Lovell.

You may get some real steals on flights. For example, Ryanair offers return flights from Bristol to Sofia from around £40.99.

4. Tallinn in Estonia

“I’d also recommend visiting Tallinn in Estonia – this one is really popular on TikTok,” says Carden-Lovell.

“Stay in the heart of the old town, which is UNESCO-listed. It has wonderful fairytale streets and colourful buildings.”

After you’ve wandered around the charming old town, check out Telliskivi Creative City, the creative hotspot of Tallinn.

open image in gallery The Patkuli Viewing Platform offers a panoramic view of Tallinn’s medieval Old Town ( Alamy/PA )

“It’s a bit more modern than the old town and there are lots of independent cafes, local artists, street art and bars to explore here,” says Carden-Lovell.

She also suggests relaxing in one of the city’s public saunas.

“Saunas are a big part of the culture in Estonia, so I definitely recommend going to a sauna somewhere, especially in the colder shoulder season,” recommends Carden-Lovell.

Wizz Air offers return flights from London Luton to Tallinn from around £58.53.

5. Riga in Latvia

“Another great city to visit in shoulder season is Riga in Latvia,” says Carden-Lovell. “You can explore the medieval town on foot, and soak up all the history.

“Transportation is also super-cheap and there are loads of independent coffee shops to pop into.”

Make sure you visit St. Peter’s Church, which is one of the most recognisable landmarks in the city.

open image in gallery St. Peter’s Church is one of the most recognisable landmarks in Riga ( Alamy/PA )

“On the observation tower of St. Peter’s Church you get a great 360-degree view of the city,” says Carden-Lovell.

It usually costs around €3 to look inside the church, but if you want to go to the observation tower it costs €9, according to Tripadvisor.

Riga also has a vibrant and growing food scene.

“I would really recommend trying Latvian honey cake here,” recommends Carden-Lovell.

Ryanair offers return flights from London Stansted to Riga from around £60.99.

The 2026 NFL season begins on Wednesday with a rematch of the Super Bowl, launching an unpredictable race for the championship featuring a record nine international fixtures played across four continents before concluding on Valentine's Day in Los Angeles.

An offseason filled with extensive roster overhauls, coaching adjustments, and shifting title odds has left the path to Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium on February 14 wide open and difficult to predict.

The Seattle Seahawks will launch the 2026 campaign by raising their championship banner before facing the New England Patriots, marking the league’s first Wednesday opening game since the 2012 season.

This unusual scheduling clears the runway for the NFL’s most ambitious international push yet.

open image in gallery Seattle Seahawks cruised past the New England Patriots in last season's Super Bowl ( Getty )

The NFL's slate of international fixtures this season will span seven nations and eight venues, starting Friday in Australia at the Melbourne Cricket Ground where the San Francisco 49ers face the Los Angeles Rams in the league's inaugural regular-season game Down Under.

From there, the global tour heads to Rio de Janeiro's Maracana Stadium for a matchup between the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys, followed by three games in London and stops in Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City.

Major roster shifts across the league

Significant turnover has swept through the league since Seattle relied on a dominant defensive performance to secure the franchise's second Lombardi Trophy in February.

Already viewed as title favorites, the Los Angeles Rams took an even bolder approach. A marquee trade brought Myles Garrett from Cleveland in exchange for Jared Verse and multiple draft selections, reinforcing belief in LA's championship aspirations. Aaron Donald subsequently ended his short-lived retirement to rejoin the squad he guided to a title in 2022.

Meanwhile, New England - which served as the league's model of parity after surging from the bottom of the AFC East to the Super Bowl in a single year - added further offensive firepower by trading for Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver A.J. Brown.

While Seattle returns largely intact in its quest to repeat, their title defense includes questions in the backfield after Super Bowl MVP running back Kenneth Walker III departed for Kansas City in free agency.

open image in gallery There is uncertainty over how Patrick Mahomes will perform on his return from an ACL injury ( Reuters )

The Kansas City Chiefs enter the campaign surrounded by uncertainty, primarily regarding how quarterback Patrick Mahomes will perform upon returning from a season-ending ACL tear sustained in his left knee last December.

Mahomes, who previously guided Kansas City to three Super Bowl crowns over a five-year stretch, did not play in any preseason matchups as a safety measure but appears ready for their September 14 opener against the Denver Broncos.

Chiefs wide receiver Xavier Worthy said he held no doubts regarding Mahomes's return, adding that his teammate's relentless focus throughout the recovery process stood out.

"His grind, his will and want-to is beyond anybody I’ve ever seen," said Worthy. "Whatever he puts his mind to, that’s what he’s going to do. He kind of leads the team in that way."

Significant attention has surrounded top overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza in Las Vegas, but the rookie's regular-season debut will have to wait after the Raiders named veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins as their starter under center.

New head coaches take to the sidelines

Sidelines underwent just as much transition as playing lists. A record-tying 10 franchises appointed new head coaches during the offseason, with six earning their first opportunity in the role.

Among the first-time leaders, Jesse Minter inherits a talented Baltimore Ravens roster centered around two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson, while the Buffalo Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to replace Sean McDermott following years of postseason frustration.

Few storylines illustrate the league's combination of youth and longevity quite like Pittsburgh's. Four-time MVP Aaron Rodgers, who at 42 is the league's oldest player, returns for his 22nd season to reunite with new head coach Mike McCarthy - the duo previously won a Super Bowl together with the Green Bay Packers in February 2011.

open image in gallery Jesse Minter has taken charge of a talented Baltimore Ravens roster ( AP )

Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin, who stepped down in January after 19 seasons at the helm, believes the veteran pairing has the potential to surprise rival teams.

"I think that's the only reason Aaron comes back. He believes it, I believe it. I don't think he comes back if he doesn't believe that," Tomlin said on "The Rich Eisen Show".

"They're probably not being talked about in the ways that some others are being talked about, but that can be a good motivator and a catalyst for them as well. I think they got high expectations, and I think they should have high expectations."

When Killing Eve ended, many fans expressed their frustration with how the series concluded – and Jodie Comer has now reflected on this, revealing that she instead “reverts to the memory” of making the show.

The US drama, in which British actor Comer played Russian assassin Villanelle, received huge acclaim for its debut season. But the final episode received a backlash from dedicated fans, with some calling it “the worst finale since Game of Thrones”.

Much of the anger surrounded the fact that Villanelle was killed off in the closing moments, despite a happy romantic ending being teased for her and Sandra Oh’s character, Eve Polastri, throughout the final season.

open image in gallery Jodie Comer in 'Killing Eve' ( BBC America Original )

Comer acknowledged the fan outcry in The Independent series Life in Pictures, stating: “I think as an actor you just have to have your blinkers on in a sense. Of course, you want people to be fulfilled or happy – they’ve spent such a long time with your story and your character, you know?

“You want them to feel satisfied in some way, but it’s always ultimately out of your control, so it’s tricky really.”

However, Comer, who won an Emmy for the series, said that she chooses to look back at her time making the show when thinking about its legacy.

“I always revert back to the memory of being on the set and working with the crew, and people worked so tirelessly to honour that moment,” she commented.

When the series finale aired in 2022, writer Laura Neal said killing off Villanelle had been “really difficult to find the best ending”, and claimed the show’s team “talked about it loads”.

open image in gallery Jodie Comer reflects on career in new 'Independent' interview 'Life in Pictures' ( The Independent )

Comer herself told Elle at the time “It would have been easy for it to feel very maudlin, I think, or to go completely the other direction and make it feel too funny. So striking the right balance between the two of them felt really important.”

Comer said her character’s death was “inevitable”, adding: “She’s like a cat with nine lives. What I loved about the moment [she gets shot] was that was a really selfless act that she did that caused it.

“It felt right that in that moment she protected Eve. There was something about that shielding, I think, that signified how much she had changed.

“She was trying so desperately to change at the beginning and I don’t think she ever realised how much she had, which is so sad. That moment really shows how Eve changed her life.”

open image in gallery 'Killing Eve' fans were hoping the lead characters would have a happy ending ( BBC )

The following year, Comer told interviewer Josh Horowitz that she anticipated “a mixed reaction” and admitted that she doesn’t like to think of Villanelle “floating around the River Thames”, joking: “Perhaps she crawled out.”

Watch The Independent’s full interview with Comer here. The actor can currently be seen in Hugh Jackman film The Death of Robin Hood, which is in cinemas now.

Mathew Davis, a resident of an Austin, Texas homeless shelter, dreams of securing an apartment of his own. Yet with the minimal earnings he receives from donating blood plasma, even a $450-a-month tiny home without running water and with a shared bathroom remains a major stretch.

Meanwhile, more than 4,500 properties the city deems affordable — nearly 16% — sit vacant.

"I don’t make enough money really to afford anything," Davis, 49, said, referring to the couple hundred dollars he makes each month. "I just keep trying to swim uphill."

America’s most impoverished individuals confront the most severe shortage of affordable places to live. But most low-income housing funded in recent years is intended for people earning 50% of an area’s median income or more, according to a survey of state housing agencies.

Several cities are now recording higher vacancy rates as rental prices for these units near market levels. Consequently, apartments classified as affordable remain unoccupied because the poorest individuals simply cannot afford the rent.

Meanwhile, some individuals are driven onto the streets, while others face severe hardships trying to pay for costly shelter.

America has just 4 million affordable homes for 11 million families who need them

open image in gallery A person sweeps outside during the grand opening of the Rose on Colfax, a new affordable housing community with a co-located childcare center in Denver ( Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

America has just 4 million affordable rental homes for 11 million extremely low-income households, exposing a vast gap between the people most in need of housing and the homes being built for them.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition defines extremely low-income households as those earning below the federal poverty line — just under $16,000 for a single person — or 30% of their area's median income, whichever is higher.

The group accounts for roughly a quarter of U.S. renters and includes low-wage workers, older Americans and people with disabilities living on fixed incomes.

About 75% of these households spend more than half their income on rent and utilities, leaving little for food, transportation and other necessities.

open image in gallery A window lets light into an empty bedroom in an affordable housing building run by Central City Concern, a homeless services nonprofit in Portland, Oregon ( Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Yet only 12% of affordable homes financed through the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit in 2024 were reserved for extremely low-income residents, according to the National Council of State Housing Agencies.

Most were targeted at people earning at least 50% of their area's median income. In Austin, for example, that can mean a single person earning about $47,000 a year, compared with less than $28,000 for someone classified as extremely low-income.

The tax-credit program has financed nearly 4 million affordable homes since it was created 40 years ago, but critics argue its complexity drives up construction costs.

"If you're going to subsidize affordable housing, you should give the money directly to tenants," said Chris Edwards, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, who favors housing vouchers.

open image in gallery Cabin-like tiny homes are seen at a micro community in Denver ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

But vouchers face their own severe shortage. Only about one in four eligible families receives one, with waiting lists in some areas stretching for years.

Developers say that without additional subsidies, building apartments affordable to the poorest Americans can be financially impossible.

"The math does not lie," said Carmen Romero, president and CEO of True Ground Housing Partners in the Washington, D.C., area.

"Our expenses don't make it really possible to create a 30% AMI unit, unless there was this extraordinary amount of subsidy that just doesn't exist."

Thousands of ‘affordable’ apartments sit empty as renters choose market rates instead

Across U.S. cities like Austin, Denver, and Portland, Oregon, rents for 60% area median income (AMI) housing are nearing market-rate apartment prices. As a result, some renters are choosing slightly higher market-rate rents to gain faster approvals and undergo less income verification, leaving a growing number of affordable units unoccupied.

open image in gallery In Austin, the vacancy rate across all affordable housing has reached nearly 16%, with over 4,500 vacant units, according to real estate data and analytics firm CoStar ( Getty )

In Austin, the vacancy rate across all affordable housing has reached nearly 16%, with over 4,500 vacant units, according to real estate data and analytics firm CoStar. A healthy market vacancy rate typically sits around 5%.

Affordable housing builder LDG Development reported a 12% vacancy rate for its 60% AMI units in Austin. Chief portfolio officer Rebekah Fischer noted that LDG is "in direct competition" with thousands of recently built market-rate apartments in the city.

Regarding the extensive paperwork required for affordable housing applicants, Fischer said: "I have to have every bank statement, every paycheck, every bill, every Venmo transaction that you had with your friends."

She added: "When we’re almost going after the same renter, you can be approved within two minutes at a market-rate deal, where unfortunately in affordable housing … it takes time."

open image in gallery In Denver, 60% AMI units financed through the federal tax credit program show a 13% vacancy rate, while 80% AMI units have a 21% vacancy rate ( (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) )

In Denver, 60% AMI units financed through the federal tax credit program show a 13% vacancy rate, while 80% AMI units have a 21% vacancy rate, according to the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority. Meanwhile, housing remains drastically scarce for the city's poorest residents.

In Portland, where a housing shortage also impacts the lowest income brackets, the Portland Housing Bureau reports over 1,700 vacant affordable units, creating a 7.5% overall vacancy rate.

Most of these empty properties target those earning 60% AMI—roughly $54,000 for a single-person household—with rent capped at $1,444 monthly. Bureau data from CoStar shows this is close to the $1,581 average rent for a market-rate one-bedroom apartment.

Portland resident Jaiden Barbee earns about 55% of the area median income and remains on waitlists for affordable housing. However, he said he'd prefer to pay higher market rates to skip the complex application process.

"I’d rather spend the $200 extra just to get into a place easier that’s wherever I want" and doesn’t have "all these hoops," he said.

Austin promised 20,000 homes for its poorest residents. It has built just 543

According to city records, Austin has constructed just 543 units toward a 2018 to 2027 target of 20,000 for extremely low-income residents, who represent 17% of all households in the city.

By contrast, local officials successfully met their entire goal of 15,000 units designated for individuals earning between 60% and 80% of the area median income.

Responding to inquiries from The Associated Press, the Austin housing department acknowledged the urgent need to expand options for the poorest populations. It said it is taking steps, including prioritizing funding applications that feature 30% AMI units.

The shortage remains frustrating for residents like Davis, who spent a year living in his car before finally obtaining a bed at an Austin shelter.

"I want to shut the door at night and be able to sleep," he said. "I really just want to find the right place."
