World.title: Security, activism and the burden of proof, By Mukhtar Ya’u Madobi
World.content:
The Nigerian Armed Forces, the Nigeria Police Force and the country’s intelligence agencies comprise thousands of dedicated officers and men who continue to confront terrorism, insurgency, banditry and organised crime under extremely challenging circumstances. Their collective sacrifices should not be overshadowed by allegations that remain untested or unsupported.

The foremost responsibility of any government is to protect the lives and property of its citizens, maintain public order, and safeguard the territorial integrity of the state. In fulfilling these constitutional obligations, governments rely on security institutions — the military, police, intelligence agencies and other law enforcement bodies — as the backbone of national defence and public safety.

In Nigeria, where terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, communal violence and organised crime continue to test the resilience of the state, the role of these institutions cannot be overstated. Every day, thousands of security personnel operate under difficult and often life-threatening conditions, making enormous sacrifices in the service of their country.

Those sacrifices deserve recognition.

Yet recognising the commitment of security personnel does not place them above scrutiny. In a democratic society, accountability is indispensable. Allegations of misconduct, corruption, abuse of power or collusion with criminal elements must be thoroughly investigated, and where wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the full weight of the law.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The challenge arises when grave allegations are presented to the public as established facts without credible evidence to support them.

This concern has once again come to the fore following comments attributed to social media activist Martins Vincent Otse, popularly known as VeryDarkMan (VDM), during the 2026 Annual General Conference of the Nigerian Bar Association in Rivers State.

Speaking on the country’s security challenges, Otse reportedly argued that politics lies at the root of Nigeria’s insecurity and alleged that some government institutions benefit from the persistence of the crisis. More significantly, he accused elements within the military and the police of collaborating with kidnappers and other criminal groups.

According to reports, he alleged that some police officers stationed at highway checkpoints provide criminal gangs with information about travellers, including their identities and movements, thereby facilitating kidnappings and ransom demands.

He was quoted as saying:

“The root of insecurity is politics. The government benefits from this. The police benefit. The military men benefit. Since insecurity started, generals get higher pay.”

These are weighty allegations.

There is an important distinction between criticising the performance of security institutions and accusing their personnel of systematic collaboration with criminals. The first is a legitimate exercise of democratic oversight; the second is an allegation of serious criminal conduct that requires credible evidence.

It was therefore unsurprising that a military representative at the conference reportedly cautioned against making allegations that could not be substantiated.

Similarly, the Nigeria Police Force, through its Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Ani Iniedu, invited VeryDarkMan to provide evidence in support of his claims.

Public institutions have both a responsibility to investigate credible allegations and a duty to protect their personnel against unfounded accusations capable of damaging institutional integrity.

The issue is not whether citizens have the right to criticise security agencies — they unquestionably do. The issue is whether individuals with significant public influence should be held to the same standards of accountability they demand from others.

This is not the first time VeryDarkMan has found himself at the centre of controversy over serious allegations against security officials.

He had previously accused Assistant Inspector-General of Police Moshood Jimoh, then overseeing Zone 2 Command, Lagos, of frustrating investigations into high-profile criminal cases, including allegations relating to murder and land disputes.

Following the allegations, the police invited him to substantiate his claims. He did not honour that invitation in Lagos. Instead, both he and the senior police officer were subsequently invited to the Force Headquarters for further engagement.

According to available reports, subsequent investigations cleared the senior police officer Jimoh Moshood of the allegations. Yet despite the reputational implications of the accusations, there appeared to be no further legal consequences to the activist if indeed the claims could not be substantiated.

Another example arose when VeryDarkMan publicly criticised the Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) over the interrogation of a retired military officer accused of involvement in an alleged coup plot. After publishing excerpts of the interrogation online, he questioned both the professionalism of the intelligence officers involved and the evidence reportedly linking the retired officer to the alleged offence. His outbursts simply expose security and intelligence services to public ridicule.

Again, citizens have every right to question government actions, especially where national institutions are concerned.

However, allegations touching on national security, senior public officials and ongoing investigations require a high degree of responsibility. Such claims should be supported by verifiable evidence and pursued through appropriate legal and institutional channels.

This is not merely about protecting institutions. It is about protecting the integrity of public discourse.

Where evidence exists, those implicated — regardless of rank or position — must be investigated and prosecuted. Where allegations prove to be false, reckless or malicious, the law should also take its course. Accountability must apply equally to institutions and individuals.

The objective should never be to suppress dissent, investigative journalism or civic activism. Democratic societies depend on robust public scrutiny.

But activism is most effective when it is anchored in facts rather than speculation.

The influence of social media has made this responsibility even more important. Today, an allegation posted online can reach millions of people within minutes. Unfortunately, corrections, clarifications or investigative findings rarely receive comparable attention. Consequently, reputational damage may persist long after allegations have been disproved.

Against this backdrop, the Coalition for Security Awareness and National Stability (CSANS) has previously expressed concern over campaigns it believes unfairly undermine the reputation of security institutions and their personnel.

Whether or not one agrees with every position taken by the coalition, its broader concern deserves consideration.

Public confidence in security institutions is itself an essential component of national security.

The Nigerian Armed Forces, the Nigeria Police Force and the country’s intelligence agencies comprise thousands of dedicated officers and men who continue to confront terrorism, insurgency, banditry and organised crime under extremely challenging circumstances. Their collective sacrifices should not be overshadowed by allegations that remain untested or unsupported.

Equally important, effective policing depends on public cooperation. Communities provide intelligence, report suspicious activities and support law enforcement because they believe security agencies are acting in the public interest.

If that confidence is systematically eroded through unverified accusations, criminal organisations stand to benefit most. Distrust between citizens and security institutions weakens intelligence gathering, hampers investigations and ultimately strengthens those who threaten national security.

This does not mean criticism should cease.

Rather, criticism should be evidence-based, responsible and constructive.

If anyone possesses credible evidence that security personnel are collaborating with kidnappers, terrorists or other criminal networks, such evidence should be presented to the appropriate investigative authorities. Where wrongdoing is established, prosecution should follow without hesitation.

Conversely, allegations that cannot be substantiated should not become accepted public narratives merely because they have gone viral. The rule of law demands that accusations be tested through evidence rather than public sentiment.

Nigeria needs a more mature national conversation about insecurity — one that simultaneously honours the sacrifices of security personnel, demands professionalism and accountability from security institutions, and insists on responsibility from those who shape public opinion.

Activists have a duty to speak truth to power.

Security agencies have a duty to respect citizens’ rights while responding professionally to criticism.

Both are equally bound by the rule of law.

At a time when terrorists, bandits, kidnappers and organised criminal networks continue to exploit every weakness in Nigeria’s security architecture, the country cannot afford an endless war of narratives between security institutions and their critics.

What Nigeria requires today is not louder accusations or defensive denials, but verifiable facts, transparent investigations, institutional accountability and responsible public engagement.

Facts must prevail over speculation.

Evidence must triumph over sensationalism.

Accountability must replace impunity.

And above all, the national interest must always outweigh personal confrontation.

Only by upholding these principles can Nigeria strengthen public confidence in its security institutions, reinforce democratic accountability and build a safer and more secure nation.

Mukhtar Ya’u Madobi is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Crisis Communication (CCC) Abuja.

World.title: After initial ‘capture’, army declares notorious terror kingpin wanted, places ₦30 million bounty
World.content:
The Nigerian Army has declared a notorious terror kingpin, Ifeanyi Eze, wanted.

Eze, popularly known as Gentle De Yahoo, hails from Imo State, South-east Nigeria.

He was earlier declared “captured” by the military authorities before resurfacing in January.

A top military official confirmed to PREMIUM TIMES on Monday that the Nigerian Army issued the wanted notice.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

₦30 million bounty

The wanted notice, which has a photograph of Mr Eze, was circulated by the Joint Task Force in the South-east, known as Operation Udo Ka.

The notice also bears the logos of the Nigerian Army and Udo Ka.

Udo Ka is an ongoing army-led joint security team in the South-east tasked with clearing criminal networks and armed groups, particularly targeting activities linked to the outlawed Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB).

“A reward of ₦30,000,000 awaits anyone who provides credible information leading to the capture of Gentle De Yahoo threatening peace in the South-east,” the notice reads in part.

The army provided phone numbers and urged Nigerians with credible information about the terror kingpin to contact the security authorities using them.

The information could be provided anonymously, the notice said.

Who is Gentle De Yahoo?

Mr Eze, who claims to be a Biafran agitator, has been linked to some deadly attacks in the Okigwe Local Government Area of Imo State, including the murder of three of his fighters in the area.

The terror kingpin is a commander of the Biafra Liberation Army in Okigwe, which was established by Simon Ekpa, a controversial Biafra agitator and leader of Autopilot, a faction of IPOB.

IPOB is a group leading agitation for an independent state of Biafra, which it wants carved out from the South-east and some parts of the South-south Nigeria.

Mr Ekpa was jailed last year for terrorism in Finland, a Nordic country.

Meanwhile, PREMIUM TIMES reported in September that Mr Eze and his boys were feared killed when Nigerian troops raided their hideout in Aku-Ihube, a community in the Okigwe Local Government Area of Imo State.

‘Initial capture’

This newspaper earlier reported that the Defence Headquarters had announced that troops of Operation Udo Ka of the Nigerian Army “captured” Mr Eze during an operation in the south-eastern state between eight and 13 October 2025.

But on 28 January this year, a video clip which went viral showed the terror kingpin announcing his return from an undisclosed location and threatening those he accused of betraying him.

In the clip seen by PREMIUM TIMES, Mr Eze, who was also dancing to celebrate his survival, suggested that he had been in Akwa Ibom State, South-south Nigeria, where he had gone to receive medical treatment after he and his militants were poisoned.

READ ALSO: Court strikes out suit filed against APC candidate for Imo federal constituency

‘It could be AI, but we’ll investigate it’

At a press briefing in late January, the Director of Defence Media Operations, Michael Onoja, said the video clip might have been AI-generated.

“What I can say is that in this current dispensation of AI, it is possible to create anything just to destabilise and cause panic within the society,” Mr Onoja, a major general, had said.

“Notwithstanding, we will initiate necessary action with relevant security agencies to confirm if it is that he (Mr Eze) is back,” the director added.

He vowed that if the military authorities confirmed the return of the terror kingpin, they would immediately take action to prevent him and his group from causing more harm to people.

World.title: From Wimbledon to the US Open: How Oluwaseun Ogunsakin Is Rewriting Nigeria’s Tennis Story
World.content:
For Nigerian tennis, Wimbledon was supposed to be a breakthrough moment.

Oluwaseun Peter Ogunsakin, popularly known as The Shark, is ensuring it is only the beginning.

Barely two months after making history at Wimbledon, the Nigerian has followed up by qualifying for the US Open Junior Championships main draw, firmly establishing himself on the biggest stages of junior tennis.

At Wimbledon, Ogunsakin became the first Nigerian in decades to compete at the tournament and the first Nigerian in more than a decade to feature in a Grand Slam main draw. Having never played on grass before and with less than a week to acclimatise, he went on to reach the semifinals of the doubles event.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Historic.

But the question after Wimbledon was whether it marked the beginning of something bigger or was merely a one-off.

The US Open has provided an answer.

Ogunsakin came through qualifying with straight-set victories over Poland’s Tymon Litwic, 6-3, 6-0, and Canada’s newly crowned No. 1 junior, Felix Roussel, 6-3, 6-4.

Two Grand Slam main-draw appearances in one season.

And that distinction matters.

For years, Nigeria has served as a pipeline for exceptional talent, particularly in tennis. The challenge has often been turning that talent into sustained international success.

Ogunsakin’s rise represents something slightly different: a Nigerian player not simply participating on the international circuit, but progressing, winning and advancing at major events.

That progress has not happened by accident.

Behind the player is a development structure focused not only on training, but also on preparing him for the demands of international tennis.

At the centre is Aurum Tennis Academy Abuja, where Ogunsakin has developed under the guidance of a dedicated team with more than 100 years of combined coaching experience.

His career development plan, curated by Aurum Tennis Academy, has involved international exposure, carefully selected tournaments, training opportunities and high-performance development through the Aurum Tennis Academy, the African Regional Training Centre in Tunisia and the Grand Slam Player Development Programme.

The idea is simple: talent has to be matched with the right environment, the right competition and the right opportunities at the right time.

The result is beginning to show.

Wimbledon was not a one-off.

The US Open has followed.

And that consistency may be the most important part of Ogunsakin’s emergence.

With the Nigerian flag now appearing on the biggest stages in tennis, Ogunsakin’s journey could represent more than the rise of one player.

It could offer a blueprint.

Nigeria has never lacked tennis talent. The bigger challenge has always been building a sustainable pathway that can take talented young players from local courts to the highest levels of international competition.

His story also raises a bigger question for Nigerian tennis: what happens if this pathway is replicated?

What if the next Ogunsakin does not have to be an exception?

What if Nigeria could create an environment in which reaching the Grand Slam stage becomes an expected part of the journey for its best young players, rather than a historic rarity?

Those are questions that extend beyond one player.

For now, Oluwaseun “The Shark” has another milestone in front of him.

He turns his attention to the US Open main draw and the next target: a maiden Grand Slam main-draw victory.

From the distinguished grass of Wimbledon to the bright lights of New York, the Shark continues to make his mark.

The Nigerian flag will be showcased at the US Open as Oluwaseun Ogunsakin adds more pages to the country’s history books.

World.title: Senator Buba, banditry and the social media mercenaries, By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
I approach national security and intelligence operations with deliberate caution. Revealing successes too early can compromise ongoing missions; failures narrated without context can sound like conspiracy theories. Allegations against individuals working at the sensitive intersection of intelligence, non-kinetic security strategy, and politics can inflict irreversible reputational damage — even when entirely fabricated.

That caution explains my initial reluctance to write on the recent viral video purporting to show “high profile bandit kingpins” on a visit to the residence of Senator Shehu Umar Buba of Bauchi South. But the scale of the circulation, and the pattern behind it, now demand public clarification.

I have known Senator Buba for about two years, during investigations into non kinetic approaches to counter insurgency in Northern Nigeria. In that period, senior security and intelligence officials — including the Office of the National Security Adviser under Malam Nuhu Ribadu — provided information that did not support any of the banditry allegations repeatedly circulated against him. This does not certify perfection; it simply reflects what the evidence showed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The campaign against him is not new. The allegations took formal shape in September 2024, when Bauchi State Governor Bala Mohammed, once an ally of Senator Buba, petitioned President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. The petition claimed that the senator, through an aide named Yahaya Ibrahim, sponsored a bandit kingpin to the 2024 Hajj and distributed motorcycles to bandits. Senator Buba denied the claims, insisted he had no aide by that name, and explained that his Hajj sponsorships — like his scholarships, medical outreach and other empowerment initiatives — are based on recommendations from community and religious leaders, and that he does not personally screen or identify the beneficiaries. No investigation has contradicted his explanation.

After the petition failed to gain traction, the same narratives resurfaced through social media influencers with far lower evidentiary thresholds. Since mid 2025, photographs and videos alleging Buba’s support for bandits have surfaced periodically. In professional verification chats with mainstream media organisations and senior editors who had received similar allegations and multimedia content — including a respected Abuja bureau chief who is also a media scholar with strong investigative credentials, the publisher of Zagazola, and a US‑based northern Nigerian journalist‑activist — all examined the materials and declined to publish them because they found no substantiation. Their restraint was professional judgment, not fear.

Nevertheless, Senator Buba petitioned security agencies to investigate the disinformation network. Several suspects — including a lawyer and three influencers — were arrested, while a fifth suspect, Hassan, fled the country.

On 30 October, 2025, the suspects were arraigned before Justice Rita Ofili Ajumogobia on charges of criminal conspiracy, cyberstalking, defamation, advance fee fraud, and extortion. The prosecution alleges that they broadcast false videos accusing Senator Buba — the then chairman of the Senate Committee on National Security and Intelligence — of sponsoring banditry and causing a breakdown of law and order in the country. The extortion charge suggests the campaign may have been more commercial than political at that time.

In July 2026, a fresh petition emerged — this time against Muhammad Abdullahi Abubakar (SAN), former Bauchi governor and APC gubernatorial candidate — for defaming Senator Buba. Filed by Jay Adl Attorneys, it alleged cyberstalking, criminal defamation, incitement, and disturbance of public peace, following viral statements in which Abubakar questioned the senator’s wealth and insinuated that it had to do with “blood money.” The political context is clear: Senator Buba defected from the APC to the PRP and is now the PRP’s gubernatorial candidate. The disinformation campaign, the rivalry, and the legal proceedings are intertwined.

Meanwhile, the latest episode came in August when a content creator known as “D English Alhaji” circulated a video claiming to show bandit kingpins at a senator’s residence. PRNigeria’s factcheck established that the video was a splice of two unrelated clips: Kaduna based Hajj returnees visiting Senator Buba in 2023, speaking Fulfulde/Fulani, and a separate group of individuals displaying passports and speaking English. Neither clip involved bandits. The content creator later interviewed Hassan — the fugitive suspect — who supplied the footage. The interview went viral with some funny allegations.

By the way, how can anyone seriously believe a narrative by the same Hassan in the interview claiming that bandits were brought to Abuja — of all places — to be trained by security agencies? How does such an implausible story even survive a moment of scrutiny.

This pattern reveals the architecture of modern disinformation: an old fabrication, rejected by responsible media, is retrieved, re-edited, and repackaged for amplification by social media operators who understand that novelty can make old lies feel new. Algorithms reward outrage, giving reckless content creators a competitive advantage over those who exercise restraint. This is not accidental; it is structural.

I am cautious about character testimony, but after two years of engagement with Senator Buba in contexts where performance matters more than presentation, some observations are relevant. He is a man of few words, not given to the theatrics of Nigerian politics. His work in non-kinetic security — persuasion, community engagement, de-radicalisation — has, by credible accounts, helped reduce abductions along the Abuja Kaduna expressway and in Birnin Gwari, among others. Such work cannot be publicised without compromising community leaders or inviting sabotage from actors who profit from instability.

His philanthropic record is independently documented. A Trust TV documentary captured the breadth of his medical outreach across Bauchi and Plateau, showing Muslims and Christians among the beneficiaries. Monthly medical support programmes of that scale leave traces in communities and hospitals; they are not easy to fabricate.

None of this places Senator Buba beyond scrutiny. Public officials must be examined. But the evidence consistently shows that the allegations against him — sponsoring banditry, hosting bandit kingpins — are manufactured, and the machinery producing them is driven by electoral competition rather than civic concern.

When recycled footage, political rivalry, and social media algorithms converge, even a debunked falsehood can acquire a second life. In such an environment, a public figure’s communication strategy becomes as important as the truth itself.

Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of An Encounter with the Spymaster and MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS. Email: [email protected]

World.title: Beyond the rule of 70: Why subsidy should never crawl back into Nigeria’s economic discourse, By Gboyega Nasir Isiaka
World.content:
…reversing the removal of the subsidy would be a step in the wrong direction. It would restore the fiscal burden, revive the price differential that encouraged smuggling and arbitrage, and weaken incentives for efficient domestic refining. More fundamentally, it would address the immediate price of petrol, while leaving the structural weaknesses that produced the wider economic problem largely untouched.

I have followed with considerable interest the continuing debate over Nigeria’s economic reforms, particularly the arguments surrounding the removal of the petrol subsidy and the direction of economic policy under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Such debate is necessary. Government policy must remain open to scrutiny, especially when its consequences are felt directly in the daily lives of citizens.

It was against this background that I viewed Professor Bongo Adi’s recent intervention on Nigeria’s growth trajectory, including his reference to the Rule of 70. Professor Adi is an economist whose contribution to public discourse I respect. The mathematical rule he cited is quite straightforward. It provides an estimate of the time required for a quantity to double when a constant growth rate is assumed. So, for instance, an economy growing at a constant rate of 4 per cent annually will take 17.5 years to double its size.

The difficulty arises when this calculation is treated as a prediction of Nigeria’s economic growth. Economic outcomes are dynamic, shaped by emergent trends, while, the Rule of 70, by its nature assumes constancy. Indeed, the purpose of economic reform is to alter the conditions that constrain growth and ultimately, improve the growth rate, which delivers better development outcomes.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

As a result of the foregoing, Professor Bongo further suggested that the subsidy regime should be reversed. For me, a call for the reversal of petroleum subsidy on the strength of a mathematical rule is too simplistic. Nigeria’s economy is far more complex than what a simple and linear mathematical rule can capture and predict its growth trajectory.

Subsidy is a legitimate instrument of public policy. Governments use it to protect consumers, support strategic industries, correct market failures and cushion temporary economic shocks. Nigeria’s petroleum price intervention developed over several decades, beginning with a broader regime of price regulation in the 1970s. Its objectives included moderating inflation, supporting industrial development and providing affordable energy to citizens. As domestic refining capacity weakened and dependence on imported petroleum products increased, the subsidy component became progressively more pronounced, and its cost to the economy became increasingly difficult to sustain.

As the fiscal burden expanded, however, subsidy became increasingly difficult to reconcile with Nigeria’s limited public resources and enormous development needs. What NNPC Limited described in its accounts as “under-recovery” represented, in economic substance, the cost of selling petrol below its supply cost. The price differential also created powerful incentives for smuggling and arbitrage, while regulated pricing weakened incentives for investment in domestic refining. Nigeria could export crude, import refined petrol, and devote enormous public resources running into trillions of naira to maintain an artificially low domestic price.

Many interventions have been introduced to mitigate the effects of subsidy removal, while the economy adjusts. NELFUND reduces the immediate cost of tertiary education through interest-free student financing. CREDICORP is expanding responsible consumer credit for vehicles, energy solutions and essential assets. The MOFI Real Estate Investment Fund is widening access to long-term mortgage finance. Cash-transfer programmes provide direct support to poor and vulnerable households.

The question eventually became one of priorities. The resources required to sustain the arrangement had to be weighed against the nation’s needs for infrastructure, education, healthcare, human capital and productive investment. The issue was never whether Nigerians deserved protection from high fuel prices. The issue was whether a universal petrol subsidy remained the most effective and sustainable means of providing that protection to Nigerians.

The impact of the removal of subsidy, alongside other reforms on macroeconomic stability, is equally noticeable. Its removal has substantially improved the government’s fiscal space by eliminating a large and wasteful expenditure obligation, thereby reducing fiscal pressure. Alongside foreign exchange market reforms, it has reduced foreign exchange distortions associated with fuel importation and smuggling, strengthened the external position and supported greater confidence in Nigeria’s fiscal and monetary stance.

The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has recognised the removal of fuel subsidies and exchange rate reform as important steps in addressing deep-rooted structural weaknesses and creating fiscal space. The broader reform programme has also received improved assessments from international credit-rating institutions. These are meaningful gains because fiscal stability and external resilience are essential foundations for sustainable investment and growth.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu therefore deserves commendation for the courage to confront this difficult situation. The decision to remove the subsidy carried an immediate social cost, and Nigerians have felt it. It is a necessary pain on the paths towards an enduring recovery.

Universally, such pains are relieved through various interventions. Nigeria has not shied away from these global policy practices. Many interventions have been introduced to mitigate the effects of subsidy removal, while the economy adjusts. NELFUND reduces the immediate cost of tertiary education through interest-free student financing. CREDICORP is expanding responsible consumer credit for vehicles, energy solutions and essential assets. The MOFI Real Estate Investment Fund is widening access to long-term mortgage finance. Cash-transfer programmes provide direct support to poor and vulnerable households.

The Bank of Industry and related SME interventions are supporting businesses, manufacturing, agriculture and employment, while the Federal Government’s TVET programme combines skills training with stipends and start-up support. Investment in compressed-natural-gas buses and vehicle conversion is providing succour and reducing transport costs. Pro-poor and pro-business provisions in the new tax law are another important component of this response.

The measure of reform is ultimately the quality of the economy it leaves behind. The responsibility is to ensure that the sacrifice produces something worthy of it: greater productivity, stronger institutions, broader opportunity and ultimately, a more prosperous Nigeria.

Nigeria’s approach also finds support in international experience. Countries that have undertaken difficult energy subsidy reforms have generally found that the durability of reforms depends on credible social protection, clear communication and visible use of the resources released. Indonesia’s experience shows how cash transfers can help build public acceptance for fuel subsidy reform, while Iran replaced broad price subsidies with direct cash transfers as part of its 2010 reform. The Philippines, meanwhile, demonstrated the importance of sustained public communication and consensus-building in securing support for fuel price reform.

Ghana also commissioned independent poverty and social impact assessments before its reform and accompanied subsidy reform with measures covering education, transport, healthcare and rural electrification. The lesson here is that economic arithmetic may explain the need for reform, but social protection, transparency and competent governance give reform legitimacy and durability.

For that reason, reversing the removal of the subsidy would be a step in the wrong direction. It would restore the fiscal burden, revive the price differential that encouraged smuggling and arbitrage, and weaken incentives for efficient domestic refining. More fundamentally, it would address the immediate price of petrol, while leaving the structural weaknesses that produced the wider economic problem largely untouched. It would simply return the government to financing the difference between the regulated price and the underlying cost of supply, at the expense of competing national priorities.

Nigeria has made a difficult but necessary choice. The wiser course is to make the post-subsidy economy work for every citizen.

The measure of reform is ultimately the quality of the economy it leaves behind. The responsibility is to ensure that the sacrifice produces something worthy of it: greater productivity, stronger institutions, broader opportunity and ultimately, a more prosperous Nigeria.

Gboyega Nasir Isiaka (GNI), FCA, FCS, a member of the House of Representatives representing Yewa North/Imeko-Afon Federal Constituency also serves as chairman of the House Committee on National Planning and Economic Development.

World.title: Intersociety: 3,083 Christians killed, 3,193 abducted in eight months
World.content:
By Jeff Agbodo

The International Society for Civil Liberties and Rule of Law (Intersociety) has claimed that 3,083 Christians were killed and 3,193 abducted in attacks allegedly linked to Islamic extremist groups between January and August 2026.

The organisation also claimed that 400 churches were attacked during the period, while 25 priests and pastors were either killed or abducted.

Chairman of Intersociety, Emeka Umeagbalasi, disclosed this in a statement on the group’s assessment of attacks on Christian communities in Nigeria.

According to him, 437 Christians were killed while 393 were abducted in July and August 2026.

Umeagbalasi said 138 Christians were killed and 180 abducted in August alone, with several of the reported incidents occurring in Plateau and Benue states.

He said the organisation’s figures were based on information gathered from residents, survivors and eyewitnesses in affected communities.

Umeagbalasi claimed that attacks attributed by the organisation to armed groups of Fulani origin accounted for a significant proportion of the incidents recorded during the period.

He said Intersociety’s reports focused specifically on attacks it considered religiously motivated and linked to Islamist extremist groups.

The organisation claimed that 299 Christians were killed and 213 abducted in July 2026.

Umeagbalasi also cited several incidents allegedly recorded in August, including the reported killing of Christians in Plateau, Benue, Kaduna and Adamawa states.

He said Intersociety had also included what it described as “dark figures” in its estimates to account for victims whose fate could not be independently established.

On abductions, Umeagbalasi claimed that at least 92 Christian travellers were abducted in incidents recorded in Benue, Kogi and Ondo states in August.

He also cited the reported abduction of Christians in Imo, Edo, Kaduna, Plateau, Enugu and other states.

According to him, Intersociety’s analysis indicated that about 120 of the 180 Christians it recorded as abducted in August were from the South-East.

He said the organisation had identified several Eastern travellers among those reportedly abducted while travelling to Lagos and Abuja.

Umeagbalasi further cited the reported abduction of passengers travelling in commercial vehicles in the South-West, including an incident in Ondo State.

However, the casualty and abduction figures contained in the statement are claims made by Intersociety and were not independently verified in the statement.

The organisation called for greater protection of vulnerable communities and improved security measures to prevent further attacks and abductions.

World.title: Nollywood mourns actress Nimmy Ferrari
World.content:
By Ayo Onikoyi

Nollywood actress and social media influencer, Nimmy Ferrari, has died, reportedly shortly before she was scheduled to celebrate the completion of her new home in Sagamu, Ogun State.

News of her death was announced by her colleague, Oluwakemisola Apesin, popularly known as Kemity, who expressed grief over the actress’ passing in a social media post.

“Everybody is back home, we left only you IDERA Nimmyferrari, it is well,” Kemity wrote.

Ferrari’s immediate younger sister was also reported to have confirmed her death following earlier uncertainty over reports of her passing on social media.

The actress was reportedly preparing for a housewarming ceremony at her newly completed property in Sagamu before her death.

Videos circulating on social media showed people gathered at the property, with reports suggesting that funeral arrangements were underway.

Ferrari had been building a following as an actress and social media personality before her death.

Meanwhile, reports circulating on social media have linked her death to alleged complications following surgery for fibroids. However, neither her family nor any official source has publicly confirmed the cause of death.

The circumstances surrounding her death remain unclear as colleagues, friends and fans continue to mourn her.

Her passing has sparked reactions across the entertainment industry, with fellow practitioners and fans expressing shock and sadness over the loss of the young actress.

World.title: Dangote Refinery IPO: 10 things Nigerian investors must know before buying
World.content:
By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor

The Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC’s approval clears the way for a potential ₦2.15 trillion Initial Public Offering, IPO, giving public investors an opportunity to own a stake in one of Africa’s largest industrial assets.

Businesses suffer as FG’s domestic borrowings surge 90% to N24.7trnRead Also:

The proposed IPO of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE is shaping up to be a landmark transaction for Nigeria’s capital market.

The SEC approved the commencement of the offering, clearing the refinery’s draft offer documents and moving the transaction into its next phase.

Under the proposal, 4.1 billion ordinary shares will be offered at ₦525 per share. The SEC has also registered the company’s existing 120.13 billion ordinary shares.

For investors, however, the significance of the IPO goes beyond its headline size. The offer raises questions about valuation, future earnings, dividends, expansion, risks and the potential impact of owning a stake in a business at the centre of Nigeria’s energy and industrial ambitions.

Here are 10 key facts Nigerian investors should understand.

1. The IPO could raise ₦2.15 trillion

At an offer price of ₦525 per share, the proposed sale of 4.1 billion shares could generate approximately ₦2.15 trillion if fully subscribed.

That would make the transaction one of the biggest capital-market offerings in Nigeria’s history.

The size alone could have implications for the Nigerian Exchange, potentially increasing market capitalisation and providing investors with access to a major company outside the traditional banking and telecommunications heavyweights that dominate Nigerian equities.

For the company, the proceeds could provide additional capital for its business and expansion plans, subject to the terms set out in the final offer documents.

2. Investors would become shareholders in the refinery business

The IPO changes the relationship between Nigerians and the refinery.

Instead of the facility being viewed solely as a major infrastructure project owned by a private group, the public offering would allow investors to acquire shares and participate in the company’s ownership.

That means shareholders could potentially benefit from future capital appreciation and dividends if the company performs well and declares distributions.

But ownership also comes with investment risk. Shareholders would be exposed to the company’s financial performance and the wider risks affecting the refining and petrochemical industries.

3. ₦525 is an entry price, not a guaranteed return

One of the most important distinctions for prospective investors is that the ₦525 IPO price does not guarantee that the shares will later trade above that level.

Once listed and actively traded, the share price will be influenced by supply and demand as well as the company’s earnings, outlook and broader economic conditions.

The stock could appreciate if investors believe the company is undervalued or its earnings prospects are improving. Conversely, it could fall below the offer price if expectations deteriorate.

Investors should therefore approach the IPO as an equity investment rather than a guaranteed-return opportunity.

4. The refinery operates at an extraordinary scale

Located in Ibeju-Lekki, Lagos, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals Complex covers approximately 2,635 hectares.

The refinery currently has a stated refining capacity of 700,000 barrels per day, making it the world’s largest single-train refinery.

Its scale gives investors exposure to a business capable of processing enormous volumes of crude oil and producing refined petroleum products for domestic and international markets.

The company’s ability to operate efficiently at that scale will be a critical factor in determining its long-term profitability.

5. Expansion could fundamentally change the company’s earning capacity

The refinery is also undergoing an expansion programme expected to increase capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day.

If completed successfully, the expansion would more than double the current capacity and position the facility as the world’s largest refinery.

For shareholders, increased capacity could mean greater production, higher revenues and stronger export potential.

But expansion also introduces execution risks. Investors will need to consider the capital required, the timetable for completion, financing arrangements and whether additional capacity ultimately produces attractive returns.

6. It is an integrated energy and petrochemical complex

The investment story extends beyond petroleum refining.

The complex includes a 900,000-tonnes-per-annum polypropylene plant, a dedicated 435-megawatt power plant, extensive storage facilities and marine infrastructure.

Its storage network consists of 177 tanks with a combined capacity of approximately 4.742 billion litres.

The company also has a dedicated marine facility designed to improve logistics and freight efficiency, including multiple quays capable of handling Panamax vessels, liquid cargo and roll-on/roll-off operations.

For investors, this integrated infrastructure could provide operational advantages and multiple sources of commercial activity.

7. Domestic demand gives the business a huge potential market

Nigeria is one of Africa’s largest oil-producing countries, but it has historically relied heavily on imported refined petroleum products because of inadequate domestic refining capacity.

The Dangote Refinery was developed partly to address that structural gap.

At full production, the facility is designed to meet a substantial portion of Nigeria’s demand for refined petroleum products while also supplying export markets.

That creates a potentially significant domestic market for the business while giving it the opportunity to earn foreign revenue through exports.

However, the company’s actual financial performance will depend on factors including crude availability, refining margins, domestic demand, export economics, operating costs and market prices.

8. Investors will need to understand the company’s ownership and share structure

The SEC has registered 120.13 billion existing ordinary shares, while the proposed public offer covers 4.1 billion shares.

This makes the final ownership structure particularly important for investors.

Before subscribing, investors should examine the final prospectus and offer documents to determine the percentage of the company being offered to the public, the resulting free float, the rights attached to the shares and the concentration of ownership after the IPO.

The structure matters because a company’s free float and shareholder composition can influence liquidity and how easily investors can buy or sell shares after listing.

9. Profitability matters more than the refinery’s impressive headline numbers

The refinery’s capacity, size and infrastructure make for compelling headlines, but investors ultimately need to focus on the company’s ability to generate sustainable profits and cash flow.

Key indicators to watch will include revenue growth, operating margins, refining margins, production volumes, utilisation rates, operating expenses, debt obligations and cash generation.

Other important risks include crude supply, foreign-exchange movements, global oil prices, petroleum-product prices, regulatory changes, maintenance requirements and competition in domestic and international markets.

The refinery can be strategically important to Nigeria and still be an investment that requires careful valuation.

10. The IPO could reshape the Nigerian investment landscape

Perhaps the biggest significance of the transaction is what it could mean for the relationship between Nigerian investors and large-scale domestic businesses.

A successful listing would allow individuals, pension funds, institutional investors and other market participants to own shares in a company operating one of Africa’s most significant industrial assets.

It could also inject fresh activity into the Nigerian equity market and encourage more companies to consider public listings as a way of raising long-term capital.

For retail investors in particular, the IPO could become an important test of whether Nigerians are willing to commit substantial savings to large domestic companies when the investment case is compelling.

What investors should check before subscribing

SEC approval is an important milestone, but it is not an investment recommendation.

Prospective investors should wait for and carefully study the final offer documents, paying particular attention to the company’s historical and latest financial results, profitability and cash-flow performance, debt and other financial obligations, the proposed use of the IPO proceeds, the valuation implied by the ₦525 offer price, dividend policy and prospects, the percentage of shares available to the public, expected listing and trading arrangements, expansion costs and execution risks, as well as exposure to crude supply, foreign exchange movements and global refining margins.

The proposed Dangote Refinery IPO therefore presents two stories at once: a landmark opportunity for the company to raise long-term capital and a potentially significant investment opportunity for Nigerians seeking exposure to one of Africa’s largest industrial assets.

The ₦2.15 trillion potential fundraising figure makes the transaction impossible to ignore. But for investors, the more important question will ultimately be whether the company’s future earnings and cash flows justify the price at which those shares are being offered.

If successfully completed, the IPO could become a defining moment for Nigeria’s capital market. For individual investors, however, the landmark status of the transaction should be the starting point for due diligence — not a substitute for it.

World.title: Osun poll: APC, PDP file petitions challenging Adeleke’s re-election
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

The Osun State Governorship Election Petition Tribunal has displayed two petitions filed by the All Progressives Congress (APC) and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), challenging the re-election of Governor Ademola Adeleke.

The petitions, which were dated September 5, 2026, were pasted on the notice board of the tribunal secretariat in Osogbo on Monday, formally commencing the process of hearing disputes arising from the August 15 governorship election in the state.

The development followed the confirmation by the Secretary of the Tribunal, Pefe Belemore, that petitions challenging the outcome of the election had been filed before the tribunal.

When Vanguard visited the tribunal Secretariat on Monday, the secretary was in the courtroom alongside other officials of the secretariat as preparations were underway for the commencement of proceedings.

The APC and PDP are challenging the outcome of the governorship election which returned Adeleke for another term in office.

The display of the petitions is expected to set in motion the legal process, including the service of processes on parties and subsequent proceedings before the tribunal.

The APC’s petition with suit number EPT/OS/GOV/01/2026 was filed by its candidate, Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, against Governor Adeleke, Accord Party and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The PDP’s petition EPT/OS/GOV/02/2026 was filed by one Adebayo Olugbenga Adedamola against Adeleke, INEC and the Accord Party.

Also, officials of the Accord Party and their legal team were seen entering the court before Vanguard correspondent exited the building.
