Three requests, three separate points on the calendar, and still no trial — not because a witness failed to appear, not because evidence was incomplete, but because the docket never made room. Now the defense wants the case thrown out entirely, under a law written to punish exactly the kind of foot-dragging that, in this instance, the paper trail shows the prosecution did not do.

A JUSTICE SYSTEM THAT CANNOT tell the difference between a prosecutor who asked and a prosecutor who didn’t is not neutral. It is broken in a way that happens to favor whoever is charged.

THIS IS NOT A ONE-OFF. Corruption cases against former NOCAL chief Rustolyn Suacoco Dennis and former Bureau of State Enterprises head Arthur Massaquoi both went the same way — dismissed after sitting for terms at a time while the court’s attention went elsewhere. Add the Margibi case, and what looked like an unfortunate pattern starts to look like a design flaw. Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law gives defendants a real and necessary protection: if the state doesn’t bring you to trial by the next court term, absent good cause, the case gets dismissed. That protection exists so people are not left to rot under an accusation indefinitely. It was never meant to be a technicality that rewards a court’s own scheduling failures at the expense of the public’s interest in seeing corruption prosecuted.

THE COST NOBODY IS COUNTING



EVERY DISMISSED CORRUPTION case is not a wash. It is a loss. Behind every indictment the LACC secures are months of forensic accounting, subpoenaed bank records, witness interviews and legal drafting, performed by an agency that does not have unlimited money or unlimited staff. When a case dies for lack of a docket slot, the state does not get that investment back for free. It either lets a serious corruption case disappear for good, or it asks an already-stretched commission to redo the work from scratch, against the same clock, in the same courts. Neither outcome serves the public that pays for the LACC’s work and is told, case after case, to wait for the accountability it was promised.



THERE IS ALSO A COST that will not show up in any LACC annual report: what the public concludes when it watches indictment after indictment vanish before a single witness is sworn in. Liberians do not need to believe in a conspiracy to lose faith that corruption prosecutions go anywhere. They only need to keep seeing this outcome. A court system does not have to intend to protect the well-connected for it to end up doing exactly that, term after term, simply by failing to prioritize.



WHAT THE COURTS OWE THE PROCESS



NOBODY IS ASKING judges to rubber-stamp the LACC or fast-track cases in a way that tramples a defendant’s rights. Due process cuts both ways, and it is not this paper’s place to prejudge any individual’s guilt, including in the Margibi case. But due process for the accused cannot be the only interest a court weighs when a docket fills up. The public has an interest in these cases too, and prosecutors who do their part — who file, who write, who ask, on the record, for a hearing — deserve a system that credits that effort rather than one that quietly erases it.



THAT MEANS LIBERIA’S circuit courts need an honest accounting of how corruption cases are prioritized against everything else competing for courtroom time, and it means the judiciary, the Ministry of Justice and the Legislature need to treat docket congestion as the structural crisis it has become rather than an excuse that arrives after the fact, case by case, dismissal by dismissal. A dedicated calendar for LACC prosecutions, firmer rules for how “good cause” gets weighed when the delay traces back to the court rather than the state, and basic transparency about why cases sit for terms at a time would cost far less than what Liberia is currently losing every time one of these cases dies untried.

THE LACC CANNOT do its job if the courts will not give its cases a trial date. That is not a defense of any defendant or any prosecutor. It is a minimum condition for an anti-corruption fight that Liberians have been promised for years and are still, mostly, waiting to see delivered. The courts do not have to decide anyone’s guilt to fix this. They only must decide that a case is worth trying.

World.title: MoM urged to expedite processing of artisanal licences
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary, Milner Mwanakampwe has called on the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development to expedite the processing of artisanal licences to enable young people engage in safe and legal mining activities.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the lengthy process of acquiring artisanal mining licences is contributing to challenges faced by young people in the mining sector.

He was speaking when officials from the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

Dr Mwanakampwe observed that people are losing their lives in mining pits, making it important for artisanal miners to be adequately trained and supported to conduct their activities safely.

He said the ministry should encourage artisanal miners to open bank accounts so that they can receive payments through formal financial channels and contribute more effectively to the economy.

Dr Mwanakampwe said training of artisanal miners is important as it promotes safe mining practices which can help reduce accidents and loss of lives.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Assistant Director for Policy and Development Cooperation, Mercy Zulu said her team is in the Central Province for 20-days training artisanal miners on safe and responsible mining practices.

Ms Zulu said 400 artisanal miners will be trained to equip them with the knowledge and skills needed to conduct mining activities safely.

She said the ministry is also facilitating access to finance for artisanal miners so that they can increase their contribution to the country’s economy.

World.title: Chisamba Councils calls for 2027 CDF applications
World.content:
Chisamba Town Council is calling for applications from members of the public for the various components under Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

This is according to a public notice dated September 2, 2026, signed by Chisamba District Council Secretary, Chamuka Muwamba and made available to the media in Chisamba.

Mr Muwamba said the call for applications is in respect of the 2027 CDF, stating that Chisamba District is expected to receive slightly over K80 million for both Chisamba and Mwomboshi Constituencies.

“Each constituency will receive an equal share of K40, 032, 549.91 to finance community projects, youth and women empowerment, and skills development bursaries,” Mr Muwamba said.

He urged members of the public in the two constituencies to seize the opportunity and apply for the various components of the CDF.

Mr Muwamba explained that 60 percent of the funds is designated for community projects to facilitate critical infrastructure development in the district.

He stated that the applications should be submitted using the recommended application forms, which are available free of charge from area councillors, constituency offices, or the Civic Centre under the Planning Unit.

Mr Muwamba said the deadline for submitting applications is October 16, 2026.

He has also urged applicants to follow the eligibility criteria for each component of the CDF to avoid having their applications rejected.

Mr Muwamba said one of the eligibility criteria for community projects is that the proposed project must appear in the Integrated Development Plan (IDP) for Chisamba District, which can be viewed through area councillors or the local authority.

“The project must be identified and prioritized by the local authority, must be of benefit to the wider community, should use approved designs by the planning authority and take into account persons with disabilities.

“Proof of a bank account or mobile wallet registered for the group, the proposed project is being undertaken within the constituency, applicants must have been residents in the constituency for over six months,” Mr Muwamba said.

He disclosed that local citizens aged between 16 and below 35 years, who are in possession of a Green National Registration Card, as well as out-of-school entrepreneurs requiring up-skilling and re-skilling, are eligible to apply for skills development bursaries.

“The applicant must be a resident of the constituency for more than six months, and must be in possession of an admission or acceptance letter from any of the public TEVET institutions or the Zambia National Service,” he said.

Mr Muwamba said all application letters must be addressed to his office and submitted not later than October 16, 2026.

World.title: Police apprehend Kalulushi girl over dumped baby’s body
World.content:
Police in Kalulushi have apprehended a 15 year old girl for allegedly dumping the body of a newborn baby at a dump site.

Copperbelt Police Commanding Officer, Rae Hamoonga, who confirmed the development to ZANIS, said the incident occurred between August 27, 2027 at around 17:30 hours and September 05, 2026 at around 17:00 hours at Kafulafuta Lane in Milemu Clinic area.

Mr Hamoonga said the matter was reported to Kalulushi Police Station by a 39 year old woman who discovered the body of a new born baby boy wrapped in a plastic bag lying on top of garbage at the dump site near Milemu clinic.

Mr Hamoonga said the information obtained by Officers who visited the scene led to the apprehension of the girl suspected to be connected to the incident which is being investigated as suspected infanticide.

He said the girl was taken to Kalulushi General Hospital together with the body and during preliminary inquiries, disclosed that she had unexpectedly given birth while using the toilet after which she is alleged to have wrapped the baby in a plastic bag and disposed of the body at the dumpsite.

He said the body has since been deposited at Kalulushi General Hospital Mortuary, awaiting a postmortem examination to establish the circumstances leading to the death of the baby.

Mr Haoongaa disclosed that the girl has been admitted at the same hospital for further medical examination and treatment under Police guard.

He stated that a medical report has been issued and a docket opened.

World.title: RUGBY: Mufulira opens 10-point lead
World.content:
Defending Champions Mufulira Leopards have extended their lead at the top of the National Rugby League to ten points with five games remaining in the 2026 season.

Mufulira at the weekend beat their closest rivals Arrows 19-15 at home in Mufulira to move to 39 points after playing nine games.

Second placed Arrows, who have one un-played game, have 29 points from eight matches played.

On the road to victory, Mufulira posted one try which they converted and later scored three penalties and had one drop goal.

Arrows converted one of the two tries they placed and later scored a penalty.

Nkwazi are third on the table with 29 points as well after edging Buffaloes 26-23 in a tightly contested Lusaka derby.

Buffaloes are fourth on the table just two points behind third placed Nkwazi.

Elsewhere struggling giants Diggers returned to league action after a lengthy absence with a 13-8 away loss to Eagles in Kabwe.

Eagles are fifth on the table with 21 points in nine matches and are placed one slot above Diggers, who are six points behind the Zambia National Service side.

Meanwhile, the bottom two sides KPF and Kansanshi shared the 15-15 spoils to stay in their respective positions.

Seventh placed Kansanshi have six points in nine matches while bottom positioned KPF sits on one point from eight games.

KPF remains the only team without a win so far in the 2026 National Rugby League.

World.title: Findlay Needs Urgent Medical Care, Says Family
World.content:
Findlay’s Health Deteriorating In Detention, Family Says

The family of detained Lusaka businessman Harry Valden Findlay says his health has deteriorated sharply after he was denied access to his prescription medication, with the 63-year-old now on a drip and his whereabouts unknown to relatives for extended periods during his detention. The family has emphasized the urgent need for medical attention for Findlay.

In a statement issued at the weekend, the family said it remained deeply concerned that the State had continued moving Findlay between different detention facilities without informing them, leaving them without knowledge of his location for 12 days at a stretch. They called for immediate action to ensure Findlay receives the care he urgently needs.

“We have waited… we have pleaded for humane treatment… we have asked that the law be followed despite the gravity of the charges, to no avail,” the family said.

The statement described a pattern of repeated transfers that left relatives struggling to track Findlay’s condition. “But we are afraid, Harry keeps getting moved between facilities, for 12 days we did not know his whereabouts, he was denied access to his prescription medication and now he is unwell,” the family said.

According to the statement, Findlay has been on a drip since Wednesday, September 2, but has not been taken to hospital despite the seriousness of his condition. The family said the State was fully aware of his medical history and appealed for that awareness to translate into action.

“He needs specialised medical treatment. The State is aware of his medical condition! Regardless of the charges, every human being has constitutional rights! We are seeing someone we love become weaker day by day!” the family said.

The family stressed that detention should never be allowed to become a form of punishment in itself, insisting that Findlay’s wellbeing could not be treated as secondary to the legal process against him. “His life matters, his health matters! We plead that Harry is treated humanely!” the statement read.

Efforts to have Findlay brought before a court to address the concerns around his detention have similarly stalled. The family said it had applied for a writ of habeas corpus seeking to have him produced before the court, but the process was repeatedly delayed because the State failed to bring him to the scheduled hearings.

After several adjournments linked to Findlay’s continued absence, the court proceeded to hear the application without him present, a development the family said undermined the very purpose of the habeas corpus process, which exists to establish the lawfulness of a person’s detention through direct judicial scrutiny.

“Harry has rights! We appeal that these rights are afforded to him!” the family said, framing their appeal as one rooted in constitutional principle rather than a dispute over the underlying allegations against him.

The family was careful to separate the question of guilt or innocence from the question of humane treatment, stating plainly that whatever the outcome of the case against Findlay, no set of allegations could justify the permanent loss of his life or health while the matter remained before the courts.

“Whatever the allegations against Harry, his life cannot be restored if it is lost!” the family said, closing their statement with a direct appeal for the authorities to act before his condition worsens further.

As of the time of the family’s statement, Findlay had not been transferred to hospital despite being on a drip for several days, and his exact custodial location was not confirmed publicly. The family said they intended to continue pressing for both his medical treatment and his right to appear before a court to challenge the legality of his continued detention.

The case adds to a wider pattern of concern raised by rights groups and opposition figures in recent weeks over the treatment and welfare of individuals held in custody following the disputed August general election period, with families of several detainees separately calling for greater transparency around detention conditions and access to medical care.

World.title: Zambia chase 13th COSAFA U-20 crown
World.content:
‎Zambia will be hoping to extend their record number of COSAFA titles at Under-20 level to

‎13 when they compete in the TotalEnergies CAF Under-20 Africa Cup of Nations | COSAFA

‎Qualifier in Mozambique from September 18-27.

‎They have been remarkably consistent at this level. In the 11 tournaments they have played

‎since 2010, they have won five titles, finished runners-up once and third once, with two

‎fourth-place finishes and two exits in the pool stages.

‎This time around they have been drawn in a pool with old foes Malawi, Comoros and

‎Botswana. Only the top team in each group advances to the semi-finals, along with the best

‎runner-up across the three pools.

‎The two finalists in the competition will qualify for the continental finals next year.

‎Zambia finished third in 2025 after losing to Malawi in the semi-finals, having reached that

‎stage as the best runner-up from the pool phase. They edged Angola on penalties in the

‎bronze-medal match.

‎It was a similar story the year before as they qualified for the semi-finals as the best runner-

‎up, having lost to Angola in the pool stages, and then beat Zimbabwe on penalties following

‎a 2-2 draw in the last four.

‎But they came unstuck against South Africa in the decider, losing 2-0 to the side who would

‎go on to be crowned African champions. Their road to the title in 2022 included group-

‎stage wins over Mauritius (3-0), Eswatini (2-0) and Botswana (1-0), before they edged

‎Angola on penalties in the semi-finals and beat then-holders Mozambique 1-0 in the

‎decider.

‎Prior to 2022, their previous victory came in 2019. It was a commanding performance from

‎the side as they claimed a full haul of nine points in the pool stages before seeing off Angola

‎3-0 in the semi-finals.

‎That was followed by victory against old foes South Africa by the same comprehensive

‎margin in the decider.

‎Zambia were also rampant in 2016 as they stormed through that competition and inflicted a

‎2-1 defeat on hosts South Africa in the decider.

‎

‎

‎They went on to claim the 2017 Africa Under-20 Championship title on home soil and also

‎excelled at the FIFA Under-20 World Cup in South Korea.

‎But the side disappointed in the COSAFA Men’s Under-20 Championship that year, bowing

‎out in the first round after a defeat to East African guest nation Uganda was followed by a

‎draw with Malawi and a win over Eswatini.

‎They did make the semi-finals in 2018 but lost 2-1 to Zimbabwe and were then beaten 2-1

‎by Angola in the bronze-medal match.

‎They reached the semi-finals again in 2020, a competition played in South Africa, winning all

‎three pool matches against Namibia (1-0), Comoros (2-0) and Malawi (2-0).

‎They came unstuck in the semi-finals, though, when they were held 0-0 by Mozambique

‎before losing 5-4 on penalties. They were then beaten 2-1 by Angola in the bronze-medal

‎match.

‎Zambia have also been fairly regular visitors to the Africa Under-20 Championship and have

‎appeared at the continental tournament on 11 previous occasions.

Apart from their gold medal in 2017, they also finished fourth in 1991, 1999 and 2007.

World.title: Musoma, Kalaba Push For Release Of Political Detainees As Prison Numbers Grow
World.content:
Zambia Republican Party leader Wright Musoma has appealed to President Hakainde Hichilema to grant clemency to political prisoners, describing it as the defining legacy opportunity of his second term. Musoma, a member of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, wrote to the Head of State appealing for the immediate and unconditional release of all those detained for political reasons, arguing that mercy at this stage would signal strength rather than weakness.

“Behind every prisoner is a mother waiting, children asking questions, and a home that has gone quiet. No Zambian should suffer or die in detention simply because they hold opposing views from those holding power,” Musoma said. He named former Pambashe Member of Parliament Ronald Chitotela, former Kawambwa MP Nickson Chilangwa, former Patriotic Front Secretary General Raphael Nakacinda, former Kabushi MP Bowman Lusambo, and New Revolution Party for Unity and Prosperity President Brian Mundubile together with his running mate Makebi Zulu as political detainees.

“I write this with tears. Please Mr President, release these comrades. They have suffered way, way too much. Let families be reunited,” he said. The Zambia Republican Party leader added that the country remained politically divided following the August general election, and that reconciliation required a decisive gesture from the Executive.

“It will show that his second term is about healing and reconciliation. It is an act of statesmanship that will unite a polarised country. The fact remains that this country is politically torn apart and it is the responsibility of those with state instruments to unite it and move forward for the better,” Musoma said. He argued it was not right to punish citizens simply because they disagreed with those in power, noting that his appeal echoed calls already made by church leaders, the European Union, the United Nations, traditional leaders and civil society.

Citizens First President Harry Kalaba separately condemned what he termed the selective application of the law and rising political intolerance under the United Party for National Development government. Kalaba said it was concerning that the ruling party had denied Zambians the opportunity to validate the outcome of the presidential election by closing the courts, only for the same courts to now be used to challenge duly elected parliamentary candidates.

“This contradiction exposes a troubling pattern of expediency over principle and undermines public confidence in the justice system,” he stated, calling on authorities to investigate reports concerning the safety of elected leaders and to guarantee protection for all of them regardless of political affiliation. Kalaba raised further concern over what he described as prolonged detentions of opposition supporters, with some individuals allegedly held for up to 14 days without being brought before a court.

“Such actions amount to an abuse of the justice system and point to a dangerous trend of its weaponisation. This must come to an immediate end,” Kalaba said. Several opposition figures remain in custody on treason charges following a military raid in Kabulonga last month, a development that has drawn continued criticism from opposition parties, civil society organisations and international observers.

Musoma’s appeal placed particular weight on the symbolism of mercy shown at the height of political power, arguing that Zambians already believed several detained former officials were being held because of their political standing rather than the strength of evidence against them. “Former ministers Hon. Ronald Chitotela, Hon. Nickson Chilangwa, Hon. Raphael Nakacinda, Hon. Bowman Lusambo, and NRPUP President Brian Mundubile with his running mate, all these are political detainees,” he said.

Kalaba’s statement, delivered separately, focused less on individual clemency and more on the structural pattern he said the current wave of arrests represented. He described the situation as an erosion of the constitutional protections that ordinary citizens and elected representatives alike were entitled to, framing his intervention as a defence of process rather than a defence of any particular individual.

Both leaders presented their appeals as being made in the interest of national unity rather than partisan advantage. Musoma stressed that his call joined appeals already lodged with the Presidency by religious and international bodies, while Kalaba maintained that his concern was with the integrity of the justice system as a whole rather than the fate of any one detainee.

Neither leader specified a timeline for the response they expected from the Presidency, though both indicated that continued silence on the matter risked deepening the divisions that emerged from the disputed election period. For now, the detained figures remain in custody as the political temperature around their cases continues to rise, with pressure mounting from multiple fronts for the Head of State to act.

World.title: Daka dropped to bench as Hamburg suffer 5-0 loss
World.content:
Chipolopolo striker Patson Daka was dropped to the substitute bench as his side Hamburg suffered a heavy 5-0 defeat to Mainz on day-two of the Bundesliga campaign at the weekend.

Daka had started Hamburg’s season opener against Borussia Dortmund, which ended in a 2-0 defeat in Dortmund.

The Zambian forward was a casualty of the four changes coach Merlin Polzin made to his starting eleven following the opening-day loss.

Polzin handed debuts to David Møller Wolfe, Zakaria El Ouahdi, Bilal Nadir and Terem Moffi.

Daka, however, came off the bench at halftime. He was introduced by Polzin just after the break with Hamburg already 2-0 down.

He replaced Martin Adeline in the 46th minute and played the entire second half.

The defeat leaves Hamburg bottom of the Bundesliga table* with *no points and no goals after two games.

They have conceded 7 goals in that period.

According to BBC Sport statistics, Daka made 12 passes and created one chance in his 45 minutes but did not have a shot on target.

Daka joined Hamburg in July 2025 after five years at Leicester City, a spell that saw the club suffer two relegations from the Premier League to League One.

Before England, he starred in Austria with Red Bull Salzburg.

Internationally, Daka is expected to lead the Chipolopolo frontline in next month’s back-to-back Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Zambia will face Algeria away on 25 September in match-day One, before hosting Togo at home three days later on 28 September.

World.title: Angola: Cotton Revival In Busia - Hope Grows Amid Small Farms, Dry Spells And a Silent Ginnery
World.content:
The roads leading into the interior of Busia County tell a story of a region that is slowly changing, but perhaps not fast enough.

From Luanda to Bumala and Finyula, the journey is punctuated by dusty roads, boda bodas and stretches where getting to the farms is an exercise in patience. Away from the main roads, infrastructure remains a challenge, with motorcycles often providing the only practical means of reaching some farming areas.

It is here, amid small farms and modest homesteads, that cotton is quietly making a comeback.

But unlike Lamu County, where cotton farmers are taking advantage of the revival of the industry to expand production, farmers in this part of Busia are still growing the crop on very small pieces of land.

Most farmers cultivate no more than two acres, according to Bonventer Barasa, an accountant and manager at Luanda Farmers Cooperative Union.

“Currently, not more than two acres. Very small acreage hence low production despite what our modern ginnery can handle,” Barasa says.

For a crop whose revival is being seen as an opportunity to reconnect farmers to a market that once supported entire communities, the small acreage presents a major challenge.

Without enough cotton coming from farmers, the ginnery cannot operate at full capacity. And without a reliable market and attractive returns, farmers have little incentive to increase production. It is a cycle that the region is still trying to break.

For Vincent Okumu, however, cotton is more than just another crop. The farmer has grown cotton for more than two decades, taking over the enterprise from his parents. What began as a family livelihood became an important investment in his own future. Cotton proceeds helped him pursue his education. Today, he is using the same crop to educate his children. Two of his children have already graduated from university, while another is preparing to enrol.

For Okumu, this is proof that even small-scale cotton farming can change a family's fortunes when the crop performs well and farmers receive a fair return.

He farms about one and a half acres and expects to make at least Sh100,000 in profit from the current crop.

He also chairs Bwiri Farmers Cooperative Society, where he says the benefits of cotton are becoming visible beyond individual households. Livelihoods in his village, he says, have improved, with the gradual disappearance of thatched-roof houses among families whose incomes have increased. The transformation may not be dramatic, but it is visible. The same crop that helped one generation access education is now helping another pay school fees and improve their homes.

Yet Okumu's experience also exposes the limitations holding cotton farming back in Busia. He would like to increase his acreage from one and a half acres to five. But expanding production is easier said than done.

One of the biggest challenges is mechanisation. Land preparation is still largely done manually, making cotton production expensive and time-consuming. The county's available machinery cannot meet the demand from the number of farmers seeking the service.

The problem is particularly important in cotton because timing matters. Okumu says delayed distribution of seed affects production because farmers are working within a narrow planting and growing window.

By the time some farmers receive seed and prepare their land, they may have already lost valuable time.

It is a challenge that echoes concerns raised by the cooperative leadership.

Bernard Ojiambo, chairman of the Luanda Farmers Cooperative Union, says the cooperative has been seeking machinery, including tractors that farmers can hire to prepare their land. Without tractors and other equipment, farmers can fall behind the rains. “When it reaches time for planting farmers can hire, they go and plow to make it earlier plantation. We delay because we don't have machines like tractors and other things to support farmers,” Ojiambo says.

The consequence is a chain reaction of delays in planting and harvesting. The rains hold the key This year's crop has also had to contend with insufficient rainfall.

The cotton plants are about two months old, but the season has not been ideal. The dry conditions have affected the crop, with farmers now looking to the rains for a turnaround. During the visit, temperatures climbed to around 30 degrees Celsius. The heat was compounded by dusty roads and the dry conditions in the interior. Yet farmers remain hopeful. Ojiambo says the area's soils and climate can support cotton when rainfall comes at the right time. “It is the soil itself and the climate, though we don't have much rain, but once we get it between April and August, the harvest comes out well,” he says.

AllAfrica Vincent Okumu, a cotton farmer from Busia County inspecting his crop at his one and a half acre farm

For farmers like Okumu, a good harvest could provide the incentive to expand.

He praises the cooperative's buying price of Sh76 per kilogram, saying the price offers farmers a reason to remain in the crop. His own target of at least Sh100,000 in profit from one and a half acres shows why the crop continues to attract interest despite the difficulties.

At Luanda Ginnery, however, there is currently little evidence of the activity associated with harvest. The machines are silent. The last season ended about four months ago, and the ginnery is now waiting for the next crop to mature.

Inside the modern facility, the process is straightforward. Once cotton arrives, it is weighed and stored before being fed into the machinery. A suction system moves it from the store to a bale opener, where compacted cotton is loosened.

The cotton then passes through a pre-cleaner that removes dust and separates poor-quality cotton from the good lint. The good cotton is taken to the ginning machine, where the lint is separated from the seed.

The seed moves through a conveyor while the lint is transferred to a press, where it is compressed and tied into 200-kilogram bales ready for collection. But the ginnery's ability to operate depends entirely on what farmers bring from their fields. “If they don't grow cotton, then we don't have raw materials. That means we won't move on,” Barasa says. It is a simple relationship: the strength of the ginnery depends on the strength of the farmer.

Cotton has a long history in Busia. Ojiambo says cotton growing in the region dates back decades, when the crop was promoted among local farmers. But the industry eventually declined, with farmers becoming discouraged by delayed payments and poor returns. When cotton lost its appeal, many turned to maize. But maize also requires adequate rainfall, while cotton, Ojiambo argues, remains better suited to the area's conditions. “Cotton is more of a value than maize,” he says. With maize, the small acreage available to farmers is often used to feed the household. Cotton, on the other hand, is primarily a cash crop. Once harvested and sold, the money can be directed towards school fees, food and other household needs. That distinction is important in an area where many families are still farming on very small plots.

The challenges extend beyond production. Barasa says farmers also struggle with access to chemicals and implements, while limited working capital makes it difficult for both farmers and the ginnery to operate efficiently. The ginnery has also struggled to add value to cotton seed. A machine supplied by the Agricultural and Food Authority to process cotton seed has not performed efficiently, according to Barasa. He says a better-performing machine could allow the facility to produce cottonseed oil, seed cakes and soap. Such value addition would give the crop additional economic importance and potentially create more income from the same harvest.

The ginnery has, however, received a major boost through investment in solar energy. Barasa says the government provided solar panels worth Sh40 million. The move has reduced the facility's monthly electricity bill from about Sh150,000 to approximately Sh75,000. But the question remains whether there will be enough cotton to keep the machinery busy.

Busia's cotton revival is therefore a work in progress. The crop has a history here. Farmers know it. Cooperatives understand it. The ginnery has the machinery to process it. What is missing is scale. Farmers are still cultivating small pieces of land. Seed distribution needs to be timely. Mechanisation remains inadequate. Rainfall is unpredictable. And the market needs to offer farmers sufficient confidence to invest more.

For Vincent Okumu, however, the argument for cotton is already settled. The crop paid for his education and is now paying for his children's education. He believes the same opportunity exists for his neighbours. As chairman of Bwiri Farmers Cooperative Society, he is encouraging other farmers to return to cotton and take advantage of the improving fortunes of the crop. His own ambition is to move from one and a half acres to five. But for that ambition to become reality, the tractors must arrive, seed must reach farmers on time and the market must remain attractive.

For now, the cotton plants are still young. The ginnery remains quiet. The roads remain dusty and difficult. But the clouds are gathering, and with them comes the possibility of a better harvest. In the small farms of Busia, cotton may not yet be the booming commercial enterprise seen elsewhere. But for farmers like Okumu, it has already proved that a small farm can produce something much bigger than cotton—a pathway to education, better homes and a more hopeful future.

World.title: Sudan: Human Rights Chief Türk Renews Call for End to Spiralling Sudan War
World.content:
The ongoing war in Sudan took centre stage at the UN Human Rights Council on Monday where the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, led calls for an end to attacks on civilians in "markets, hospitals [and] fuel stations".

Key points

Türk calls for an immediate ceasefire and end to foreign involvement

Civilians face growing attacks, including from long-range drones

SAF and RSF may have committed war crimes

Sudan's healthcare system has suffered extensive damage

Now well into its fourth year, the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created a massive humanitarian emergency, with more than six million people displaced internally and another 4.5 million forced to seek shelter across Sudan's borders.



In his appeal for an end to the violence, UN rights chief Mr. Türk warned about the deteriorating situation in Kordofan, Blue Nile, and North and West Darfur, stressing that civilians remain at "imminent" risk.

Ceasefire call

"There needs to be an immediate ceasefire, an end to foreign involvement, and a return to inclusive civilian rule," he insisted.

The High Commissioner's appeal follows the publication of a new report into the conflict by senior independent investigators appointed by the Human Rights Council. The investigators are not UN staff and they are not paid for their work.

Their key findings include the increasing use of long-range drones against civilians and the significant support allegedly provided to paramilitary rebel fighters by "individuals and entities" in the UAE, Chad, southeastern Libya and Puntland in Somalia.

"Both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are increasingly using long-range drones, resulting in attacks now reaching far beyond traditional front lines," said Mohamed Othman, chair of the Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, which was created by the Council in Geneva in October 2023.

Mr. Othman also stressed that drone strikes had injured and killed civilians "in their homes, schools, hospitals, markets, displacement sites and places of refuge and while attending weddings, funerals and other community gatherings".

Turning to El Obeid city in North Kordofan, where access is heavily contested, the human rights investigator warned that "repeated RSF drone attacks" had impacted water, energy and other vital civilian infrastructure.

"These attacks underscore that these risks remain acute, as civilians continue to face repeated aerial threats, displacement and pressure on already strained essential services", he said, in a city under partial siege by the RSF.

Close 

The fact-finding mission's report highlights how both parties to the conflict have carried out attacks on civilians.

These included "successive" RSF drone strikes on a kindergarten and a hospital in Kalogie, South Kordofan, that left 114 dead including 60 children, along with SAF attacks on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital that killed at least 70 people.

"Based on the evidence gathered, we found reasonable grounds to believe that both the SAF and the RSF committed serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law which may amount to war crimes," Mr. Othman told the Council.

Healthcare devastation

In a separate update from Khartoum, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) reported on Monday that the devastation of three key hospitals in the capital has been repeated across the country.

Before the conflict, Khartoum Teaching Hospital, the Ophthalmology Hospital and the Dental Hospital were major referral and teaching hospitals. Today, their buildings and medical equipment have sustained extensive damage.

"Operating theatres have been destroyed, imaging equipment lost and several wards have collapsed," said WHO Representative in Sudan, Dr Abdinasir Abubakar. "Entire blocks and departments are out of service. The buildings need urgent structural repair before patients can be admitted safely."

Despite the difficult working conditions, hospital staff remain present to treat patients "in the parts of the buildings that remain usable", Dr Abubakar continued, in an appeal for assistance to repair the "immense" damage.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto's Remarks On Foreign Traders Were 'Taken Out of Context'
World.content:
Nairobi — Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Korir Sing'Oei has sought to clarify President William Ruto's remarks on foreign traders, saying they were taken "out of context" and should not be interpreted as a blanket restriction on foreigners doing business or working in Kenya.

Sing'Oei said the President was responding to an ongoing debate over the Local Content Bill before Parliament, which proposes restrictions on certain businesses that may be reserved for Kenyan citizens.

"President's statement has been taken out of context, as he was responding to ongoing debate on the Local Content Bill presently before Parliament," Sing'Oei said.

He assured foreign nationals that those operating legally in Kenya would remain protected, provided they have the necessary documentation.



"As such, we assure that small or large traders & employees of all nationalities, with requisite documentation--work permits & licenses--are legally protected to operate in Kenya," he said.

Sing'Oei also sought to reassure citizens of neighbouring countries and other African nationals, saying they would remain free to live and work in Kenya as long as they complied with Kenyan law.

"Burundian nationals and all East Africans--and Africans for that matter--are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our law," he said.

His remarks come after President Ruto told small traders at State House that certain businesses could be restricted to Kenyans under legislation being considered by Parliament.

"There are businesses that a foreigner will not be allowed to engage in here in Kenya. We already have a Bill before Parliament dealing with matters of business. In that Bill, we have proposed that there are certain businesses that foreigners will not be allowed to undertake here in Kenya," Ruto said on September 2.

The President urged MPs to scrutinise the proposed legislation to "seal all the loopholes", citing foreigners entering Kenya and engaging in hawking and small-scale retail businesses.

"We should not have a situation where someone comes from China or elsewhere and starts working as a hawker, or comes here to engage in small-scale retail business, such as selling goods in a small shop," he said.

The remarks sparked renewed attention on the growing presence of foreign nationals in Kenya's informal and retail sectors, with local traders for years raising concerns about competition from foreigners in businesses such as food vending, second-hand clothing and small retail outlets.

The government has, however, drawn a distinction between illegal activity and legitimate foreign investment and employment.

The Ministry of Investments, Trade and Industry (MITI) has said visa-free entry into Kenya does not automatically give a foreign national the right to work, trade or operate a business.

Kenya introduced visa-free entry for visitors from around the world in January 2024, while the government subsequently removed Electronic Travel Authorisation requirements for citizens of most African countries in January 2025.

MITI said the measures had helped boost tourism and investment but warned that visitors must still comply with immigration, work permit and licensing requirements when engaging in economic activities.

"Visa-free entry or exemption from eTA requirements does not in itself confer the right to engage in employment, trade or business in Kenya," the ministry said.

It added that such activities remain subject to "the applicable immigration, work permit and other regulatory requirements."

The ministry said some foreigners had entered the country under tourist or investor status before engaging in activities outside the terms of their permits.

"There has been deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors, leading to persons on investor or tourist status engaging in activities contrary to the provisions of the grant," MITI said.

The government has particularly raised concerns over foreigners operating in the retail and local trade sectors.

Close 

"Owing to the high number of foreigners involved in the retail and local trade sectors, there is therefore a need to align their activities and ensure compliance with work permit provisions," the ministry said.

Foreign nationals found violating applicable visa conditions could have their visas revoked, MITI warned.

At the same time, the ministry said enforcement would not amount to a blanket crackdown on foreign investors.

"Kenya remains open and welcoming to legitimate investors and businesses that operate within the law and contribute to the country's economic growth, job creation and development," it said.

The government has also pointed to Kenya's obligations under the East African Community, including commitments on the movement of people and goods among member states.

"Kenya is a signatory to the East African Community and has assented to the free movement of goods and people across the Customs Union," MITI said.

World.title: Tanzania: President's Husband Dies
World.content:
Hafidh Ameir Hassan, husband of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, has died while receiving heart treatment in Zanzibar.

Nairobi — Tanzania is mourning the death of Hafidh Ameir Hassan, the husband of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who died on Monday morning while receiving treatment in Zanzibar.

Tanzania Vice President Deogratius Ndejembi announced the death, saying Hafidh died at around 8:00am on September 7, 2026, at Mlimani Mzena Memorial Hospital.

"It is with great sadness that I inform you of the passing of Honorable Hafidh Ameir Hassan, husband to the President of the United Republic of Tanzania, Her Excellency Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan," Ndejembi said.

The Vice President said Hafidh had been receiving treatment for a heart condition before his death.

"I offer my deepest condolences to Her Excellency the President, the family, relatives, friends, and all Tanzanians during this time of mourning," Ndejembi said.

According to the Vice President, burial arrangements are already underway in Kizimkazi, Zanzibar.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 7, 2026
World.content:
Egyptian TV Presenter Sentenced to Death Over Drug Charges

Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drug charges. According to state-owned media, the group was found guilty of operating a criminal gang that imported ingredients used to manufacture narcotics for sale. They also had illegal firearms and ammunition. Authorities reportedly seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials during the investigation. Prosecutors also relied on testimony from 20 witnesses and electronic evidence, including conversations and video clips. Khalifa, 39, who is known for hosting the crime-focused television programme Mission Impossible, has denied the charges and maintained her innocence. Nine other defendants were sentenced to life imprisonment, while seven were acquitted. The death sentences were confirmed after the court obtained the legally required opinion of Egypt's grand mufti, and Khalifa's lawyer has said she will appeal the ruling.

UN Approves Resolution to Replace Mercator Map With Accurate Africa Size



The UN General Assembly has voted in favour of replacing the widely used Mercator world map with a projection that more accurately reflects the size of Africa. The non-binding "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo and backed by African Union member states, received support from 164 countries, including France and the United Kingdom. The United States was the only country to vote against it, and six nations abstained. The Mercator projection, created in the 16th century to assist navigation, has long been criticised for distorting the size of countries and continents by making areas near the poles appear larger and regions near the equator smaller. Africa, for example, appears to be roughly the same size as Greenland on some Mercator maps, despite being around 14 times larger. Supporters of the resolution argue that such distortions shape political and economic perceptions of Africa and can minimise the continent's size, resources, population and development potential. The African Union adopted the Equal Earth projection earlier this year, saying it provides a more accurate representation of the relative sizes of continents.

Zimbabwe Unions Urge Jobs, Not Vendor Crackdown

The Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) has urged the government to focus on repairing the country's struggling economy and creating jobs rather than pursuing a crackdown on illegal street vendors. The call followed an ultimatum by Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe ordering vendors and informal traders to vacate undesignated trading sites by September 9. Thereafter, law enforcement and municipal police will dismantle and demolish all irregular stalls, structures and informal vending sites. The directive initially targeted Harare's central business district and surrounding metropolitan areas. However, it has since expanded into a nationwide campaign. ZCTU secretary-general Tirivanhu Marimo said thousands of Zimbabweans had been forced into street vending by unemployment and poor economic policies. He argued that the informal economy had become the country's largest employer and should be treated accordingly. He also criticised the government for failing to provide vendors with alternative trading spaces or permanent solutions. He accused politicians of encouraging informal trading during election periods before later treating vendors as a nuisance.

Ruto, Governors to Meet Over Kenya Nurses' Strike

Kenyan President William Ruto and the country's governors are expected to meet as pressure grows to resolve a nationwide nurses' strike that has severely disrupted healthcare services. The meeting will involve the national and county governments. It is expected to focus on outstanding issues surrounding the implementation of the 2017 Collective Bargaining Agreement, which remains at the centre of the industrial dispute. County governments have argued that limited resources have made it difficult to meet the financial obligations contained in the agreement. The Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives insists that the deal is binding and has rejected claims that it is financially unsustainable. The strike has left patients struggling to access routine, specialized and emergency care, posing serious concerns about the impact on mothers, newborns and other vulnerable patients. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights has called for urgent intervention. They described the dispute as a public health and human rights crisis. It cited reports of 79 deaths between August 31 and September 2, and called for independent verification of the reported deaths. The talks are also expected to address longer-term concerns around health financing, workforce management and the welfare of healthcare workers.

Close 

At Least 25 Killed in Cape Verde Bus Crash

At least 25 people, many of them schoolchildren and teenagers, were killed when a bus veered off a mountain road and plunged into a steep ravine on Cape Verde's Fogo Island. The crash occurred in the northern part of the island. The bus fell about 30 metres into the ravine. Several injured passengers were taken to Sao Francisco de Assis Regional Hospital for treatment. According to national news agency Inforpress, many of those travelling on the bus were primary and secondary school students. Education officials said the trip had not been organised by local schools but was an annual outing privately arranged by the driver, who was also among those killed in the crash.

World.title: Zimbabwe: MP Says Learners, Teachers Stranded in Rural Kariba Ahead of Schools Reopening
World.content:
AS schools re-open in less than 24 hours on September 8, 2026, dozens of school children and teachers in Nyaminyami, Kariba rural, are stranded.

The crisis follows the sinking of government-owned Mbuya Nehanda ferry on Lake Kariba last month, cutting off the cheapest route from Kariba urban to rural communities such as Mola and Chalala.

With no connecting ferry, families now face a $30+ detour via the Karoi-Siakobvu-Mola road. Most of the affected pupils and teachers had crossed to Mola for holidays and cannot afford the road alternative.

"This is what happens when rural areas are forgotten," said a parent.



"We live next to the biggest lake in the world by volume, yet we cannot even get our children to school safely."

Most of the 97 victims who perished in the ferry accident were children, according to the Local Government ministry.

Citizen Coalition for Change (CCC) Proportional Representation Member of Parliament for Mashonaland West Province, Mutsa Murombedzi, this Sunday called on government to urgently provide a shuttle bus for returning learners and teachers, and to fix the Karoi-Binga road so more transport operators can ply the route safely.

According to reports, government recently turned down a proposal by a private Kariba operator to provide the much-needed service, saying the vessels did not meet required safety standards.

This past weekend, Saturday, Presidential spokesperson George Charamba posting as @Jamwanda said President Emmerson Mnangagwa had ordered government to source boats and ferries for inland waterways, "principally Kariba which recently saw a maritime tragedy."

"On the instruction of His Excellency the President of Zimbabwe Dr E.D. Mnangagwa, government is in the market for boats and ferries to service our inland waterways, principally Kariba which recently saw a maritime tragedy."Charamba said a two-stage probe led by the chief secretary to the President and Cabinet Martin Rushwaya is underway to deliver immediate relief and a long-term solution, with emphasis on "safety, cargo and passenger services."The two-stage probe looks at providing immediate relief and long-term solutions to maritime transport in the country."

Hours later, Presidential advisor Paul Tungwarara posted from Dubai on his X handle that he had met Vikas Goel, a billionaire ship and yacht manufacturer.

Tungwarara said he first engaged Goel in 2017 to bring investment and expertise to Zimbabwe.

"Unlocking strategic international partnerships like this is key to opening new economic horizons for our nation. Watch this space!" he said.

The development signals government wants compliant vessels immediately, while building local capacity to service lakes and dams long-term.

Close 

It is not clear how soon the government will provide this much needed service for the affected school children, teachers and other people residing in this area.

World.title: UN agency accused of Hamas ties sees another European nation cut funding
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Another European nation has stopped funding the U.N. agency that aids the Palestinians. Finland has followed the U.S. and Sweden in halting donations to the terror-tainted agency.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), is presently being investigated for ties to the terrorist rulers of Gaza. Recently, organizations including the USAID Office of Inspector General (OIG) and NGO UN Watch have uncovered further evidence of what they allege is Hamas infiltration of UNRWA and its members’ participation in the Oct. 7, 2023 terror attacks in southern Israel.

Finland announced it would discontinue funding to the organization at the end of 2026. Finland’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agreement with UNRWA would conclude at the end of 2026 but that "As of yet, no decision has been made on what are the international partners through which Finland’s support will be channeled next year to meet the acute needs in the region."

Finnish officials did not respond to Fox News Digital’s questions about what prompted the change to the country’s funding for UNRWA.

US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION

While other nations still continue to fund UNRWA, President Donald Trump fully banned funding to the organization in February 2025 and Sweden ended funding to UNRWA in December 2024. Sweden redirected aid to other U.N. bodies for its Gaza response.

The future of aid provision in Gaza matters for the Trump administration-backed Board of Peace as it seeks to shape a conflict-free future for the region.

An official affiliated with the Board of Peace reconstruction effort told Fox News Digital that "the international community’s concern about UNRWA in Gaza continues to rise and is supported by damning evidence. The Board of Peace has been clear: New Gaza will be both demilitarized and deradicalized, and we will only be working with trusted, credible delivery partners to achieve our goals. We anticipate responsibly replacing UNRWA with vetted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza."

WATCHDOG DEMANDS APOLOGY AFTER UN MEMORIAL ERRONEOUSLY HONORS HAMAS TERRORIST

The USAID OIG is investigating about 1,500 members of UNRWA for terror participation, and has referred 108 UNRWA staff to the State Department to suggest they be suspended or excluded from further work with organizations in receipt of U.S. funds.

A senior U.S. official briefed on USAID OIG’s ongoing investigation told Fox News Digital that the USAID OIG’s "independent findings are prompting several other countries to reassess the stale and conventional thinking that UNRWA is the best and only option to provide aid to civilians in Gaza." The official said that the USAID OIG’s "findings also will prevent Hamas and October 7 affiliated staff from circulating across future, more responsible, aid organizations operating in Gaza."

WORLD'S HUMANITARIAN SYSTEM BUCKLING, 'NO LONGER FIT FOR PURPOSE,' US-BASED RESEARCHERS SAY

UN Watch’s Terror Network report claims that about 12% of UNRWA staff in Gaza are members of terror organizations, based on "cross-checking UNRWA employee rosters with Hamas records seized by the [Israel Defense Forces.]"

Executive director of UN Watch Hillel Neuer told Fox News Digital that "Finland’s principled decision to defund terror-infested UNRWA will not deprive Palestinians of aid, as it will be redirected through genuine humanitarian agencies such as the World Food Programme that are not systemically infiltrated by Hamas."

He said that "other democracies should follow" the examples of Finland, Sweden, and the U.S. "Contrary to what UNRWA supporters claim, the agency is not ‘indispensable’ — assistance can and must be delivered through responsible alternatives."

Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, told Fox News Digital that "UNRWA has taken note of the announcement, and they are grateful to Finland for the disbursement of the 2023–2026 funds under the multi-year agreement. UNRWA looks forward to continuing our discussions with the government." He explained that "the Secretary-General continues to encourage member states to support UNRWA's vital work."

Finland's four-year funding was around $23.23 to UNRWA and will now end after this year. UNRWA did not respond to Fox News Digital questions about Finland’s decision.

Neuer said "defunding UNRWA is a prerequisite for deradicalization, the first step in the Gaza peace plan. Far from harming the prospects for peace, dismantling UNRWA is essential to achieving it. For decades, the agency has perpetuated the conflict by teaching generations of Palestinians that their future lies not in building their own society, but in a so-called ‘right of return’ that would eliminate Israel."

He concluded by noting that USAID OIG and UN Watch’s exposes on UNRWA prove that "the agency is unreformable. Nations that genuinely want peace should stop financing this machinery of hate, and invest instead in humanitarian relief, deradicalization and Palestinian self-reliance."

World.title: NASCAR race turns ominous as driver delivers chilling warning, Hooters Gianna gets racy in the pool & Hocevar!
World.content:
Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

Last week, Carson Hocevar told me he didn't expect any drama in The Chase.

NASCAR RACE INCLUDES HALF THE FIELD WRECKING, FURIOUS DRIVERS & HOLLYWOOD ACTOR RIPPING A 'LEFTIST, WOKE' MOVE

"You know, I've had people try to wreck me and they just end up wrecking themselves lately. So I don't foresee anybody really having to, you know, wanting to do anything like that that where I would have to really be worried about it.

"So, yeah, I mean, I'm not really worried about."

Carson, buddy, it's time to start worrying. If your head wasn't on a swivel before Darlington, it HAS to be on one now.

Welcome to a Labor Day edition of Monday Morning Pit-Stop! We're gonna keep this one brief today because A) it's a holiday, B) it's a holiday, and C) I've got meat to smoke ... because it's a holiday.

We're gonna dive into Carson's antics last night at Darlington here in just a minute.

We'll also get into Ryan Blaney putting another few dollars in NASCAR's new 'Swear Jar,' Dale Jarrett got a nice little Sunday night wakeup call, and Hooters Gianna Blaney gave us one final summer photo dump from the pool.

And what a summer it was!

Four tires, enough fuel to get us to Gateway, and maybe some secret service protection for Carson ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Watch Out, Carson' edition — is LIVE!

Let's just jump right in

Look, I'm not gonna break down the race. It's a holiday, and it was a relatively "meh" finish.

Christopher Bell finally won after seven runner-ups this season.

Denny Hamlin was surprisingly bad, but still grabbed a bunch of stage points so he maintains his point lead after the first Chase race.

The Toyotas continue to be the dominant car this season, followed by the Fords, followed by the Chevys.

Kyle Larson led a bunch of laps early, but you knew it was only a matter of time until a Toyota took over.

OK, we all caught up? Good! Now, let's check in with Carson and Brad Keselowski:

When entertainment crosses a line

Thoughts? First impressions?

First of all, Brad didn't just spin, as Hocevar says with a s–tgrin on his face 14 times. That's obviously false. Hocevar washed up the track and got into Brad, which caused the spin.

Now, here's where I veer a bit with the rest of the pitchfork crowd today ...

He barely — and I mean barely — tapped him. You have to squint to see it. If anything, it looks like he really just got Brad loose enough to spin him out. I don't think it was intentional. I think it was a mistake on Carson's part, and he's too embarrassed/proud to admit it.

"His day’s coming and it’s coming hard. Watch out, Carson."

You don't hear Brad Keselowski talk like that often — not this version of Brad, at least. He was hot, and I get it. At some point over the next few weeks, he's going to end Carson Hocevar's day. This sport has a way of policing itself, and you will see it unfold.

Now, the question becomes ... is this good for NASCAR?

Of course it is. It's great for NASCAR.

The series desperately needs a villain, and they have one in Carson Hocevar. He's also an extremely popular villain, given he LEADS the series in merchandise sales right now.

Hocevar talked to me a lot last week about the state of the sport, and even compared it, to a degree, to WWE.

"They don't understand the new guys," Hocevar said when asked about balancing old and new NASCAR fans. "'This guy is popular, and I don't understand why.' A lot of my friends, some of them love WWE and all the intricacies of that world. But the casuals of it, they're like, 'Man, I loved Stone Cold when he walked out. I never even watched him wrestle, but I liked him, and the Undertaker and their shticks.

"It's very similar to how NASCAR fans describe everything and become negative to everything. A lot of times, they're not sure what they're looking for."

Blaney adds to the Swear Jar, Dale Jarrett's jump scare & Sam Busch

That's an actual social media post from Brad Keselowski's RFK racing team, if you were wondering how the rest of the garage felt about Carson Hocevar.

They hate him.

By the way, they also hated Kyle Busch and Brad Keselowski back in the day. I can remember a time when those two were HATED. Kyle especially.

Carson Hocevar is young and stupid. He's got a hot TikTok influencer girlfriend. He was just told he's the most popular driver on the circuit. He won at Talladega earlier this year, and he's in the Chase.

He's good for NASCAR. He also needs some humbling. Both things can be true.

PS: Massive sale going on over at Carson's pro shop right now!

Amazing. The kid doesn't care. Can't wait to see the fight in a few weeks!

OK, let's put the pedal to the floor and get on outta here ... it's a HOLIDAY.

First up? NASCAR has a new initiative where they are going to put $5 in a swear jar over these next 10 weeks every time a driver cusses over the radio.

That's A LOT, by the way. These guys are disgusting over the radio in the heat of battle. Trust me.

Anyway, if you can guess how much money is in the jar by the end, you, apparently, get ALL of it!

Hat's off to NASCAR. I give them a bunch of crap (rightfully so), but this is a smart promotion. Perhaps they took a page out of Carson's WWE playbook?

Also ... what a liner there from Angry Ryan Blaney!

"Christ, it's f—ing plowing my d–k off."

That's $10, by my count!

Next? Let's check in with Dale Jarrett on the way out:

Amazing. That gif, I assume, will get some good play this football season. It's not often that 40 stock cars can sneak up on you, but Dale was genuinely taken aback here.

No clue what he was doing, but I'm glad the cameras were rolling. Well done.

OK, that's it for today. Some solid laboring on Labor Day, everyone. Let's go have a big week.

World.title: Discovery beneath soccer field reveals massive medieval convent lost for centuries
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Researchers recently uncovered a long-lost medieval convent in an unusual location in Denmark: a soccer field — with an expert sharing details with Fox News Digital about the "rare" find.

The discovery, made in Roskilde, was announced last month by ROMU, a state-recognized Danish museum organization.

St. Clare's Convent, which was built in the 13th century, was found through a ground-penetrating radar survey ahead of plans to build an underground parking facility.

FORBIDDEN PASSAGE? SECRET MEDIEVAL TUNNEL FOUND BENEATH ANCIENT PAGAN GRAVES, ARCHAEOLOGISTS SAY

"The survey revealed a well-preserved convent complex approximately one meter [three feet] below ground level," officials said in a press release.

The scans also "revealed traces of the convent’s buildings, including rooms, columns, cloisters and a church in the southern wing," officials said.

"The eastern wing, in particular, is exceptionally well-preserved, with clearly defined rooms and vault pillars," the statement said.

St. Clare's was one of five monastic sites in medieval Roskilde. Unlike the other four, it was not protected as an ancient monument because it was believed to have been lost.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH REMNANTS OF FORGOTTEN CITY 'MARKED BY CONFLICT' BURIED BELOW BUSTLING HUB

Researchers are working with the municipality on plans for trial excavations at the proposed parking site.

Excavations of monasteries and convents are "rare," said Jesper Langkilde, an archaeologist and museum curator at ROMU.

Langkilde told Fox News Digital he was "quite surprised" by the discovery.

"I almost didn’t believe my own eyes that so much was still there, and that we got such a clear image of it," he said.

The convent was a large complex, measuring roughly 230 feet by 230 feet.

Although the convent was demolished in the 16th century and hundreds of thousands of its bricks were removed, much of its underground footprint survived.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER LOST MEDIEVAL CITY THAT VANISHED WITHOUT A TRACE: 'TRUE TIME CAPSULE'

Langkilde said the radar is detecting the lowest portions of the walls and foundations, which were made with large boulders that were often left in place when medieval buildings were torn down.

Historical records show that about 500,000 bricks were sold after the convent was demolished, but Langkilde said a complex of its size could easily have contained twice that number.

Though there hasn't been an excavation of the site yet, Langkilde said archaeologists expect to find "quite a lot of artifacts," especially those from daily medieval life.

Excavators expect to find everything from "lots of pottery sherds and animal bones" to "religious objects, like pendant crosses, rosary beads and pilgrims' badges" and objects related to writing and books, he said.

CLICK HERE TO 

"The convents and monasteries were centers of literacy and had libraries and book production," added Langkilde, noting that book fittings, writing utensils and personal effects like combs and needles are also expected.

If organic remains are well-preserved, archaeologists could learn more about the nuns' diets and the plants grown in the convent gardens.

"[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archeological point of view."

Researchers also expect to find burials at the site, which "can tell us about who the nuns were and who else was buried at the convent," Langkilde said.

The discoveries could also reveal the convent's international connections. Its first nuns are believed to have come from a convent in Strasbourg, according to Langkilde.

"The convents were part of international networks, so it would be interesting to look for signs of international relations in the [material] from this site," he said.

"[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archaeological point of view," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The expert also called the discovery "a very big step forward for our knowledge of the medieval monasteries."

"[They] played a key part in the development of Roskilde as one of the most important and wealthiest towns in medieval Denmark," he said.

Langkilde added, "It is an excellent example of how much archeological knowledge a geophysical survey can contribute — under the right circumstances — without even putting a shovel to the ground."

World.title: Pilotless cargo aircraft could change how packages move
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A broken pump on an offshore platform, or medical supplies needed after a hurricane can be tough to move quickly. The FAA just tested one possible solution: a hybrid-electric cargo aircraft that can take off vertically and fly without a crew onboard.

The FAA announced that Elroy Air and the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development conducted a cargo demonstration at Houma-Terrebonne Airport in Louisiana. The agency says it was the first remotely piloted aircraft test flight under its eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) Integration Pilot Program, known as eIPP.

That may sound like a specialized aviation test, but the bigger story is what aircraft like this could eventually do. Elroy Air's Chaparral can carry more than 500 pounds, putting it in a very different league from the small delivery drones you may picture hovering over a driveway.

So, could pilotless aircraft like this eventually change how everything from emergency supplies to everyday goods moves across the country? Here's what the FAA is testing and why it could be a big deal.

MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

Why this pilotless cargo aircraft test stands out

The FAA created eIPP to help the government learn how next-generation aircraft can operate safely in U.S. airspace. In March, the Department of Transportation selected eight projects across 26 states. Louisiana is one of the participants, and more test flights are planned through the rest of 2026. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the Louisiana demonstration provides data that can help "turn these concepts from trial to deployment."

That line gets to the heart of this test. Chaparral has flown before. In December 2025, Elroy Air completed its first point-to-point cargo delivery with the aircraft. During that demonstration, Chaparral autonomously carried 213 pounds over a 2.6-mile flight. What changed here is the regulatory setting. The FAA now gets to study these flights as part of a federal program focused on bringing advanced aircraft into the national airspace.

How Elroy Air's Chaparral works

Chaparral looks more like a small cargo aircraft than the drone that might bring dinner to your house. It uses electric propulsion for vertical takeoff and landing. Then it transitions to wingborne flight for the longer part of the trip. A hybrid-electric powertrain gives the aircraft longer-range capability without requiring charging infrastructure at every stop. Elroy Air's current Chaparral specifications list a maximum range of 450 miles and a payload of more than 500 pounds.

The cargo system is unusual, too. Elroy designed modular pods that workers can load before the aircraft arrives. Chaparral can pick up a pod, fly it to another location and leave it there. That could reduce the amount of ground equipment needed at remote sites. Because it can take off vertically, Chaparral can serve locations that lack a traditional runway.

Pilotless still involves human oversight

There is an important detail behind the word "pilotless." The FAA described the Louisiana demonstration as remotely piloted. Elroy Air later said Chaparral completed a week-long series of flights autonomously with no pilot onboard while operating under Air Traffic Control oversight.

That means humans still play a role in overseeing these operations even when the aircraft handles the flight autonomously. As testing continues, regulators will have to determine how much human supervision is required and how the aircraft should respond to communication failures, changing weather or other unexpected problems.

DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES

Where Chaparral could be useful first

You probably will not see a Chaparral dropping an Amazon box onto your front lawn anytime soon. The aircraft targets what the logistics industry calls the middle mile. That means moving cargo between larger points in a delivery network rather than carrying one small order to your doorstep.

Elroy Air has pointed to offshore energy operations and industrial supply chains as potential uses. The company also sees an opportunity in disaster response, where damaged roads can make moving supplies far more difficult. For example, Chaparral could carry replacement equipment to an offshore facility without sending a crewed helicopter. After a major storm, aircraft like it could eventually help move heavier supplies into areas that ground vehicles struggle to reach.

Elroy Air said when it joined eIPP earlier this year that the program could include cargo operations across the Gulf Coast, including energy industry locations in Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi.

How this fits into the delivery boom

Delivery drones are starting to show up in more places, but most of them are still carrying pretty small loads. Amazon plans to expand Prime Air drone delivery to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026. Those drones are built for lightweight packages delivered directly to customers. We recently took a closer look at Amazon's huge drone delivery expansion and what it could mean if you live in one of the communities getting the service.

Meanwhile, other companies are working on the last part of the trip. Robot.com's R-dog uses wheeled legs to get over obstacles such as stairs and curbs while carrying deliveries.

Chaparral takes on a much bigger job. Instead of carrying one sandwich or a small box, it is built to move substantial cargo between locations. That could make heavy-duty delivery one of the first places where this kind of aircraft proves especially useful.

What happens next for the FAA program

The Louisiana flight represents one step in a much broader federal test program. The FAA says it will study these demonstrations, identify problems and refine procedures for advanced air mobility. Louisiana and the other eIPP participants plan additional flights through the rest of the year.

Watch how much human supervision the FAA requires as the technology develops. Regulators will also have to decide where these aircraft can operate routinely. Another major test will come when something goes wrong. Communication can fail. Weather can change. The aircraft will need dependable ways to respond safely when either happens. Those answers will tell us much more about how close pilotless cargo aircraft are to regular commercial use.

100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS

What this means to you

The biggest change could happen behind the scenes before you ever see one of these aircraft overhead. If heavy cargo can move faster between remote locations, companies could shorten some supply routes. Communities that are expensive or difficult to reach could gain another delivery option.

Emergency response could benefit as well. An aircraft that takes off without a runway could potentially keep supplies moving when damaged infrastructure slows trucks or traditional aircraft.

However, communities will want answers about noise and flight paths. Safety questions will be even bigger as these aircraft begin sharing more airspace with conventional aviation.

For you, the FAA's work now could eventually influence which autonomous delivery services reach your area and what safeguards come with them.

Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much work this aircraft could actually take on. We have watched small delivery drones inch closer to everyday use for years, but Chaparral is built for a much bigger job. It can move hundreds of pounds over real distances without needing a runway at every stop. I also like that the FAA is testing this in a real-world program instead of rushing it into wider use. Regulators need to see how these aircraft handle shared airspace, changing conditions and unexpected problems. The bar should stay high when you are talking about hundreds of pounds flying overhead. For now, I would keep an eye on remote worksites, disaster response and other places where moving cargo is difficult or slow. If these aircraft prove they can do that safely and reliably, they could end up changing a much bigger part of the delivery network.
