World.title: Sen Jim Justice finds way through Senate polarization to bring WWII hero memorial to DC
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., found a way to get something passed unanimously, despite what he rebukes as "romper-room behavior" of political polarization in the Senate.

In an interview Saturday with Fox News Digital, Justice detailed how he worked around the Senate’s bitter partisan divide to get a monument honoring late World War II Medal of Honor hero Hershel "Woody" Williams onto the National Mall.

"I've never seen anything like this, never in my life seen anything to where it is, it is so preposterous," Justice lamented. "You know, no one could make any sense out of what in the world is going on a lot of times."

"I don't know why we don't talk to one another," he added. "I don't know why we're disrespectful to one other."

DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE

Using good, old-fashioned dialogue, Justice's effort ultimately succeeded in getting his first Senate law passed for his late friend. The Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act directs the National Medal of Honor monument to a prominent location within the Reserve on the National Mall.

The legislation is Justice’s first bill as a senator. It honors Williams, a West Virginia native who received the Medal of Honor for extraordinary heroism during the Battle of Iwo Jima and who was the last surviving World War II Medal of Honor recipient before his death in 2022 at age 98. The monument will honor Williams by name while commemorating Medal of Honor recipients as a whole.

The House approved the measure on Aug. 31 after the Senate passed it unanimously in March. The legislation is now awaiting Trump’s signature.

"We're really hopeful he's going to sign it this coming week," Justice said. "There's been a lot to make all that happen and everything, and I can't be more proud."

Justice, describing the partisan fight in the interview, said the path to unanimous approval was anything but smooth.

EXCLUSIVE: NEW AMERICA 250 MONUMENT LETS FAMILIES FIND MILITARY RELATIVES IN SECONDS: 'I HAD TEARS IN MY EYES'

"I mean, we had it shot down," he said, adding, but "I just wouldn’t turn it loose."

"And the reason I wouldn’t turn loose is because it was just real simple: I mean Woody’s unbelievable, or was unbelievable, that’s for sure. But all these Medal of Honor recipients and everything, the ones we’ve lost and all those that are still living, they are so deserving."

Justice described how the measure initially had become caught up in the same divisiveness that has locked up the Senate on a much broader range of issues.

"All we managed to do is keep a food fight going to where – because it was a Republican thing or Republican Jim Justice introducing – well, I’m telling you, if I’m a Democrat, by God, we’re not gonna let that happen and everything," he lamented. "And then it’s just, it’s the same thing on both sides. Way, way, way too much for a guy that’s got white hair and wants to try to get things done."

EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE

Justice said the breakthrough came just before he was preparing to take the matter to the Senate floor with four Medal of Honor recipients present.

"I was about three feet from going into the Senate chambers," Justice recalled. "And we sat down right there, you know, kind of on the steps and really just started talking."

The senator was Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. The two serve together on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Justice said he had developed a personal relationship with Heinrich over the years, including through Justice’s well-known bulldog, Babydog.

SEN RICK SCOTT: AMERICANS WORK FIVE DAYS A WEEK, WHY CAN’T THE SENATE?

"I said, Martin, I don’t understand. I mean, how in the world can we do this?" Justice said. "And I said, Martin, you know, I’m getting ready to go on the floor, and it’s not going to be good. It’s not gonna be good for you. It’s not going to good for a lot of folks and everything. A lot of people are going to be upset. A lot of people are going to be really sad."

Justice said he appealed directly to Heinrich to find a way forward.

"And I just said, Martin, I don’t know any way to tell it other than just to tell you the truth. And you’re a good guy. And I don’t know why in the world we just can’t talk with one another."

Heinrich responded with a blunt explanation of the broader problem, Justice said.

MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH'

"And he looked right at me, and he said, you know, people here don’t talk to one another," Justice said. "And I really appreciate you doing that, and I’m not going to object."

Justice said the measure then moved "in three minutes, boom, boom, boom, done."

"It was an amazing moment really, and like I said, Martin's a good guy, and I just think that maybe we could all learn from that just a little bit," he said.

"Now we're going to honor, you know, another great, unbelievable, courageous group of people, and it's way, way, way overdue."

HOUSE REPUBLICANS DID WHAT VOTERS ASKED AND WE HAVE THE RECEIPTS. IT’S UP TO THE SENATE

On other issues in the Senate still in gridlock, Justice urged dialogue like that above and for everyone to "grow up."

"Why in the world would you carry on with just childishness, and in all fairness, that's what it is," Justice said. "You can't make sense of it. There's no point in us trying to do that. This is Romper Room behavior. And if there's anything in the world I could do, I wish to goodness that I could tell everybody, you know let's grow up a lot. Let's absolutely grow up and let's behave."

Justice said he does not expect the Senate’s structural problems to be fixed easily, pointing to the 60-vote threshold associated with overcoming a filibuster and arguing that lawmakers have little incentive to change a system that protects the political status quo.

HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER'

"You’ve got a lot of people there that have never had a job," Justice said. "They’ve been there forever, and they’ve never made a payroll."

He said his former chief of staff Brian Abraham once gave him an even simpler explanation for the paralysis.

"I said, ‘guys, we’re really missing something here because we can really get stuff done here and everything,’" Justice recalled. "And he looked right at me, and he said, ‘you don’t understand, do you?’

"People here don’t wanna get something done. All they want to do is just keep it going. Round and round it goes. Fundraiser, fundraiser, fundraiser. Round and around it goes, get reelected, get re-elected."

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

Justice said the monument fight was especially important because Williams himself embodied the opposite of that kind of self-interest.

"Woody Williams was all about us," he said. "Woody Williams was never about Woody Williams. And he just was an amazing man. I got to know him really well, and we became really good friends."

Williams’ Medal of Honor citation stems from his actions on Iwo Jima, where, under intense enemy fire, he used a flamethrower to destroy Japanese positions and help clear a path for advancing Marines.

Justice said the symbolism of the monument extends beyond Williams and into future generations.

"Now, I’m going to take them there," Justice said of his future descendants. "I’m going to show them this and tell them, maybe I was only a grain of sand, but I had something to do with this. And I really stood up hard for it and everything. We got it done."

World.title: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them
World.content:
DES MOINES, Iowa — Dawn Vogel, a Republican county supervisor in rural Buchanan County, Iowa, doesn’t have a lot in common with the leading democratic socialists in Congress. But on this bit of policy they agree: Data centers are proliferating across the American landscape too fast.

Vogel voted earlier this year for a moratorium that temporarily bans data centers from setting up shop in her heavily Republican county, which favored President Donald Trump 63% to 35% in 2024. In Washington, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. — the nation’s two most prominent democratic socialists — have proposed a similar moratorium that would cover the entire country.

“I don’t think this is a Republican or Democratic issue,” Vogel said on the sidelines of the Iowa State Association of Counties’ annual conference here in late August, adding that she hasn’t talked to a single voter at home who wants data centers.

Dawn Vogel, a Republican supervisor in Buchanan County, Iowa, voted for a temporary moratorium on data centers in the county. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

“It’s an issue of what’s the best use for the land, what’s the best use for our natural resources,” she said. “You can have all the data you want to in the world, but if you don’t have water to drink, you don’t have humans to use the data.”

That point of view places Vogel in a loose, but very large, populist coalition that is fighting the rise of data centers at the ballot box, with yard signs, in courts and at all levels of government as November’s midterm elections approach.

An NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey, conducted from Aug. 20 through Sept. 1, found that 69% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local area, with 45% saying they “strongly oppose” the idea.

They are all at odds with President Donald Trump.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the end of August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

But it’s more about backyards than being seen as backward, according to voters who spoke to NBC News on a recent road trip along Interstate 80 from Nebraska to New Jersey — a swath that includes eight swing districts key to determining which party will control the House next year and two marquee Senate races. These voters, who span the political spectrum, said they don’t want data centers anywhere near their communities.

For some, the issue has become a touchstone for the feeling that the powerful are taking advantage of the powerless.

“All of the data centers that are starting to pop up in areas, I find that troublesome because it drives utility costs for citizens in the area,” said Tamara Clark, 49, a Democratic voter who works in the healthcare industry. “I don’t feel like the rich should continuously get rich while we have to grovel for what we need in our everyday necessities.”

In Clark’s congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, a 22-term incumbent, is using the issue against her rival, Republican Derek Merrin, who cast a 2017 vote in the state Legislature that helped extend tax breaks to companies that build data centers in the state.

Tamara Clark, an Ohio Democrat, said she finds it "troublesome" that data centers drive up utility costs for nearby residents. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is seeking to hold his seat against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown, was a full-throated advocate for data centers when he was the state’s lieutenant governor. But in July, he introduced legislation in the Senate that would require utility companies to charge large-scale data center operators enough money to cover the costs of increased electricity and water use.

His change of tune reflects a broader shift among elected officials who embraced data centers as a way to bring jobs and tax revenue to their cities, counties and states. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, D-Pa., who is on the ballot in November, signed a new batch of data center regulations in August after having encouraged companies to locate them in his state.

While Republican voters are more supportive of data centers than Democrats and independents, the majority of them remain opposed — 57% to 43% — according to the NBC News Decision Desk poll. The survey found that 81% of Democrats and 71% of independents are against data centers being built in their communities.

While supporters have been less demonstrative, their ranks extend beyond the AI companies building data centers and the politicians who have looked to them as economic development engines.

National and local labor unions involved in the construction and maintenance of data centers tout them as a boon for workers, both as a source of jobs and for high rates of pay. Several data center workers in Ohio spoke to NBC News about those benefits on the condition of anonymity because, according to one of them, they have agreed not to discuss their jobs with the media.

That worker said he can make as much as $5,000 in a week, including overtime, at a relatively low-level union job.

“It’s helping a lot of people — a lot of work going on, a lot of people benefiting from it,” the data center worker said, adding that he was warned by friends about problems, from overuse of water resources to weird ringing sounds, that he has not witnessed at his workplace.

“It’s scary,” he said. “You got a lot of people that say all these horrific things. I was told all these negative things about data centers, and then I started working at one, and I didn’t see any of the things I was told about.”

He said he would like to see proponents and critics work together to fix any problems with data centers so that they can continue to be built and operate without disruption to the surrounding communities.

Jordan Cloe, an electrician, is concerned about a data center's water consumption in Altoona, Iowa. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

But Jordan Cloe, 47, an electrician from Bondurant, in Iowa’s hotly contested 3rd Congressional District, said he’s worried about the resources used by a data center in neighboring Altoona.

“Did we have any data on what the implications were about water consumption or anything? Like, we just built a power grid where that thing sits,” he said. “Did we get to use that? No, they gobbled that up.”

Cloe, who said he aligns more with Democrats, said he doesn’t know anything about Sarah Trone Garriott, the Democratic challenger to Republican Rep. Zach Nunn, but that he plans to vote for her in November.

For Vogel, the county supervisor, the unresolved questions are enough reason to keep data centers out of her county — at least for now.

“We need to do what’s best for Buchanan County and then, you know, if the companies want to come knock on the door,” she said, “then we’ll talk.”

Wait until sales in October and November to save on denim, boots, coats and sweaters, for example, says Porwal. Are there better Labor Day sales online or in stores? There are comparable Labor Day sales online and in stores, especially at big box retailers, so you’re guaranteed to find strong deals wherever you shop. A few things to keep in mind while deciding whether to leave your couch: Shopping online makes comparing prices and stacking savings easier , letting you consider the total value of a deal, not just the sale price, says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, a shopping and savings expert at Rakuten. Open a few tabs and search for the exact same product at a handful of retailers to weigh which one offers the lowest price and lowest shipping fee. You can also shop through cash back apps and browser extensions online, which help you find additional promo codes and rewards, she says.

Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.” How can you save the most money during Labor Day sales? All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend. Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you. Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.

World.title: DOJ’s civil rights unit tasked with voter fraud and 5 dead after cargo plane crashes in Miami: Morning Rundown
World.content:
Federal election monitors traditionally focused on protecting voter rights are tapped to tackle fraud. Police arrest an armed man suspected of lunging at an Ohio gubernatorial candidate. And five people are dead after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashes at Miami’s main airport.

Here’s what to know today.

DOJ civil rights unit retooled to focus on voter fraud

A voter casts their ballot at a polling location inside Farewell Recreation Center in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. Emily Elconin / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has for decades sent election monitors to polling sites to protect voters from discrimination based on race, disability or language.

Now, the Trump administration is giving it a new focus: voter fraud.

This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

Harmeet Dhillon, a Republican who co-chaired Lawyers for Trump during the 2020 election, helms the division. She emailed employees asking them to serve among the 1,000 monitors she wants in place for the midterms, a person familiar with the matter said.

The division has solicited staff lawyers to serve as monitors before. But the number nationwide has never reached 1,000 and it’s unusual for fraud to be on the agenda.

Many employees have also been replaced by conservative hires, some of whom back the president’s false claim that he won in 2020.

NBC News spoke with a half-dozen Justice Department veterans. Some worry the monitors could be used to help undermine confidence in elections if Trump is unhappy with the results.

More about the concerns.

Related news:

Exclusive: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them.

Poll: Most Americans are using AI, but they’re not happy about it.

Alarm in Europe after far-right’s historic German victory

AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund at an election party in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sunday. Matthias Schrader / AP

A regional election victory put the far-right on the brink of holding power in a German state for the first time since the Nazis. The Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, crushed its mainstream rivals but fell just short of a majority in the eastern Saxony-Anhalt region.

The pro-Russia, anti-immigration AfD is now seeking outside support in its bid to become the first far-right party to govern a state since World War II.

As those high-stakes talks began, the shockwaves of Sunday’s vote were being felt across the continent.

“It clearly sends out a very, very worrying signal,” French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told RTL ​radio, according to Reuters. “This shows that we face a ​major challenge in the face of a populist wave ‌which ⁠is spreading around the world today and which we must resist,” he said.

In Poland, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also said the regional election was “a very worrying sign,” according to Reuters. “Only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD,” Poland’s center-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Suspect arrested after armed man confronts Ohio gubernatorial candidate

A suspect was arrested after an armed man lunged at Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, and injured several people at a fair.

Acton was speaking at the event when Patrick Havas, 38, “started pushing his way through the crowd,” a spokesperson for the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said. Security confronted him, and two people were knocked to the ground in the process.

After law enforcement officials arrested Havas, they recovered two handguns and a set of brass knuckles, the spokesperson added.

Acton, a physician, was not hurt, and she remained on-site to attend to one of the injured people, according to a photo an attendee shared with NBC News.

Here’s what else we know.

Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes in Miami

Five people were killed and five others injured after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashed just outside Miami International Airport yesterday, officials said.

The Boeing 767-300 aircraft overran the runway while it was landing, struck multiple vehicles and came to rest at a field, according to officials. It took off from San Juan, Puerto Rico, the Federal Aviation Administration said.

Three people were in critical condition, the Miami-Dade fire chief said. A hotline has been set up for relatives of people who may have been involved in the accident.

Staff Pick: The U.K.’s approach to postpartum psychosis may be saving lives

Sofii Lewis, now 27, smiling as she holds her daughter, Evie, 3, years after her recovery. Courtesy of Sofii Lewis

Lindsay Clancy’s devastating trial over the killing of her three children has sparked an important dialogue around maternal mental healthcare and how cases of postpartum psychosis are treated in the U.S.

We looked at an approach across the Atlantic that prioritizes the treatment of mothers alongside their babies through specialist inpatient care facilities called Mother and Baby Units, or MBUs.

While the United Kingdom is not the only country to provide care that keeps mothers and babies together during treatment, the scale of its MBU program is “pretty unique to the U.K.,” Dr. Sally Wilson, the National Training Coordinator for Action on Postpartum Psychosis, a British charity supporting women and families affected by the condition, told me. My reporting highlights how that trailblazing effort may very well be saving lives, including that of one mom, Sofii Lewis, who says she and her daughter Evie, now 3, might not be alive today had it not been for the care she received in an MBU.

World.title: 25 years after 9/11, Taliban rules Afghanistan again, but with U.S. firepower
World.content:
Kabul — As Americans reflect this week on the 25 years that have passed since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, CBS News has returned to Afghanistan, where the war those attacks triggered ended five years ago with the Taliban's stunning return to power.

When the last U.S. and allied soldiers left after a brutal two-decade war, the Taliban's fighters seized billions of dollars worth of American-purchased military hardware. President Trump, whose first administration negotiated the deal to end the war with the Taliban, has accused the Biden administration of "totally botching" the withdrawal.

Five years later, the hardware of America's longest-ever war is still easy to spot on the streets of Kabul. Taliban fighters patrol in armored vehicles once supplied to Afghan forces, wearing American tactical gear and carrying American weapons.

A convoy of Taliban security personnel take part in a parade in front of the former U.S. Embassy building in Kabul, Afghanistan, Aug. 15, 2026, as they celebrate the fifth anniversary of the Taliban's return to power. Wakil KOHSAR/AFP/Getty

CBS News saw one Humvee in the Afghan capital still adorned with a faded Green Bay Packers decal — a remnant from its past operators.

President Trump has been fiercely critical of the former Biden administration, accusing his predecessor of allowing the U.S. military to abandon billions of dollars in military hardware. Mr. Trump has demanded that the Taliban hand it back.

But the Taliban has proudly shown off its American-funded arsenal, even staging military parades through Kabul's streets.

Pentagon figures released last year show some $7 billion in hardware and weaponry fell into the group's hands when the Afghan National Army collapsed.

Shortly after the 2021 withdrawal, CBS News filmed as "Badri 313," an elite Taliban special forces battalion, patrolled in their American vehicles, American commando gear and with their American weapons.

Members of the Afghan Taliban's Badri 313 military unit stand guard as newly recruited Taliban members attend a ceremony in Kandahar, Afghanistan, in a Feb. 15, 2022 file photo. JAVED TANVEER/AFP/Getty

Asked about President Trump's determination to reclaim the equipment, Taliban Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News the hardware now belongs to "the state of Afghanistan, and we are not in the business of doing transactions and deals on the assets of the state of Afghanistan."

When it was pointed out that American taxpayers purchased the equipment, Balkhi said: "The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should we not be paying for that first?"

The Taliban waged a vicious insurgency during a war that killed more than 2,400 U.S. service members and tens of thousands of innocent Afghans.

But critics of the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. withdrawal say it's allowed the Taliban to transform from insurgents into a state military force armed with billions of dollars in American-funded firepower.

They have used those weapons to impose a draconian interpretation of Islamic rule on Afghanistan's people, almost completely depriving women and girls of the right to work and study, and restricting life for everyone in the country in ways that some analysts say are even harsher than during the group's previous reign.

Biden has offered little public commentary on the Afghanistan withdrawal, but he said in September 2021, a month after the Taliban took back control, that he "was not going to extend this 'forever war,' and I was not extending a 'forever exit.'"

"If anything, the developments of the past week reinforce that ending U.S. military involvement in Afghanistan now was the right decision," said the then-president in August 2021, as the Taliban reasserted their rule 20 years after being ousted by the U.S.-led military campaign. "American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves."

In 2023, the Biden White House released a 12-page summary of a classified review of the Afghanistan exit that largely blamed the Trump administration for the deal it struck with the Taliban to withdraw U.S. forces from the country by May 2021.

The so-called Doha Agreement brokered by the first Trump administration laid out a series of conditions for the Taliban to fulfill in order for U.S. forces to leave. Another report partially declassified and released by the State Department in 2023 faulted both the Trump and Biden administrations for "insufficient" planning surrounding the withdrawal.
