World.title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
World.content:
At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Authorities in Florida on Monday were investigating a plane crash in Miami International Airport that killed at least five people a day earlier.

Five people were also injured in the crash, though it is not yet clear how many of the people killed or hurt were on board the plane or on the ground.

An Amazon Prime cargo plane was landing at the airport around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday when it overran the runway, crashed and rammed into vehicles on the ground, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Amazon says the plane was operated by 21 Air, a contract cargo carrier.

Sponsor Message

Rosie Cordero-Stutz, the Miami-Dade County sheriff, said that the plane came to rest in a field adjacent to the airport.

Photos from the scene showed the Prime Air plane, a Boeing 767, off the runway, in a parking lot, its wings charred.

In a statement to NPR, the FAA said that Flight 7598 originally took off from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA said it will investigate the crash.

The Miami-Dade Aviation Department said in a statement that the plane overran the diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport.

"What we found was a very complex situation here," Miami-Dade County Fire Chief Ray Jadallah told reporters on Sunday. Jadallah said the airplane struck a couple of vehicles, requiring extrication of trapped victims. He also said emergency teams were engaged in a search and rescue operation of the pilot and co-pilot.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said over 60 MDFR units had responded. Jadallah said there was a fuel leak from the aircraft, which they were working to mitigate.

On the ground on Monday also were National Transportation Safety Board investigators as they looked into all factors, from potential mechanical failure to environmental variables or flight crew performance.

Sponsor Message

Following the crash, the FAA on Sunday issued a ground stop on planes until 3 p.m. that was later extended until 5:30 p.m. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was ordered so that first responders could assess the scene and warned travelers of "significant delays and potential cancellations."

The closure caused delays, flight cancellations and long lines at the airport with passengers rebooking flights. Miami International Airport said on Monday morning that two of the four runways were back open, but cautioned that it was still dealing with the "impacts of this incident."

"This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel in a post on social media. "Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."

World.title: Germany's far-right achieves an electoral breakthrough in key state election
World.content:
Germany's far-right achieves an electoral breakthrough in key state election

toggle caption Matthias Schrader/AP

BERLIN — Germany's populist, far-right Alternative for Germany party has declared victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt after more than doubling its share of the vote in the first of several regional elections this fall.

Falling just shy of an absolute majority, it's not yet clear whether the AfD will be able to govern the state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the outcome is already causing a political earthquake.

According to preliminary final results, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote — its strongest performance in any German state election, which puts the far-right party within reach of power for the first time since the time of Nazi Germany.

Sponsor Message

The center-right Christian Democratic Union more than halved its share of the vote, falling to a historic low of 17.2%. The centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) received 9.3%, the Greens 8.9%, and the Left party 8.6%.

All of these parties refuse to form a coalition with the AfD. But the AfD can come to power with the help of BSW, a small, anti-immigration, left-wing populist party. BSW got 5.3% of the vote on Sunday, potentially giving it enough seats to form a parliamentary majority with the AfD — something the party has not ruled out.

AfD's candidate for state governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said the result "sends a very clear signal to Berlin: this is the end of the line; people don't want to go on like this."

"They want their good, old, secure Germany back," Siegmund told German public broadcaster, ARD.

Christian Democrat candidate Sven Schulze took to the stage on Sunday evening to congratulate the AfD on its win. While polls had shown the AfD with a comfortable lead for weeks, the CDU fared worse than predicted.

Whether Schulze will attempt to cobble together a "firewall" coalition — a platform by Germany's main political parties to keep the AfD out of government — is unclear. Such a strategy would require the Christian Democrats and others to work with the far-left party, Die Linke — something the conservatives refuse to do.

Sponsor Message

Addressing supporters, Schulze sounded resigned.

"Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say this is democracy," he said.

Alice Weidel, co-chair of AfD at the federal level, told public broadcaster ZDF that the CDU will never win another election. She said the AfD is seeing "explosive growth" across the country.

In Saxony-Anhalt, that growth is down to 35-year-old Siegmund, a former marketing executive and a salesman who, observers say, showed a knack for packaging his party's policies in positive slogans and pop-star-like appearances at campaign events and on TikTok.

His personable and amiable style is uncharacteristically upbeat for the AfD and he distinguishes himself from others in the party for being more happy-go-lucky than angry.

Germany's domestic intelligence classifies the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as extremist. Its regional platform is the party's most radical and is seen by the AfD as a blueprint for the rest of Germany.

If Siegmund ends up as state governor, he will be privy to foreign and domestic intelligence, which is a major concern for the other parties considering the AfD's push to revive relations with Russia. Several state interior ministers from Germany's other 15 states say they are already preparing to meet separately.

At the top of their platform agenda is what the AfD calls its "remigration" policy, which promises mass deportations. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD on Sunday night, Siegmund spelled out the policy in more detail.

"Remigration is far more than just deportation," he said, adding that "remigration applies to anyone who does not contribute to society." He included Ukrainian refugees without jobs.

The AfD also wants to segregate refugees and disabled children in schools and revamp the curriculum to focus on what it refers to as a "more positive" teaching of Germany's history.

After the results, Siegmund declared: "We have made history in this country."

Sponsor Message

"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," he told supporters, "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."

On Sunday evening, President Trump posted a screenshot of the projected election results on Truth Social . Trump's post was shared by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who described the result as a "historic win."

The AfD has called for an end to support for Ukraine and seeking to revoke the refugee protections currently granted to Ukrainians.

Also among those hailing AfD's success was Tesla CEO Elon Musk. In response, Siegmund thanked Musk for his "support" and "clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time."

But neighboring Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk took a very different view, posting on X that "in Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany."

World.title: American Muslims are giving Texas barbecue a halal makeover
World.content:
American Muslims are giving Texas barbecue a halal makeover

toggle caption Fiona André/Religion News Service

FORT WORTH, Texas (RNS) — At 9 a.m. on a scorching summer Saturday, nearly 100 people were already lined up outside Goldee's BBQ, a small, wooden-shack restaurant.

First in line was 30-year-old Thanh Huynh, who had been sitting in a lawn chair on the joint's rustic porch since 6:30 a.m.

"I have, like, a whole list, and I'm going to spend lots of money here. It'll be worth it," he said, laughing while rattling off a long order of meats and sides from his phone's Notes app as a sweet, smoky scent from nearby pits hung in the air.

Sponsor Message

Opened in 2020 by a group of his friends, the restaurant was named the No. 1 barbecue spot in the state by Texas Monthly a year later, and then won a Bib Gourmand award from the prestigious Michelin Guide, given for "great food at a great value."

The restaurant serves classic Texas barbecue like craft pork belly, sausage and ribs. But it also offers halal brisket, turkey and lamb — meat raised and butchered in accordance with Islamic guidelines.

toggle caption Fiona André/Religion News Services

At a time when Republican leaders are increasingly targeting the state's growing Muslim communities, barbecue joints like Goldee's that offer halal options are thriving in Texas. Across the state, Muslim pitmasters are gaining recognition for putting their own spin on one of Texas' most iconic culinary traditions.

At least a dozen barbecue spots now serve halal meats, including Yearby's Barbecue & Waterice, run by Black Muslim couple CJ and Sabrina Henley, soon-to-be in Plano, and Levant Mediterranean BBQ, a restaurant with locations in Houston and Frisco and whose all-beef menu includes a brisket shawarma sandwich.

"Now there are so many options, and for us to have highly rated barbecue, it's a blessing," said Haris Ghaffar, who drove an hour from Celina and stood in 90-degree weather for nearly two hours with a friend for the halal options at Goldee's.

Sponsor Message

Growing up in the 1990s, Ghaffar said a McDonald's Filet-O-Fish sandwich was one of the few halal meals he could eat while dining out. Back then, halal food was seen as serving a small community. Today, it's a multibillion-dollar industry that's part of the American culinary mainstream, said food writer Farhan Mustafa, who wrote about the rise of American halal barbecue for Bon Appétit magazine in 2025.

"Halal food is American food," said Mustafa. "It belongs on your plate. It belongs in the casual chat. It belongs in hip-hop tracks. It's the most American thing there is."

Mustafa said Muslims are part of a growing list of communities putting their stamp on Texas barbecue. "Whether they're first, second or third-generation Muslims or Muslim Americans or just Americans, they're bringing what they know and what excites them," he said.

Texas barbecue is typically defined by salt-and-pepper brisket and pork ribs, but this new crop of halal pitmasters is adding inventive twists, often based on their own family heritages.

Zain Shafi, a pitmaster and co-owner of Goldee's, previously ran Sabar Barbecue, a food truck that offered Pakistani-infused halal dishes, such as brisket with rub that included spices like bay leaf and coriander. He brought tandoori smoked turkey to Goldee's menu. And sourcing halal cuts, he said, was a natural choice because they are "the highest quality" meats.

toggle caption Ulaa Kuziez/Religion News Service

At Kafi BBQ in Irving, owner Salahodeen Abdul-Kafi brings halal Wagyu beef and Iraqi spices to classic Texas barbecue, challenging what he said is the "traditional old guard of Texas barbecue."

"My goal at Kafi BBQ is to make the best barbecue in Texas," Abdul-Kafi said. "I have not been shy about that at all, and making the best barbecue in Texas does not necessarily have to include pork."

A former Silicon Valley tech worker, he moved to Texas six years ago in search of a Muslim community. On weekends in his backyard, he smoked brisket for friends. By 2024, he bought a smoker and opened Kafi BBQ.

He said he spent months testing and perfecting recipes and finding local producers. Abdul-Kafi attributes his obsession with crafting a stand-out menu to the Islamic concept of "Ihsan" — a term meaning doing something with excellence for the sake of God.

Sponsor Message

On a Sunday afternoon this summer, the restaurant's red booths were packed with diners, drawn to menu items like the 13-spice Wagyu brisket, pomegranate-glazed beef belly burnt ends and Iraqi-inspired spicy beef sausage.

"That sausage, I'd probably put it at the top sausage I've ever had, and we eat barbecue a lot. This place is unique," said Jonathan Tate, a Fort Worth resident who came to Kafi BBQ with a friend after reading about it on a Facebook foodie group.

"I don't necessarily have to have it halal, but it's nice to know they took good care of the food, the meat," his friend Jon Sklar said, before going back in line to order oxtail.

Although political rhetoric against Muslims in Texas has become increasingly hostile — some GOP lawmakers even discussed a ban on halal food — pitmasters like Abdul-Kafi see the rise of halal barbecue as an effective counterargument.

"It's an example of exactly the opposite of what the Islamophobes talk about, right?" he said. "They say, 'Oh, Muslims don't integrate, they stay alone, they don't help society and all this stuff.' And it's like, I'm sitting here contributing to the most well-known cuisine of Texas."

toggle caption Ulaa Kuziez/Religion News Service

After finishing a big lunch with 10 relatives, Areeba Ali, a Dallas native of Indian heritage, said the restaurant's appeal cuts across communities, which she said is evidence that halal barbecue isn't a niche but resonates broadly with Texans. "If you look around in the restaurant, you see everybody in there — it's not just one demographic in there," Ali said.

For Mustafa, that success is ultimately a testament to the resilience of Muslim American communities.

"No matter how much they try to erase us, our food is here to stay," he said. "You will see the power of just good food and the fact that most people really seem to understand that this is just as American as anything else."



Sponsor Message

This story was produced through a collaboration between NPR and Religion News Service.

World.title: Stephen Fuhr was mocked for opposing purchase of F-35s. Now he's in charge of Canada's defence procurement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stephen Fuhr got his "Picasso" nickname back in his days as a fighter pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF).

He'd been ordered to produce detailed attack maps, but his abstract scribbles earned him a call sign inspired by the cubist master, according to former military officials.

Today, the 57-year-old holds a more serious title: Canada's secretary of state for defence procurement.

In this role, he leads the Defence Investment Agency, an organization created last year by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to speed up the procurement of tens of billions of dollars worth of military acquisitions.

It's been a quick rise for the former CF-18 pilot who, after retiring from the Armed Forces in 2009, drew mockery from members of the military community by vigorously opposing the purchase of American F-35 aircraft.

Multiple sources indicate that relations remain strained to this day between Fuhr and the RCAF, whether over fighter jets, radar planes or helicopter replacements.

Several sources told CBC News that Fuhr's RCAF career had its share of ups and downs, and that he's seen as an outsider by many prominent members of the fighter pilot community. Fuhr retired from the Armed Forces in 2009 with the rank of major. (Stephen Fuhr/Submitted)

In an interview with CBC News, Fuhr said he is always ready to fight for his convictions.

"I'm not afraid to stand out on the hill by myself," he said. "It's just a principled place to be. And sometimes it's lonely, but that's just the way it is."

CBC News spoke with a dozen people who have interacted closely with Fuhr over the years. Some requested confidentiality to avoid harming commercial relations with the government, or were not authorized to speak publicly.

Fuhr — who is from Edmonton but now lives in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley and is MP for Kelowna — first became interested in aviation when his grandfather took him to model airplane competitions. He never lost his taste for speed and flight.

In addition to his pickup truck, he enjoys getting behind the wheel of his sporty Porsche 911 or flying his own aircraft, a two-seater Van's RV-8 featuring a shark mouth on the nose.

Stephen Fuhr flies in his RV-8 plane. (Stephen Fuhr/Submitted)

Sitting in the cockpit in a hangar at the Kelowna airport, he tells CBC News this plane is his "happy place."

But he rarely gets time to fly over the nearby mountains. After travelling the world in recent months, his summer schedule was once again disrupted by wildfires in the area. Fuhr's house in West Kelowna was burned to the ground by a wildfire in 2023 and was only recently rebuilt.

Now, his political career is set to become even more demanding. Under the Liberal government's Bill C-31, he could soon inherit new powers as head of the Defence Investment Agency to award sole-sourced contracts in order to protect Canada's "economic security."

The measures proposed in Bill C-31 would create a "super minister" in charge of military procurement, said Justin Massie, a defence expert at Université du Québec à Montréal.

"He would have more power than Mélanie Joly at industry or [David] McGuinty at national defence, because he would combine many of the powers that were usually or historically delegated across several departments," Massie said.

Fuhr is in line to oversee a dramatic increase in Canada's defence budget, amid a promise to reshape the military relationship between Canada and the U.S.

He says he's aiming for a sweeping transformation of the military procurement system, either by producing more equipment in Canada or by finding new global partners.

"We are going to become less reliant and more resilient," he said.

"The good news is we have friends in every time zone. And everybody wants to work with Canada."

Fuhr gets an obvious political boost from being a former CF-18 pilot. Being a member of Canada's select "top gun" club is an enviable calling card.

Still, sources said Fuhr is seen as an outsider by many prominent members of Canada's fighter pilot community.

Fuhr receiving the chief of the air staff commendation. (Stephen Fuhr/Instagram)

During his four years in a CF-18 squadron at CFB Cold Lake in Alberta, from 1999 to 2003, he was known for standing up to his commanding officer and his career had its share of ups and downs, according to several sources.

Fuhr did not wish to comment on personal issues during the interview.

Some former pilots argue Fuhr lacks "operational credibility" within their community, having never been part of deployments in conflict zones.

He counters by pointing to a defining moment of his piloting career after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, in which airliners were turned into missiles. He said he had trained for war, but not the scenario in which he took to the skies to protect North American airspace as commercial planes were redirected to Canada.

"When you've got hundreds of civilian airliners full of people coming your way, and that is now a threat you have to work through, that's a different mind space," he said.

After leaving CFB Cold Lake, he worked in Winnipeg managing Canada's fighter fleet and then training pilots and instructors. He retired from the RCAF after 20 years with the rank of major.

Fuhr made more of a name for himself after returning to civilian life in the early 2010s.

WATCH | What Canada's fighter jet decision could mean for NORAD: What Canada’s fighter jet decision could mean for NORAD | Duration 5:13 As Canada weighs a choice between American F-35s and Swedish Gripens for its fighter jet fleet, CBC’s David Common goes to NORAD headquarters to ask top generals about the implications of operating a mixed generation fleet for North American airspace defence.

While many in the fighter pilot community were tireless supporters of the F-35, he became a fierce critic.

"It may be a great airplane, it's not the right plane for Canada," he said on CBC's Power & Politics in 2011.

Friends and former colleagues speak of his fixation against the Lockheed Martin aircraft, which had been chosen by the Stephen Harper government to replace the CF-18s.

F-35 proponents say the aircraft is superior to any other Western fighter jet due to its stealth capabilities and the extraordinary amount of data it can process.

Still, Fuhr objected to the purchase for Canada, citing the project's staggering costs, numerous delays and some of the technical difficulties faced by some air forces. His opinion was based on a thorough review of every major study on the aircraft, including various public reports from the U.S. and Canadian governments on the program's failures.

He knew by publicly attacking the F-35, he was taking on many of his former air force colleagues.

"From the fighter pilot community, the F-35 has basically been considered the be-all and end-all," said Mike Reyno, a military magazine publisher and friend of Fuhr.

"What Stephen has done, and this is all with publicly available documentation, is [point out] the F-35 has actually failed to meet almost every critical point along its development."

Stephen Fuhr first ran with the Liberals in 2015. (Stephen Fuhr/Submitted)

A former supporter of the Conservative Party of Canada, Fuhr ran as a Liberal Party candidate in the 2015 federal election alongside Justin Trudeau, drawn in part by the Liberal promise to cancel the F-35 purchase.

He won the Kelowna-Lake Country seat but lost it to the Conservatives in 2019. He then became a consultant for Boeing, among other roles, and continued to criticize the F-35, describing the aircraft as "unaffordable" in 2021.

Two years later the Trudeau government announced the purchase of 88 F-35s, signing a firm contract for 16 aircraft.

Fuhr returned to politics last year, this time alongside Carney, who responded to growing tensions with the U.S. by subjecting the F-35 purchase to a review.

There is no doubt Canada will integrate F-35s into its air force, but the real question is how many aircraft the government will ultimately buy, and whether it will decide to add Swedish Gripen fighters to its military arsenal.

WATCH | Canada quietly makes payments related to 14 more F-35 jets: Canada quietly makes payments related to 14 more F-35 jets | Duration 3:57 The federal government has started to make payments for key components for 14 additional U.S.-built F-35 fighter jets, sources have told CBC News. The Department of National Defence says it is reviewing future fighter jet purchases in the context of trade tensions with Washington.

Easygoing and approachable, Fuhr is a fixture at defence trade shows, announcements, business trips and media interviews.

He is a prime target for lobbyists and executives hoping for a share of the new defence investments.

"He talks to everyone," said a lobbyist whose clients find it easier to get meetings with Fuhr than the defence minister.

Numerous procurement files are moving ahead much faster than expected under his leadership, including Swedish GlobalEye radar planes, German-Norwegian submarines and the purchase of over 60,000 assault rifles from Colt Canada.

But Fuhr has ongoing tensions with the RCAF regarding the diversification of equipment supply sources.

"The Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Navy have welcomed the change," said Reyno. "I would say that the air force hasn't been as welcoming to that because the Royal Canadian Air Force basically wants to operate everything the Americans operate."

A Swedish Gripen fighter jet is fitted with air-to-air missiles as part of a training exercise during a NATO air policing mission in Iceland. (Murray Brewster/CBC)

Fuhr is not closing the door to new mixed fleets of aircraft or helicopters, while the RCAF has stated its objections to the purchase of Gripens.

"Many of our allies … run a mixed fleet with fighters," says Fuhr. "I don't necessarily subscribe to the fact that we can't do it. We certainly can and we've done it and our allies do it now. So it's a function of 'do we want to do this or not?'"

Despite disagreements on the matter, a former pilot says he wishes Fuhr the greatest success in his bid to modernize Canada's sclerotic military acquisition process.

"Stephen Fuhr has to succeed. Whether anyone likes him personally or not, it is crucial for Canada to procure the right equipment to do the right job in a timely manner," they said.

Fuhr is aware he carries the reputation of an unyielding politician who holds firm views on various procurement projects. He says he is always ready to change his mind — but only if he is given compelling evidence.

"That evidence better actually bring something to the table and be credible. And if it doesn't do those two things, then I don't see a reason anyone should change their position," he said.

Throughout the interview, Fuhr made an effort not to speak directly about the F-35, a particularly sensitive topic given the trade and diplomatic tensions with the U.S.

Still, he smiled as he was asked about recent comments by U.S. Gen. Gregory Guillot, the commander of NORAD, who said F-35s weren't necessarily the best aircraft to protect the Canadian and American borders.

"He is the commander of NORAD. So I think what he says, I take him at his word," Fuhr said, breaking into a laugh.

World.title: Far-right AfD wins German state election but falls short of majority
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alternative for Germany is projected to win the Saxony-Anhalt state election, marking a major breakthrough for the far-right party and a major defeat for the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

AfD win seen as big victory for far right politics in Germany

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged to a resounding victory in a regional election on Sunday but fell a little short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country's first far-right state government since the Second World War.

The party of Germany's unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The anti-immigration and Russia-friendly AfD's candidate for governor said, "We have written history" and that the party has a clear mandate to govern.

Ulrich Siegmund, 35, told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this." He said that "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz."

Alternative for Germany was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with AfD.

WATCH | How the AfD rose to prominence in Saxony-Anhalt: Why people are voting for Germany’s far-right AfD party | Duration 7:09 For the first time since the Nazi era, a far-right German political party is eyeing victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. For The National, CBC’s Marina von Stackelberg goes there to find out how Alternative for Germany (AfD) went from fringe to frontrunner.

Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund said it wouldn't engage in "games" such as a minority government. But it wasn't evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it.

Blow to Chancellor Merz

A first state government would be the biggest prize in the anti-migration party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with a national government that has yet to persuade voters that it can get the country's sluggish economy moving.

Whether or not AfD ends up governing, the result is a blow to Merz, whose centre-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.

Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn't yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.

Sven Schulze, the premier of Saxony-Anhalt and member of the German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) reacts to initial results in Saxony-Anhalt state elections on Sunday. (Jens Schlueter/Getty Images/Getty Images)

The AfD is already Germany's most popular party at the national level and is seeking to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.

A poll from the ARD broadcaster showed 87 per cent of the state's voters were unhappy with the federal government. Siegmund has described Merz as the AfD's best campaigner, given his unpopularity in the state.

"This election result is, above all, a vote of no ⁠confidence in the federal government," Marcel Fratzscher, the president of the German Institute for Economic Research, told Reuters.

Merz, who leads the centre-right Christian Democratic Union, has vowed to revive Europe's largest economy with business-friendly reforms and increased spending while warning that an AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt would damage the state and deter foreign companies from investing there.

Officials prepare absentee ballots for the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sunday. (Liesa Johannssen/Reuters)

Germany's mainstream parties have all refused to work with the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of Germany's domestic intelligence service.

One outlier is the small Sahra ‌Wagenknecht Alliance party (BSW), which looked set to clear the threshold to enter parliament. The BSW has floated the idea of rule for Saxony-Anhalt by a non-partisan state premier relying on shifting majorities, including with votes from the AfD.

Siegmund, however, rejected the BSW's idea as a "mess" and ruled out any arrangements with other parties that would prevent the AfD from delivering on his promise of change. "If push comes to shove, there will simply be new elections," he said.

Merz's conservatives said they would explore talks with other parties, although that could require pulling together parties with vastly different policy agendas. In the neighbouring ​eastern German state of Thuringia, the conservatives run a minority government with passive tolerance from the Left party.

Although Saxony-Anhalt, formerly part of communist-run East Germany, is one of the smaller German states with a population of just over two million, the result underlines the rapid advance of the AfD since it was created ⁠in 2013.

The AfD is now Germany's most popular party nationally, polling at 28 per cent, according to a recent INSA poll — putting it comfortably ahead of the conservatives with 20 per cent.

Hard line on immigration

While hard-right parties have gained ground elsewhere in Europe, ⁠Germany's Nazi past has contributed to a reluctance among mainstream parties to co-operate with the AfD.

The AfD has dismissed accusations of extremism as scaremongering and an insult to the party's millions of supporters.

During the campaign, ⁠the AfD tapped ⁠into growing disillusionment with established parties, which it characterizes as tired and out of touch, ​offering instead a range of hardline policies and a nostalgic vision of a return to cleaner and safer streets and taking pride in being German.

"It is clear that we need change in Germany and in western Europe. And ​I believe a starting signal is definitely going out from here — whether ⁠you like it or not," said Antony Lee, an attendee at the AfD's election party. "I am a father, I am an entrepreneur, and I know that things cannot continue like this in Germany."

The AfD's program includes plans to push schools and cultural institutions toward what it views as more traditional values, while curbing immigration and overhauling public broadcasting. It wants the children of refugees to be taught in segregated classes.

It has called for rainbow flags in schools to be banned and for the German national flag to be hoisted every day. The national anthem would be sung by students and staff at school celebrations. Other proposals include citizen patrols, more teaching of Russian in schools and a halt to building new wind farms.

World.title: It's back to school season. Here's why there's a push to get rid of cars at dropoff and pickup
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Lily Dejnicki prepares to get back to the classroom, she hopes to see fewer cars during the morning and afternoon rush hours outside her school.

The 13-year-old would like to see the return of a pilot project to get cars out of the regular dropoff zone at her school, Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary in Mississauga, Ont.

As part of the School Streets project promoted by a non-profit environmental association, volunteers directed cars away during dropoff and pickup times by using barricades and signs. Kids and parents were encouraged to cycle and walk to and from school, as opposed to driving.

"It was lots of fun," said Lily, who is going into Grade 8.

"Kids … wouldn't rush home," she said. "Instead, they would … take a couple minutes to play and stuff outside."

Anita Dejnicki, Lily’s mom, sits on the school’s parental advisory council and said more parents were talking to each other and more kids were active and playing compared to before.

"Once it ended, it just seemed like it was quiet again."

Lily Dejnicki, 13, is about to start Grade 8 at Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary in Mississauga, Ont. She says she hopes the School Street at her school will return. (Anita Dejnicki)

As the school year starts, environmental association Green Communities Canada is continuing its efforts to implement School Streets across the country .

The pilot at Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary, which ran for a month, is part of a bigger push led by the organization called the National Active School Streets Initiative. It received $3 million in funding from the Public Health Agency of Canada in 2024.

At least 20 School Streets are planned for the 2026-2027 academic year. Over the past few years, they have been piloted in six provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia.

Nicole Roach, sustainable mobility director at Green Communities Canada, said School Streets usually take the form of a temporary barrier installed on both ends of one street next to a school.

The street is typically one that is not on a major thoroughfare or one that is going to cause issues for buses or students with disabilities, she said.

For those who need to drive, one al ternative is to drive to a nearby parking area and walk together the rest of the way, Roach said.

Volunteers help enforce a School Street project at Corliss Public School in Mississauga, Ont., in 2025. (8 80 Cities/City of Mississauga)

Roach points to safety and air pollution from cars as among the reasons to implement School Streets.

"Many schools at pickup and dropoff are just absolute chaos," she said. "We see a lot of dangerous driving behaviour, really unsafe environments for the children walking or wheeling or even just getting to their vehicle for pickup."

Lily, who walks to and from school, said the usual lines of cars at dropoff and pickup can be bothersome.

"It would kind of be not … too safe because it would be really, really crowded," she said.

"Most of my friends … liked [the School Street]. But some people didn't really like it. They would … say that there's no point in doing it."

A bumpy road

Although it's estimated that at least 36 schools across Canada have tested School Streets, implementing them long-term has proven challenging.

Just two permanent, year-round School Streets exist, and at least one pilot ground to a halt after pushback.

Last year, a School Street project a t Corliss Public School in Mississauga was cancelled after a parent started a petition, raising concerns about safety and disruption.

"Every day, children and parents are forced to navigate confusing road closures and restricted areas, which not only causes delays but also increases the risk of accidents," the petition, which collected nearly 200 signatures, said.

A year-long School Street runs at Lord Selkirk Public School in Vancouver. Most School Street projects across Canada have been temporary pilot programs. (City of Vancouver)

"The setup leads to congestion in nearby areas, forcing parents to opt for potentially unsafe detours or parking in locations that are less supervised."

Kerstyn Lutz, who studied four School Street pilots in the Greater Toronto Area in 2022, recalls witnessing disruption first-hand.

"At least at the beginning, [it] felt like chaos. You have cars driving up to these barriers, they don't know what to do," said Lutz , a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto at the time of her research. "We have to have vehicle diversion plans…. The reality is not everyone is going to walk."

What do the experts say?

But Raktim Mitra, an urban planning professor at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies sustainable transportation behaviour, said there’s no evidence to suggest School Streets push congestion onto nearby roads or lead to more unsafe driving.

Over the past year, Mitra collected data on travel patterns close to two School Streets pilots in Mississauga.

More cars drove below the designated speed on the street, and a "significantly" higher number of cars were yielding to pedestrians in nearby streets, he said.

As for clogging up nearby streets, Mitra said none of the data suggests that to be a likely problem.

A School Street project ran for a week at Gilmore Community School in Burnaby, B.C., in April. Only two permanent School Streets exist in Canada. (Xuedan Xu/Green Communities Canada)

"None of the nearby roads … reached a congested condition."

While children who travel to school by themselves may encounter more people, there's no evidence that more walking as a result of such an initiative would lead to more potentially problematic interactions with strangers, said Lewis Smith, spokesperson for the Canada Safety Council.

"We believe that the bigger concern is teaching children to recognize unsafe situations, to recognize unsafe behaviors and be able to respond to them accordingly."

As for benefits, Mitra and Lutz noted more kids cycled or walked to school.

The absence of cars outside the school also led to a reduction in air pollution in the immediate area, Lutz said.

Canada's 'culture of mobility'

School Streets began in Italy in the 1990s and has spread to other countries.

Mitra said Canada's "culture of mobility" is a factor that can make School Streets face opposition, particularly in suburbs where car travel is the dominant mode of transportation.

He said many parents are used to driving and that "asking them to change that culture … is always difficult."

WATCH | Bogotá goes car-free for a day to combat air pollution: Bogota goes car-free for a day to combat recent air pollution | Duration 1:00 The streets in Bogota, Colombia, were clear of traffic and instead filled with pedestrians and cyclists on Thursday, as only vehicles related to public transportation were permitted on the roads. The restrictions were only in effect for one day as a means to combat traffic and air pollution after the city was recently blanketed in smoke from nearby wildfires.

Resources to enforce School Streets programs have posed another challenge.

In 2023, a year-round program at Lord Roberts Elementary School in Vancouver ended because there weren’t enough volunteers to supervise the School Street.

The volunteer burden is the reason why many School Streets only run as short pilots, said Lucy Maloney, a Vancouver city councillor who was president of the parental advisory committee at Lord Roberts at the time.

"Trying to run a School Street all year round where parents are required to set it up and dismantle it and supervise it is just too much for people to manage."

Maloney, who plans to push for more School Streets as a councillor, said there are measures that could reduce reliance on volunteers such as retractable bollards or camera enforcement.

Lutz is skeptical whether School Streets with permanent, physical infrastructure would work for Canada’s suburban streets.

"Is it going to work the same way it works in a country like Italy? Probably not, because they're already better built for walkability than we are."

A street outside Condorcet Elementary School in Lyon, France, is permanently reserved for pedestrians. Some experts doubt whether permanent School Streets are feasible in Canada, particularly in suburban areas. (Antoine Boureau/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

For urban areas, Mitra sees School Streets as a possibility.

"About half of our children who attend elementary school … live within half a mile [0.8 kilometres] from their schools, which technically is a 10- to 12-minute walking distance," he said.

While he doesn’t foresee every child walking to school, he said the program can help those who live close by convert short car and bus trips.

"I think that would have significant impact in reducing localized congestion and improving the health and well-being and safety of children."

Lily, for one, sees many positives.

"When I come to school … I'm actually looking forward to doing something … rather than just, like, going straight home."

World.title: Concerns over flood-compromised roads remain in Cape Breton after torrential rain batters island
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A state of emergency remained in place across much of Cape Breton on Sunday after northeastern Nova Scotia was battered by wind and a heavy rain storm.

But there was some hope that state of emergency could be lifted in the island's central and northern areas on Sunday night.

Warden Lois Landry said Richmond County on the island's southeast corner bore the brunt of the weekend storm.

"We're a community that has experienced hurricanes regularly over our history," she said Sunday afternoon.

"I think [it's] safe to say we would get at least one a year. This one seems to have hit differently.

"We saw trees down across roads on people's property. That's really Category 1 hurricane-level damage and that just wasn't in the forecast."

The St. Georges Channel bridge on West Bay Road, Richmond County, washed away early Saturday morning, leaving some people stranded on the other side. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

The storm brought strong winds and rainfall totals upwards of 200 millimetres in several communities, but it was not forecast to be nor was it declared a hurricane.

However, it wreaked havoc on roads and bridges Friday night and Saturday across the island, including the heavily populated Cape Breton Regional Municipality.

CBRM escaped the worst of the storm though, with some streets and roads closed due to rising water being reopened later in the day Saturday.

Richmond, Inverness and Victoria counties declared a state of emergency Saturday, along with the Town of Port Hawkesbury.

Richmond County Warden Lois Landry says the first priority is to get emergency access for people stranded on West Bay Road and in River Bourgeois, where washouts have cut roads. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Trees were knocked down, there were widespread power outages and streams and ditches overflowed just about everywhere, but in some cases little damage was left behind.

Two communities in different parts of Richmond County, River Bourgeois and St. Georges Channel on West Bay Road, remained cut off by wash-outs Sunday.

Landry said that's a priority concern for emergency access, but there are also questions about the infrastructure underneath roads and bridges that got submerged and appear to be OK.

"We have had road washouts before. We have had power outages before that have not required a state of emergency," she said.

"What gave us pause and what directed our action in this instance was really not having a confident sense that the roads we were driving on, the bridges we were driving over, were safe."

Municipality 'staggered' by storm

The storm also seems to have produced one fatality, although RCMP would not confirm the cause of death.

Landry said the province and the municipality are still assessing the storm damage.

"We're staggered by the extent of the damage and the likelihood of what all that's going to cost," she said.

"All of that pales in comparison to waking up and getting confirmation of a death of a resident as a result of this weather event."

Residents are rallying around each other to help out, Landry said, including those who volunteered to stay up overnight to warn motorists about compromised roads in areas where there wasn't time or resources to put up barricades.

Inverness County Warden Bonny MacIsaac says electricity had mostly returned by Sunday afternoon and the damage was being tallied, but integrity of the roads is the main concern. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

In Inverness County, on the west side of the island, water spilled over roads, some trees were down and there were scattered power outages, said Warden Bonny MacIsaac.

However, she said, the electricity had mostly returned by Sunday afternoon and the damage was being tallied.

"The integrity of a lot of roads [is] certainly a main concern right now," MacIsaac said.

Provincial road crews busy

In an email Sunday, Public Works spokesperson Gary Andrea said highway crews have been busy.

"At one point, we had more than 120 roads closed or damaged by flooding," he said.

"Currently, 54 roads are closed. The rest have either fully or partially reopened. Eight bridges were also damaged and two will need to be replaced."

WATCH | Torrential rain in N.S. brings widespread damage: Unexpected rainfall clobbers Cape Breton | Duration 2:29 What locals expected to be a typical rain event turned into an emergency in Cape Breton after roughly 200 millimetres of rain fell, accompanied by powerful wind and thunderstorms. The storm brought flooding and washed out roads, and it stranded many people.

In Victoria County, which runs from the middle of Cape Breton to its northern tip, Warden Jackie Organ said residents were very lucky.

She said damage was minimal and the state of emergency might end Sunday.

"I am waiting to hear back from public works and our [emergency management] office and ... it will be probably lifted sometime this evening," Organ said.

Port Hawkesbury expects significant bill

Roads throughout much of the three rural counties are provincially owned, but most of Port Hawkesbury's streets are the town's responsibility.

Mayor Brenda Chisholm-Beaton said it will likely be days before the full impact of the storm is known in Port Hawkesbury, but the cost is likely to be significant.

A large tree fell and damaged Prince Street and the asphalt will need to be repaired near the corner of Old Sydney Road and Bernard Street.

The town is built on a hill leading down to the Strait of Canso, so low-lying areas got submerged by runoff from the rain, Chisholm-Beaton said.

World.title: Trailblazing Indigenous actor and director Georgina Lightning dead at 63
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

First Nations filmmaker and actor Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63.

Her daughter, Crystle Lightning, announced the news online late Saturday night, just before 11 p.m., though no details about the cause of death were shared.

Social media posts link her death to the Enoch Indian Relay World Championship at the Enoch Park Race Track, an event Lightning posted about on her Facebook page just one day before her death was made public.

Enoch Cree Nation announced in a statement on Saturday that it “is mourning the loss of a community member following an incident that occurred during [Saturday’s] Indian Relay event.” The nation did not confirm the identity of the person who died.

It was always about taking space and bringing others with her. - Jodi Calahoo Stonehouse

RCMP told CBC News on Sunday that officers were called to the Enoch Park Race Track shortly after 6:30 p.m. Saturday, where a woman had died before police arrived.

Police said the woman who was killed was standing in the media area, but would also not confirm her identity.

RCMP said that Occupational Health and Safety will take over the investigation.

Michelle Thrush worked with Lightning on the TV series Blackstone. While she wasn't there when Lightning died, she said she received a call in real time from a mutual friend who was there, and was looking for Lightning's son Cody.

"It was just so incredibly tragic and shocking that it was just unbelievable," said Thrush in an interview with CBC News.

Thrush said she called Lightning's daughter Crystle while the family was waiting for news. Thrush said the loss of Lightning has been a huge hit to their community.

Thrush said she was told that Lightning was filming a documentary about the relay sport, and that it was a project she was passionate about.

"As Indigenous artists, we all know each other," said Thrush. "We're like family."

WATCH | Video from 2020 shows Trickster, a television production starring Lightning: What is Trickster? | Duration 3:09 Epic. Crazy. Fun. The cast gives us a taste of what to expect from Trickster. Premieres October 7 at 9/9:30 NT on CBC and CBC Gem.

Close friend Jodi Calahoo Stonehouse said that the impact Lightning had on the community was unimaginable.

Despite her many accomplishments, awards, and recognition, Lightning always brought her work back to the community, and advocating to mentor young students in the industry, Calahoo Stonehouse said.

"You know what's special about Georgina? It wasn't about the awards for her," said Calahoo Stonehouse, who is also an NDP MLA in Edmonton.

"It was always about taking space and bringing others with her."

WATCH | Georgina Lightning appeared in Blackstone and Trickster: Georgina Lightning — trailblazing Indigenous actor, filmmaker — dead at 63 | Duration 2:02 Indigenous director, producer and actor Georgina Lighting, known for roles in Trickster and Blackstone, died at a race in Enoch Cree Nation, just outside of Edmonton. She was 63.

According to Calahoo Stonehouse, Lightning loved horses, and echoed Thrush in saying she was working on a documentary about the history and tradition of the Indian Relay.

Calahoo Stonehouse said Lightning was in her last phase of shooting the film on Saturday when she passed.

"She wanted to produce a film about the horse spirit and the medicine of the horse that it brings to the people," said Calahoo Stonehouse.

She said Lightning's children made the decision on Saturday night that they wanted to see her documentary completed. Calahoo Stonehouse will be the one to see the documentary's completion.

Calahoo Stonehouse, seen here in Lethbridge, Alta., in 2024, said her friend Georgina Lightning was a special person who will be so missed. (Ose Irete/CBC)

"The legacy of her stories need to be finished," said Calahoo Stonehouse.

"And I have the honor to be here today, to step in her shoes. And they're mighty big shoes. Mighty big moccasins."

Born in Edmonton, Lightning was a member of the Samson Cree Nation, located about 100 kilometres south of the city.

In addition to her impact in the film industry, she was widely known as an outspoken advocate for First Nations causes.

"She was a beautiful human being," said Calahoo Stonehouse. "She didn't just share our stories, she shared our hopes, our fears, our sadness, our pain. And she also shared love. And you know, she's going to be missed."

World.title: Manitoba family searches for answers nearly 2 years after daughter died following dental procedure
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The parents of a 23-year-old woman who died after she went to have her wisdom teeth removed at a southern Manitoba dental clinic say they've been left "shattered" and searching for answers nearly two years after their daughter's death.

Virginia Blatz was pronounced dead in hospital on Nov. 27, 2024, after going to the Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden, Man., to have her wisdom teeth removed that morning.

An autopsy found Virginia's death was caused by local anesthetic systemic toxicity — when levels of the pain-blocking medication become too high in a person's blood — "resulting from an inadvertent intravascular injection of local anesthetic," according to the family's lawyer Troy Harwood-Jones.

CBC News has not independently viewed the autopsy report.

Virginia's mother Victoria Blatz said her daughter was keen to get her wisdom teeth removed because she had been suffering with a sore mouth in the days leading up to the procedure.

Victoria dropped Virginia off at the dental clinic on the morning of Nov. 27, 2024, and planned to pick her up as soon as the appointment was over.

The clinic called Victoria a short time later, saying her daughter was having a seizure.

Virginia Blatz's family says the 23-year-old had been excited to start a new job as a welder just a few days after she went to the dentist. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

Victoria said the clinic was frenzied when she returned. It was as if she "walked into a nightmare" when she saw her daughter there, she said.

"It's obviously the worst thing I've ever seen. It's the worst experience I've ever had. It was terrible," Victoria said.

As the two-year anniversary of Virginia's death creeps closer, her father Dulaney Blatz says the family is still searching for answers about what happened in the dentist's chair.

"Maybe we will never know the truth," he said.

The Manitoba Dental Association began investigating the incident , which happened when Virginia was under the care of Dr. Ronald Janz, shortly after it occurred.

Janz is still listed as a general dentist on the Boundary Trails Dental Centre's website . According to the dental association's registry , he is currently restricted in his ability to administer local anesthetic drugs.

Dulaney said the family didn't hear from the dental association until several months after Virginia's death. And they're still unsure what's happening with the investigation after many more months have passed, he said.

Victoria said the lack of answers has been "massively frustrating" for the family.

"We were a shattered family for quite some time after Virginia's death. We just really could not function properly. And we had so many questions and we were so unsure and we were really, really struggling," she said.

"We've just come to the point where we're so tired of being patient."

WATCH | Southern Manitoba woman dies after dental procedure: Southern Manitoba woman, 23, dies following dental procedure | Duration 1:30 A 23-year-old woman from southern Manitoba died following a dental appointment, the Manitoba Dental Association disclosed Monday. The woman, who lives in the Morden-Winkler area, was undergoing a procedure in a dentist's office on Nov. 27 when a medical emergency took place, said Dr. Daron Baxter, president of the dental association.

The family filed a separate formal complaint about Janz in June.

The dental association's lawyers said in a Sept. 1 letter sent to the Blatzs' legal counsel that information about the initial investigation wasn't being shared with Virginia's loved ones because the MDA's registrar is the official complainant under rules set out in the Dental Association Act — not the family.

That letter was in response to an Aug. 21 letter sent by the family's lawyers asking for updates on the initial investigation and the status of the Blatz family's new complaint. CBC News has viewed both letters.

In a statement to CBC News on behalf of the Manitoba Dental Association, Rodrigo Sanches Cunha, the association's president, acknowledged the family's frustration, and said that while they understand why Virginia's family wants answers, they have "a legal and regulatory responsibility to conduct a thorough and fair process."

"As you can appreciate, details of the investigation cannot be shared because this matter has not reached its final adjudicative conclusion," the statement said.

"We recognize that the length of this process, together with confidentiality requirements that limit what we can share, has compounded an already unbearable situation for Virginia's family."

"We will contact them directly this week to explain where the process stands, what happens next, and what information we can appropriately share without compromising the integrity of the proceeding."

CBC News has also reached out to the Boundary Trails Dental Centre.

Dulaney said Virginia — the youngest of their five children — was set to start a new job as a welder just a few days after her final dental appointment.

Her father said she was hard-working and kind, with dreams to settle down on a little farm like the one her parents run near Lowe Farm, about 70 kilometres south of Winnipeg.

"We lost a wonderful daughter who was kind and caring to everybody," he said, adding she loved people and animals dearly.

Victoria said Virginia was a "bright light" who had a happy future ahead of her.

The family wants justice for their daughter.

"We've suffered a monstrous loss and the community has suffered a monstrous loss and our family will never be the same again. It's shattered us all completely," Victoria said.

"We want answers and accountability and assurances that this is not going to happen to other families."

World.title: At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off Miami runway and smashes into cars: authorities
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Amazon Prime Air cargo flight overran a runway and struck multiple vehicles on the ground while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others. Keith Mackey, an aviation safety consultant and former captain, breaks down how the investigation will likely proceed.

An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. ET after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.

Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to determine whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.

The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said another person was trapped under a vehicle.

It also halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.

More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the crash, arriving to find the aircraft on fire as crews worked to extinguish the flames and assess patients.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, according to images from the scene. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

250 flights delayed Sunday

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

WATCH | The cargo plane skidded off the runway, striking vehicles: 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane leaves runway, smashes into cars | Duration 2:21 An Amazon cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, slamming into cars, killing five people and injuring several others. An investigation into what caused the crash is underway.

About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it is sending a team to Miami led by Chair Jennifer Homendy to investigate.

Amazon said in a statement that it would co-operate with any investigation.

"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."

Amazon said in an email to CBC News that it was also gathering details and "working closely with local authorities and officials" to understand what happened.

Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport's fences, Lee said.

"We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I'd got used to it," Lee said. "I never thought it could come this close to us."

World.title: Ben Woodfinden: ‘Blame Canada’ conservatives are no better than woke statue topplers
World.content:
Article content

None of this is an argument for uncritical patriotism. You can think this country has serious problems, that the last decade has been a lost one for younger Canadians, that Ottawa is dysfunctional, and that Carney’s government has mismanaged the relationship with Washington, and still want the place fixed precisely because you love your country and not the opposite. Criticism of the government of the day or present state of affairs is not oikophobia, and the danger in times like the moment we are living in right now where passions are high is to create a binary where unless you are blindly uncritical of the government you are disloyal. This is wrong, but conservatives must guard against the impulse to go further and sink into a national form of self-loathing that leads you to siding with a foreign president insulting and demeaning our country.
