World.title: Perfect Day Mexico wasn’t dead after all. Now its opponents are headed to the Supreme Court
World.content:
Perhaps someone should have driven a stake through its heart.

Royal Caribbean’s Perfect Day Mexico was widely believed dead in May, when Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena announced that the massive water park planned for Mahahual, Quintana Roo, would not be approved.

But the massive, US $1 billion extreme water park proposal wasn’t buried after all. Royal Caribbean withdrew its environmental application before authorities could formally reject it, leaving the cruise giant free to return with a revised proposal.

Now the residents’ battle has reached Mexico’s Supreme Court, which on Aug. 10 agreed to hear three challenges to fast-tracked land-use changes that helped make Perfect Day possible.

The stakes reach well beyond the fate of a water park. The fight involves development alongside the Mesoamerican Reef, the world’s second-largest barrier reef system; a national campaign that drew more than 5 million petition signatures; and now a potentially precedent-setting question: How much opportunity must Mexican citizens be given to challenge development decisions that could permanently alter the places where they live?

A reef transformed

When Luis Fernando Amezcua first began diving off Mahahual nearly three decades ago, he remembers a very different Caribbean: water about 5 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit cooler, with coral reefs alive with color and an extraordinary variety of marine life.

The reef is still remarkable. A first-time visitor could easily be dazzled by its diversity. But to Amezcua, the losses are impossible to miss.

If he could take a visitor anywhere in Mahahual, he said, he would dive with them directly in front of town. Then he would show them photographs of that same reef 20 years ago, and let the contrast speak for itself.

Mahahual’s problems don’t stop at the shoreline. Amezcua says the wastewater system is already overwhelmed in a town of roughly 3,000 residents, where a single cruise ship can arrive with 6,000 passengers — and as many as four ships may call in a day.

And on the Yucatán Peninsula’s porous limestone, what happens on land doesn’t necessarily stay there. Contaminated water can quickly move through the underground aquifer toward the sea, adding another source of stress to an already vulnerable reef.

For Amezcua, who has lived in Mahahual for about 17 years and belongs to the citizens’ collective Salvemos Mahahual, the issue isn’t whether the town should develop. It’s what kind of development — and how much the ecosystem can withstand.

From four stories to 20

Accommodating the company required changing the rules.

In December 2025, the municipality of Othón P. Blanco approved changes to the urban development plan covering 107.67 hectares — roughly 200 football fields — in less than three weeks, a process attorney Irma Morales says normally takes eight months to a year.

Among the changes: The maximum permitted height on part of the property jumped from roughly four stories to about 20 — just what Royal Caribbean needed for the record-breaking water park it was proposing. The company had touted Jaguar’s Peak, at more than 170 feet tall, as the tallest waterslide tower in North and South America.

Morales, an attorney with Defendiendo el Derecho a un Medio Ambiente Sano (DMAS), said the changes were approved without the studies and public participation required by law.

Residents challenged them in federal court.

Their cases never got as far as the environmental questions. They were dismissed because judges found that residents had filed them too late — in one case applying a 15-day deadline for citizens to respond.

But Morales said the residents hadn’t even known the land-use plan had been changed while that clock was running.

Environmental justice and the rights of communities

That dispute has now landed Mahahual before the Supreme Court. At stake is a broader question of environmental justice: How meaningful is the right to challenge decisions capable of transforming a community and its environment if residents have only weeks to discover those decisions, understand their implications and get into court?

The justices are not deciding whether Royal Caribbean can build Perfect Day. But their ruling could establish new ground rules for when and how communities across Mexico can challenge land-use decisions with potentially irreversible environmental consequences.

That could affect communities fighting tourism, real estate and industrial projects far beyond Mahahual.

How a local fight went national

Long before the federal government intervened, Mahahual’s fight had become a national cause. Local residents had been organizing for months when Greenpeace Mexico and other national organizations joined.

The response surprised even veteran campaigners. A Greenpeace petition opposing Perfect Day ultimately drew 846,646 signatures. High-profile Mexican content creators, including film critic Javier Ibarreche and travel creator Alan Estrada, spoke out against the project, while Mexican BTS and Taylor Swift fan networks mobilized their formidable social media reach behind the cause.

For Ornela Garelli, campaigns director for Greenpeace Mexico, Mahahual tapped into a wider backlash against tourism, real estate and industrial megaprojects that communities say threaten ecosystems while giving residents too little voice over what happens to their territory.

Perfect Day became a particularly potent symbol: an enormous artificial attraction proposed beside one of the planet’s great natural ones.

The project anticipated as many as 21,000 visitors a day — seven times Mahahual’s resident population — while a Greenpeace analysis warned of impacts to vegetation, groundwater and biodiversity.

The campaign appeared to work.

The victory that wasn’t

In May, Bárcena announced that Perfect Day would not be approved. Semarnat requested additional information from Royal Caribbean, later saying the company failed to show how significant environmental impacts would be avoided.

On May 19, before Semarnat issued a final ruling on the main Perfect Day application, Royal Caribbean withdrew it. Morales says developers sometimes withdraw applications facing likely rejection to avoid a formal denial, allowing them to return later with another proposal.

Amezcua and his fellow activists understood immediately what that meant.

Asked whether Salvemos Mahahual believed in May that the fight was finally over, his answer was emphatic: “Not for a moment.”

Royal Caribbean, meanwhile, has made clear it is not walking away from Mahahual. On a July 28 earnings call, CEO Jason Liberty told investors the company was continuing to work “to develop a tourism destination” there, saying negotiations with government and community stakeholders would “affect our previously planned timeline.”

That is precisely what worries Amezcua: that attention will fade before Perfect Day returns in another form.

After nearly three decades watching Mahahual’s reef change, his message is simple: “Everything we do has consequences for the ecosystem we inhabit.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: What would a move from CONCACAF to CONMEBOL mean for Mexican soccer?
World.content:
Following arguably Mexico’s best World Cup finish since 1986, rumors have circulated online about El Tri potentially moving from its throne in CONCACAF to the much tougher South American confederation known as CONMEBOL. With FIFA’s presidential election coming up on March 18, 2027, rumors have swirled around current FIFA president Gianni Infantino granting the Mexican Football Federation’s ambition to switch over to CONMEBOL and host Club World Cup tournaments in exchange for its vote.

Historically, Mexico has dominated in CONCACAF, with its biggest rival being the United States in World Cup qualifiers, Gold Cup matchups and even friendlies. The occasional scare from countries like Costa Rica, Honduras and most recently, Canada, has threatened Mexico’s throne at the top. But it never fell lower than the third-best team in the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football.

The reality of a move to CONMEBOL

That narrative changes if Mexico switches over to CONMEBOL, where it would have to win or tie enough games against nations like Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay to even think about qualifying for future World Cups.

It’s also worth noting that Liga MX teams would be eligible to play in the Copa Libertadores, which is the South American version of Europe’s Champions League, creating opportunities for Mexican pro teams to compete against the best of Latin America every season.

Even though it may be a daunting task for some fans, Mexico’s stellar performance in the 2026 World Cup gives lifelong fans like myself hope. El Tri won all of its group-stage games for the first time without conceding a single goal. Then, it won a knockout-phase game for the first time in 40 years. Then, it took eventual third-place finisher England down to the wire in a 3-2 loss at the historic Estadio Azteca in the round of 16.

A great mix of emerging talent like Julián Quiñones and young players like Gilberto Mora gives fans reason to be excited for the future if Mexico actually switches over to CONMEBOL.

New and greater challenges

There’s an old saying in sports: If you want to be the best, you need to beat the best. And if Mexico ever hopes to build off its momentum from the last World Cup, playing against quality footballing nations will benefit the squad.

Brazil has won the World Cup five times and has plenty of top players in Europe, including Vinicius Junior, Raphinha and Alisson Becker. Argentina has Lionel Messi and back-to-back World Cup finishes where it either won or finished runner-up. Colombia and Uruguay are also teams not to be taken lightly. But the good news is this will force players like Brian Gutierrez, Gilberto Mora, Mateo Chavez and Raul “Tala” Rangel to level up their games. All of them had their moments in the last World Cup, and that momentum needs to continue.

Being part of CONMEBOL also means playing in the Copa America, a tournament that will be Mexico’s next big test, whether it makes the switch or is simply invited to compete in 2028. A solid finish would strengthen Mexico’s position as an improving footballing nation capable of making deep runs among the elite.

Revival of old-school rivalries

Despite Brazil’s accolades on the global stage, Mexico has proven to be a worthy opponent over the years. In the 1999 Confederations Cup final, Mexico prevailed over Brazil 4-3 in front of 110,000 fans in Estadio Azteca. Mexico also upset Brazil in the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, beating a prime Brazilian squad 2-1 that included players like Neymar, Thiago Silva and Marcelo.

Mexico and Colombia also go way back, having played against each other in the 2001 Copa America final. The Mexican national team also has Colombian influence via Julián Quiñones, a Colombian-Mexican striker who was Mexico’s leading goalscorer in the last World Cup with four goals in five matches. It’s also worth noting Colombia was set to be the original host of the 1986 World Cup, but withdrew due to overwhelming stadium demands from FIFA — leading Mexico to step in its place, hosting what is now considered one of the greatest World Cups of all time.

The parallels between Mexico and many South American countries are endless, which can strengthen rivalries if El Tri ends up switching over to CONMEBOL. Looking at the drama leading up to Mexico’s 2-0 win over Ecuador in the round of 32, new rivalries may also be in the works.

Great economic opportunities

Though watching Mexico face off against the U.S. is always a treat, there isn’t much else for Mexican fans to look forward to between World Cups. It’s no secret that the Mexican Football Federation loves hosting friendlies with its American neighbors in cities like Los Angeles and Houston due to economic opportunities, but other nations within CONCACAF don’t present the same level of excitement.

Playing in CONMEBOL will change that and add more variety to El Tri’s calendar. Regular matches against Brazil, Argentina and Colombia will also attract South American fans — millions of people ready to pay top dollar to watch their respective national teams.

Not only can Mexico continue to play against the United States in friendlies, but it can also strategically host games in American cities with large Brazilian, Argentinian and other South American populations.

Would you rather see Mexico vs. a tiny island in a Gold Cup group-stage match or against Uruguay in a World Cup qualifier? Regular matchups against steep competition will not only make Mexican players better, but will also create buzz and excitement that won’t fade after a World Cup ends.

Do you think Mexico can thrive in CONMEBOL?

Like most rumors, the idea of Mexico switching over to CONMEBOL probably won’t materialize unless real action takes place. But if you want a taste of how well Mexico’s current national team could stack up against South American competition, three of its next four games are against Colombia, Peru and Chile.

So, do you think Mexico is good enough to compete against South America’s best? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: From the archive: To friend or not to friend other expats in Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a humorous look at the often thorny issue of friendships among expats.

Any foreigners who’ve been in Mexico for more than two minutes know this truth: expat relationships are complicated.

I read with interest Louisa Rogers’ article on expat relationships, and found myself nodding along to much of it. Feeling threatened by large numbers of new foreigners moving to my area? Check! Hyper awareness of my ratio of Mexican-to-foreign-born friends? Check! Complaining about “those other gringos” who are messing up some designated “elsewhere”? Oh my goodness, please don’t make me look in the mirror.

Friends unless proven otherwise

My policy these days is to keep a very light grip on everything from my friendships to my own ideological musings. I pre-like everyone now, purposefully rather than by default. I haven’t met you, but I am sure you are a friend, until and unless you prove otherwise.

And I would really appreciate it if you wouldn’t prove otherwise.

But this attitude was hard-won, not discovered in a sudden stroke of coolness. It’s been over 20 years — uh-oh, am I bragging? — and it’s taken a long time to make peace with my identity both as an individual and as part of the greater foreigner-in-Mexico population. I don’t know if it’s my time here or just my age. Maybe it was a really good mushroom trip. But I just refuse to get worked up: if you want to be friends, we’re friends. I’ll try to help you if you need help. If you don’t like me, then, oh well. I guess we’re not friends.

The comment section of this humor piece I wrote made the “not friends” column abundantly clear; self-sorting, even.

And it got me thinking: is online communication among us all helping or hurting? After all, no one would be as nasty to people’s faces as we might be online. Online, we’re anonymous; we could be anyone; and we can’t get punched in the face for being rude as hell.

A polarized society, at home and abroad

Perhaps it’s a reflection as well of the general polarity we find in the United States. I’m certainly not immune from self-sorting, of course: finding common ground with friends who are openly enthusiastic about a felon president is not always easy. In any case, everyone has strong opinions either way.

Yes, we foreigners are a varied bunch, each of us as unique as a snowflake. Complicating matters is the fact that the average U.S. or Canadian citizen is not someone who would voluntarily move to Mexico. Right off the bat, then, you’re dealing with someone whose type you might not be too familiar with.

Overall, the most even-keeled people I’ve met have been retirees, though this isn’t a hard and fast rule. You can be a weirdo at any age!

People closer to my own age are a bit of a mixed bag, though, and I’ve had a few relationships with other paisanos end abruptly at this point. This has only happened once with a Mexican friend, a neighbor who blocked me after I friended her husband, who I thought was also my friend, on Facebook. Given the demographics, I’d say the number of times it’s happened with those from my own culture makes it conspicuously likely.

Abrupt endings to friendships

The first cut off was by a couple from the U.S. who wanted help translating and getting paperwork done upon arrival. We’d had some great conversations online beforehand, but in real life, our chemistry was pretty tense and weird. No matter; they were paying me for my help, and I was going to do whatever I could to make it worth it. Mostly, it was fine.

But then there was a misunderstanding about what exactly was being charged, and I suddenly found myself buried under some very intense, urgent messages. I gifted them some extra live interpretation time as a sign of goodwill and thought we were fine. Later, though, when I wanted to send a message to see how their house hunting had gone, I realized I’d been blocked on WhatsApp and Facebook.

Since then, I’ve found I’m not the only person to have received that treatment. A clear picture of kookiness has emerged, so I guess it’s not just me. The experience did convince me, however, that I definitely did not want to make a career of helping people settle down here.

Another cut-off came from someone who’d been a friend and mentor to me for over 20 years. That one was completely unexpected, and it hurt. I’d excused myself from what I saw as a minor favor, an action which my friend apparently interpreted as a sign of deep disrespect. I was oblivious that he was upset with me, and only learned that he was months later from another friend. By the time I wrote him to apologize, that was it. I never heard from him again.

The last incident was quite recent, with a friend of three years. I thought we were really close, but when I unwisely hounded her about getting her dog fixed so it wouldn’t get all the dogs in the neighborhood pregnant, that was it, too. I was asked to leave her house immediately, even though home was over three hours away.

Keeping an open mind on other expats

What is with these gringos and abruptly cutting people off? Mexicans may have a reputation for being dramatic, but my relationships with them have gone through rocky patches and come out just fine. Only my own paisanos have been so mad that they banished me from their lives. Is it something about North Americans, or is it just something about North Americans who live in Mexico? I will probably never know.

But I have not sworn off other U.S. Americans. Currently, we have a small breakfast group of foreigners in Xalapa that meets once a month. We share a nice meal and chat. We wouldn’t all necessarily be best friends were we in the U.S.

But this is different. When you’re in a foreign country without family, it’s nice to know people who know your culture and language on a native level. Real friendships, I still believe and have proven, are possible.

But for people who I know will definitely still be my friend even if I berate them about their unsterilized pets, I’m sticking with Mexicans.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: US Senators Want Sudan’s War Cut Off From Gold and Gum Arabic
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

SUDAN · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —Who wrote: Senator Chris Murphy led seven colleagues in a letter to the US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz. —The core ask: They want Washington to push for additional Security Council measures limiting the money reaching the warring parties. —Gold chemicals: The letter calls for international prohibitions on the sale of precursor chemicals used in certain forms of gold extraction. —Gum arabic: It also asks for due-diligence guidelines covering gum arabic procurement, a commodity the senators say is smuggled to finance the fighting. —Naming names: The senators want the Security Council’s Panel of Experts to identify explicitly which states have circumvented restrictions to arm or fund the belligerents. —The deadline: The Council’s Sudan sanctions regime expires on 12 September, with a vote on renewal expected, according to Security Council Report. —The stakes: The letter describes Sudan’s war as the largest humanitarian crisis in the world.

Eight US senators have asked Washington to push for Sudan sanctions that reach the commodities financing the war, specifically the chemicals used in gold extraction and the trade in gum arabic. The request lands days before the Security Council’s Sudan mandate expires on 12 September.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

What the Sudan sanctions letter asks for

Senator Chris Murphy and seven colleagues wrote to Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations, urging Washington to seek additional measures at the Security Council.

Two of the proposals are unusually specific. One would prohibit international sales of precursor chemicals used in certain gold-extraction processes, and the other would create due-diligence guidelines for buyers of gum arabic.

A third asks the Council’s Panel of Experts to report more transparently, naming the states that have circumvented restrictions to supply weapons or money to the warring parties.

Why gold is the centre of the war economy

Sudanese gold is portable, high-value and easy to move across desert borders, which makes it the ideal financing instrument for armed groups on both sides.

Targeting the metal directly has proved difficult because the buyers are dispersed and the refining chain runs through jurisdictions with limited appetite for enforcement.

Going after the inputs instead is the interesting move. Extraction chemicals are manufactured industrially, sold by a small number of firms and shipped through documented channels.

It is the same logic applied to drug precursors and to dual-use components. Control the narrow part of the chain rather than the wide part.

Whether it survives negotiation is another matter, because legitimate mining across the region uses the same inputs. A blunt prohibition would hit Ghana and Tanzania as well as Sudan.

Gum arabic, and why a soft drink ingredient is in a sanctions letter

Sudan is the world’s dominant supplier of gum arabic, the acacia resin used as an emulsifier in soft drinks, sweets and pharmaceuticals. There is no easy substitute at scale.

That makes it both a lifeline for rural producers and, the senators argue, a smuggling channel for belligerents. The two facts are uncomfortable together.

Due-diligence guidelines rather than a ban is the compromise. The aim is to make Western buyers document their chains without cutting off the farmers who depend on the crop.

The gum belt runs across Kordofan and Darfur, precisely the areas the war has torn through. Harvesting is done by smallholders who have no say in who taxes the road out.

Any measure that raises the cost of buying Sudanese gum risks pushing buyers to Chad and Nigeria. That would punish producers rather than combatants.

The timing is not accidental

The Security Council’s Sudan sanctions regime expires on 12 September, and a vote on extension is expected, according to Security Council Report’s monthly forecast.

Renewal debates are when the scope of a regime can realistically be widened. Outside those windows, adding measures requires a fresh negotiation nobody wants.

Whether the Council has the appetite is another question. Recent Sudan votes have passed with abstentions rather than consensus.

The existing regime dates from the Darfur arms embargo and has been criticised for years as too narrow geographically. Extending it to the whole country has been proposed repeatedly.

Senators have raised that specific point before in a formal resolution. This letter is the latest attempt to move it from the Senate to the Council.

What this means for commodity buyers

Confectionery, beverage and pharmaceutical companies would carry the compliance cost of any gum arabic guidelines. Most already run voluntary schemes of varying seriousness.

Chemical manufacturers face a sharper version of the same problem, because a precursor prohibition would place liability closer to the point of sale.

For African exporters more broadly, the precedent matters. A commodity can now be brought into a sanctions conversation on the basis of who moves it rather than what it is.

What to watch next

The immediate marker is the 12 September vote and whether any of the senators’ proposals appear in the text rather than the debate.

The second is the Panel of Experts’ next report, and whether it names states directly. That single change would do more than most listings.

The third is the gum arabic market itself. Buyers tend to reprice risk in advance of rules, and rural Sudanese producers would feel that before any resolution passes.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the senators want added to Sudan sanctions? Prohibitions on selling precursor chemicals used in gold extraction, due-diligence guidelines for gum arabic procurement, and more transparent reporting by the UN Panel of Experts. Who sent the letter? Senator Chris Murphy led seven colleagues in writing to Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations. Why does gum arabic feature? Sudan is the world’s dominant supplier, and the senators say belligerents smuggle it to finance their operations. When does the current sanctions regime expire? On 12 September 2026, with a Security Council vote on renewal expected, according to Security Council Report. Would this stop the fighting? No single measure would. The proposals aim to narrow the financing available to the warring parties rather than to end the conflict directly.

World.title: A White Stone at Glidji, and Togo’s Guin Community Exhales
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

TOGO · CULTURE

Key Facts —The verdict: The stone lifted at Glidji this year is white, which the Guin read as peace and prosperity, Africanews reported on 6 September. —The rite: Priests and initiates enter the sacred wood at Glidji Kpodji before dawn, find a stone believed placed there by the ancestors, and read its colour aloud to the crowd. —The calendar: Epe Ekpe, also called Ekpessosso, marks the start of the Guin ancestral year and falls between late August and early September. —The colours: White means peace and a good year, blue is broadly favourable, red signals blood and conflict, and black is worse still. —The age of it: The Guin trace the taking of the stone to 1663, which makes it one of West Africa’s longest continuously observed civic rituals. —Where it happens: Glidji sits in south-east Togo, inland from Aneho, the coastal town that anchors Guin community life. —Why it draws crowds: The reading is public, and the diaspora returns for it, which turns a religious rite into the region’s largest annual gathering.

The Togo sacred stone taken from the wood at Glidji this weekend came out white, and for the Guin of the south-east that is the best of the four possible answers. It reads as a year of peace and prosperity.

How the Togo sacred stone is taken

Long before dawn, priests and initiates walk into the sacred wood at Glidji Kpodji. What they are looking for is a single stone, which believers hold to have been placed there by the ancestors.

When it is found it is carried out and shown to the waiting crowd, and its colour is announced. That announcement is the whole of the ceremony’s public meaning.

Africanews, reporting from the ground on 6 September, said this year’s stone was white. The reading given was a year of peace and prosperity.

What the colours mean

White is the outcome people hope for: peace, good harvests, a year without rupture. Blue is generally favourable without the same weight.

Red is the warning. It stands for blood and conflict, and a red year is one in which the community is told to be careful.

Black is worse again. The scale is not a forecast in the meteorological sense, but it does shape how a season is entered.

The reading is also a purification. The year is closed before the next one is opened, and grievances are meant to be left on the wrong side of that line.

Elders address the crowd after the colour is announced, setting out what the community should attend to. It functions as an annual address as much as an oracle.

A rite older than the modern state

The Guin trace the taking of the stone to 1663, when the community settled in what is now southern Togo. Very few civic rituals anywhere in West Africa have been observed that continuously.

It survived the slave-trading era on this coast, German and then French colonial administration, and independence. Governments have come and gone around a ceremony that did not require their permission.

That longevity is part of why the reading carries authority. It predates every institution now listening to it.

The Guin themselves arrived on this coast from what is now Ghana, and the festival preserves that migration story. The stone is a claim to place as well as a prediction.

Neighbouring Benin holds its own Vodun calendar, and the two traditions are closely related. The Gulf of Guinea coast shares a religious grammar that national borders cut across.

Epe Ekpe as an economic event

The festival is the largest annual gathering in the Aneho area, and the diaspora returns for it from Lome, Accra, Paris and beyond. Hotels, transport and markets in the south-east work to its calendar.

Togo has been building a tourism proposition around exactly this kind of heritage, alongside its ports and its coastline. Cultural depth is one of the few assets a small country cannot have copied.

The rite is also a piece of soft power. It is one of the very few Togolese stories that reliably reaches an international audience each year.

Visitors who come for it stay in guesthouses that would otherwise be empty in early September. For Aneho, the festival is a season rather than a day.

Handled carefully, that is a durable form of tourism, because it is not built on infrastructure that has to be financed. Handled carelessly, it becomes a spectacle that the community stops recognising.

Vodun, misread abroad and ordinary at home

Foreign coverage tends to reach for the word voodoo, with everything that has accumulated around it in film and fiction. The tradition on this coast is Vodun, a structured religion with priesthoods, calendars and law.

In Togo and neighbouring Benin it is practised openly and alongside Christianity and Islam, often by the same families. Treating it as exotic misses how ordinary it is here.

For readers used to seeing African religion described only as folklore, the Glidji reading is a useful corrective. It is a civic institution that happens to be sacred.

What follows a white year

Practically, the reading opens the Guin year and the round of ceremonies, reconciliations and appointments that go with it. Disputes are expected to be settled in its light.

It arrives in a country that has spent 2026 in the news for its port, its climate advocacy and a constitutional reordering. A white stone will not change any of that.

But it sets a tone, and communities that keep a calendar of their own tend to weather the ones imposed on them rather better.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Togo sacred stone ceremony? It is the central rite of Epe Ekpe, the Guin ancestral new year, in which priests take a stone from the sacred wood at Glidji and read its colour aloud. What colour was the stone this year? White, which the Guin read as a year of peace and prosperity, according to Africanews on 6 September 2026. What do the other colours mean? Blue is broadly favourable, red signals blood and conflict, and black is worse still. How old is the ceremony? The Guin trace it to 1663, making it one of the longest continuously observed civic rituals in West Africa. Where does it take place? At Glidji Kpodji in south-east Togo, inland from the coastal town of Aneho.

World.title: Five Turbines Come Ashore at Owendo to Give Libreville 100 MW
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GABON · ENERGY

Key Facts —What moved: Five gas turbines with a combined announced capacity of 100 MW began leaving Owendo commercial port on 6 September, according to SEEG. —How long it takes: The convoy runs over three days, from 6 to 8 September, moving daily from about 4 am to 6:30 pm under police escort. —Where they are going: The Akournam thermal plant, which supplies Greater Libreville and has been the weak point in the capital’s power supply. —The stated purpose: SEEG describes the delivery as a renewal of the Owendo gas plant’s production equipment, to make operation more reliable and improve service quality. —The caveat: Announced capacity is not delivered capacity. Installation, commissioning and grid connection all sit between the convoy and the network. —Why it matters now: Greater Libreville has been running with recurrent outages, and the capital concentrates most of Gabon’s formal economic activity. —Fiscal context: Gabon cut its revenue forecast by a fifth this year while holding spending, which leaves little room for slippage on capital projects.

Five Gabon power turbines with a combined announced capacity of 100 MW began moving out of Owendo port this weekend, bound for the Akournam thermal plant that supplies Greater Libreville. On paper it is the largest single addition to the capital’s generation in years.

What the Gabon power turbines are meant to fix

The Akournam site is the backbone of supply to Greater Libreville, and its equipment has been the constraint. SEEG, the national water and power utility, calls the delivery a renewal of the plant’s production facilities.

The utility’s stated aims are reliability and quality of service rather than expansion for its own sake. That is the language of an operator managing outages, not one chasing growth.

Greater Libreville holds the great majority of Gabon’s formal employment, public administration and services. Power failures there are national economic events.

A convoy that shuts a city’s roads

Moving five turbines from the quay to the plant takes three days, from 6 to 8 September, with transport each day from about 4 am until 6:30 pm under police escort.

Direct Infos Gabon warned drivers that the route would be disrupted throughout. Loads of this size travel slowly and cannot share a carriageway.

The logistics are a reminder of how physical energy policy remains. A hundred megawatts arrives on a low-loader, not in a press release.

Owendo is Gabon’s main commercial port and the entry point for almost everything the capital consumes. Its handling capacity is itself a constraint on national investment.

That the operation was announced in advance, with hours and routes published, is a small sign of a utility communicating better than it used to.

Why the announced number should be read carefully

One hundred megawatts is the nameplate figure. What reaches customers depends on installation, testing, fuel supply and the state of the transmission network.

Gabon Review made the point plainly: after transport comes the decisive challenge of turning announced capacity into electricity actually available on the grid.

Thermal plants in the region routinely run below rating because of gas supply interruptions or deferred maintenance. The turbines are necessary and not sufficient.

Gabon also draws on hydropower, which varies with rainfall and has left the system exposed in dry spells. Thermal capacity is the buffer that covers those gaps.

The right question for households is not how many megawatts arrived but how many hours of supply they get in December. Those are different measurements.

The fiscal frame around it

Gabon cut its revenue forecast by roughly a fifth this year while keeping spending largely intact, a combination that has drawn attention from the Fund and from bondholders.

The country nonetheless raised US$920 million in a Eurobond that outperformed much of the emerging-market field. Investors have been more relaxed than the fundamentals alone would suggest.

Capital equipment for the capital’s grid is one of the more defensible uses of that money. Deferred power investment tends to be repaid with interest in lost output.

Gabon’s authorities have been keen to show delivery on visible infrastructure since the political changes of recent years. A convoy through Libreville is, among other things, a photograph.

That is not a criticism. Governments everywhere sequence their spending for visibility, and electricity is one of the few areas where the public verdict is immediate and honest.

Gas, and what Gabon does with it

The plant is gas-fired, which ties the capital’s electricity to domestic hydrocarbon production at a moment when Gabon’s mature oil fields are in decline.

Central African producers are all facing versions of the same question. The regional central bank has warned that oil dependence has thinned reserves across the monetary union.

Using gas domestically rather than exporting it is at least a decision about value retention. Whether the supply holds for the life of the turbines is a separate matter.

What to watch next

The first marker is a commissioning date. Equipment that sits on site through the rainy season is a familiar outcome in the region.

The second is outage statistics for Greater Libreville over the next two quarters, which are the only honest measure of whether this worked.

The third is tariffs. New capacity has to be paid for, and SEEG’s balance sheet is not separate from the state’s.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Gabon power turbines being delivered? Five gas turbines with a combined announced capacity of 100 MW, landed at Owendo port and moved to the Akournam thermal plant. When is the convoy running? From 6 to 8 September 2026, moving each day from about 4 am to 6:30 pm under police escort. Who is behind the project? SEEG, Gabon’s national water and electricity utility, which describes the delivery as a renewal of the Owendo gas plant’s production equipment. Will Libreville immediately get 100 MW? No. The 100 MW is announced capacity, and installation, commissioning and grid connection all have to follow before power reaches customers. Why does this matter for the economy? Greater Libreville concentrates most of Gabon’s formal economic activity, so recurrent outages there translate directly into lost national output.

World.title: Zimbabwe Says 720 Tonnes of Lithium Ore Left on Forged Papers
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ZIMBABWE · CRITICAL MINERALS

Key Facts —The charge: A finance director at Orequest was remanded by a Harare magistrate on Saturday over an alleged attempt to move lithium ore on fraudulent export documents, NewsDay reported. —The volume: The State alleges the syndicate had already exported 720 tonnes of un-beneficiated lithium ore in 23 trucks before the case was brought. —What was recovered: Investigators account for 420 tonnes: 300 tonnes at a yard in Ruwa, 60 tonnes in abandoned containers and 60 tonnes stopped at Forbes Border Post. —The document: The State describes the paperwork as fraudulent Bikita Minerals documents. A separate case in July involved an actually cloned Bikita permit. —Who brought it: The anti-corruption commission and the revenue authority have worked lithium smuggling cases jointly, including a separate cloned-permit case in July. —The legal backdrop: Zimbabwe suspended raw mineral and lithium concentrate exports in February 2026, then replaced the blanket ban in April with quotas for six large producers. —Value undetermined: The loss to the State has not been quantified. Ministry of Mines evaluators have yet to assess it.

A Zimbabwe lithium smuggling case brought before a Harare magistrate on Saturday alleges that 720 tonnes of unprocessed lithium ore left the country in 23 trucks on fraudulent export documents. A further 420 tonnes was recovered before it crossed.

What the Zimbabwe lithium smuggling case alleges

The accused, a finance director at a private company, appeared before a magistrate in Harare on Saturday and was remanded, NewsDay reported. She is represented by counsel and the allegations have not been tested at trial.

The State’s case is that a syndicate obtained an export permit belonging to an established lithium producer, reproduced it, and used the copy to move ore that could not lawfully leave in that form.

Twenty-three truckloads are said to have gone out before the scheme was interrupted. The interception at Forbes Border Post, on the Mozambique frontier, is what brought the rest into view.

Why raw lithium cannot legally leave Zimbabwe

In February 2026 the government suspended exports of all raw minerals and lithium concentrates, citing export malpractice and leakage of value. Al Jazeera reported the measure at the time.

The policy is beneficiation by decree. Ore must be processed domestically so that the country captures refining margin rather than shipping rock at spot prices.

Zimbabwe is not alone in this. A run of African producers has moved the same way, betting that access to reserves is leverage enough to force processing onshore.

The logic is sound and the execution is the difficulty. Refineries need power, water and financing, and Zimbabwe has been short of all three for most of the past decade.

Until domestic capacity exists at scale, a ban converts legal exports into stranded ore. That is the pressure the alleged syndicate was working with.

The gap the ban created

Export bans raise the price of a legal tonne and leave the illegal one untouched. That spread is the whole business model of the syndicate the State describes.

A forged permit is a low-technology solution to a high-value problem. It requires no mine, no plant and no licence, only a document and a border post that does not check it against the issuer.

That is a control failure rather than a policy failure, and it is fixable. Digital permit verification at crossings would close most of it.

The choice of a real producer’s permit is the telling detail. A forged document from a company that genuinely exports is far harder to question at a weighbridge at night.

It also means a legitimate miner’s name was attached to loads it did not send. That is a reputational cost carried by a firm that appears to be a victim here.

What is genuinely at stake in the numbers

Zimbabwe’s lithium export earnings rose 229.8% to US$782 million, on official figures we reported in August. Against that, 720 tonnes of ore is small.

The significance is not the tonnage but the demonstration. If the permit system can be copied once, the assumption behind the entire beneficiation policy is weaker than the government has claimed.

Investors building processing capacity inside Zimbabwe price that risk directly. A refinery only works if the feedstock it was promised cannot quietly leave the country.

The regional picture

Southern Africa now holds a decisive share of the world’s hard-rock lithium, and the region’s governments have discovered they can set terms. Enforcement is the part that lags.

Border posts on the Beira and Maputo corridors handle enormous volumes with limited inspection capacity. Ore is heavy, visible and slow, which makes it an unlikely thing to smuggle and an easy thing to miss.

The same corridors carry chrome, gold and tobacco under the same paperwork regime. A weakness proven on lithium is a weakness available to all of them.

Zimbabwe has already extended its deadline for regularising small-scale miners to the end of December, an admission that the informal end of the sector is larger than the formal one.

Two enforcement problems are therefore running at once: unlicensed production upstream and unverified paperwork at the border. Neither is solved by a further restriction on exports.

What to watch next

The first question is whether the prosecution reaches anyone beyond the company officer in the dock. Syndicate cases in the mining sector have often stopped at the first arrest.

The second is the valuation. Until Ministry of Mines evaluators price the 720 tonnes, the State cannot quantify what it says it lost.

The third is procedural. Whether the permit system is rebuilt, or simply patched, will tell investors more about Zimbabwean mineral policy than any further export restriction.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much lithium ore is the Zimbabwe smuggling case about? The State alleges 720 tonnes of un-beneficiated ore was exported in 23 trucks, with a further 420 tonnes recovered before it left. How was the ore allegedly moved? On an allegedly fraudulent set of Bikita Minerals documents, which the State says allowed the loads to pass as authorised shipments. Where was the intercepted ore found? Three hundred tonnes at a yard in Ruwa, 60 tonnes in abandoned containers and 60 tonnes stopped at Forbes Border Post. Why is exporting raw lithium banned in Zimbabwe? The government suspended exports of raw minerals and lithium concentrates in February 2026 to force domestic processing and stop value leaving as unrefined rock. Has anyone been convicted? No. The accused was remanded by a Harare magistrate and the allegations have not been tested at trial.

World.title: Sierra Leone’s Former President Comes Home, Two Years After a Treason Charge
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

SIERRA LEONE · POLITICS

Key Facts —Home after two years: Ernest Bai Koroma, 72, arrived in Freetown on Sunday and was received by the foreign affairs minister, Bloomberg reported. —The charge that sent him away: He left for Nigeria in 2024, days after being charged with treason and other offences over the November 2023 uprising. —A three-month leave that ran long: Judicial authorities had cleared him to remain in Nigeria for three months of medical treatment. He stayed more than two years. —How it ended: In July 2026 the attorney-general filed a notice of discontinuance under Section 45 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2024, ending the proceedings and his bail conditions. —No reasons given: The attorney-general did not explain the decision, and the office has not published one since. —What 2023 involved: Armed men stormed a military armoury, two barracks, two prisons and two police stations. Twenty-one people were killed and hundreds of prisoners escaped. —Who travelled with him: Former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo accompanied him on the flight, according to Bloomberg.

Sierra Leone Koroma, president from 2007 to 2018, returned to Freetown on Sunday after the attorney-general discontinued the treason case brought against him over the November 2023 attack on a military armoury. He had been in Nigeria for more than two years.

Why Sierra Leone Koroma left in the first place

In November 2023 armed attackers hit a military armoury, two barracks, two prisons and two police stations in Freetown. Twenty-one people were killed and hundreds of prisoners walked out.

The government called it an attempted coup. Koroma, who had led the country for eleven years, was charged with treason and other offences the following year.

He was then permitted to travel to Nigeria for three months of medical treatment. That window closed in 2024 and he did not return until this weekend.

What the attorney-general actually did

On 14 July 2026 the attorney-general and minister of justice filed a notice of discontinuance under Section 45 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2024, and parliament endorsed the decision two days later. The filing ended the proceedings and released the bail conditions attached to them.

Section 45 gives that office the power to stop a prosecution without a verdict. It is a discretionary act, not an acquittal, and it carries no finding either way.

No reasons were given. That silence is the point of contention in Freetown, because it leaves the question of what happened in 2023 formally unanswered.

The Criminal Procedure Act 2024 is itself recent legislation, passed as part of a broader overhaul of Sierra Leonean criminal justice. This is one of its more consequential early uses.

Lawyers in Freetown have noted that a discontinuance does not bar a future prosecution in principle. In practice, cases dropped at this level rarely return.

The politics of a homecoming

Koroma remains the dominant figure in the All People’s Congress, the main opposition party. His absence had left it without a settled centre of gravity through a difficult electoral cycle.

His return was staged with care. A former Nigerian head of state on the aircraft and a cabinet minister on the tarmac are both signals aimed at domestic audiences.

Regional mediation has shaped Sierra Leonean politics before, and the fingerprints of that tradition are visible here. West African elder statesmen have long served as the region’s release valve.

The governing party has said little in public. That restraint suggests an arrangement reached quietly rather than a concession forced in the open.

For the opposition, the calculation is delicate. A returning leader unifies a party and also freezes the succession that his absence had begun to produce.

Why investors were watching

Sierra Leone is trying to rebuild a minerals economy around iron ore, rutile and newer critical-minerals ambitions. Every one of those projects is a fifteen-year commitment.

A former president facing a capital charge in absentia is a specific kind of country risk. It signals that the transfer of power between administrations has not fully settled.

Removing that overhang is worth something at the margin. It does not by itself change the fiscal position, the power supply or the cost of capital.

Sierra Leone has also been rebuilding its relationship with international lenders after a difficult few years. Political normalisation is a soft input into those conversations.

The country’s pitch to investors rests on stability rather than scale. Anything that makes the recent past look settled is therefore worth more here than it would be in a larger market.

What is unresolved

Others charged over the 2023 events have faced the courts, and their cases sit uncomfortably alongside a discontinuance for the most senior accused. Consistency is the obvious question.

There is also the matter of what the state now says happened. Without a trial there is no judicial account of the armoury attack, only competing political ones.

For a country that spent the 1990s in civil war, an authoritative record matters more than usual. Amnesia has been tried here before and did not hold.

What to watch next

The immediate test is whether Koroma resumes an active political role or accepts an elder-statesman position outside party structures. The APC will press for the former.

The second is whether the government pairs the discontinuance with any wider reconciliation process. Nothing of the kind has been announced.

The third is the mining calendar. Licensing rounds and the winding-up of the state minerals vehicle both proceed this year, and both are easier to sell into a calmer political room.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was Ernest Bai Koroma charged? He was charged with treason and other offences in 2024 over the November 2023 attack on a military armoury, barracks, prisons and police stations in Freetown. How did the case end? The attorney-general filed a notice of discontinuance in July 2026 under Section 45 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2024, which ended the proceedings and his bail conditions. Was he acquitted? No. A discontinuance stops a prosecution without a verdict, so there is no judicial finding either way. Why was he in Nigeria? Judicial authorities cleared him to travel for three months of medical treatment in 2024, and he remained there for more than two years. What happened in the 2023 uprising? Armed attackers struck a military armoury, two barracks, two prisons and two police stations. Twenty-one people were killed and hundreds of prisoners escaped.

World.title: Ghana Returns to the Medium-Term Curve as Bids Top US$390m
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GHANA · MARKETS

Key Facts —Demand: Investors submitted GH₵4.46 billion (US$392 million) in bids for the new four-year cedi bond, according to MyJoyOnline. —Accepted: The government took GH₵3.15 billion (US$277 million), or 70.57% of what was tendered, for a bid-to-cover ratio of 1.41 times. —Price: The paper cleared at 12.00%, the bottom of a pre-auction range that ran to 13.50%. —The spread: That is roughly 130 basis points above the post-restructuring four-year secondary reference of about 10.7%. —Mechanics: The Finance Ministry opened the book-built offer on 1 September and settlement falls on 7 September, with maturity in 2030. —Who was targeted: The issue was marketed primarily to resident investors, and six institutions acted as bond specialists, among them Absa, CalBank, GCB and Stanbic. —The backdrop: Ghana completed the sixth and final review of its IMF programme in July 2026, unlocking a last disbursement of about US$371 million.

The Ghana 4-year bond drew GH₵4.46 billion (US$392 million) of bids and cleared at 12.00%, the state’s first medium-term cedi issue since the domestic debt exchange reset the local curve. The government accepted GH₵3.15 billion (US$277 million) of what was offered.

What the Ghana 4-year bond result actually shows

A bid-to-cover of 1.41 times is respectable rather than spectacular. It means demand exceeded the amount taken, but not by the multiple that signals a market straining to buy.

The clearing yield is the more interesting number. Settling at 12.00%, the floor of the expected range, tells you the book had enough depth for the issuer to price on its own terms.

Accepting 70.57% of bids rather than the whole book is consistent with that. The Finance Ministry chose price over volume, which is a position only a confident issuer takes.

Why a four-year tenor matters here

Ghana’s domestic debt exchange in 2023 pushed local investors out of the medium part of the curve and into short bills. Rebuilding the middle is the slow work of the recovery.

Every successful medium-term issue lengthens the average maturity of the domestic stock and reduces the rollover the Treasury must manage each quarter.

It also gives pension funds and insurers something to buy. Those institutions need duration, and for three years they have had almost nowhere to find it in cedis.

Book building rather than a straight auction is itself a signal. It lets the issuer gauge demand before committing to a coupon, which is how a market is coaxed back rather than tested.

Six bond specialists were engaged to distribute the paper. That infrastructure had gone quiet after the restructuring and is now being used again.

The 130 basis points nobody should ignore

The bond cleared about 130 basis points above the post-exchange four-year secondary reference of roughly 10.7%. That is the price of a new issue rather than a seasoned one.

Some of that spread is illiquidity premium and some is memory. Investors who took losses in the exchange do not lend at the theoretical curve.

Narrowing that gap on the next issue is the real test. A single auction proves appetite exists, not that the market has repriced Ghanaian duration.

Analysts in Accra have already noted that a strong headline can mask a soft price. A book that clears at the floor of the range is not the same as one that clears through it.

For foreign investors the comparison is with other frontier local-currency markets. Twelve per cent in cedis has to compete with Nigerian, Kenyan and Egyptian paper on a currency-adjusted basis.

How this fits the fiscal story

Ghana completed the sixth and final review of its Extended Credit Facility in July, with a final disbursement of about US$371 million and a request for a successor policy instrument.

The country has also been retiring external obligations early, having settled a US$700 million Eurobond ahead of schedule this year. Domestic and external strategies are pulling in the same direction.

Together those steps are an attempt to leave crisis management and re-enter normal debt operations. This auction is the domestic leg of that argument.

Ratings agencies have been moving in the same direction, though slowly. Domestic issuance history is one of the inputs they weigh when assessing a post-default sovereign.

None of it removes the underlying arithmetic. Ghana still has to run primary surpluses to make the restructured stock sustainable.

What could still go wrong

Cedi stability is doing a great deal of work in these numbers. A currency move would reprice the whole domestic curve regardless of fiscal performance.

The gold-backed foreign exchange programme has helped hold the line, but it is an administrative fix rather than a structural one.

And the successor arrangement with the Fund has not yet been finalised. Investors are pricing the continuation of discipline, not the fact of it.

What to watch next

The immediate marker is whether the Treasury returns with a five- or seven-year offer before the end of the year. Extending further is the natural next step.

The second is secondary trading in the new bond after settlement. If it trades in from 12.00%, the premium was about newness rather than credit.

The third is participation. This issue was aimed at residents, and drawing foreign accounts back into cedi paper would be the genuine signal of normalisation.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the Ghana 4-year bond raise? The government accepted GH₵3.15 billion (US$277 million) out of GH₵4.46 billion (US$392 million) in bids, or 70.57% of what was tendered. What yield did it clear at? 12.00%, at the bottom of a pre-auction expectation that ran from 12.00% to 13.50%. How does that compare with the secondary market? It is about 130 basis points above the post-restructuring four-year secondary reference of roughly 10.7%. When does it settle and mature? Settlement falls on 7 September 2026 and the cedi-denominated bond matures in 2030. Why is a four-year issue significant? The 2023 domestic debt exchange pushed local investors into short bills, so rebuilding the medium part of the cedi curve is central to Ghana’s recovery.

World.title: Benghazi Hosts the Second Libya-US Reconstruction Forum
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

LIBYA · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —When and where: The second Libya-US Forum for Development and Reconstruction opened in Benghazi on Sunday 6 September, according to Libya Herald. —Who attended: Libyan and American officials, private-sector executives, development institutions and technical experts, the organisers said. —The agenda: Infrastructure and public works, energy and communications, health and education modernisation, and economic diversification. —The first edition: The inaugural forum was held in Washington in April 2025, making this the first to convene on Libyan soil. —A timed showpiece: Benghazi University reopened on 4 September after a full rebuild, one day before delegates arrived. —How it was arranged: Preparations were discussed between Belqasim Haftar and the US adviser Massad Boulos, according to Al Wasat. —Also on the circuit: A Spanish business mission visited Tripoli the same week, and a Korean business forum is scheduled there this month.

The second Libya United States forum for development and reconstruction opened in Benghazi on 6 September, bringing American officials and contractors to eastern Libya for the first time under this format. The agenda runs from infrastructure and energy to health, education and economic diversification.

What the Libya United States forum is for

The stated purpose is to convert political contact into contracts. Organisers listed infrastructure and public works, energy and communications, health and education, and diversification as the four working areas.

The first edition met in Washington in April 2025. Moving the second to Benghazi is the substantive change, because it puts American delegations physically inside the eastern administration’s territory.

That matters in a country whose institutions are still divided. Where a forum meets is itself a statement about who is being treated as a counterparty.

Libya has no shortage of investment conferences. What distinguishes this one is that it carries an American government presence rather than a purely commercial delegation.

The organisers framed the aim as tangible results rather than dialogue. That phrasing is an implicit acknowledgement that the first edition produced mostly the latter.

The choreography around it

Benghazi University reopened on 4 September, rebuilt after being destroyed in the fighting that flattened much of the city. Delegates arrived the following day.

Reconstruction of that kind is the eastern authorities’ principal argument to foreign partners. It is easier to point at a finished campus than at a constitutional settlement.

Preparations for the forum were handled in part by Belqasim Haftar, who runs the reconstruction effort, in discussions with the US adviser Massad Boulos, Al Wasat reported.

Why Washington is in the room

Libya holds Africa’s largest proven oil reserves and sits directly opposite Italy and Greece. The National Oil Corporation reported output of about 1.49 million barrels a day in June 2026, the highest since 2013.

It is also the main departure point for migration across the central Mediterranean, which gives European partners an interest that Washington can trade on.

And it is contested. Russian networks have been active in the country since the Wagner period, and the reconstruction file is one of the few areas where American commercial presence can be built quickly.

Turkey has held a strong position in the west of the country for years, largely through defence and construction. Washington is arriving late to a market with entrenched competitors.

Egypt and the United Arab Emirates have their own long-standing relationships in the east. An American forum in Benghazi enters a room that is already crowded.

What Libyan hosts want out of it

Capital, technology and legitimacy, in roughly that order. Eastern institutions have money from oil transfers but limited access to Western engineering firms and export credit.

American participation also carries a reputational dividend that no amount of domestic spending provides. Being received as a partner is part of the product.

Tripoli is running the same play in parallel, hosting a Spanish trade mission this week and a Korean business forum later this month. Both administrations are courting the same shortlist.

The obstacles nobody announced

Contracting into a divided state is legally awkward. Which authority signs, which central bank pays and which court hears a dispute are unresolved questions rather than technicalities.

Sanctions exposure and compliance costs remain high for American firms. Reputational screening in Washington will be tougher than the welcome in Benghazi suggests.

Security is the third constraint. Libya’s roadmap between rival camps has been signed, but it has not yet produced a national government able to guarantee a contract for a decade.

Payment mechanics are the fourth. Oil revenue flows through institutions in Tripoli, and eastern projects have historically been funded through arrangements that Western auditors find difficult.

None of this stops memoranda being signed. It does explain why so few of Libya’s announced projects reach financial close.

What to watch next

The first measurable output is signed memoranda, and specifically whether any convert into financed projects rather than statements of intent. The 2025 edition produced little that has been built.

The second is whether US export credit or development finance takes a position. Private contractors will not lead without public risk cover in this market.

The third is Tripoli’s response. If the western administration secures a comparable American event, the reconstruction file becomes another arena of the same competition rather than a bridge across it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Libya United States forum? A development and reconstruction forum bringing Libyan and American officials, companies and development institutions together. The second edition opened in Benghazi on 5 September 2026. Where was the first edition held? In Washington, in April 2025. The Benghazi meeting is the first to convene inside Libya. What is on the agenda? Infrastructure and public works, energy and communications, modernisation of health and education, and economic diversification and capacity building. Why does the location matter? Libya’s institutions are divided, so hosting American delegations in Benghazi signals which authority is being treated as a working counterparty. Is Tripoli doing anything similar? Yes. A Spanish business mission visited Tripoli the same week and a Korean business forum is scheduled there this month.

World.title: Petrol in Antananarivo Passes 5,300 Ariary as the State Steps Back
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MADAGASCAR · ECONOMY

Key Facts —The move: From Saturday 5 September, a litre of SP95 petrol rose from 5,100 to 5,300 ariary, according to Moov.mg and Madagascar Tribune. —What did not move: Diesel stayed at 4,860 ariary a litre and kerosene at 3,710 ariary. Only petrol was adjusted this month. —Why now: The automatic price adjustment mechanism, restored in July, is running again after being suspended in April when international prices climbed. —The lapsed shield: The energy state of emergency adopted in August was not renewed, removing the cover that had held pump prices flat. —Who says so: Cydolain Raveloson, director general of the Office Malgache des Hydrocarbures, described the increase as a decision of the State. —The pattern: An earlier round in February raised prices by 130 to 190 ariary a litre, so this is the second significant step of the year. —The political temperature: Fuel is the most politically sensitive price in Madagascar, in a year that has already seen large youth-led protests.

Madagascar fuel prices rose on 5 September, taking SP95 petrol from 5,100 to 5,300 ariary a litre as the automatic adjustment mechanism resumed and August’s energy emergency was allowed to lapse. Diesel and kerosene were left unchanged.

What changed in Madagascar fuel prices this month

Only petrol moved. SP95 went from 5,100 to 5,300 ariary a litre on Saturday, a rise of 200 ariary, while diesel held at 4,860 and kerosene at 3,710.

The Office Malgache des Hydrocarbures publishes the maximum pump prices, and its director general said the increase was a decision of the State rather than an automatic calculation alone.

That distinction matters. It concedes that the mechanism operates with political discretion attached, which is exactly what motorists suspect.

The mechanism, suspended and restored

Madagascar operates an automatic adjustment formula that is meant to pass international product prices through to the pump. It was suspended in April when those prices climbed sharply.

It was restored in July, and August was then covered by an energy state of emergency that held prices flat. That emergency has not been renewed.

So the September increase is less a new policy than the removal of two successive cushions. The underlying cost had not gone away while the price was frozen.

Automatic mechanisms exist to depoliticise the pump, and they work only if governments let them run in both directions. Madagascar has now suspended and restored the same formula twice inside a year.

Each suspension teaches the market that the rule is provisional. That expectation gets priced into fuel importers’ terms long before it reaches the forecourt.

Why diesel was spared

Diesel is the freight and agricultural fuel. Raising it feeds directly into rice, transport and construction costs across the island within weeks.

Kerosene is the household fuel for lighting and cooking outside the grid, which covers most of the rural population. Both were politically expensive to touch.

Petrol falls disproportionately on urban private motorists and on the taxi-be minibus fleet in the capital. It is the least bad of three uncomfortable options.

That said, the taxi-be network carries a very large share of Antananarivo’s working population. A petrol rise is a commuting cost for people who do not own a vehicle.

Fare adjustments in the capital are negotiated rather than automatic, which usually produces a public argument and then a rise. The lag is where the hardship sits.

The fiscal arithmetic behind the decision

Holding pump prices below cost creates arrears to distributors, and those arrears eventually appear either in the budget or in fuel shortages at the pump.

Madagascar has been trying to keep an IMF-supported programme on track while managing a fragile electricity sector and a weak ariary. Fuel subsidies are the first line to be examined in that conversation.

The choice made this month is to take the smaller political cost now rather than the larger fiscal one later. That is the orthodox answer and it is rarely the popular one.

Madagascar imports all of its refined product, so every ariary of subsidy is ultimately a foreign-currency commitment. A weak local currency makes that commitment heavier each quarter.

The state electricity utility carries its own arrears on fuel for generation, which links the pump price to the reliability of the grid. The two problems are one problem.

A country already on edge

Madagascar has had a turbulent year, including youth-led protests that drew international attention and a photojournalism prize. Fuel prices were among the grievances.

The island is also reopening its mining register after sixteen years, which brings its own arguments about who benefits from resource revenue.

Against that background a 200 ariary rise is not a rounding error. It is a signal about who absorbs adjustment costs.

What to watch next

The first question is whether October brings a diesel adjustment. If the mechanism is genuinely running, that is the next uncomfortable step.

The second is the taxi-be fares in Antananarivo, which historically follow petrol within a month and are negotiated in public.

The third is whether the state of emergency returns. Reaching for it twice in a year would tell investors that the automatic mechanism is automatic only when prices fall.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Madagascar fuel prices rise? SP95 petrol rose from 5,100 to 5,300 ariary a litre on 5 September 2026, an increase of 200 ariary. Did diesel and kerosene change? No. Diesel remained at 4,860 ariary a litre and kerosene at 3,710 ariary. Why did prices rise now? The automatic price adjustment mechanism resumed after being restored in July, and the energy state of emergency adopted in August was not renewed. Who sets the prices? The Office Malgache des Hydrocarbures publishes maximum pump prices, and its director general said the increase was a decision of the State. Has this happened before this year? Yes. An earlier adjustment in February raised prices by between 130 and 190 ariary a litre.
