World.title: Ireland hails EU tax agreement on carbon imports and electronic waste
World.content:
The president of the European Council, António Costa, urged national leaders to home in on several potential taxes during their next gathering in Brussels on Oct. 15. Supporters argue that own resources are essential to generate more revenue and reduce national contributions to the EU from 2028 to 2034.

With less than four months to go until the informal deadline, the bloc's governments have shown openness towards a tax on foreign carbon imports, officially known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a separate levy on non-collected electronic waste.

“Of the Commission’s proposals for new Own Resources, the most consensual among Member States is CBAM, with many open to increasing the call rate further,” the Irish Council presidency, which is steering discussions, wrote in a note to EU governments seen by POLITICO.

Under current rules, capitals must funnel 75 percent of CBAM revenues to the EU budget, and retain 25 percent for their domestic budgets.

CBAM is expected to generate, on average, €1.644 billion per year, roughly adding up to €11.5 billion for the whole budget cycle, according to an updated estimate by the European Commission seen by POLITICO.

The Irish presidency also noted “a broad degree of support” among governments towards the electronic waste tax, which is expected to generate €17.9 billion per year. They added that criticism towards the levy largely focuses on statistical issues.

World.title: Renew MEPs to press Macron on his political future at Paris meeting
World.content:
A Renew official, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the meeting agenda, said lawmakers are growing particularly concerned about the prospect of far-right parties taking power in Germany and France, where Marine Le Pen has a commanding lead in the polls for the spring 2027 presidential race.

“Pro-Europeans … are worried about what happens after Macron because they recognize his vision and ambition for Europe,” said the official.

The burning question on everyone’s lips is what Macron, who cannot run for a third consecutive term, can and will do next. The 48-year-old has given little indication of his plans after he steps down in May 2027, but he has hinted at once again running for the presidency when he is eligible in 2032.

“Lawmakers will question the president on his political future, many would like to see him play a role at a European level,” said the Renew official.

But Macron has also indicated that he will focus on his role as French president until the very last day, raising fears he is not preparing the future of his centrist movement when he leaves office. Last May, he said he would “think about what comes next” after the end of his mandate.

The talks in Paris will also focus on the upcoming State of the Union speech by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the Multiannual Financial Framework, social media bans, European preference measures and Ukraine.

World.title: Bardella-Farage immigration deal faces backlash across French political spectrum
World.content:
Nigel Farage, right, joins Jordan Bardella onstage during the signing of a memorandum of understanding in Birmingham, England on Sept. 4, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

The agreement was blasted as a capitulation to British interests by much of the political class in France.

PARIS — French presidential candidates from the far left to the far right are blasting the memorandum of understanding on stopping migration across the English Channel that National Rally President Jordan Bardella signed with Reform U.K.’s Nigel Farage on Friday.

Critics of the deal, which says in English that France “will ordinarily accept” migrants intercepted in the English Channel and sent back to French shores, accused the far-right MEP of attempting to cede French sovereignty on immigration matters. The pact only goes into effect if Reform UK and the National Rally take power in the United Kingdom and France, respectively.

On X, Xavier Bertrand, the conservative president of the Hauts-de-France region that includes some of the most well-known launch points for the so-called “small boats” trying to reach the U.K. from France, accused Bardella of “bowing down” to Farage and wanting to make France the U.K.’s “subcontractor” on border enforcement.

World.title: EU to crack down on short-term rentals in bid to slash housing prices
World.content:
But those efforts have often triggered legal action. Homeowners and tourism operators sued Florence over its restrictions, and Airbnb challenged a €64 million fine imposed by Spain after authorities determined the platform was carrying illegal listings. Although courts ruled in favor of the city governments, the lawsuits nevertheless tied up local authorities in costly, protracted court battles.

Jørgensen said the new legislation would “give the possibility to local authorities which want to take action, to do so in a way that is effective and that does not expose them to litigation risks.” The commissioner rejected industry allegations that restrictions could hurt tourism-dependent economies and homeowners who depend on rental income, insisting that “housing is a right, not just a commodity” and “people need to come before profit.”

He also dismissed industry claims that the Commission is overreaching by legislating on housing, an area where the EU has limited direct competence. Jørgensen pointed out that, under the new plans, national, regional and local authorities will determine which areas are under housing stress and decide whether and how to intervene.

“The goal is not to impose restrictions from Brussels,” he said. “But housing affordability is one of Europe’s most pressing challenges and European institutions cannot be blind to the very concrete daily problems our citizens are facing.”

“If we fail to address this crisis, we risk losing our people’s trust in democratic institutions,” he added. “And that would lead to the rise of extremist political forces.”

The legislation comes almost one year after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the EU’s housing shortage as a “social crisis” and pledged to take action.

Jørgensen said the new act represented a “key step to support cities, regions and countries that want to bring immediate solutions to the areas and the people most affected,” but stressed that it was not a panacea.

“The housing crisis is a complex issue,” he said, adding that the bloc still needed to “act on investment, simplification of rules, supply and pressures on the existing housing stock.”

World.title: Merz to skip Macron’s space summit
World.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrives for the Christian Democratic Union's leadership meeting in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026. | Ralf Hirshberger/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is pulling out of a space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.

A spokesperson for Merz said Monday that he was canceling his trip because of his busy agenda this week, just hours after the chancellor’s party suffered a humiliating defeat at the hands of the far-right Alternative for Germany in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.

Merz is set to meet with with European Council President António Costa and speak at the Bundestag on Wednesday, while on Thursday he will have meetings with United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and with German diplomats.

World.title: Musk celebrates, Tusk despairs: How the world reacted to the AfD’s election win
World.content:
The AfD ultimately took 43.8 percent and 39 of 83 seats — three short of an outright majority — delivering its strongest-ever state election result and moving closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since World War II.

The result had the party’s allies around Europe exulting. Italy’s right-wing Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini congratulated his “friend” Weidel and declared: “Another Europe is possible.” Austrian far-right leader Herbert Kickl said voters had torn down the political “firewall” around the AfD, while Spain’s Vox leader Santiago Abascal wrote on X that the result was “a great hope for Germany and Europe.”

Hard-right Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe called the AfD “an inspiration.” Dutch far-right leader Geert Wilders also congratulated the party after the election results rolled in.

Notably, Britain’s preeminent populist-nationalist leader Nigel Farage had not publicly commented on the result as of Monday morning, with France’s far-right leaders Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella also remaining tight-lipped.

Mainstream shock

While Musk and Europe’s right rejoiced, centrist and left-wing heavyweights around the continent sounded the alarm.

French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs slammed the AfD as a “neo-Nazi, anti-European, pro-Putin” political force whose program is “a betrayal of the European spirit,” and called on “all those who refuse the poison of extremism” to “provide an urgent response” to voters’ cries of anger.

World.title: ‘Turning point for our country’: German mainstream reels after huge far-right win
World.content:
Saxony-Anhalt’s incumbent premier Sven Schulze, from the CDU, struck a more sober note on Sunday night. “Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say: That’s democracy,” he told ARD. “The people went to the polls today.”

The rout piles pressure on Merz, who once vowed to cut the AfD in half but has been chancellor while the far-right party has boomed in the polls.

Social Democratic Party co-leader Lars Klingbeil called the vote a “signal to Berlin” and said the result should prompt the federal government to reflect on its policies. Co-leader Bärbel Bas said the result was “frightening many people,” while Green co-chair Felix Banaszak described the AfD surge as “dramatic.”

The Left’s Heidi Reichinnek branded the result “catastrophic,” blaming federal government policies for creating fertile ground for the far right. But the CDU’s refusal to cooperate with The Left makes constructing an anti-AfD majority harder.

Left-populist BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht declared the “firewall policy” a failure in a post on X, warning another coalition built purely to exclude the AfD would be an “affront” to voters.

The AfD, meanwhile, claimed a mandate to govern. Co-leader Alice Weidel hailed a “historic result,” while fellow co-leader Tino Chrupalla declared: “Ulrich Siegmund will be our new minister-president,” referring to the party’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt.

World.title: Is the chancellor really a risk taker?
World.content:
Can the chancellor deliver growth without breaking his own self-imposed fiscal rules?

John Healey will set out his vision for the economy this morning, but with pressure mounting on the public finances, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy ask whether he is preparing to stretch the rules to make it happen.

Amid an increasingly turbulent economic backdrop, the duo examine the warning lights beginning to flash – from the rising cost of borrowing to the instability of mortgage rates – and what it could mean for households and the government’s room for manoeuvre.

Plus, as the AfD clinch victory in a German state election, Anne gives her take on where it all goes next.

World.title: Latvia bans Russian and Belarusian books, citing propaganda concerns
World.content:
Latvia has banned the import of books, newspapers and other printed materials from Russia and Belarus, citing "disinformation and war propaganda," its foreign ministry told AFP on Monday — a move with implications for how EU and NATO members handle information warfare from Moscow.

 

"The import ban is intended to protect Latvia's security interests and further reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus, which continue to wage and support (the) war of aggression against Ukraine," the ministry said.

Latvia, a NATO and EU member bordering both Russia and Belarus, has positioned itself firmly behind Kyiv since the 2022 invasion. Riga says it has faced sustained "hybrid attacks" from Moscow since the war began — a term covering cyberattacks, drone incursions and disinformation campaigns — and has invested heavily in security, believing it could become one of the Kremlin's next targets.

The country also has a significant Russian-speaking population, with around a quarter of Latvians identifying as ethnic Russian, according to official statistics.

The ban, in effect since 1 September, is the first of its kind imposed on Russian consumer goods anywhere in Europe. It also covers other goods including clothing, toys and sports equipment. Latvia's government said the aim was "strengthening the resilience of society and reducing vulnerabilities in the information space."

Overall imports from Russia and Belarus have fallen roughly 91% since the war began, the foreign ministry said — but books and printed materials remained one of the largest consumer import categories still flowing from Russia, as the ministry put it, having "constituted one of the largest remaining consumer goods import categories from Russia."

Latvia has already scrapped VAT incentives for Russian-language publishing domestically and moved to reduce Russian-language instruction in schools, citing the need to counter Kremlin interference and better integrate Russian-speaking residents.

The move comes against a backdrop of rising friction between Moscow and the Baltic states. In May, Russia signalled plans to take Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia to the International Court of Justice over alleged rights violations against Russian speakers — claims the three countries reject, instead accusing Moscow of exploiting an ethnic Russian minority that grew substantially during decades of Soviet occupation to stoke regional tensions.

World.title: Italy rail strike: Here's what passengers need to know
World.content:
Rail staff across Italy are set to strike from 9 pm on Monday, 7 September through to 9 pm on Tuesday, 8 September.

 

Passengers may also experience disruption in the hours leading up to the walkout and after it ends due to adjustments to the rail network.

Here's everything you need to know about the strike.

What to expect on regional trains

For passengers who rely on regional trains each day, there are guaranteed service periods, but outside of these hours, trains may be cancelled or disrupted.

On weekdays, guaranteed services operate from 6 am to 9 am and from 6pm to 9 pm.

Outside of these time slots, passengers face possible cancellations, delays and changes to routes across the national rail network.

Trenitalia has advised passengers to check the status of their service before travelling, either through the app or the official website.

High-speed services and Intercity trains are also affected by the strike, and unlike the regional trains, they are not covered by guaranteed service periods.

Passengers are therefore also advised to check on the status of their journey in advance.

How to get a ticket refund

Passengers can request a full refund, although the deadline for doing so varies depending on the type of service.

For Frecce and Intercity trains, refund requests can be made from the announcement of the strike up until the scheduled departure time of the train.

For regional trains, requests must be submitted by midnight on the day before the strike.

As an alternative to a refund, passengers can also reschedule their trip on another service under the same conditions, subject to seat availability.

The unions are striking to demand better working conditions, improved safety and better-organised shifts across the railway sector.

World.title: Preserving the past: Kyrgyzstan's World Nomad Games continues as new village brings history to life
World.content:
The World Nomad Games may be over for another year but the impact of the event is likely to echo throughout Central Asia for some time.

 

After the grand opening at Kyrgyzstan's Bishkek Arena, the games and more than 3,000 athletes from 110 nations moved to a lake-side venue in the Isyk Kul region, a popular tourist destination.

Traditional equestrian and archery skills filled every corner of the Kyrchyn Gorge, as competitors pitted their wits and strengths against each other, giving visitors a lookback in time travelling experience at an ancient style settlement.

Exhibition of handicraft Euronews

Village people

Each region of the Kyrgyz Republic built their own village by erecting age-old nomadic dwellings and yurts, all traditionally decorated.

Yurts - tent-like structures with wooden framework covered with felt, animal skins and heavy canvas - have been used by Asian nomadic tribes for millennia. A yurt houses a single nuclear family who can assemble and disassemble it in about half an hour, making it suitable for nomadic lifestyle.

Among the decorated yurts, people from all parts of Kyrgyzstan, dressed in traditional colourful costumes, displayed their works of folk art, alongside handicraft like embroidery and carpet-weaving.

During the first two days, more than 150,000 visitors were treated to traditional songs and folk tunes and offered the chance to taste national dishes often prepared right on the spot.

The attraction, named “The Universe of Nomads”, was opened with a theatrical performance on a hillside that included a dramatic village raid where horsemen and women amazed the crowds by showing off extremely impressive defensive riding skills.

Opening performance Euronews

At the opening, Kyrgyz Prime Minister Adylbek Kasymaliyev, said that the village would not be a one-off. The plan is for it to remain open as a tourist attraction and help educate visitors about the country's past.

“We do not preserve the heritage of our ancestors only behind the museum glass – we are bringing it back into the people’s lives. We build yurts today – that is a living heritage," said Kasymaliyev.

"We are raising shyrdaks, smelting metal, making horse tack – that is a living heritage. The craftsmanship of the father passes onto the son, the skills of the mother to the daughter,” he added.

Related World Nomad Games open in Bishkek before an audience of world leaders

Bone crush bonaza

Opposite the village, a reconstruction of an ancient fort houses a bazaar where one can enjoy the atmosphere of an ancient town bustling with activity and acrobats performing high jinks.

Right next to the fort, Nomad games athletes were engaged in archery and strength games, such as tug of war and arm-wrestling and the more unusual sport of bone crushing.

In this Mongolian and Central Asian popular game participants show their strength by breaking the back bones of animals (not live ones). It is frequent sight at festivals and folk fairs. This year, the Mongolian world champion managed to defend his title with 58 bones crushed in a minute.

Archer prepare to compete at the World Nomad Games in Bishkek, 3 September 2026 Euronews

Whille the World Nomad Games aim to promote nomadic heritage, culture and influence on different civilisations, they are usually accompanied by scientific and cultural events. This year, the highlight among dozens of such events was the International Scientific Conference “Nomadic Civilisations: Heritage, Paradigms and Prospects”.

“Nomadic civilisation represents a vast body of humanity’s historical experience, knowledge and cultural practices," said Gylzat Isamatova, Kyrgystan's Minister of High Education. "Today, its study is particularly relevant in the context of climate change, environmental challenges, the sustainable use of natural resources and the preservation of cultural heritage.”

World.title: Germany's shocking far-right surge rattles Europe's political foundations
World.content:
The radical-right Alternative for Germany's landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt region election may be the first real crack in the power structure that has held European politics together since the Second World War.

 

On Sunday, Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a resounding victory in the eastern German region, taking 43.8% of the vote. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the governing coalition in Berlin, collapsed to 17.2%, while its junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD), managed just 9.3%.

For the first time since the Nazi period, a German region could be led by a far-right force, as local leader Ulrich Siegmund could become president if the far-left party BSW decides to support him or to abstain in the election.

Beyond dealing a further blow to an already deeply unpopular government in Berlin, the results drew mixed reactions across Europe, with far-right forces eager to capitalise as key EU states head to the polls next year.

"This result is not an outlier - it is a signal to the rest of Germany and to Europe," René Aust, the head of the AfD delegation to the European Parliament, told Euronews.

"We are on course to become the country's leading governing party, and I am convinced that at the next European elections we will return to the European Parliament with more than twice our current strength," Aust said.

European repercussions

"The region Saxony-Anhalt is a small part of Germany. 1 out of 16 regions," Andreas Schwab (Germany/EPP) said, playing down the impact of the vote. "The [AfD] party has no real power in Berlin, where the great coalition has a clear majority."

For Schwab, the vote's impact in Brussels will likely be limited to reinforcing the EU's simplification agenda — cutting red tape, including for farmers — and pushing for a more nationally oriented EU budget.

Svenja Hahn (Germany/Renew) echoed that view. "We can only hold up a democratic majority in 2029 by finally delivering on economic growth and prosperity and taking the regulatory burden off of people and businesses," she said.

Still, the result is bound to raise alarm bells across Europe, not just for its impact on German domestic politics, butbecause Germany’s grand-coalition tradition provided a foundation for the political consensus at the heart of European integration for much of the postwar era.

The centre-right European People's Party (EPP) and centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) have been the linchpin of Brussels politics since the European Parliament was created, at times with the support of the centrist Renew Europe group.

But the rise of extremist parties and the steady erosion of the political centre is now calling that approach — born in Germany, exported to Brussels — into question. Last month, Europe Elects projected that the three centrist forces would, for the first time, fail to secure an absolute majority if European Parliament elections were held today.

"It is no more about who can speak with whom and how different factions of democratic society can unite. It is about how to get their joint share larger, not by stealing the electorate from one another, but by convincing those who are disappointed by all of us, democrats," MEP Sergey Lagodinsky (Germany/Greens-EFA) told Euronews.

Far-right into power

The AfD's growing electoral gains across Europe have raised the prospect that far-right parties could enter government outright. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell short of a majority to govern alone but could reach one in coalition with the BSW.

How much power-sharing traditional parties allow has depended on national context, and on whether mainstream forces are willing to ally with the far right.

In Italy, for instance, Giorgia Meloni has steered her coalition government towards the centre, making her European party, the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), increasingly mainstream. As a result, she now faces competition from a new far-right force led by Roberto Vannacci (Italy/ESN), a former army general turned MEP.

In Spain, the centre-right Popular Party has partnered with the hard-right Vox to govern several regions, including Andalusia and Castilla y León, a model some would like to see exported to Brussels.

"In each country, it really depends on how radical the far right is and how much there can be any kind of collaboration. But, in general, collaboration with the far right was not good for us. We have stayed weak," MEP Hildegard Bentele (Germany/EPP) told Euronews.

Within the European Parliament, the EPP group led by the Bavarian Manfred Weber has throughout this legislative term kept a flexible approach to forming variable majorities, at times seeking support from hard-right parties over specific files.

While Weber's strategy has strengthened the EPP's negotiating hand and drawn the ire of other centrist forces, moving from case-by-case alignment to a more structural alliance would entail a fundamental reshaping of power-sharing at the EU level.

As of now, Weber has always excluded structured cooperation with far-right forces, while some parties forming the EPP have often wished for it.

Elections loom

In 2027, voters in France, Italy, Poland, Spain, Estonia, Greece, Finland, Malta and Slovenia will all go to the polls in high-stakes national elections. In France, in particular, far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is projected to win against any other candidate in the run-off.

These upcoming elections will reshape Europe's political landscape ahead of the next EU elections in 2029, which, if current trends hold, could be the first not to hand mainstream parties a governing majority.

"[The Saxony-Anhalt election] It's a very strong warning signal, but we have three years ahead of elections, so we have a lot of time to become stronger again. The warning signal is out. We have to work on our own strengths," Bentele said.

Bentele drew two main lessons from the results: the need to mobilise people who had not voted in the last elections — the main driver of the AfD's surge — and the need to choose better-suited candidates.

Meanwhile, Aust noted that only voters over 70 kept the AfD from securing an absolute majority at the regional level, which he considers clear evidence that the future belongs to patriotic forces and that the CDU will soon become "the party of yesterday," as was the case for Democrazia Cristiana in Italy.

For Lagodinsky, the challenge ahead is nothing less than restoring disappointed voters' faith in liberal democracy. "If we don't get our act together on that, our democracy is doomed," he concluded.

World.title: UN rights chief warns how AI could pose ‘existential risk to humanity’
World.content:
The United Nations human rights chief has warned that advanced artificial intelligence could pose an “existential risk to humanity”, calling for immediate action to make the technology safer.

 

Addressing the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Volker Türk said people faced “unfamiliar, even unprecedented” threats to their rights.

"The need for AI governance is widely acknowledged, but where is the action?" he asked, warning that "delay only benefits the massive tech companies, their owners and enablers".

Türk said that “a handful of men has almost unlimited power over AI, which we are repeatedly told has unimaginable computing capacity”.

“They talk about freedom, but on closer inspection, this turns out to be little more than the freedom to exploit our data,” he said.

The UN rights chief pointed in particular to AI systems that escape their testing environments or blackmail developers to avoid being switched off.

According to AFP, Turk warned in particular that "AI that escapes its testing environment or blackmails developers to prevent itself from being turned off, is AI that is too powerful".

His comments appeared to refer partly to revelations in July that OpenAI agents had escaped supposedly controlled environments and gained access to servers belonging to Hugging Face, a widely used platform where developers share AI software.

OpenAI later said the agents had executed code on dozens of Hugging Face servers and gained full access to one of them.

The incident renewed calls for tighter oversight of advanced AI systems.

Anthropic, Meta and other technology companies have reported similar incidents involving agents during testing.

“I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity,” Türk said.

“I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late.”

Calls for international safeguards

The UN rights chief said he would write to AI companies in the coming days, urging them to take immediate steps to reduce the risks within their control.

At a minimum, he said, "we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines".

Related How the EU AI Act is reshaping company rules from Washington to Tokyo

“We need independent verification, and much stronger collaboration on security within the industry,” Türk added.

"We also need to consider the human rights impacts of AI on employment practices, on fundamental principles of democracy, and on our environment," he said.

In the European Union, the AI Act provides a legal framework for AI.

Under the law, high-risk systems have to meet strict requirements before they can enter the EU market, while uses considered an unacceptable threat to people’s safety or rights are banned.

The law prohibits AI designed to manipulate or exploit people, score them based on their behaviour, predict whether an individual will commit a crime, or indiscriminately collect images to build facial-recognition databases.

It also prohibits emotion recognition at work and in schools, some forms of biometric profiling and most real-time police facial recognition in public places, while a ban on AI-generated sexual images made without consent and child sexual abuse material takes effect in December 2026.

World.title: Rescuers search rubble for survivors after New Delhi hostel collapse kills seven
World.content:
Search and rescue teams combed through the debris of a collapsed hostel building in the Indian capital New Delhi as the death toll climbed to seven, officials said on Monday.

 

The five-storey building, which housed a boys’ hostel, collapsed on Sunday in Satya Niketan, a densely populated neighbourhood known for its private student accommodations near a Delhi University campus.

Police, firefighters and crews from India’s disaster response agency continued their search for a second day as earthmovers cleared debris and sniffer dogs worked the site to help rescuers reach those still trapped inside.

Rescue crews pulled at least 12 people from under the rubble, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta told reporters at the site on Monday.

About 80% of the debris had been cleared and only rubble from the basement remained, she said, adding that six people died and six others were injured in the incident.

Later Monday, rescuers recovered a body, raising the death toll to seven, officials said.

Rescue workers continue to search for people trapped under the debris of a collapsed building in New Delhi, 7 September, 2026 AP Photo

According to residents, the building was at least 55 years old and had been under renovation for months before reopening to tenants, mostly students, in August despite work remaining unfinished.

Prakash Chand, a resident, said labourers were in the basement carrying out digging work when the building collapsed.

Preliminary findings suggest water accumulation in the basement and ongoing repair work on the aging building may have caused the collapse, Gupta said.

She said the government will draft a policy requiring periodic structural audits and safety certificates for buildings used by the public, including student accommodations, nursing homes and schools.

“No public activity will be permitted” in buildings that fail to comply, Gupta said.

After Gupta’s visit, police arrested the building owner and filed a case against him. Authorities also suspended at least five municipal employees responsible for building safety oversight in the area, the Press Trust of India news agency reported.

Building collapses are a recurring hazard in parts of India during the June-to-September monsoon season, when heavy or prolonged rain can weaken older structures.

World.title: Paris flight searches surge ahead of Céline Dion's comeback concerts
World.content:
We’re just days away from Céline Dion’s major return to the stage after a six-year hiatus from the spotlight, and fans have been busy planning trips to see the star in one of her favourite cities.

 

Paris is proving increasingly popular with international travellers ahead of Dion’s upcoming residency, with new data from Amadeus Travel Intelligence showing an 11% surge in international flight searches to the French capital compared to last year.

Searches from the Americas are driving much of this demand. The US accounts for 26.5% of searches, followed by Brazil at 11% and Canada at 7.4%, together almost representing 45% of global search traffic growth to Paris in the run up to her performances.

The “My Heart Will Go On” singer has described Paris as her “second home” and is set to take the stage at La Defense Arena for 16 concerts in September and October this year, where she will perform her French and English hits. She will then return in May 2027 for a further 10 shows.

In Asia-Pacific markets, the “Céline effect” has seen bookings from Thailand grow by 200% compared to the same period last year, while bookings from Japan have grown by 40%. Other regional markets with a notably greater appetite for Paris travel include Australia, South Korea and India.

Meanwhile, in Europe, travellers account for 26.5% of all searches to Paris during the residency dates, with Italy, Spain and the UK among the markets showing the strongest interest.

The Amadeus data also found that flight bookings are up, too, citing a 5% boost led by the Americas, especially US, Brazilian, Canadian and Mexican travellers.

In Europe, however, searches don’t seem to be translating to actual bookings. The travel analytics platform found Europe taking just a 5% share of booking to Paris, with the majority coming from would-be Spanish and Italian travellers.

The singer’s residency is driving search and booking demand to the French capital AP Photo

Even closer to home, eight out of the top 10 domestic bookings to Paris during Dion’s dates hail from Toulouse, Nice and Ajaccio in Corsica. Bookings from southern France accounted for nearly 79%, Amadeus said, adding that bookings from the Corsican cities of Bastia and Ajaccio show a 55% and 35% year-on-year growth, respectively, during Dion’s residency.

In what Amadeus dubs the “culture tripping” trend of pop culture being at the heart of travel plans, it also points to Dion’s concerts as being a potential factor driving demand for longer hotel stays. It cited hotel data, which pointed to a 6% spike in medium-length stays of six to 13 nights.

Earlier research by Natixis CIB expects her 16 dates this autumn to attract 480,000 spectators to the French capital.

Across spending on tickets, accommodation, transport and dining, Natixis projects that the “impact of Céline Dion's concerts on activity is estimated between €570 million and nearly €1billion in 2026, with a big impact for the Île de France region”.

World.title: Can tech giants curb AI data centres’ growing thirst for water?
World.content:
AI’s boom has a water problem.

 

Data centres are facing growing public anger in the United States over the amount of water and electricity they use. The technology giants spending billions of dollars on them say the water problem, at least, can be addressed.

Data centres are warehouses filled with computer servers that power the internet and, increasingly, artificial intelligence.

Those computers generate heat, and keeping them cool can require large amounts of water.

Data centres worldwide consumed 222 billion litres (59 billion gallons) of water for cooling in 2025, according to consultancy Rystad Energy.

Without measures to reduce consumption, that figure could nearly triple to 644 billion litres by 2030, Rystad estimates. It says steps to curb water use could keep the increase below 100%.

US chipmaker Nvidia said in a report published in June that its newest system for designing and managing AI data centres, known as DSX, could almost eliminate water consumption at some facilities.

It is a bold claim – and one the industry is under growing pressure to deliver on.

Nvidia’s system uses closed-loop cooling, with liquid flowing directly through servers and as close as possible to the chips, which can reach temperatures above 80°C (176°F).

But reducing water consumption can come at a cost.

“There’s a pretty direct trade-off between how much water is used and how much energy is used” to control temperatures, Andy Masley, an independent researcher covering AI and data centres, said.

Using less water usually requires more electricity because the liquid circulating through sealed pipes still has to be cooled, often by blowing air over it.

Nvidia gets around some of this by letting the liquid enter the servers warmer than usual, at 45C.

Most other closed-loop systems ran at about 32°C in 2024, according to the Uptime Institute, which certifies data centres.

By starting with warmer water, Nvidia does not need to pump in cooled air year-round.

"Simple fans circulating the air" are often enough, though sometimes a mix of methods is needed, Josh Parker, Nvidia's head of sustainability, said.

At sites in extremely hot climates, or during heatwaves, chilled air or evaporative cooling may still be needed.

Public pressure over water use

Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Meta told AFP that they also use closed-loop cooling systems, which they said do not result in any net water loss.

Microsoft and AWS, two of the world’s largest cloud-computing companies, used more water overall between 2022 and 2025 as they expanded their data-centre operations.

However, their water-use efficiency improved by 25% at Microsoft and 37% at AWS, according to their latest sustainability reports.

Comparisons are difficult because there is no industry-wide standard governing how companies report their environmental, social and governance efforts.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which became a major data-centre operator after acquiring his artificial intelligence company xAI, has never published an ESG report.

In June, ratings agency MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG score.

"Because water is generally much cheaper than electricity," companies have less incentive to cut water use on cost grounds alone, Shaolei Ren, an engineering professor at the University of California, Riverside, said.

“There are incentives,” Ren said, adding that these are driven more by public relations as opposition to data centres grows across the United States.

Another problem is the cost of upgrading older data centres with newer technology that uses less water.

However, older facilities are generally smaller and less powerful than the enormous data centres now being built, meaning they require less cooling in the first place, according to Minh K. Le, who leads research on data centres and hydrogen at Rystad Energy.

The water used directly by data centres is also only part of their overall footprint.

Water is also required to generate the electricity that powers them and to manufacture their chips and servers.

In the United States, this indirect water use can be twice as high as the amount consumed by data centres themselves.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
World.content:
Leaked addresses and phone numbers have reignited fears among Hindu government employees who returned to Muslim-majority Kashmir under a rehabilitation scheme.

A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits — members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s — has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme.

The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their Jammu residential addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers.

Personal details exposed

"Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media," Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak.

The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan-based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters' authenticity or the existence of the group behind them.

The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore "safe" — and those recruited under New Delhi's rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for "masters" outside Kashmir.

The fresh threats have also triggered a political row.

Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a "conspiracy" aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019.

Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats.

His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community's fears.

Familiar fears

Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu.

For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem.

Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns.

"Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing," Tickoo told DW. He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees' personal details.

"How are these details being posted on social media?" Tickoo asked.

Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022.

One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022.

The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district.

Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook.

"There is nothing new in this," Vaid told DW, calling it "a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society." He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley.

The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been so easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided.

Kashmir: Fears dampen celebrations at Hindu festival To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The return dilemma

The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir.

But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging.

Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of "Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir," said the government's record on rehabilitation was inadequate.

"The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus," Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.

Some land has been returned and cases of killings investigated, he said, but "it is too little and too late."

Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return.

"No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return," he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region, Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted.

"It's for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk," he said.

Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said.

"That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley," he said.

Pandits accuse the government in New Delhi of not doing enough to protect them from alleged Islamist threats Image: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Security beyond protection

Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox.

"Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential," Barve told DW.

She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir's statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region.

Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified.

"The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice," Mattoo told DW.

"A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties."

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
World.content:
09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference

In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state.

Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.

Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.

Weidel said Chancellor Friedrich Merz had become "a major burden" on Germany Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.

Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.

After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.

After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.

Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.

Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."

Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.

"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."

World.title: Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea
World.content:
Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River as political, economic and military ties between the two countries deepen.

Russia and North Korea on Monday cut the ribbon on the first road bridge linking the two countries as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen their strategic partnership.

The crossing spans the Tumen River and marks another expansion of transport links between the two countries.

Where is the new bridge?

The road crossing is near the existing Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge commissioned in 1959 following the Korean War.

Russia and North Korea already have direct rail and air connections, but until now there had been no road bridge between them.

The new bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life. Relatives of Novichenko attended the opening ceremony.

Nikolai Shcherbitsky and Tatyana Shcherbitskaya joined the ceremony to unveil the bridge named after their grandfather and father respectively Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance

Construction began in April 2025 after the project was agreed during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.

Why is the road bridge being opened now?

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the new crossing should boost economic development, tourism and employment.

"I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," the TASS news agency quoted Mishustin as saying by video link at the opening ceremony.

Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened considerably since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

North Korea sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion launched in 2024.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?
World.content:
Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without a majority?

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in this eastern German state quite difficult.

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund announced on public broadcaster ARD: "As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround." At the same time, he acknowledged that there are currently no political parties that he considers suitable for a coalition government.

Above all, he was referring to the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds power in coalitions both in Saxony-Anhalt and on the federal level in Germany. Siegmund, along with the entire AfD leadership, has characterized the CDU's policy of refusing to work with the AfD a failure.

On public broadcaster ZDF, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel sharply criticized the CDU for stonewalling the AfD: "The CDU will not win another election — not a federal election. And this clearly gives the AfD a mandate to govern. Because we are democrats, we do not refuse to work with others."

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me." Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.

The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: it has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an ARD interview that these issues are non-negotiable.

Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.

AfD: Saxony-Anhalt result will 'shake all of Germany' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel told ZDF television: "Who ultimately forms the government — perhaps through a tolerance agreement or even a coalition — remains to be seen."

On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."

Could the BSW help the AfD form a government?

The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), should it manage to move into the state parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

Take, for example, Oliver Kirchner, co-chair of the AfD caucus in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt: "If we end up behind the lectern as the opposition, it will be brutal for the others," he warned during an AfD livestream.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Middle East: Israeli strikes kill several in Lebanon
World.content:
09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case

Germany's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel, should be thrown out.

The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted."

Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

"Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges.

Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings.

It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court.

Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law.

"Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said.

The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza, where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year.

However, Germany only instituted this policy in 2025, and continued to ship defensive equipment worth hundreds of millions of euros this year.

World.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says war looks set to go on into winter
World.content:
09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 Zelenskyy says Russian drone targeted SBU chief's office

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that a Russian drone which struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday had been aimed directly at the office of the agency's chief.

The revelation adds to the significance of one of the most high-profile Russian strikes on a Ukrainian government building since the start of the full-scale invasion.

SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad was not there at the time and was unharmed.

Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to prepare an "appropriate, tangible response" and suggested Ukraine could retaliate in a similar manner.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike a "major escalation."

Black smoke was seen rising from the SBU building, close to the UNESCO-listed St. Sophia Cathedral.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 12 people were wounded in the wider attack on the capital, although it was not immediately clear whether any of them were injured at the SBU headquarters.

The strike also damaged nearby buildings and shattered windows in the area.

It was the first time the SBU headquarters had been hit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

The SBU plays a central role in Ukraine's war effort and has carried out long-range and covert operations against Russian military targets. It was behind Operation Spiderweb in 2025, when drones targeted Russian strategic bombers at air bases deep inside Russia, as well as the 2022 bombing of the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

World.title: UK government condemns 'thuggish' anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
World.content:
Hundreds gathered in Portsmouth after some refugees arrived by boat from France, a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at the port of Dover.

British minister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth.

Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported.

"This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control.

The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port.

Masked protesters in Dover

On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups, in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."

The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port.

Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France, although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year.
