Villar acknowledged that hospitals must remain financially sustainable and have the right to collect valid debts, but stressed that financial considerations should not take precedence over a patient’s freedom and dignity. /atm

World.title: Marcos calls for job-focused education amid skills shortages
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. —AFP file photo

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Monday called on schools and businesses to ensure that education and training programs equip Filipinos with skills that match the needs of a changing labor market.

He said this during his visit to Lipa-Malvar Estate, Batangas State University (BSU) LIMA Campus, in Malvar and Lipa City, Batangas.

His visit also marks the 1st Anniversary of JERA-Aboitiz Power Global Technical Center of Excellence (GTCOE).

Article continues after this 

READ: Zero funding for DepEd’s Aral Program under 2027 NEP

“Our people deserve the skills that allow them to find meaningful work, build careers, and contribute to the growth of our economy and our country. At the same time, education should also address the needs of our industries and demands of our society,” Marcos said.

“The challenge before us is clear: As our industries evolve, we must ensure that our people are equipped to grow with them,” he also said.

Marcos cited a 2021 study by the Asian Development Bank, which revealed that around a third of college graduates are employed in jobs that are designed specifically for those with non-college education.

The same study said two-thirds of technical-vocational education and training graduates are employed in occupations unrelated to the expected outcomes of their training programs.

Article continues after this 

Additionally, the labor force surveys show the prevalence of hard-to-fill occupations, which Marcos said signals a skills shortage.

“These figures call on us to bring education and training closer to the needs of our industries, and to better prepare our people for the opportunities that lay ahead,” he said.

Article continues after this 

The BSU LIMA Campus was established on June 19, 2025, in partnership with Aboitiz Infracapital Economic Estates, which donated 10 hectares of land within the LIMA Estate to the BSU for the development of its new engineering and technology campus.

The GTCOE, meanwhile, which celebrates its first anniversary, is a technical training facility for engineers and technical professionals in the power sector located at the LIMA Commercial Center in the LIMA estate. /gsg

World.title: LTO revokes license of driver of Torre’s vehicle over plate misuse
World.content:
INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Office (LTO) on Monday announced that it had revoked the license of the driver of the vehicle owned by Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) General Manager Nicolas Torre III.

A video-recorded incident showed the driver operating the vehicle bearing MMDA markings and identifiers, including a body number, siren, and blinker.

“However, an LTO verification found that the vehicle’s license plate did not match its records and that the SUV was registered as a private vehicle,” the LTO said.

Article continues after this 

A show cause order was issued against the driver on Aug. 28, and in a Sept. 4 order, the LTO imposed a one-year suspension of his driver’s license after declaring him an “Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle.”

READ: MMDA: Torre admitted to owning vehicle that passed through Edsa busway

But the investigation found that the same driver was also involved in another incident involving the same vehicle, prompting the LTO to issue another show cause order.

The LTO confirmed that the driver involved in the first incident was also operating the vehicle when the second incident occurred.

The incidents pointed to repeated violations and misrepresentation involving the vehicle’s use and unauthorized markings and identifiers.

Article continues after this 

“As a result, the LTO declared the driver an ‘Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle’ and ultimately revoked his driver’s license,” the LTO said.

Meanwhile, the MMDA-marked SUV remains impounded at the LTO Central Office.

Article continues after this 

LTO chief and Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao said, “Regardless of your rank, position or office, if you violate traffic laws, I will not let it pass.”

“We in government clearly understand the law. Let us follow it, do what is right and be responsible on the road,” he pointed out. /mcm

World.title: Romualdez suffers from ‘cardiovascular event, panic attack’ – Remulla
World.content:
Former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez. Videograb from the official Facebook page of Martin Romualdez

MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez suffered a “cardiovascular event” and a purported panic attack, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Monday night.

Romualdez was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City around 4 p.m. on Monday, Remulla said in an interview with reporters.

“According to the doctors, he’s suffered from a cardiovascular event. His blood pressure was unstable and he was having an anxiety attack,” Remulla explained.

Article continues after this 

READ: Martin Romualdez arrested

“The Philippine National Police’s doctors are here to determine his status in conference with his doctors,” he added.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered the Leyte 1st District representative taken into government custody.

Romualdez was charged by the Office of the Ombudsman before the Sandiganbayan on Monday for allegedly receiving P7.44 billion worth of kickbacks from flood control, infrastructure and other government projects from 2022 to 2025.

“We will check every day until he is well enough to be presented to the court,” Remulla said.

Article continues after this 

“We assure you, he cannot hide behind his wealth. No matter how rich he is, he cannot pay the law to allow him to stay in a place of this caliber. This isn’t a permanent situation,” he added.

“His room in Payatas is just waiting if the court commits him. The fight is fair here,” he stressed, referring to the New Quezon City Jail, where other personalities allegedly involved in the infrastructure corruption scandal have been jailed.

Article continues after this 

Remulla did not say when Romualdez would undergo booking procedures.

This is a developing story. /mcm

World.title: Sara Duterte trial: Ridon says senator-judges aren’t being influenced
World.content:
Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon — Screengrab from House of Representatives/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said Monday that senator-judges will decide Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment case based solely on evidence, rejecting her claim that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. controls the Senate.

Ridon made the pronouncement after Duterte earlier issued a statement claiming that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. controls the Senate, court judges, the police, and fiscal matters.

READ: Duterte trial Day 22: PSA official to testify on CF payees’ identities

Article continues after this 

“We have high regard for our senator-judges: We trust that they will make decisions based solely on evidence,” he said.

“They are not influenced by anyone, and contrary to the Vice President’s view, they are not controlled by anyone,” he added.

Duterte is currently facing the Senate impeachment court amid allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and grave threats.

Much like in the impeachment complaint against her, Duterte was also recently ordered arrested by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Friday for three counts of grave threats stemming from alleged threats she made during a November 2024 virtual press conference against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then-House Speaker and presidential cousin Martin Romualdez.

She has since posted bail of P120,000 for each count. /mcm

World.title: World Nomad Games: Where Sport Meets Spirit of Steppe
World.content:
ASTANA – The sixth World Nomad Games (WNG) came to a close in the Kyrgyz Republic on Sept. 6, leaving a lasting impression on athletes, visitors, volunteers and everyone who helped bring the event to life.

For six days, the games were filled with color, energy and the competitive spirit of athletes determined to win, while upholding one of the most important values of sport – respect for their opponents. Beyond the medals and victories, the event offered a powerful reminder that nomadic culture is not simply a chapter of the past. It remains an important part of the region’s identity, roots and living heritage.

From the horse races and wrestling arenas to eagle hunting and kok boru, the games brought centuries-old traditions into the present, giving thousands of participants and visitors a chance to experience the spirit of the steppe firsthand.

Kazakhstan finished the WNG with 74 medals, including 32 gold, 20 silver and 22 bronze, reported the Kazakh Ministry of Culture and Sports.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Kazakhstan’s national team on its performance, saying the results reflected the athletes’ dedication, hard work and determination.

Tokayev expressed gratitude to the medalists, coaches and specialists who contributed to Kazakhstan’s strong showing and helped strengthen the country’s international standing as a center for the development of traditional sports.

Experiencing the spirit of the games

Beyond the sporting results, the games also offered visitors and participants an opportunity to experience nomadic culture and traditional sports.

For Kazakh volunteer Miras Yauda, the games were an unforgettable experience.

“Every day, we were at the heart of the events, watching teams compete across various sports. We felt the spirit of nomadic culture, saw the genuine interest of foreign visitors and shared in victories that left no one indifferent,” Yauda told The Astana Times.

He also highlighted the high level of preparation and skill demonstrated by the athletes.

Among the events he watched were eagle hunting and archery, where Kazakh athletes competed for the top honors.

“It was spectacular. I got goosebumps when I heard that our athletes had won gold. It is important to showcase our nomadic heritage and draw attention to our traditional sports,” he said.

World-famous Japanese blogger Yuji Beleza also attended the games and paid particular attention to kok boru (a martial equestrian art of the Kyrgyz people) matches.

Speaking to local media, Beleza said the competition in the Kyrgyz Republic appeared more intense than what he had seen previously, while describing it as entertaining and energetic.

Beleza had previously watched kok boru at the fifth WNG in Astana in 2024, but this was his first time attending the event in the Kyrgyz Republic.

He said he enjoyed the local atmosphere and the energy of the fans and strongly recommended experiencing kok boru live at least once.

The U.S. kok boru players attending the games also highlighted the welcoming atmosphere, strong fan support and significance of the event.

“This is my first time here, and I can see how strong these athletes are. For me, lifting a goat is difficult, yet even children here can do it using the proper technique. I am learning from everyone and am grateful for this experience,” said U.S. athlete Jason Speta.

Held in the Kyrgyz Republic from Aug. 31 to Sept. 6, the games brought together about 3,000 athletes from 113 countries, making the 2026 edition the largest in the history of the competition.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks For New Deposits as Expert Points to Investment Challenge Beyond Exploration
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to increase exploration drilling over the next three years, with up to 200 exploration and appraisal wells expected to be drilled by 2028. While the expansion could help replenish the country’s resource base, experts say the real challenge will be turning geological discoveries into economically viable projects.

Speaking at the KAZDRILLING conference in Atyrau, Vice Minister of Energy Yerlan Akbarov said exploration and appraisal drilling could reach around 80 wells in 2026 and increase to up to 120 wells annually in 2027–2028, reported the Ministry of Energy on Sept. 7.

The government sees higher drilling activity as necessary to identify new deposits and replenish Kazakhstan’s hydrocarbon resource base. The plans come as Kazakhstan seeks to increase geological exploration while also developing the domestic drilling and oilfield services sector.

More drilling targets underexplored basins

Particular attention is being given to relatively underexplored sedimentary basins that are considered to have significant oil and gas potential. The government has also simplified the process for allocating such areas. Following submission of an application, the Ministry of Energy is to hold an auction within 10 working days.

The work programs for selected areas require seismic surveys covering at least 30% of the relevant block during the first three years, followed by the drilling of exploration wells. This approach is intended to accelerate the movement from identifying prospective areas to obtaining more concrete geological data.

However, the number of wells drilled will not by itself determine whether the programme succeeds.

Discovery is only the beginning

For investors, the key distinction is between identifying a resource and establishing that it can support a commercially viable project.

“Much work is being done by companies to find these resources, but this is only the beginning of the journey,” said Nurlan Saurambayev, the managing partner of Aurin Capital, an investment and strategic advisory firm focused on mining and natural resources in Kazakhstan.

For a discovered resource to become a developed project, reserves need to be confirmed, appropriate extraction and processing technologies identified, and infrastructure requirements addressed to establish whether the project is feasible. He stressed that this process requires more than geological expertise.

“Mining projects are long-term and capital-intensive, so they need to be implemented sequentially: geological exploration, resource assessment, technological studies, engineering, financing and construction,” Saurambayev said.

Skipping stages in this chain can lead to incorrect investment decisions, capital losses and other risks, according to the expert.

The point is particularly relevant as Kazakhstan increases exploration activity. A larger number of discoveries can strengthen the country’s resource base, but it does not necessarily translate into a proportional increase in production, exports or government revenues.

The economic value of a discovery ultimately depends on whether companies can demonstrate that the resource can be extracted and processed at a competitive cost and supported by the necessary infrastructure and financing.

Domestic drilling industry expected to benefit

Alongside exploration, the government is seeking to increase the share of domestic companies and equipment in the drilling industry. Kazakhstan already has manufacturing capabilities in the sector. The Atyrau-based Zhigermunaıservis plant, for example, produces drill bits, stabilizers and other drilling equipment.

The development of local suppliers could allow the expected increase in drilling activity to generate benefits beyond the discovery of new reserves, including demand for domestic equipment, services and skilled workers.

“Our task is to create a sustainable and competitive market for drilling services,” Akbarov said. “The result should be new geological discoveries, replenishment of reserves, development of domestic production, creation of qualified jobs and increased tax revenues.”

The extent to which those benefits materialize will depend partly on whether domestic companies can develop capabilities that remain competitive as exploration and production projects become more technically demanding.

Critical minerals add another dimension

The exploration push also has implications beyond oil and gas. Kazakhstan is seeking to expand exploration for critical and rare-earth minerals as global demand for materials used in energy, technology and advanced manufacturing increases. Saurambayev said the country has an opportunity to strengthen its position in global value chains, but stressed that geological resources alone are insufficient.

“It is possible, but the presence of resources alone is not enough,” he said. “It is necessary to develop processing and move up the value chain where economically justified.”

That would require technologies, capital, infrastructure and experienced project teams, he said.

Kazakhstan’s expanded drilling programme could provide the geological foundation for future production, but there is a considerable distance between a promising well and a functioning industrial project.

For hydrocarbons, this means establishing commercial reserves and production potential. For critical minerals, the challenge can be even broader, extending from exploration and resource assessment to beneficiation, processing and access to markets.

World.title: Kazakhstan Enters Top 50 Most Peaceful Countries As Global Peacefulness Declines, Report Shows
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked 44th among 163 countries in the 2026 Global Peace Index (GPI), placing it among the world’s 50 most peaceful countries and reflecting an improvement from the previous year as Central Asia continues to diverge from a broader global decline in peacefulness.

Kazakhstan recorded a score of 1.771 points, improving from 1.791 in 2025 and marking the country’s best result since 2008. It was also the second consecutive year in which Kazakhstan improved its own GPI score.

Among Central Asian countries, Kazakhstan ranked second after Uzbekistan, which placed 37th with a score of 1.726. Tajikistan ranked 47th (1.799), the Kyrgyz Republic 61st (1.853) and Turkmenistan 66th (1.903).

All five Central Asian countries were classified by the Institute for Economics & Peace (IEP) as having a high level of peacefulness. Three – Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan – entered the global top 50. Kazakhstan was ranked between Uruguay and Romania, and ahead of Armenia, Greece and South Korea.

Central Asia moves against global trend

The regional results stand out against the overall deterioration recorded by the index. The global average level of peacefulness deteriorated by 0.7% over the past year, marking the 12th consecutive year of decline. Of the 163 countries covered by the index, 99 became less peaceful while only 62 improved. A total of 119 countries are now less peaceful than they were in 2008.

Eastern Europe and Central Asia were the only one of the eight GPI regions to record an improvement in average peacefulness. The other seven regions deteriorated, with South Asia experiencing the most significant decline.

The long-term trend is also favorable for Central Asia. Over the past decade, GPI scores have improved in all five countries. In 2016, Uzbekistan had a score of 1.911, Tajikistan 1.971, the Kyrgyz Republic 1.984, Kazakhstan 1.883 and Turkmenistan 1.979. The most substantial improvements over the period were recorded in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

The progress, however, has not been linear. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan experienced a notable deterioration in 2023, when their scores reached 1.964, 1.959 and 2.033, respectively. Their indicators subsequently improved in 2024 and 2025.

Conflicts drive global deterioration

The improvement in Central Asia contrasts sharply with the global security environment. One of the principal factors behind the worsening global score is the growing number of armed conflicts. According to the latest available data cited by the IEP, 61 active state-based armed conflicts were recorded in 2024, the highest number since 1945.

The economic cost of violence has also continued to rise. The IEP estimated the global economic impact of violence at $21.8 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 10.5% of global GDP. The deterioration is particularly visible among countries experiencing major armed conflicts. Russia ranked 163rd, the lowest position in the 2026 index. Russia’s position is notable because it marked the first time the country ranked last in the GPI.

Iceland remains the world’s most peaceful country

Iceland retained the top position in the 2026 ranking with a score of 1.161. It has held the number one position for 19 consecutive years. New Zealand ranked second with 1.343, followed by Switzerland (1.363), Slovenia (1.369) and Ireland (1.371).

Austria, Portugal, Singapore, Finland and Japan completed the top 10. Seven of the 10 most peaceful countries are located in Europe.

At the opposite end of the ranking, countries affected by major armed conflicts dominate the bottom positions. Sudan ranked 162nd, Congo 161st, Ukraine 160th and Israel 159th. Afghanistan, Yemen, Syria and Mali also ranked among the 10 least peaceful countries.

What the index measures

The Global Peace Index is published annually by the Institute for Economics & Peace, an international think tank. The 2026 edition is the index’s 20th edition and covers 163 countries and territories representing 99.7% of the world’s population.

The index uses 23 quantitative and qualitative indicators grouped into three broad areas: societal safety and security, ongoing domestic and international conflict, and militarization. Both domestic and external factors are considered. Domestic indicators account for 60% of the overall score, while external factors account for 40%.

The indicators include homicide and violent crime rates, political instability, terrorism, domestic and international conflicts, relations with neighboring countries, military expenditure, armed forces personnel, and arms imports and exports.

Scores range from 1 to 5, with lower scores indicating greater peacefulness. The IEP also classifies countries into five levels: very high, high, medium, low and very low peacefulness.

World.title: OPEC+ Keeps October Oil Output Quotas Unchanged As Focus Shifts To 2027
World.content:
ALMATY – OPEC+ has decided to keep oil production targets for October unchanged, pausing further adjustments as the alliance assesses market conditions and prepares for a broader review of production baselines for 2027.

The decision was made on Sept. 6 during a virtual meeting of Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman, the seven OPEC+ countries that previously announced additional voluntary production adjustments in 2023.

Under the decision, the seven countries will maintain their September 2026 required production levels in October.

For Kazakhstan, the October production quota will stand at 1.628 million barrels per day (bpd). Russia’s quota will be 9.949 million bpd, Saudi Arabia’s 10.478 million bpd, Iraq’s 4.431 million bpd, Kuwait’s 2.676 million bpd, Algeria’s 1.007 million bpd and Oman’s 841,000 bpd.

The seven countries also reaffirmed their commitment to full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation and agreed to continue meeting monthly to review market conditions. The next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 4.

Pause follows earlier production increase

The decision comes after OPEC+ increased production in September by 188,000 bpd, continuing the gradual unwinding of supply restrictions introduced in 2023.

In August, the group agreed to complete the phased rollback of a 1.65 million bpd reduction that had been introduced in 2023. However, actual production by OPEC+ members has remained significantly below their official targets.

According to Reuters, the unchanged October quotas therefore represent a pause in the recent process of increasing supply rather than a new production cut. The pause comes amid major disruptions to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, which have constrained the physical movement of crude and limited the ability of OPEC+ to influence actual supply to the market.

“OPEC+ currently has very limited power over the physical oil market,” said Jorge Leon of Rystad Energy, according to Reuters. “The group can change production targets on paper, but it cannot guarantee that those barrels will be produced or actually reach the market.”

2027 quotas become the bigger question

The more consequential issue for OPEC+ is now likely to be the framework for production quotas in 2027.

Another layer of production restrictions remains in place for most members of the wider 21-country OPEC+ group through the end of 2026. Before deciding how and when to unwind those restrictions, the alliance needs to assess the production capacity of its members and establish new baseline levels, Reuters writes.

Those baselines will determine individual production quotas for 2027 and could have a longer-term impact on how much oil each producer is able to bring to market. The process could also change the balance between countries with substantial spare capacity and those already producing close to their technical limits.

Reuters reported that OPEC+ is likely to pause further output increases in the fourth quarter as members prepare for the baseline review. The statement issued after the Sept. 6 meeting, however, did not specify a production policy beyond October.

Kazakhstan faces both quota and capacity considerations

For Kazakhstan, the outcome preserves the country’s October production target at 1.628 million bpd while the broader alliance considers its next stage of production policy.

The question of future quotas is particularly significant because Kazakhstan’s oil output has been affected by the expansion of production at major fields, including Tengiz, as well as its commitments under OPEC+ agreements.

The seven countries will meet again on Oct. 4 to review market conditions.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Logistics Diplomacy: Ambition, Leverage and Constraints
World.content:
ASTANA – Long constrained by its landlocked geography, Kazakhstan is seeking to turn its position between Europe and Asia into a source of economic and geopolitical leverage. As trade disruptions and competition drive demand for diversified supply chains, Astana is investing in new transport corridors to establish itself as an indispensable transit hub and translate connectivity into diplomatic influence.

“Transport diplomacy has long been a pillar of economic diplomacy. Today, efficient transport and logistics networks are becoming strategic assets that shape economic competitiveness, and a country’s role in regional economic cooperation,” Head of Research Department of the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) Alexey Kuznetsov told The Astana Times.

Located between China, Europe, Russia, Central Asia and the Caspian Sea, Kazakhstan is developing railways, roads, ports and logistics hubs while expanding connections along several international transport corridors.

The scale of the sector is reflected in recent figures. Kazakhstan transported 540.5 million tons of cargo in January-July, up 0.9% from the same period a year earlier, according to the Bureau of National Statistics. Cargo turnover increased 1%, while road freight transportation grew 6.2%.

Government data shows that transit freight reached 21.7 million tons in January-June, up 24% from 17.5 million tons a year earlier.

Building Eurasian connectivity

Kazakhstan is seeking to strengthen its role not simply as a transit country but as a major regional connectivity hub.

“For Kazakhstan, modern transport, logistics, and warehousing infrastructure are essential for addressing the challenges of a landlocked geography. At the same time, the country has become one of Eurasia’s most important transit hubs,” said Kuznetsov.

He said international transport and logistics partnerships are central to Kazakhstan’s connectivity diplomacy, positioning the country as an influential player in shaping Eurasia’s regional agenda.

According to the EDB’s Transport Projects Observatory, Kazakhstan accounts for 53% of transport corridor investments planned or under implementation in Central Asia through 2035.

“More than $32 billion is expected to be invested in 55 major transport projects, including construction of the Center-West motorway, the Uralsk-Atyrau and Kyzylorda-Saksaulsk roads, and the Moiynty-Kyzylzhar railway. These investments will strengthen East-West and North-South trade routes and further position Kazakhstan as a strategic transport crossroads linking Europe and Asia,” Kuznetsov said.

Road construction, reconstruction and repairs cover around 11,000 kilometers nationwide in 2026. Kazakhstan also plans to repair 11,000 kilometers of railway tracks by 2029.

International financing is supporting part of the expansion. In February, the World Bank approved an $846 million guarantee to mobilize $1.41 billion in commercial financing for a major railway connectivity project along Kazakhstan’s section of the Middle Corridor.

However, Kuznetsov emphasized that infrastructure alone cannot determine whether a transport route succeeds.

“Transport connectivity depends equally on ‘soft infrastructure’: harmonized regulations, efficient border-crossing procedures, coordinated corridor development, and digitalization of transport services and documentation,” he said.

The World Bank estimates cited by Kuznetsov suggest that cutting border delays by 50% through regulatory harmonization and digital solutions could increase exports from Central Asian countries along transport corridors by an average of 18%.

For Kazakhstan, this means that the competitiveness of its routes will depend not only on the number of roads, railways and terminals built, but also on how efficiently they operate.

The Middle Corridor and geopolitics

At the center of Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy is the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which connects China with Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Europe.

For political scientist Tair Naumov, the importance of such routes extends beyond trade.

“Investment in transit infrastructure requires a certain level of trust between countries, including confidence in political relations and the security of investments,” Naumov said in an interview with The Astana Times.

Once a route becomes operational, however, it can also strengthen those relations by creating greater economic interdependence.

“When countries rely on the same transport routes, their interests become more closely connected. If a corridor becomes important to foreign trade, there is a stronger incentive to maintain stable relations and keep existing agreements in place,” he said.

Naumov noted that this interdependence can eventually acquire a security dimension.

“If a country becomes an important transit hub, its stability becomes an interest not only for the country itself but also for its neighbors and major trading partners,” he said.

Damir Kayumov, PhD, with a bachelor’s degree in economics and law, takes a similar view, emphasizing the economic interests created by shared logistics networks.

“Good logistics creates mutual interest between countries. The more participants there are, the safer it becomes. And the more economic ties pass through Kazakhstan, the greater its role in the region,” Kayumov told The Astana Times.

The Middle Corridor illustrates this dynamic. While it does not yet account for a dominant share of Kazakhstan’s transit flows, its rapid growth could give it greater strategic importance.

From transit to economic value

For Kazakhstan, stronger economic ties along these routes are only part of the opportunity. The bigger question is how the country can turn growing transit flows into broader economic value at home.

“I would not reduce the transport strategy to transit alone. If a container simply passes through Kazakhstan, the country earns comparatively little. It is much more interesting when logistics centers, warehouses, manufacturing and service companies emerge alongside the route,” Kayumov said.

Such an approach would allow Kazakhstan to capture more value from its position in Eurasian supply chains.

“Then the transport corridor begins to work for the regions and for our industry. Kazakhstan receives much more income. The service model that develops around the entire flow allows us to earn more and create more jobs,” he said.

Kayumov noted that attracting cargo also requires competitive and predictable routes. Border delays, limited port capacity, container shortages and differences in procedures can increase costs and make a route less attractive to businesses.

“A convenient route must be fast, clear and predictable. For business, it matters how long cargo remains at the border, how quickly documents are processed and how much railway capacity is available,” he said.

According to Kayumov, digitalization can help address some of these challenges. Electronic document management, for example, can reduce corruption risks while speeding up operations.

TRIPP and the wider connectivity network

The development of new routes beyond Kazakhstan could expand the country’s connectivity options.

The Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) is a proposed transport link through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan proper with its Nakhchivan exclave. Kazakhstan has expressed interest in participating in the project and linking it with the Middle Corridor.

“For the Trans-Caspian route, TRIPP provides an additional option for moving cargo after the Caspian Sea toward Türkiye and Europe. The more such branches there are, the more resilient and attractive the entire corridor becomes,” Kayumov said.

For Kazakhstan, the interest is largely pragmatic. As a landlocked country, it needs several reliable routes to major markets.

However, Kayumov noted that the project’s value for Kazakhstan would depend on how effectively it is integrated into the country’s existing transport network.

“What is more important for us is not formal participation in the project, but its integration with our existing transit hub. This means having unified tariffs, digital borders, digital document management and clear, predictable delivery times,” Kayumov said.

“The more reliable routes connect Central Asia with Europe through Kazakhstan, the greater the economic and political value of our geography and our role in connecting different markets,” he added.

World.title: Expert: Higher Foreign Currency Supply Supports Tenge Strengthening Amid Changing Market Flows
World.content:
ASTANA – The Kazakh tenge strengthened 2.6% against the US dollar in August, reaching 461.57 per dollar at the end of the month, as foreign currency supply continued to exceed demand amid increased market activity and changing capital flows, according to Saltanat Igenbekova, head of the Analytics Center at Halyk Finance.

According to the center’s analysis of the National Bank’s monthly foreign exchange market data, trading activity remained high in August, while the structure of currency flows changed.

The total trading volume on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) reached $8.7 billion, up from $8.6 billion in July. Average daily trading volumes increased to $415 million, reads the analysis published on Sept. 4.

The tenge strengthened despite a decline in some traditional sources of foreign currency supply. Net foreign currency sales by the National Bank fell to $284 million in August from $617 million in July.

Sales of foreign currency from the National Fund amounted to $200 million, within the announced range of $200-300 million.

At the same time, the National Bank purchased $721 million in foreign currency for the investment portfolio of the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund, twice July’s $375 million.

Non-resident capital supports tenge

The analysis attributes much of the stronger currency supply to foreign portfolio capital.

“In our assessment, the high level of foreign currency supply on the market was largely supported by the inflow of non-resident capital through several channels,” Igenbekova said.

She linked investors’ interest in tenge-denominated assets to their attractive real returns, growth in Kazakhstan’s combined foreign exchange reserves and the country’s sovereign credit rating upgrade by S&P this year.

The role of the quasi-public sector as a source of foreign currency supply was more limited following the suspension in July of the requirement for quasi-public entities to sell 50% of their foreign currency earnings.

The center also noted that the National Bank conducted no foreign exchange interventions in August.

Trading activity rises

Foreign exchange trading on KASE reached $60 billion in January-August, up $21.8 billion from the same period in 2025.

Unlike the previous year, when higher trading volumes coincided with a weaker tenge, the currency strengthened from 501.2 tenge per dollar at the start of this year to 461.6 at the end of August.

“The observed strengthening points to the continued predominance of foreign currency supply over demand during the period under review,” Igenbekova said.

September outlook

Foreign currency sales from the National Fund are planned at $200-300 million in September. The National Bank also expects to sell foreign currency equivalent to 374 billion tenge under its gold-operations mirroring mechanism.

Igenbekova said it will update the tenge outlook following changes in the expected use of National Fund transfers.

“The main factors influencing the exchange rate remain the balance of foreign currency flows in the domestic market, global oil prices, and the activity of non-residents,” Igenbekova said.

According to the analysis, the interaction of these factors will determine the tenge’s direction in the coming months.

World.title: Kazakhstan Is Upgrading Its Oil Export Strategy—Here’s How
World.content:
Astana is looking for more ways to move its oil.

Russia, its principal export outlet, is rife with disruptions. Damage to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) Black Sea terminal in November 2025 suppressed exports into early 2026, while the recent July attacks on tankers threatened roughly 1.5 million barrels per day.

The vulnerability would not be so enormous if 80% of Kazakh oil exports did not move through the CPC terminal near Novorossiysk.

But is Kazakhstan merely searching for emergency alternatives amid instability? Or is this a transformation it has been preparing for?

The answer is consequential: Kazakhstan is attempting a wholesale upgrade of its oil-export strategy, one befitting a rising regional power. It is moving from rational efficiency toward strategic resilience, from accepting routes toward shaping them, and from concentrated dependence toward managed interdependence. Although the CPC will remain dominant through 2030, Astana is seeking greater control over the risks, partnerships and infrastructure connecting its oil to international markets.

From rational efficiency to strategic resilience

The CPC transports Kazakh oil, particularly from Tengiz, to global markets, making it the most commercially attractive route.

When it was created in 1992, a fledgling independent Kazakhstan was looking to enter international energy markets. The CPC was the rational choice. It, for instance, transported up to 1.3 million barrels per day back in 2021; avoided the additional loading, shipping and crossing costs of a Trans-Caspian route; and its 1,510-kilometer pipeline, according to area studies analyst Ilya Roubanis, would be extremely difficult to replicate. Astana selected efficiency while adjusting to a new geopolitical environment.

Contrast this with Azerbaijan. According to Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, Azerbaijan chose the expensive option. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline through Georgia and Türkiye required what he called an “insurance premium for strategic autonomy” to avoid dependence on competing producers. Kazakhstan captured the CPC’s immediate savings but accepted greater concentration risk.

The stakes will rise alongside production. The KazEnergy 2023 National Energy Report anticipated high output from Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak, with national production potentially reaching 105 million tons. Higher output requires dependable market access; otherwise, its advantage can be undermined by one constrained route.

The lesson is simple: the cheapest route is not necessarily the least costly once the consequences of interruption are included. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev affirmed as much in 2024: “With unprecedented international turbulence, the priority is to further diversify export routes.” Diversification, however, requires more than identifying alternatives. It requires Kazakhstan to help shape the infrastructure and partnerships behind them.

From route-taker to route-shaper

As a landlocked, post-Soviet producer, Kazakhstan has historically been constrained by existing pipelines and neighboring states. Its role was simple: produce oil and insert it into available routes.

But Kazakhstan does not have to remain a route-taker. Although it cannot independently control its export geography, it can shape the terms on which that geography operates. It can negotiate access to multiple corridors, invest in tankers, coordinate with transit states and treat infrastructure as an instrument of foreign policy.

Nowhere is Kazakhstan assuming this route-shaper role more clearly than in the Caspian. Tokayev identified the Trans-Caspian route as a “priority” in 2022. KazMunayGas and Azerbaijan’s SOCAR subsequently agreed to transport approximately 1.5 million tons annually through BTC, while Kazakhstan added the Caspian’s Taraz and Liwa tankers to its fleet, each with an 8,000-tonne capacity.

This gradual Caspianization continues. KazTransOil supplied 155,000 tons of Kazakh oil to BTC through Aktau in July, an 11.5% increase over the previous year. Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan plans to transport 2.2 million tons through BTC in 2026. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have also discussed using the idle Baku–Supsa pipeline for between three million and five million tons of Kazakh crude.

But this role has limits. According to Andy Kuchins, a senior fellow at the Center for the National Interest, major expansion would require high capital expenditure, long-term purchase commitments and several years of construction. Oil majors like ExxonMobil and BP are “more reluctant now as compared to the 1990s” to finance large projects in remote markets.

The direction is nevertheless clear: Kazakhstan is moving from accepting the routes geography provides toward assembling the infrastructure and partnerships it needs. It is not yet a fully fledged route-shaper, but it is steadily behaving like one—using new routes not to eliminate dependence, but to distribute it more strategically.

From concentrated dependence to managed interdependence

Every export option depends on another state, infrastructure operator, or external market. Self-reliance is not realistic. Kuchins nevertheless argues that Astana can “reduce concentration of its dependence on Russia.”

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy reported 73.4 million tons of oil exports during the first eleven months of 2025. Separately reported full-year route data show 64.8 million tons transported through the CPC, 9.3 million through Atyrau–Samara, 3.5 million through Aktau, 1.1 million through Atasu–Alashankou toward China, and approximately 100,000 by rail. Of the 78.8 million tons accounted for in this route-level data, approximately 94% moved through the two Russian corridors. Kazakhstan therefore possesses several export routes, but its portfolio remains highly asymmetrical.

Herein lies its greatest oil-policy shift: managed interdependence. This means distributing export relationships so that no transit state possesses overwhelming influence over Kazakhstan’s market access. Each direction performs a different function.

And at the moment, Kazakhstan is assessing four directions—some mainstay, some new.

The Russian route

The CPC will remain dominant because it offers unmatched capacity, established infrastructure and lower costs. Kuchins and Roubanis expect structural dependence to persist through 2030. Following the Tengiz expansion, Kazakhstan may become more dependent on the CPC in the short term even as its long-term strategy diversifies. Diversification does not require abandoning the CPC; it requires making an interruption less damaging.

The Trans-Caspian route

BTC could absorb Kazakh crude as Azerbaijani production declines, while Baku–Supsa could provide another outlet. Neither would match CPC volumes, but together they would widen access to global buyers.

Europe also has a stake in this.

The European Union imported 52.4 million tons of Kazakh crude just in 2024, making Kazakhstan its third-largest external supplier. If Europe wants westward diversification, it must help make projects bankable through financing and long-term commitments. Brussels and its partners are therefore mobilizing 10 billion euros to improve transport connections with Central Asia. According to Roubanis, “building ties with the region in the short run is necessary for the EU’s long-term positioning.” The push indicates that Trans-Caspian connectivity is not just a Kazakh interest, but one shared by the whole region.

The Chinese route

China may offer the easiest immediately available opportunity to reduce dependence on Russia. The Kazakhstan–China pipeline transported 19.5 million tons in 2025, but that included domestic deliveries and Russian transit. Direct Kazakh crude exports through Atasu–Alashankou were planned to be 1 million tons in 2025, compared to the more than 11 million tons per year flowing with non-Kazakh suppliers.

China remains a credible expansion market and willing financier. Yet the fastest way to reduce Russian dependence could deepen dependence on China. Moriyasu similarly argues that Kazakhstan does not want to exchange one concentrated dependency for another. Unlike the Trans-Caspian route, China provides access to one principal market rather than multiple global buyers.

The Southern route

A corridor through Iran—possibly toward Pakistan and India—could be compelling but faces formidable political and economic obstacles. But it should not be dismissed altogether.

Moriyasu suggests that “Iran offers Central Asia one of its shortest routes to warm-water ports.” Although current geopolitical conditions severely constrain this option, he argues that “infrastructure Kazakhstan builds today will still be operating decades from now. Astana should therefore avoid making long-term infrastructure decisions on the assumption that today’s geopolitical map is permanent.”

The southern route’s present value lies in preserving a long-term option, not in providing a realistic alternative before 2030.

From east to west and north to south, Kazakhstan is not moving from dependence to independence. It is moving from one dominant dependency toward a deliberately balanced portfolio of interdependence.

A more advanced role, but not autonomy

Kazakhstan’s transformation should not be measured by whether the CPC ceases to dominate. By 2030, it will likely remain the principal corridor as Trans-Caspian volumes rise incrementally and eastbound capacity becomes more important amid regional instability and escalation. The resulting portfolio will be broader, though still asymmetrical.

The strategy is itself an upgrade—a threefold one. Resilience is becoming the objective, route-shaping the emerging function, and managed interdependence the organizing principle.

Looking forward, Kazakhstan’s strategic upgrade lies not in escaping geography, but in developing the infrastructure, partnerships and political leverage needed to manage geography more effectively.

The author is Joseph Shumunov, a Non-Resident Research Fellow at the Topchubashov Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, and a Fellow at Nightingale Intelligence.
