World.title: Abkhazia to review how effectively agricultural grants are being spent
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to review how agricultural grants have been spent. President Badra Gunba has ordered the government to return to the budget any money spent on ineffective projects.

The grants come from the Agriculture Ministry’s “Agricultural Development for 2025” programme and the Economy Ministry’s programme supporting small and medium-sized businesses.

The president’s decision to review how the grants are used was most likely prompted by numerous complaints from farmers on social media, who say the government is providing little or no support to actual producers.

Badra Gunba does not rule out some violations given the large amount of funding involved.

“If violations are found — and with such a huge amount of funding, they are bound to occur — we must respond to them. But most importantly, we should not simply punish those responsible. We must make sure they compensate the state for all the costs it has incurred and return the money to the budget,” the president said.

The opposition media outlet Respublika believes that the president’s decision to order law enforcement agencies to set up an interagency group to oversee state support programmes for small and medium-sized businesses can only mean one thing: something is clearly wrong with these programmes.

“It looks like someone has already decided to make a tidy profit from state support for entrepreneurs. Now law enforcement agencies have several options:

simply scare them so they stop stealing;

investigate what they have already managed to steal;

or get in on the deal themselves.

Which option do you think they will choose?” Respublika asks, making it clear that it believes the answer is obvious.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Agriculture in Abkhazia

World.title: EU gas consumption falls in July despite higher power demand — GECF
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Natural gas consumption in the European Union declined by 0.6% year-on-year to 17.4 billion cubic meters (bcm) in July 2026, mainly due to weaker demand from the industrial and residential sectors, the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) said.

According to the GECF, the decline was largely linked to the start of the holiday season, which reduced industrial gas use, while residential demand remained subdued due to seasonal factors.

Gas consumption for power generation, however, edged up as a heatwave across much of Western Europe boosted electricity demand for cooling. The increase was limited by stronger renewable generation, particularly from wind and solar.

EU electricity generation rose 3.6% year-on-year to 216 terawatt-hours (TWh) in July. Gas-fired generation increased by 0.5%, or 0.2 TWh, while nuclear output fell 2%, partly as high river temperatures forced several reactors to reduce or temporarily halt operations.

Solar generation surged 20% year-on-year, while wind generation increased 13%. Hydropower output, meanwhile, dropped 20% due to weaker availability.

Non-hydro renewables accounted for the largest share of the EU power mix at 44%, followed by nuclear at 23%, natural gas at 16%, hydropower at 9% and coal at 8%.

The GECF noted that the figures "highlight the complementary role of natural gas in providing system flexibility and ensuring reliable electricity supply" during periods of weaker wind and hydropower generation.

Despite the July decline, EU natural gas consumption increased 1.4% year-on-year to 190 bcm in January-July 2026.

Globally, aggregate gas consumption across major gas-consuming countries, which account for around 75% of global demand, fell 1.3% year-on-year to 1,685 bcm in the first half of 2026. The decline was recorded in North America, the Middle East and Southern Asia, while the EU posted an increase.

EU sees no immediate gas supply security risk

Despite gas storage levels remaining below those of previous years, EU member states and the European Commission see no immediate threat to the bloc's gas supply security.

Experts from the Commission and member states said at a meeting of the Gas Coordination Group in early September that global energy markets remain "exceptional" and require close monitoring, but the current situation differs significantly from the 2021-2022 energy crisis.

The EU is now better positioned due to greater diversification of supplies, expanded LNG import capacity and lower gas demand, according to the assessment.

Based on historical projections, the bloc remains on track to reach an adequate level of winter preparedness. The European Commission currently sees no need to intervene, saying the EU gas system is resilient enough to manage lower storage levels ahead of winter.

At the same time, instability in the Middle East and the continued shutdown of Qatari LNG production remain key concerns. Heatwaves in Europe have also increased gas demand from the power sector, while geopolitical uncertainty continues to contribute to significant price volatility.

The Commission said it would continue to closely monitor the situation in cooperation with member states and market stakeholders. The next meeting of the Gas Coordination Group is scheduled for September 24.

World.title: Azerbaijan to present hydrogen strategy action plan in coming days, agency director says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Azerbaijan is working on an action plan under its National Hydrogen Strategy, Javid Abdullayev, Director of the Azerbaijan Renewable Energy Agency, said, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

Abdullayev made the remarks while speaking at the opening of a modern renewable energy laboratory at Azerbaijan State Oil and Industry University (ADNSU).

He said a number of issues related to the development of a hydrogen economy in Azerbaijan remain unresolved.

“Questions related to the future are quite serious, and there is currently no definitive answer to them. The main reason is that the hydrogen economy does not yet exist,” Abdullayev said.

He said further research is needed to determine how efficient it would be to convert electricity into hydrogen for storage and then use that hydrogen to generate electricity again.

“For example, we are talking about converting electricity into hydrogen and using it as a storage system. But we need to determine where and in what form it can be applied, as well as how efficient it would be to use the energy converted into hydrogen to generate electricity again,” he said.

Abdullayev also acknowledged a degree of skepticism surrounding hydrogen energy.

“I can say that there is some skepticism on our side as well. However, we are working in this direction step by step,” he said.

According to Abdullayev, Azerbaijan is studying various areas related to hydrogen, including sustainable aviation fuel.

“Sustainable aviation fuel and other areas are quite interesting. Our colleagues have recently spent a week in Germany, at German universities and relevant institutions,” he said.

Abdullayev said work was underway to prepare an action plan under Azerbaijan’s National Hydrogen Strategy.

“In the coming days, with financial support from the European Union, we are preparing a tender for the strategy and getting ready to present our action plan. We will answer these questions specifically in the action plan,” he said.

He noted that hydrogen production and exports had previously been considered as part of interconnector projects.

“Previously, we considered hydrogen production and hydrogen exports as part of our interconnector projects. Currently, hydrogen production is being carried out in a limited number of countries and geographical areas around the world. We are also trying to assess its economic efficiency and potential,” Abdullayev said.

The agency director highlighted strong interest in hydrogen energy in China.

“In China, this issue is being advanced with a very strong initiative. China is also making major strides in renewable energy. This approach shows that hydrogen production could become economically efficient at a certain stage,” he said.

At the same time, Abdullayev said large-scale use of hydrogen remains more of a long-term prospect.

“This is very much a question for the future, and we believe that this issue will become clearer at the next stage,” he said.

He also highlighted challenges arising from the integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid.

“In a country like ours, integrating variable generation into the power grid is not particularly easy. Operational issues and even environmental problems need to be considered,” Abdullayev said.

As an example, he cited the impact of bird migration on wind turbines in the Khizi and Shurabad areas.

“For example, in Khizi and Shurabad, there is a problem related to bird migration in front of the turbines, and the turbines are shut down when birds arrive. Imagine that 70 megawatts of capacity are removed from the system at that moment. How will you restore this capacity in the system? You need to carry out certain balancing measures,” he said.

According to Abdullayev, such situations caused by variable renewable energy generation represent a major challenge for the power system.

“This is a very serious issue for the power grid. Among the problems created by variable generation, this is one of the main and major challenges,” he said.

World.title: Azerbaijan weighs membership in Global Offshore Wind Alliance (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Azerbaijan’s possible accession to the Global Offshore Wind Alliance has been discussed.

This was stated by Azerbaijan’s Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov in a post on his “X” account.

"During our meeting with Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), we discussed carrying forward the COP29 energy agenda at COP31. We exchanged views on advancing the energy storage, grids and hydrogen initiatives launched in Baku through concrete implementation mechanisms in Antalya, Azerbaijan’s accession to the Global Offshore Wind Alliance, as well as cooperation on sustainable aviation fuels and hydrogen," Shahbazov wrote.

The Global Offshore Wind Alliance (GOWA) is a diplomatic-led, multi-stakeholder initiative launched at COP27 in November 2022 by the Government of Denmark, the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC). Together with Colombia as a co-chair, it unites governments, industry, international organizations, and civil society to accelerate offshore wind deployment worldwide. Its core goal is to help unlock at least 2,000 GW of global offshore wind capacity by 2050 (with an intermediate target of around 380 GW by 2030) in support of the Paris Agreement, energy security, and the clean energy transition, by raising ambition, sharing policy best practices, and building a global community of practice.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Samsung E&A debate major oil refining and petrochemical complex
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Kazakhstan’s Minister of Energy Yerlan Akkenzhenov and Samsung E&A President and CEO Hong Namkoong discussed prospects for cooperation in oil refining, the ministry said.

This was announced by the press service of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the sides discussed prospects for cooperation within the strategic project to develop a new oil refining and petrochemical complex in Kazakhstan.

"During the meeting, Samsung E&A was briefed on the current status of preparations for the project and key areas of its further implementation. Particular attention was paid to the technological configuration of the future complex, development of petrochemical production, attraction of private investment and the use of advanced engineering solutions", the ministry said.

Representatives of the South Korean company expressed interest in further studying the project and opportunities to participate in its implementation at subsequent stages.

According to the ministry, Kazakhstan is currently preparing a preliminary feasibility study for the new complex. At this stage, various options for its technological configuration, production specialization and location are being considered, taking into account the feedstock base and infrastructure.

Following the meeting, the sides expressed readiness to continue dialogue and further develop potential areas of cooperation.

Samsung E&A is one of South Korea’s leading engineering and EPC companies, with significant experience in implementing major projects in oil refining, petrochemicals and energy.

In May, the ministry reported that the project to construct Kazakhstan’s fourth large oil refinery had entered the practical stage. Work had begun on developing a preliminary feasibility study (pre-FS) for the project. The future large-scale complex is expected to have the capacity to process up to 10 million tons of oil per year.

World.title: bp set to launch new renewable energy trainer program in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. A new “Train the Trainers” program is expected to be launched in the coming days in cooperation with the Institute for Solar Energy Research Hamelin (ISFH) in Germany and partners from eight countries, bp Vice President for the Caspian, Central Asia and Türkiye region Bakhtiyar Aslanbayli said, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He made the remark during the opening ceremony of a modern renewable energy laboratory at Azerbaijan State Oil and Industry University (ADNSU).

Aslanbayli noted that all parties involved contributed to the implementation of the project. "All sides have made their contribution to the creation of this project. Everyone has contributed to bringing the project to completion and moving it to the next stage," Aslanbeyli said.

Furthermore, he stated that the foundation of the project was laid in 2020, when renewable energy became one of the key areas of bp’s strategy. "When the initiative was first put forward in this area in 2020, one of the main issues was how to develop human capacity in the renewable energy sector in Azerbaijan. At that time, discussions were held on supporting this initiative, and the ministry expressed its readiness to provide strong support," he said.

According to Aslanbayli, after the initial investment was attracted, the program was implemented with the initiative and support of the Ministry of Science and Education. "As a result, such a dual program became possible thanks to the exceptional support of first the Ministry of Education and later the Ministry of Science and Education. The scientific and technical foundation of the program, including laboratories, was created within this project," he said.

The bp vice president emphasized that the project included improving teachers’ English language skills, as well as support programs for two groups of students. "The center we are opening today is not just an investment in equipment and laboratories. It is an investment in Azerbaijan’s human capital, human potential and the future of the new energy sector, particularly renewable energy," Aslanbayli said.

The official noted that the young specialists, scientists and experts trained at the center are being prepared not only for one company, but for Azerbaijan’s energy sector as a whole.

Aslanbayli congratulated ADNSU leadership, students and all partners involved in the project. "We are very pleased that we have been able to contribute to this project. The center has been designed with attention to the smallest details. It provides high-level facilities, including laboratory classes, practical sessions, lectures, a library and opportunities for cooperation," he said.

He added that bp’s renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan are not limited to this initiative. "This is not our first project in the renewable energy sector. So far, the first Azerbaijani-language textbook titled ‘Introduction to Renewable Energy Resources’ has been translated. In addition, smaller-scale laboratories have been established at two vocational schools," Aslanbeyli said.

According to him, a new “Train the Trainers” program is expected to be announced in the coming days together with the Institute for Solar Energy Research Hamelin in Germany and partners from eight countries. "The program envisages training 20 renewable energy instructors," he said.

Aslanbeyli also said that the establishment of a specialized laboratory on energy storage systems at Baku State University is planned. "Work is currently underway to establish an energy storage systems laboratory at Baku State University. We will hold discussions on this issue next week and are at the stage of preparing to sign the agreement," he said.

The bp vice president emphasized that the company is interested in contributing to the wider integration of renewable energy into Azerbaijan’s education system. "We are very pleased to contribute to the renewable energy sector and support the broader representation of this field in Azerbaijan’s education system. Our partnership with ADNSU has continued on a broad scale so far and will certainly continue with confidence in the future," Aslanbeyli said.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans to develop pumped hydro storage facilities — official
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Azerbaijan is planning to develop pumped hydro storage facilities for the first time, Director of the State Agency for Renewable Energy Sources under the Ministry of Energy Javid Abdullayev said, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He made the remark during the opening ceremony of a modern renewable energy laboratory at Azerbaijan State Oil and Industry University (ADNSU).

Abdullayev first noted that a conceptual approach to the deployment of energy storage systems in Azerbaijan could be presented by the end of September. He added that work is currently underway on a regulatory framework related to the integration of renewable energy sources into the energy system and the introduction of energy storage technologies. "We are currently working on regulation. Several key principles and frameworks have been identified. To address these issues, one of China’s leading research institutes is studying our grid. They will share the initial results of their renewable energy analysis with us," Abdullayev said.

Moreover, he emphasized that Azerbaijan currently has two energy storage systems, each with a capacity of 125 MW. "We currently have two energy storage systems based on lithium batteries, each with a capacity of 125 MW. Overall, this represents 250 MW of capacity," he said.

According to Abdullayev, the ongoing analysis will determine what volume of new generation capacity should be developed in the country and what share of it should be supported by battery storage systems. "After the analysis, we will understand what percentage of the installed capacity should be supported by batteries if a certain volume of new capacity is introduced. This is one aspect of the approach," he said.

The agency director stressed that it is impossible to integrate unlimited renewable energy capacity into the power system and that a careful approach is required. "It is not possible to connect an unlimited amount of renewable energy capacity to the grid. The experience of neighboring countries has also shown that a very careful approach to this issue is extremely important," Abdullayev said.

He added that Azerbaijan plans to use various types of energy storage technologies. "There are several ways to address this issue. One is, of course, the use of battery storage systems. There are different types of such systems. In addition to lithium batteries, we are already looking at other technologies as well," he said.

Abdullayev noted that a presentation on one of the energy storage technologies had been held at the Ministry of Energy and that work in this area is continuing.

Javid Abdullayev stressed that Azerbaijan is also considering the development of pumped hydro storage facilities for the first time. "At the same time, we are planning to introduce pumped hydro storage systems in Azerbaijan for the first time. Around 25% of Azerbaijan’s water resources are formed in the liberated territories. Naturally, the justified use of this potential could create certain opportunities," Abdullayev said.

He noted that work on energy storage systems is based on a comprehensive analysis. "This is a comprehensive analysis covering all aspects. It examines issues such as the types of battery storage systems, their share within the energy system, geographical distribution and spatial analysis," he said.

The agency director also touched upon the issue of rising electricity demand in Azerbaijan. "The growth of demand in the energy system is a very serious issue. Standard extrapolation methods are no longer sufficient to understand this, as artificial intelligence and other factors are affecting energy demand," Abdullayev said.

He noted that Azerbaijan currently has sufficient generation capacity to meet growing energy demand. "At present, Azerbaijan has sufficient electricity generation capacity, and there is no need to take any emergency measures in the near future to meet increasing demand," he said.

Abdullayev added that technologies for energy storage systems, their share in the energy mix, and their geographical placement are currently being studied intensively. "I hope that by the end of September we will be able to present a general conceptual approach on this issue," he said.

World.title: French burglar used ChatGPT to locate Canberra home with luxury goods
World.content:
Court documents have revealed how a French burglar used artificial intelligence and images posted to social media to locate a home containing luxury goods in Australia.

He, along with three other French nationals, stole a haul of designer jewellery, handbags and watches from a home in Canberra's south in October last year, before being arrested at a fast food outlet in Sydney just days later.

Ilyes Abdelkader, Mohamed Abdelkader, Mohamed Naimi and Antoni Voisin pleaded guilty to charges of aggravated burglary and joint commission theft in March, but their lawyers disputed the total value of the stolen items.

When charges were laid in December, police said some of the stolen goods — including designer handbags — had been recovered from a short-term rental property in Wentworthville, Sydney, while other items were located by French authorities.

But several items the victims claimed were still missing, including a Richard Mille RM88 (Smiley) watch worth $5 million, were yet to be returned.

The victims claim a Richard Mille rm88 (Smiley) watch was among the items stolen from a Canberra home in October. (Supplied: Richard Mille)

In a hearing in the ACT Supreme Court today, prosecutors tendered an agreed statement of facts, which revised the total value of the goods down from its original figure of $10 million to just under $2 million, with some of the items still unrecovered.

"The prosecution cannot prove beyond reasonable doubt that these [unreturned] items were genuine," the facts read.

"The victims have not been able to produce any documentation such as receipts, proof of purchase, transaction records, or certificates to prove the authenticity of those items."

A Patek Philippe 5711 40th anniversary watch similar to the one stolen from a Canberra home. (Supplied)

How thieves identified Canberra home

The document also noted how one of the victims had posted images of the luxury goods on Instagram.

Ilyes Abdelkader used artificial intelligence to determine a cherry blossom tree in one of those images was usually found in Canberra, while another image contained Black Mountain tower — also in the ACT.

The victim had also posted photos of her backyard containing a swimming pool and tennis court.

NSW police arrested the four men at Wentworthville KFC in Sydney on October 19. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Abdelkader used ChatGPT to search for suburbs in Canberra with tennis courts and pools and located the home.

He and the three other men then flew from Thailand to Sydney on October 7.

The group broke into the home in Canberra a few days later, while the victims were out, using tree trunks to smash a window and gaining access to a safe which the victims thought had been left locked.

Four French men came to Canberra for a $10m heist, police say Police allege the men travelled to Australia to rob a Canberra home.

The men later used a freight service to send some of the now-recovered belongings to France.

They were arrested at a KFC in Wentworthville, Sydney, on October 19 and have been in custody since.

The ACT Supreme Court will set a date for their sentencing next week.

Court documents note goods valued at $915,000 have been returned, while items with an agreed value of more than $1 million are still outstanding.

World.title: Former childcare worker's husband avoids jail for sharing child exploitation material
World.content:
A West Australian man who described children as "toys" and shared graphic video of a child performing a sexual act has avoided an immediate jail term.

Ronald Houghton was exposed and arrested after an online sting operation in 2025, making the claims and sharing the video in an online chat with WA Police investigators posing as fellow predators.

The 59-year-old was living in Ravensthorpe, 550 kilometres south-east of Perth, at the time of his arrest, and eventually pleaded guilty to producing and distributing child exploitation material.

He appeared in the Albany District Court for sentencing today, with District Court Judge Martin Flynn handing him a suspended 12-month jail term.

Houghton was sentenced in the Albany District Court. (ABC News: Toby Hussey)

Judge Flynn took into account several mitigating factors in sentencing Houghton, including his traumatic and unhappy life that was characterised by isolation, trauma and unhappiness.

Houghton's early guilty plea also saw him receive a 20 per cent discount on his sentence.

He wore a red covering to hide his face as he left Albany Courthouse.

Undercover op

The court heard that in messages exchanged with the undercover officers, Houghton bragged about touching the children of former partners.

The messages saw him refer to children as "toys" and included the graphic exploitation video.

But the court heard that during a subsequent interview with police, Houghton said his actions were the result of "sheer boredom" and that he did not know he was committing an offence at the time.

Houghton's defence counsel denied he had a sexual interest in children, telling the court the 59-year-old was sexually abused as a child, and using the chatroom to meet paedophiles so he could confront them in person.

Jail term avoided

Prosecutor Asha Healy pushed for an immediate term of imprisonment, telling the court Houghton's offending represented a pattern and that he "continues to be a risk to the community".

But Judge Flynn said Houghton had no prior convictions of this manner and had shown sufficient remorse.

"I accept that you know that you have done the wrong thing," he said.

Houghton will have to attend counselling, participate in rehabilitation programs and regularly report to authorities as part of his release.

He will avoid imprisonment if he abides by those requirements and does not reoffend over the next 12 months.

Childcare connection

Houghton's wife of 26 years was assistant operations manager at Regional Early Education and Development (REED) at the time of his arrest, sparking concern among parents in Hopetoun and Ravensthorpe.

The court heard the woman no longer works so that she can take care of him full-time.

Houghton's wife worked for Regional Early Education and Development (REED) in Hopetoun and Ravensthorpe. (ABC Esperance: Andrew Williams)

There is no suggestion that any of Houghton's offending either took place at, or involved children from, any of the childcare centres.

The ABC has contacted REED for comment in the wake of Houghton's sentencing.

At the time of his arrest, a REED spokesperson said it had "zero tolerance" for any action within or outside the organisation that compromised child safety.

'Wake-up call' for small town

Hopetoun residents had a mixed response when news of Houghton's sentencing broke on Monday.

Tabitha Franke has lived in the town for 10 years, and took her son out of daycare after Houghton was arrested.

"Honestly, the whole thing's disgusting," she said.

Tabitha Franke says children need to feel safe in the small community. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

" Our kids should feel safe, especially in a small-town community where we thought they would feel safe. "

Fellow resident Chelsea Byrne has been a childcare worker for almost two decades, and formerly worked at REED.

"When I've been going through pre-employment checks, the question has never been asked: 'Do you reside with someone who has committed crimes against children?'" she said.

She said the case had been a "rude wake-up call" for the community, with many parents scared off childcare altogether.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

World.title: Court ruling clears way for 124-home Byron Shire development
World.content:
Opponents of a controversial housing development in northern New South Wales will have a week to appeal a Federal Court ruling before excavators start digging up the site.

About 100 people gathered in Brunswick Heads near the site known locally as "Wallum" to hear a livestream of the judgment.

The court rejected an application by Save Wallum Inc for a permanent injunction on the housing development.

Save Wallum Inc spokesperson Luciana Bowen said the judgment was "incredibly disappointing".

About 100 people gathered to watch the livestream of the judgment. (ABC News: Hannah Ross)

"You have to wonder what credibility our environmental laws have at a national level if we can't protect threatened species and their habitat from extinction," she said.

"The community has spent hundreds of thousand of dollars and countless hours trying to protect this place through the Federal Court system."

This is the site of the Wallum development at Brunswick Heads. (Source: Clarence Property)

Temporary injunction

The judgment comes more than two years after the court imposed a temporary injunction that halted work on the development.

That temporary injunction has been extended for a week to give Save Wallum and the developer Clarence Property an opportunity to consider the court's decision.

Ms Bowen said lawyers for Save Wallum would be combing through the ruling to see if there was a legal basis on which to launch an appeal.

If not, the developer can move on site from 5pm on September 14 to slash the grass and start construction on stage one which involves construction of 36 artificial frog ponds.

The Wallum development has been on the drawing board since 2013, when the site's previous owner lodged concept plans with planning authorities.

The Wallum heathland at Brunswick Heads is home to many old-growth scribbly gums. (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

Clarence Property Group bought the land in 2021, and has approval to develop 124 housing lots on 12 hectares of the 30-hectare site.

Chief executive Simon Kennedy said the company felt vindicated by the judgment.

"The applicant was suggesting that there were matters of national significance with respect to the species and the level of endangerment that may have occurred as a result of the development, and her honour has found is that is actually not true," he said.

"We have been ready to commence works for 26 months so it has been a long wait for us.

"There have been people looking to buy houses, young families ready to build houses and we've been held up for no reason.

"So we are very keen to get on site and commence works."

Activists were initially granted a temporary injunction in 2024, as the developer was preparing to bring in heavy machinery to start stage one of the development.

Tensions flared in 2024 as the developer tried to move ahead with works on the site. (ABC News)

At the time, it was celebrated by protesters who had established a camp next to the development site, with some eventually locking themselves onto machinery and occupying the branches of several large scribbly gums within the site.

Save Wallum's application for a permanent injunction under the Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity Act was heard in the Federal Court last year.

The group's submissions cited habitat loss for the critically endangered Mitchell's rainforest snail, endangered koalas and vulnerable species the long-nosed potaroo, Wallum sedge frogs and glossy black cockatoos.

The reasons for the final judgment are yet to be published and were not read to the court.

World.title: Leaked text reveals Australia's $980 million commitment to Solomon Islands
World.content:
Australia and Solomon Islands have reached an in-principle agreement on a landmark new treaty, with a leaked text message revealing the federal government has promised to plough more than $980 million in additional funding into the Pacific nation as it tries to lock in the pact.

The federal government is racing to get the treaty signed in the coming weeks after Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale successfully warded off a leadership challenge on Monday.

Mr Wale was forced to scramble back to Solomon Islands last week just hours after landing in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders meeting when his Home Affairs Minister, Manasseh Maelanga, launched a motion of no confidence, accusing the prime minister of making major decisions without consulting cabinet.

A message from Australia's High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to the deputy prime minister Francis Sade last week, which is verified by ABC News and now circulating in political circles, reveals the details of the deal, and shows how Australia was keen to buttress Mr Wale's position as he fought for his political survival.

A leaked text message from Jeffrey Roach has detailed how far Australia will go to lock in the new treaty with Solomon Islands. (Supplied: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade)

Mr Roach writes that there had been "terrific progress" on the treaty negotiations, and that Australia was willing to contribute an additional $280 million into the Pacific nation over the next two years under the deal and a further $700 million after that.

He says that will include 820 million Solomon Islands dollars ($142 million) in funding for Mr Wale's signature "free education" policy and SI$275 million ($47.8 million) to provide "visa improvements" and deal with "security requests from Solomon Islands".

Australia also looks set to ramp up support for a sometimes-contentious scheme which funnels money directly to MPs to spend on their constituencies as part of the comprehensive treaty.

The message says Australia would contribute SI$5 million ($870,000) to every constituency for MPs' "development priorities" before the end of this year, along with a further SI$3 million ($500,000) per constituency for 2027 and a further $500,000 per constituency in 2028.

Solomon Islands parliament has 50 seats, so it would see Australia funnelling a total of some $43 million into constituencies before the end of this year, along with a further $25 million in the following two years.

The message reflects Australian government anxieties that the treaty could be endangered if the prime minister was toppled and replaced by Mr Maelanga or another candidate more sceptical towards Australia, like former leader Manasseh Sogavare.

"I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity and lock this in ahead of the November budget session," he writes.

Text could spark political tension

While Mr Roach never directly endorses Mr Wale in his text, the message could still be politically contentious given it was sent in the midst of wrangling over the top job in Solomon Islands.

Opposition leader Manasseh Sogavare has repeatedly accused Australia of foreign interference in Solomon Islands, including when he was prime minister.

Mr Sade told the ABC there was nothing "political" about the message from the Australian High Commission.

"This was simply an update regarding the progress of the treaty discussions; it was never intended for political expediency," he said.

"I routinely receive these briefings to stay informed about the Community Partnerships Program."

The leak comes the day after Mr Wale managed to see off the challenge to his leadership, with the GREAT coalition winning back several defectors and recruiting additional opposition MPs to join their side.

On Sunday, Mr Maelanga announced he would withdraw his challenge, effectively acknowledging the prime minister still had the numbers.

Mr Wale told parliament on Monday morning that he wanted to "thank those that stood firm" behind him, as well as his new supporters, while praising Mr Maelanga for backing down.

"I would like to thank the member for withdrawing the motion … and bring[ing] down the temperature, both in the house, but also in the public mind," he said.

"What is clear, Mr Speaker, is that the public, not just in Honiara but right across the country … want to see the government be given adequate, reasonable opportunity to be able to deliver on its vision."

The prime minister also acknowledged that he had moved at breakneck pace since taking office, saying "many things are changing fast", adding that he had learned lessons from the whole episode.

Canberra moves to seize pro-Australia sentiment

His clear political victory will cause relief in Canberra, which was worried by the prospect of the prime minister being ousted.

Mr Wale only seized power in May, but has tacked sharply towards Australia and the US since then, signing a new agreement with the US Coast Guard and making it clear that he was deeply sceptical of China's attempts to embed itself as a security partner for the Pacific nation.

Australia has also been racing to complete negotiations on the new treaty with Solomon Islands while Mr Wale retains power, with the government keenly conscious that Solomon Islands politics remains inherently fluid and unpredictable.

The Pacific Minister Pat Conroy and senior Australian officials held multiple discussions on the treaty with Solomon Islands Foreign Minister Rick Hou and minister Peter Kenilorea Jr on the sidelines of the PIF leaders meeting last week.

Pat Conroy was tight-lipped on details of the treaty. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy, file)

In a statement, Mr Wale's office said the discussions "covered key national priorities including education, health, infrastructure, energy, agriculture, skills development, natural resource management and economic growth".

"A key focus was how Australia's development assistance can be better aligned with Solomon Islands' national priorities and contribute to tangible and measurable outcomes for communities," they said.

Treaty negotiations 'substantively concluded'

The talks came just a week or so after the Foreign Minister Penny Wong also held talks on the treaty with Mr Hou and a host of other Solomon Islands cabinet ministers in Adelaide.

While negotiations are officially ongoing, the ABC has been told that talks are rapidly coming to a close, with one source saying they are "substantively concluded."

An official from the Solomon Islands also said that the two countries had reached a "bilateral understanding" on the treaty.

Mr Conroy would not be drawn on exactly when the treaty would be signed, saying negotiations were "underway".

"Consistent with all of Australia's bilateral treaty negotiations, we will not comment on the details of the negotiations until the treaty is signed," he said.

The government has previously signalled it wanted to sign the pact before the end of the year, but the rapid progress meant the government was beginning to eye possible signing dates within the coming weeks.

Anthony Albanese and Mr Wale are both expected to attend several high-profile global gatherings, including the September United Nations General Assembly in September and possibly the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda in early November.

The former Australian High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Lachlan Strahan, said while the idea of a treaty was not new, the major commitments being made by Australia were "significant".

"If that's all new money then that's a step change in the amount of funding," he said.

James Batley from the Australian National University said Australia's decision to tip much more money into the constituency funds showed it was willing to do "whatever it takes" to get the deal over the line.

But he said while the risks around corruption and transparency connected to constituency funds were very real, they were manageable.

"I can't imagine that Australia would just tip in money and say go for it. I imagine there would be standards of transparency and accountability that they will insist on," he said.

"There's no question that it's a strongly held bipartisan view in Solomon Islands that MPs understand their constituencies best and should have a role promoting development in their constituencies."

Dr Strahan said that Australia had already been ramping up the quantities of money it was funnelling directly into local constituencies in Solomon Islands over several years.

"This is actually a fairly effective way of getting money out into constituencies and local communities. The main issue is making sure it's spent well, and ensuring it isn't used simply to prop up incumbents," he said.

However Tess Newton Cain, Associate Professor at the Griffith Asia Institute, said she was worried that Australia was trying to "pick winners" by throwing cash behind Mr Wale, which could backfire.

"It's not very strategically smart, because this is Melanesia and the politics are fluid and he's got elections on the horizon … if he's seen as Australia's man, that can have blowback," she said.

Dr Newton-Cain also said she would "need to be convinced" that the constituency funds were the best way to drive development in Solomon Islands.

"We've seen other attempts to make these funds more accountable and transparent and better governed, but they haven't really had much success," she said.

Mr Conroy did not confirm the increase in funding, but said Australian development projects would always maintain high standards.

"All Australian official development assistance is provided in line with Australia's high-quality development programming guidelines, and OECD eligibility criteria for Official Development Assistance," he said.

World.title: Fourth Tasmanian road fatality in a week sparks police plea
World.content:
A fourth fatality on Tasmanian roads within a week has led police to call for drivers to be safe "every time they travel".

On Monday, a woman died and two others left in a critical condition following a two-vehicle head-on crash at Old Beach, north of Hobart.

Tasmania Police said emergency services were called to the scene on East Derwent Highway, near Riviera Drive, about 1:30pm, where a blue Nissan and a silver Great Wall had collided.

Investigations into the crash involving a blue Nissan (left) and a silver Great Wall have begun. (ABC News: ABC News)

The female front-seat passenger of the Nissan was declared dead at the scene.

The female driver of the Nissan and the male driver of the Great Wall were taken to the Royal Hobart Hospital.

Both remain in a critical condition.

Tasmania Police Acting Inspector Amanda Hall has cautioned drivers to be safe "every time they travel on our roads".

"Every death on our roads is one too many, and today further families have received the devastating news that their loved one has died or been critically injured in a crash," she said.

Police are calling on drivers with dashcam footage of the cars to come forward. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Today's fatality comes after three people died and another two were left with "substantial injuries" when two vehicles collided on the Bass Highway, north of Elizabeth Town on Friday.

Monday's crash brings the total of road deaths this year to 25, compared to 30 at the same time last year.

Police are asking for anyone with dashcam footage of the vehicles ahead of the crash to call 131 444 or contact Crime Stoppers Tasmania anonymously at crimestopperstas.com.au.

Investigations into both crashes are continuing.

World.title: A Clockwork Orange to come to stage in eerily prescient adaptation
World.content:
When Margaret Thanos read A Clockwork Orange for the first time last year, she was struck by the similarities between the dystopia of the novel and society today.

"I couldn't help but feel Burgess was not describing some horrific imagined future, but the world I and my female friends feel like we live in right now," the director says.

Written by English author Anthony Burgess in 1962, in the shadow of World War II, A Clockwork Orange follows teenager Alex, who, with his gang of "droogs", inflicts "ultraviolence" on other people living in their near-future society.

When Alex is caught and convicted of the murder of an elderly woman, he is subjected to an experimental rehabilitation program, designed to make him severely ill at the thought of violence.

A Clockwork Orange was made into a movie by Stanley Kubrick in 1971 and will be adapted into a new play by Sydney's Belvoir St Theatre in 2027.

"I do feel like it's getting worse actually — that we're seeing a regression into a culture that not only condones but rewards behaviour of this kind: misogyny, racism, right-wing extremism," Thanos says.

Meet the 25yo director at the helm of Miranda Otto's return to the stage With two main-stage productions already under her belt in 2026, Margaret Thanos has cemented her place as a rising star of Australian theatre.

In her early 20s, Thanos worked in feminist activist spaces, including as an advocate for girls' equality non-profit Plan International, but found herself feeling despondent.

"I didn't really matter what we did inside of the feminist movement if we couldn't address the challenges inside of 'boys' club' culture," she says. "The internet was making the problem worse. It was encouraging us to stop thinking for ourselves."

That lack of thinking is something Thanos saw in Burgess's novel.

"[He] makes the central question about choice and free will and whether anyone is really choosing to be good," Thanos says.

" If we're not guided by a true sense of obligation to another human being standing in front of us, then we are more easily swayed by the structures of society around us to behave in whatever way we are told to behave. "

Thanos has directed two main-stage shows this year: A Mirror at Belvoir and The River at Sydney Theatre Company. (Supplied: STC/Daniel Boud)

Tom Wright, who Thanos approached to adapt A Clockwork Orange, was drawn to the story as a kind of fable.

"It's not a story of profound psychology," Wright says. "It's a story about a society and about how a society deals with its demons."

Wright was also excited by the chance to work with the made-up language Alex and his droogs speak to one another: the Russian-influenced "Nadsat".

"What leapt out was the quality of that spoken language and just how theatrically inventive it is," he says. "It's the language of an alienated class, but it also has a celebratory quality.

"Somehow Alex and his droogs have found a way to be almost more energetic and more exuberant than the society they belong to — they dress and speak more flamboyantly; their imaginative inner lives seem stronger than those of the people around them.

"[It's] almost as if their violent, antisocial behaviour is a legitimate response to an uncaring society."

Cross-generational collaboration

The collaboration between Thanos and Wright exemplifies the way Belvoir forges connections between artists of different generations and acts as a training ground for emerging theatre-makers.

"In theatre terms, Margaret and I are like two generations apart," Wright says. "That's a really useful collaboration.

" She can call upon my experience and I can call upon her ambition. "

It's a theme of the season, which also sees Belvoir's artistic director Eamon Flack assistant-directing the debut play from Kalkadoon writer-director Abbie-lee Lewis, Dirty Diamonds, about two Aboriginal women — played by Logie winner Lila McGuire (Goolagong) and Ruby Henaway — hitting the road to escape one of their exes.

Ruby Henaway and Lila McGuire will star in the debut play by director, writer and actor Abbie-lee Lewis, Dirty Diamonds. (Supplied: Belvoir/Daniel Boud)

Other young artists coming to the fore at Belvoir in 2027 are Ayah Tayeh and Mehhma Malhi, co-directors of Wish You Were Here, by Pulitzer Prize-winning Iranian American writer Sanaz Toossi (English); director Hannah Goodwin, and writer Grace Chapple, who are collaborating on The Landlord, Chapple's horror-comedy about intergenerational inequity, set in a pair of Sydney terrace houses.

"The only way a new generation can learn the sort of secret lore of [theatre] is for it to get passed on from one person to another," Flack says.

"We've taken artist development really seriously for a long time," Flack says. (Supplied: Belvoir/Brett Boardman)

Arts community banding together

Belvoir's 2027 season is the company's first since its workshop and warehouse were destroyed by fire in June.

The fire destroyed decades of props and sets, a ute and a forklift. (Supplied: Belvoir)

"We're through that initial stage of 'How the f*** do we keep going?', and we're now in the 'How do we rebuild?' stage," Flack says.

Thanks to the sheer willpower and efforts of Belvoir's production team — and the support of audiences through donations — The Jungle and the Sea and The Book of Everything opened as scheduled.

The former's sets had been destroyed in the fire and were re-created from scratch in just 10 days, while the latter's had already been lost after a previous tour and were painstakingly remade by both Belvoir staff and external contractors.

"We didn't have to miss an hour of [Jungle and the Sea] rehearsals because of the commitment and cunning and heart with which our production team just swung into action," Flack says.

" You could call it a miracle, but it's the people and the spirit of, 'let's get on with it'. "

The support of the arts community, including Sydney Theatre Company and Opera Australia offering space and equipment, is an example of how local companies are working together at a time when it is increasingly difficult to make theatre.

Belvoir's 2027 season Game. Set. Match. by Megan Wilding

The Lark by Daniel Keene

Stereophonic by David Adjmi

A Clockwork Orange by Anthony Burgess; adapted by Tom Wright

The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe by Jane Wagner

Dirty Diamonds by Abbie-lee Lewis

Wish You Were Here by Sanaz Toossi

The Landlord by Grace Chapple

Dancing at Lughnasa by Brian Friel

While the cost-of-living crisis is impacting audiences and artists alike, theatre companies are grappling with rising production costs, changing audience behaviours and a lack of funding.

"There's a vicious cycle going on," Flack says. "The material challenge of living the life of a theatre artist is excruciatingly difficult for so many people, and at the same time, so many companies are in such tight financial circumstances they're having to hire fewer artists."

So, companies are collaborating through co-productions and transfers, which not only extend the lives of shows, but keep artists, many of whom survive contract to contract, employed for longer periods.

Belvoir's 2027 season includes two co-productions, Stereophonic by David Adjmi, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC) and Queensland Theatre Company, and Dirty Diamonds, with MTC and in association with Yirra Yaakin Theatre Company in Perth.

It also includes two transfers, with Megan Wilding's Game. Set. Match. coming to Sydney from Melbourne's Malthouse, a decade after the Gamilaroi writer and actor first started to develop the play with Belvoir, and one-woman show The Lark, starring Noni Hazlehurst, opening after seasons in cities and regional centres around Australia.

"We're nothing on our own at Belvoir," Flack says.

"Sharing resources and giving shows future lives, letting them grow and become better and be seen by more communities across more parts of the country, that's the only strategy left."

World.title: 'Her career's finished': Fugitive Sydney developer's daughter avoids jail
World.content:
The daughter of "notorious" fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif has avoided jail for securing a $150 million loan from Westpac bank through a falsified document.

Ashlyn Nassif has been sentenced to a six-month community corrections order with no supervision after pleading guilty in June to publishing false misleading material to obtain advantage.

Ms Nassif was a solicitor and an executive at Toplace, the construction company owned by her father.

She sent a document falsifying the number of pre-sold units required to secure the loan and admitted to knowing some of the deposits were only 5 per cent of the value of the units.

Ms Nassif (back row, centre) pleaded guilty to the charges in June. (ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar)

Her lawyer Warwick Korn told the court Mr Nassif's reputation should not be a factor in considering his daughter's crime.

"He [Jean Nassif] has become notorious in this state," he said.

Ms Nassif provided a letter to the court which described how her relationship with her father influenced her decision.

According to the letter, Mr Nassif was angry with his daughter when he found out she had not sent the letter as he had asked.

According to Judge Christopher Halburd, Ms Nassif said: "I thought to myself, 'What if I continued to spiral?' I went back to the office and did what he asked, knowing that we didn't have the pre-sales required and some of the deposits were per cent."

Judge Halburd said the 32-year-old was remorseful.

"This defendant is not some sort of proxy for her father," he said.

"She's being sentenced not in relation to what he did. She's being sentenced for that one document that she didn't sign that she sent off under pressure from her father.

"She accepts that it's a serious matter and that she breached her position of trust as a solicitor."

Mr Korn told the court: "Her career's finished."

'Tyrannical father'

After reviewing several testimonies, the judge described Mr Nassif as a "somewhat tyrannical father … who seems to have escaped justice".

Former employees who witnessed her relationship with her father described him as "foul-mouth" and a "bully", who abused her almost daily.

The judge said that Ms Nassif was "not some sort of proxy for her father". (ABC News)

An affidavit provided by Ms Nassif's mother, now Mr Nassif's ex-wife, described a similar picture at home starting from a young age.

Mr Korn referenced the mother's testimony which said her ex-husband would be "telling her [Ashlyn Nassif] to lose weight, telling her to get cosmetic surgery so he could show her off".

Judge Halburd described it as a "complex matter" and a "difficult sentencing exercise", describing Ms Nassif as "a successful hard-working young woman, who would do almost anything not to disappoint her demanding father".

A psychologist's report provided to the court detailed the effects of Mr Nassif on his daughter's mental health, which the judge said was relevant to his sentencing.

"I accept that there was a life-long pattern established well before adulthood to comply with her father … and I do accept it's relevant," he said.

The judge described Ms Nassif (back row, centre) as someone who "would do almost anything not to disappoint her demanding father". (ABC News)

According to the report, abusive pressure from her father contributed to Ms Nassif's depression at the time of committing the offence and created a dynamic where she felt compelled "to placate with his demands to submit the fraudulent documents".

The judge said if the matter was concluded years earlier it would have been dealt with by way of a lengthy community corrections order.

He added there was "no point in having supervision" with her community corrections order.

World.title: ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach Matthew Knott Updated September 7, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale will move to fast-track a sweeping new $1 billion treaty after a push to overthrow Wale’s pro-Australia government imploded in a blow to Beijing’s ambitions to expand its influence in the Pacific. Wale’s success at fending off the attempt to overthrow him came as an immense relief to Albanese and foreign affairs officials in Canberra, who see him as one of Australia’s most important allies in the region. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen A leaked message from Australia’s High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to Deputy Solomons Prime Minister Francis Sade, seen by this masthead, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities. A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests.



“I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity, and lock this in ahead of the November budget session,” Roach wrote last week, as Wale was facing a no-confidence motion. The $980 million in funding by 2028, first reported by the ABC, is similar to the $1 billion pledged to support a recent set of treaties with Fiji over a 10-year timeframe. In Beijing, Xi Jinping’s foot soldiers will be lamenting a lost opportunity to install a pro-China leader in Honiara, just 2000 kilometres from the Australian mainland. The start of last week’s Pacific Islands Forum in Palau was rocked by the news that Wale had to race home to respond to a non-confidence motion lodged while he was en route to the event. As three of his cabinet ministers stepped down, Wale’s hold on power looked precarious just four months after his surprise election victory. But instead of gaining momentum, the amateurish putsch effort sputtered and flamed out. Manasseh Maelanga, the former cabinet minister who led the charge against Wale, announced on Sunday afternoon that he was withdrawing his no-confidence motion after failing to secure the numbers to bring the government down. Wale remains in power, his stature enhanced.



Related Article Pacific diplomacy The Solomons’ surprise new leader is a win for Australia, but the China challenge remains This matters to Australia because of the remarkable turnaround in foreign affairs Wale has spearheaded since coming to power in May. For most of the decade leading up to 2024, the Solomons were led by the mercurial Manasseh Sogavare, who was openly hostile towards Australia and signed a far-reaching security pact with China. That deal shocked Canberra and dominated days of the 2022 election campaign, with then opposition frontbencher Penny Wong branding it the nation’s worst foreign policy blunder since World War II. Successor Jeremiah Manele was less adversarial, but remained determined to play Canberra and Beijing off against each other. By contrast, Wale – a long-time critic of China who railed against politicians “sleazing up to Beijing” – has made clear his priority is deepening ties with Australia. Just weeks after coming to office, Wale declared he would review the China security pact and negotiate a comprehensive new treaty with Australia. He also announced he wanted to achieve an ambitious regional security pact – a move that would limit China’s ability to pick off individual countries.



When China test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile across the region in July, Wale showed no compunction in criticising the superpower, labelling it “not the act of a friend”. One of his top ministers, Peter Kenilorea Jr, has called for security and policing co-operation with China to be sidelined. This is why, despite no firm proof of meddling, Australian officials were convinced Beijing was helping to orchestrate the move against Wale. “It is just speculation, but I imagine they would have been very active,” says James Batley, a former Australian ambassador in Honiara. “They certainly have the motive.” There was even a chance Sogavare could have returned to power in a nightmare scenario for Canberra and a dream come true for Beijing. The Chinese government, for its part, angrily denies it seeks to interfere in Pacific nations’ internal affairs. The Solomons have long been known for its cycle of “grasshopper politics” in which MPs jump from one side of the aisle to another, driven less by ideology than personal advancement. Wale’s rapid attempts to drive domestic reforms and overhaul foreign relations undoubtedly rankled some of his cabinet colleagues, who found him high-handed and accused him of failing to consult on key decisions. Unlike Kevin Rudd, who faced similar accusations as prime minister, Wale has been given a chance to improve and grow in the job.



Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy China’s policing plans should be sidelined, says top Solomons minister Wale and Albanese will look to lock in their comprehensive treaty, which has largely been completed by officials. Initially slated to be struck by the end of the year, a deal could come ahead of schedule, with an Albanese-Wale meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this month the next opportunity to make progress on the pact. Wale’s proposal for a Pacific-wide security agreement will prove far more difficult, and perhaps impossible, to achieve given the diverging views within the region. Even so, Wale’s willingness to propose bold ideas that challenge Beijing shows why Albanese is delighted the push to oust him failed — at least for now. World.title: Workplace safety. Lap it up
World.content:
“Found recently in a Work, Health and Safety learning module, which I completed as part of the training for a new job: ‘Laptops must not be put on your lap.’ Oh, modern life! I really had to laugh.” Stay safe, Kerrie Wehbe of Blacktown.

“Harking back to the four-in-hand carriage drivers’ competition thread (C8) and (sort-of) defending Prince Philip, a brief internet search reveals that not only did he play a leading role in creating this competition, but that he actively assisted in writing the rules (including penalties for swearing. Ironically, he was frequently penalised),” writes Shirley Cook of Armidale. “He and other horse-loving royals did participate in the grooming, feeding and general care of their much-loved horses. At times, it was difficult to pick the prince from the groomsmen. Notably, there were two of the prince’s favourite carriage horses, plus an empty carriage, in his funeral procession.”

“Karin Viles (C8), before any fellow readers pun me out of town, know this,” declares Mike Fogarty of Weston (ACT). “Spaghetti bolognaise, lasagne and pizza supplement our national diet. The absence of these magnificent three staples, from any cafe menu or home kitchen, is long pasta joke.”

“Has anyone else noticed an abundance of the most efficient killers of the animal world suddenly swarming?” asks Dermot Perry of Mount Keira. “I’m referring to the dragonflies which have appeared in large numbers here in the Illawarra.”

“One wonders if anybody could have a legitimate reason for wearing camera glasses (C8) but now there’s the camera toothbrush!” observes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Could there be a more useless object and what will come next, the hairbrush camera?”

World.title: Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy Daniel Lo Surdo September 7, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Barnaby Joyce’s latest interview on ABC’s 7.30 program devolved into chaos when he shouted that he was One Nation’s treasury spokesman – “not Jesus Christ” – when pressed on modelling central to his party’s controversial superannuation policy unveiled on Monday. Loading Joyce was facing a grilling on Monday’s edition of 7.30 when host Sarah Ferguson challenged the One Nation MP to model the lifetime losses different Australians would incur from the policy, which would allow renters and mortgage holders to dip into a quarter of their superannuation contributions over three years. Joyce railed against the question, upset that he wasn’t provided the examples before the interview, as Ferguson pushed him for an answer. “Well, here we go folks, I’ll try and answer something which we’ll need an annuity table and will also need a sort of lineal regression, but I’ll do it for you, straight down the barrel,” Joyce said.



Ferguson responded: “Barnaby Joyce, if I may, obviously this is a policy that your party has come up with, so we would expect you as the Treasury spokesman for that party to be across it, just try it.” Joyce: “The Treasury spokesman [yes], not Jesus Christ.” Ferguson continued, listing the forecast superannuation losses for Australians aged 30, 40 and 50, earning a range of incomes. Joyce refused to engage with the question, though did say he was “happy to come back tomorrow” and give informed answers provided Ferguson was “prepared to pay my accountancy fees”. Less than two months ago, Joyce unleashed at his dog, Stella, while being interviewed by Ferguson, creating a video clip that quickly went viral across the country. One Nation capitalised on the attention by selling custom dog leads following the interview, as part of a wider push of products under the “Sit Down! Barnaby’s Dog Leads” merchandise umbrella. Barnaby Joyce yells at his dog, Stella, during a live interview on the ABC current affairs program 7.30 in July. ABC



Joyce announced the superannuation policy alongside party leader Pauline Hanson at a rare Canberra press conference on Monday, dismissing suggestions the proposed reform would raise inflation and discourage real pay rises. One Nation claim that almost two-thirds of workers would be able to access the scheme, and that a median worker would receive an additional $2300 per year under the policy. Related Article Superannuation ‘They’ll lie again’: Barnaby Joyce hits back in superannuation fight with Labor It has been panned by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, with Chalmers saying it was setting the scene for the next election to be a “referendum on super”. Chalmers said One Nation’s policy was a “recipe to make Australian workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off in retirement”, and argued that compound interest losses would negatively outweigh the short-term financial benefit of the new policy. Hanson promptly called Chalmers “hysterical” in a post on social media and blamed him for the state of the economy. “Perhaps if you hadn’t so thoroughly buggered the economy, Jim, they wouldn’t need to [access superannuation],” she wrote.



One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce hold their press conference in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Hanson and Joyce said there would be no threshold of financial difficulty for access to the scheme, meaning all renters and mortgage holders – about two-thirds of the population – could benefit. Joyce said he anticipated that “overwhelmingly” people would only access the scheme if they were in financial hardship, and would need to make applications to their superannuation funds claiming support to make rent and mortgage payments. He acknowledged that “a couple” of people may attempt to flout the system. Later in Monday’s interview, Joyce revealed he hadn’t known about allegations of illicit drug use and “sexual deviance” levelled at One Nation Victorian party leader Warren Pickering, reported in The Australian.
