World.title: Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: energy healing at police HQ, rethinking the First Nations Health Office, musical chairs at CS Energy, and more. Sometimes after a tough week serving the public, you just need your energy healed. If you work at the Roma Street police headquarters, you might turn to the volunteers at the Zi Zai Dong Zen Association, an organisation based in Brisbane’s south that offers a good cleansing through the ancient Chinese meditation technique of qi gong. Zi Zai Dong Zen Association volunteers at police HQ for a monthly session late last year. Zi Zai Dong Zen Association Inc Facebook ZZDZ gently hover their hands over the bodies of police staff, a process they say improves sleep quality, relieves stress, eliminates negative energy and even boosts immune systems and emotional stability.



Police spinners chose not to respond to direct questions about how the relationship with ZZDZ came about, but a spokesperson said it was a voluntary staff welfare program. Related Article Vale Former police commissioner Steve Gollschewski dies, months after retirement ZZDZ’s public co-ordinator Angela Nee said the not-for-profit had been healing cops’ qi since 2018. “Police officers sacrifice so much and work daily in highly stressful environments to protect our communities. Providing these sessions is our way of returning their kindness and helping them relieve stress,” she said. One participant told Circus the process is quite relaxing, and it sounds like a popular way to spend some time on a Thursday morning.



In a post from June, ZZDZ said 13 volunteers provided healing to 110 QPS staff, “with staff leaving emotionally rejuvenated and experiencing a tangible boost to their physical and mental wellbeing”. Police health coach Jarrod Presland, in a 2024 testimonial on the group’s website, said the monthly healing, chakra initiation and coaching sessions were “extremely popular”. “I would highly recommend ZZDZ energy healing to any QLD Government entity who is looking to provide wellbeing initiatives to their staff and would welcome any queries from anyone considering utilising the association’s services,” Presland wrote in a letter published by ZZDZ. Maybe we could use a session in the tent! We’d certainly like to hear any tips about the wellbeing offerings at your public sector workplace. First Nations Health Office, first downgraded, now under review



The government has denied any coordinated campaign to remove First Nations representation, but it’s been difficult not to see a trend emerging since the 2024 election. So the Circus tent was intrigued to hear of a review of the First Nations Health Office, within director-general David Rosengren’s Department of Health. Queensland’s Chief First Nations Health Officer Samantha Wild and Health Minister Tim Nicholls, announcing her appointment in a Facebook post in July. Tim Nicholls MP / Facebook Readers may recall recent criticism of Rosengren from one hospital and health service insider, who suggested he had misled estimates with remarks about the reason three legally required First Nations board roles were vacant. Neither Rosengren, nor his departmental spinners, have answered our questions about the roles, citing applicant confidentiality. Our approaches this week delivered no update on how recruitment is going, but it’s said to be “nearing an end”.



Another role recently subject to a lengthy hiring process was that of the Chief First Nations Health Officer, after it was vacated by inaugural figure, Yalangi and Tagalaka woman Haylene Grogan. January saw job ads go up for the gig – downgraded from its previous deputy director-general level in July last year, as previously reported by the ABC – with Wakka Wakka and South Sea Islander woman Samantha Wild named as Grogan’s replacement in July. Wild is said to be considering opportunities to improve the operating model of the office, which issued its first report under Grogan last September. That report noted a continued focus by the department on increasing representation and authority of First Nations leadership. In a statement, a Queensland Health spokesperson told Circus the work had been kicked off from inside the unit, which now reports “operationally” to deputy director-general for system policy and planning Peta Bryant – currently filling in as Townsville HHS chief executive – and “strategically” to Rosengren.



“To ensure we continue to deliver healthcare that drives meaningful outcomes for mob and communities across Queensland, an internal strategic review has been initiated from within the First Nations Health Office.” Related Article Public service Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show This was said to be a regular practice, part of good governance and organisational effectiveness, and something which would “help ensure the First Nations Health Office continues to provide strategic leadership and maximise its contribution to better health equity and outcomes”. We reached out to Wild independently of the department, but didn’t hear back. Musical chairs at the top of CS Energy





A check of the CS Energy website confirmed Bellas ended up taking a “temporary leave of absence” from his board duties, with Seeney in the big chair since April 9. Jeff Seeney during his time as deputy premier in the Newman government. Glenn Hunt Why the change of plans? We sought some clarity from Seeney and Bellas’ media team, and were advised by a company spokesperson it was about avoiding “any corporate governance issues that could arise from the combined role of Acting CEO and Executive Chair”. Harty starts on 28 September. A familiar face joins the TEQ board



We’d gone at least a couple of Fridays without news of new appointments on a government board. That was until 2.30pm on the final day of last week, when Tourism Minister Andrew Powell lobbed a media release with changes to the one steering Tourism and Events Queensland. Out of the chair after one term is nature-based and Indigenous tourism leader Grant Hunt AM, replaced with former Tourism Australia managing director John O’Sullivan. Also out, some 12 months ahead of the end of their terms, are Karen Bolinger, Stephanie Parkin, Rob Hudson and Brian Hennessy. Among those replacing them is former Brisbane deputy mayor and still-serving Holland Park ward LNP councillor Krista Adams, who announced last year she won’t contest the next council election.



At the time, she also stepped back from her deputy mayor and civic cabinet role – and the topped-up pay packets that come with them. But not to worry: in the past three months, Adams has picked up not only the TIQ board gig (worth about $15,000 in 2024-25) but also a spot on the Economic Development Queensland board (worth more than $80,000 in 2024-25). Then-deputy mayor Krista Adams with Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner after the re-election of their LNP administration in 2024. Cameron Atfield Others landing on the TIQ board include Jacob Cassidy, Roderic Rees and Damien Massingham – a former Tourism Noosa chief executive and LNP preselection candidate. We might hear more news from Adams before her council term is up – given City Hall’s habit of having outgoing councillors hand over the baton within a year of an election.



No fireworks for you As far as Riverfire views go, 1 William Street has one of the best. So it’s no surprise it was a hot ticket, with public servants offered the opportunity to watch the show from the Tower of Power. Not every public servant was invited. According to an email from acting DPC Deputy Director General Jaime Blackburn, only those who serve from 1 William Street in their 9-to-5 could get access to the spots. Once accepted, they could bring their families (up to four visitors, in some cases) along to the strictly no-booze viewing. Workers were asked to donate $20 to the Starlight Children’s Foundation in exchange for the privilege, and spots on some levels were gobbled up in under an hour.



A government spinner said 1 William Street employees were allowed to attend the floor they work on during Riverfire, as has been the case for years. Another reason for ladder-climbers to try and get up a few rungs before next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: Locals-focused wine bar and op shop lands in brilliant heritage location
World.content:
Eating outFood Locals-focused wine bar and op shop lands in brilliant heritage location One of the city’s cherished small-bar spots rides again, dedicated to funky small-producer wines, approachable eats and vintage threads. Matt Shea September 7, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Louise Marks couldn’t sleep. She and a colleague had gone to inspect the Valley premises previously occupied by Barry Parade Public House. “Shaun [Fugill, co-owner of Teneriffe’s Zero Fox] told me about Barry Parade closing and how beautiful the space is, and I thought, ‘We should go have look just for shits and giggles.’ And it was amazing. I could envisage exactly what it would look like.” Bar Lou Lou has opened in the premises previously occupied by Barry Parade Public House. Markus Ravik “It” would become Bar Lou Lou, a wine bar that Marks opened in the space mid-August. It completes a heady career change who Marks, who just nine months ago was working in media. In between, she’d been pouring beers with Fugill at Zero Fox.



“I literally packed up my career,” she says. “Zero Fox had always been one of my favourite venues in Brisbane, and I said when I started that my goal was to one day have my own venue. It felt like such a pipe dream.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead Bar Lou Lou demonstrates an impressive degree of vision for a first-time owner. It perhaps helps that Marks was working with such good bones with the old Barry Parade Public House. The venue’s 1920s-built heritage facade is just as beautiful as ever, and the terrazzo floors, timber bar and globe pendant lights are all present and correct. Otherwise, Marks has swapped the green paint job for a rich burgundy and filled the bar with mismatched furniture and cushions, giving it a homey and lived-in vibe. At the back, there’s the same timber outdoor area but Marks has converted a side room into a mini op shop. The heritage facade remains much the same. Markus Ravik



“People are literally buying clothes and immediately putting them on and sitting there finishing their drink. It’s so fun,” she says. “Everything in the place is second hand. Even the plates are from the op shop, which was driving chef insane at first but he loves it now.” That same unfussy approach has been applied to the drinks list. Bar Lou Lou is billed as a wine bar first but it drills down on just 12 drops, all available by the glass and bottle. Much of the fitout remains unchanged from its Barry Parade Public House days, but the venue now has a more homey, lived-in vibe. Markus Ravik Marks’ focus is the interesting and unusual. Expect the list to change regularly but you can currently order wines such as a Harrison grenache blanc from McLaren Vale, a Clare Valley Sigurd chenin blanc, and a Barossa Adlib GSM.



“I’ve just tried to pick my favourite wines that I’ve tasted over the past year at Zero Fox and other places, and arranged them from different vendors or direct from the winemakers.” The venue still boasts its winsome courtyard. Markus Ravik Alongside the wines there are three beers on tap – including Guinness – six more available by the stubbie or can, and a handful of cocktails – and that’s pretty much it. For food, chef Adnane Khattabi has created a fun but filling menu of bar eats. There’s fried chicken served with a Sriracha mayonnaise dipping sauce; toasted roti with a red curry satay sauce; banh mi crostinis; and tuna tataki served with house made blood orange ponzu, hazelnut crisp and avocado puree. The food menu is intended to be fun but filling. Markus Ravik



“I really want it to be a neighbourhood local, especially because of where it’s situated,” Marks says. “If you live in the Spring Hill area, it’s a stop before you head into the Valley. And other than The Alliance, there aren’t too many local-focused bars around here.” Open Wed-Sat 12pm-10pm, Sun 12pm-8pm 122 Barry Parade, Fortitude Valley barloulou.com.au

World.title: ‘Shameful con’: Labor proposes last-minute change to IBAC reform
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll’s promised reforms to give the state’s peak anti-corruption body greater reach and powers are at risk of collapse following a proposed last-minute change that would prevent IBAC from investigating some allegations relating to Victoria’s Big Build sites. Both the Coalition and the Greens have threatened to withdraw their support for Labor’s proposed legislation, which is set to be introduced into parliament on Tuesday, after the government confirmed its law change would declare any allegations IBAC had already dealt with under its old powers off limits. The carve-out includes allegations former premier Jacinta Allan referred to IBAC more than two years ago after a joint investigation by The Age, The Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes revealed organised crime had infiltrated government-funded major building projects. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll. Chris Hopkins The proposed legislation, which gives IBAC follow-the-money powers and a broader definition of corruption to launch investigations, prevents it from applying the broader powers and jurisdiction to matters it has already investigated, decided not to investigate or referred to another integrity agency.



The government believes the new Kourakis royal commission is the primary body for investigating allegations of corruption and misconduct associated with the Big Build, and that the commission will work closely with a special prosecutor, IBAC and Victoria Police to ensure all claims of serious wrongdoing are examined. On Monday night, shadow attorney-general James Newbury described the move as a “shameful con” and an eleventh-hour manoeuvre before parliament is prorogued ahead of November’s state election. “Ben Carroll and Labor are shamefully trying to keep covered up the worst corruption scandal in our state’s history,” Newbury said. “Labor has confirmed their proposed new powers won’t let IBAC revisit old corruption allegations it has dismissed, referred elsewhere or finished investigating. “Victorians deserve to know the extent of corruption on the Big Build. IBAC must not be blocked from that work. What a shameful con from an end of days government.”



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Integrity experts urge royal commission to look beyond crooks to deeper problem Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt rejected the criticism. “The Liberals are lying,” she said. “The royal commission will be able to investigate any allegations of crime, corruption and serious misconduct on Big Build projects. “We’re fast-tracking the new laws, so IBAC has the follow-the-money powers it needs to uncover corruption this year, not in 2027.” An opposition party room meeting scheduled for Tuesday morning is expected to withdraw support for the bill unless it is substantially amended.



Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the legislation needed to provide greater scope for IBAC to conduct public examinations of witnesses, including parliamentarians. “The Greens dragged Labor kicking and screaming to finally strengthen IBAC, but as per usual with Labor, they’ve done it in a way that has big carve-outs to protect themselves and leave Victorians in the dark,” Sandell said. Allan wrote to IBAC in July 2024, a day after the first revelations of the Building Bad investigation were published by this masthead, urging the anti-corruption body to investigate the claims. “I am concerned to ensure that any allegations of serious corruption that are within the remit of IBAC are identified, investigated and appropriate action taken by IBAC,” she wrote. In February this year, it was revealed that IBAC had assessed the premier’s referral and found it to be outside its jurisdiction at the time.



At the time, IBAC was still assessing a separate referral from Newbury about the contents of a report from anti-corruption advocate Geoffrey Watson, SC, which outlined serious misconduct in the CFMEU, the union which under the Andrews and Allan governments established an industrial monopoly over Big Build projects. In July, Newbury made a further referral over allegations that state government officials told builders to cut a deal with the CFMEU following a dispute on a key level crossing removal site. Jacinta Allan faced increasing questions about corruption in the state’s Big Build projects in the lead up to her resignation as premier. Penny Stephens The status of Newbury’s referrals is not known. IBAC does not typically confirm or deny what matters it is investigating. It responded to media requests about Allan’s referral only after the former premier publicly released her letter. The proposed changes to IBAC’s laws would allow the agency to use its new powers and jurisdiction on matters it is currently investigating, as well as any future investigations.



The government legislation would expand IBAC’s working definition of corrupt conduct beyond its current requirement that it must constitute a criminal offence punishable by five years’ jail. This jurisdictional limitation, which has been criticised by successive IBAC commissions, is more narrow than that used by any other peak anti-corruption body in Australia. Related Article Opinion

Kourakis royal commission Courage or a cop-out? Carroll faces defining test in his very first decision Nick McKenzie Investigative reporter The definition of corruption would be broadened to include any offence or serious disciplinary matter. This covers a much wider range of activity – such as misconduct and major breaches of ministerial and local government codes of conduct – and would enable IBAC to investigate what its former commissioner Robert Redlich described as “grey corruption”. Redlich, the Centre for Public Integrity, Transparency International Australia, former ombudsman Deborah Glass and other integrity advocates have repeatedly called for IBAC’s working definition of corruption to be brought into line with the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption and the National Anti-Corruption Commission. IBAC’s proposed follow-the-money powers, would allow it to pursue investigations beyond major government contractors, into subcontractors and labour hire firms who ultimately receive taxpayer funds.



Since replacing Allan, Carroll has staked his nascent premiership on restoring government integrity, promising to bring forward greater powers for IBAC and establish a royal commission into Big Build corruption on the first day of his leadership. Alongside the proposed IBAC legislation, the government will this week introduce into parliament proposed legislation to establish a special prosecutor’s office to work in tandem with the royal commission. World.title: Despite declining fertility, Gen Z do want kids – but two things are holding them back
World.content:
NationalFertility Despite declining fertility, Gen Z do want kids – but two things are holding them back Wendy Tuohy September 7, 2026 — 7:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most young Australians are still interested in having children — despite what the nation’s steep decline in fertility rates suggests — but their family plans are affected by their worry about the future. The most obvious barrier, tough economic times leading to unaffordable housing, is not what they see as their greatest hurdle. Scarlet Lee, the Youth Governor of Victoria’s Youth Parliament, says young women are career-focused but believe work and family should still be possible. Ruby Alexander Instead, in a longitudinal study of about 8000 people in Generation Z, half of those aged 19-20 years old and half aged 23-24 said lack of trust in public institutions and concerns for the climate were influencing their thoughts on becoming parents, but this had not put them off intending to do so. Australia’s birth rate hit an all-time low in 2024, but data from the Australian Institute of Family Studies’ Growing Up in Australia longitudinal study found 71 per cent of young people in both groups hope to have children, and only 17 per cent say they do not want them; 13 per cent said they had not yet considered it.



Study lead Kirsten Campbell said young people were showing a strong interest in forming families, but social cohesion, environmental degradation and trust in public institutions such as hospitals, police, education, legal and social welfare systems were affecting their choices. Related Article Motherhood ‘Thanks, Mum, but I don’t want your life’ – is the load that buckled their mothers putting off Gen Z? Those with higher trust in such social structures (79 per cent) were more likely to hope for children compared with those who trusted such supports less (59 per cent). “Overall, the story of the data shows there is still a strong interest in forming families, but what they look like is different, and those families are being formed later,” she said. “What’s driving whether their hope is translated into concrete intentions is … trust in the future state of the world.” Campbell said the researchers were surprised by this finding, as they were expecting economic stress was going to be the key influence in young people’s family intentions and projected decision-making. “The economy’s always tough, money is always tough [for young people] but what is really driving their translation of intentions is trust and hope for the future, and ‘Is this a world I would like to bring my children into?’”



Related Article Parenting The ‘failure to launch’ myth: Why adult children living at home has become the new normal Almost all young people were worried about the future economy (79 per cent), but these concerns were not linked to whether young people hoped to have children or not. The study is following the cohort though the life course, and this data is from wave 10 of the findings. About two-thirds of the Gen Z subjects were concerned about the environment (65 per cent), but those who were less concerned about it were more likely to want children. Young women were generally more concerned about the future, and had less trust in institutions, than young men, which Campbell said was likely because women believed they would need support from systems including health and childcare when they became mothers. Women still assumed the bulk of the parenting load would fall to them, so they felt they needed to have trust in the “social fabric” around them to assist. Young people said their family intentions were distant, and would not be put into action within five years.





“Young women are probably not seeing many creative solutions; it comes down to valuing care … there is still a lack of flexibility, they are probably seeing a lack of autonomy and control [for working mothers] and it’s looking quite challenging,” Gregory said. The knowledge that caring for children is still seen mainly as mothers’ work, and is still undervalued by society may also be influencing young women’s family choice. “The [Australian] household is quite consistent in expectations and norms around parenting and care, and who does the care – not just for infants but also elder care or care for family members who at any time in life might need help,” Gregory said. “It’s very gendered and quite consistent.” Teaching student and youth advocate Scarlet Lee said young women around her were highly career-focused and determined to put their educations to use in full work lives.



Related Article Fertility Seven things to know about Australia’s baby bust – and what it means for you “I am quite married to my work, I have two jobs and volunteer as Youth Governor of Victoria,” says Lee, who helped to platform the views and priorities of her generational peers in the state’s Youth Parliament of 2026. Lee aspires to eventually become a school principal, but alongside the lofty ambitions of Gen Z, young women also value having the choice whether to become mothers. “It still does factor in a little bit that women feel the pressure of having to choose between a successful career or to start a family,” Lee said. “Young women now are very aware they do have a choice.” Housing is definitely still a concern for Generation Z: “Across the board, young people are very aware of the cost of living and there being a big disparity between how accessible things were in the past compared with the present.”



Like Campbell, Lee said their peers were aware of gender roles in parenting – “norms that women are meant to be the home-makers and raise the children, and men’s work is seen as more valuable” – but their generation considered these to be no longer as relevant as they once were. Loading The Australian Institute of Family Studies data found concerns about housing affordability were widespread (85 per cent), irrespective of young people’s plans to have children. Among young people most worried about the global economy, or finding work, nearly one in five (19 per cent) did not expect to have children – particularly young women. Editor's pick Exclusive

Medical Malfunctions ‘Impossible to give consent’: Medtech giant hid bad data from patients, doctors “Often young women now know what they want for themselves, and they’re very aware of how they want their future to look: they are quite discerning in the partners they choose and the roles they choose to play in a relationship,” Lee said.



“You can find wholeness in a career and social connections – and having a family – [but] a woman’s worth isn’t defined by her ability to start a family, it is not the sole source of fulfillment.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach Matthew Knott Updated September 7, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale will move to fast-track a sweeping new $1 billion treaty after a push to overthrow Wale’s pro-Australia government imploded in a blow to Beijing’s ambitions to expand its influence in the Pacific. Wale’s success at fending off the attempt to overthrow him came as an immense relief to Albanese and foreign affairs officials in Canberra, who see him as one of Australia’s most important allies in the region. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen A leaked message from Australia’s High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to Deputy Solomons Prime Minister Francis Sade, seen by this masthead, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities. A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests.



“I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity, and lock this in ahead of the November budget session,” Roach wrote last week, as Wale was facing a no-confidence motion. The $980 million in funding by 2028, first reported by the ABC, is similar to the $1 billion pledged to support a recent set of treaties with Fiji over a 10-year timeframe. In Beijing, Xi Jinping’s foot soldiers will be lamenting a lost opportunity to install a pro-China leader in Honiara, just 2000 kilometres from the Australian mainland. The start of last week’s Pacific Islands Forum in Palau was rocked by the news that Wale had to race home to respond to a non-confidence motion lodged while he was en route to the event. As three of his cabinet ministers stepped down, Wale’s hold on power looked precarious just four months after his surprise election victory. But instead of gaining momentum, the amateurish putsch effort sputtered and flamed out. Manasseh Maelanga, the former cabinet minister who led the charge against Wale, announced on Sunday afternoon that he was withdrawing his no-confidence motion after failing to secure the numbers to bring the government down. Wale remains in power, his stature enhanced.



Related Article Pacific diplomacy The Solomons’ surprise new leader is a win for Australia, but the China challenge remains This matters to Australia because of the remarkable turnaround in foreign affairs Wale has spearheaded since coming to power in May. For most of the decade leading up to 2024, the Solomons were led by the mercurial Manasseh Sogavare, who was openly hostile towards Australia and signed a far-reaching security pact with China. That deal shocked Canberra and dominated days of the 2022 election campaign, with then opposition frontbencher Penny Wong branding it the nation’s worst foreign policy blunder since World War II. Successor Jeremiah Manele was less adversarial, but remained determined to play Canberra and Beijing off against each other. By contrast, Wale – a long-time critic of China who railed against politicians “sleazing up to Beijing” – has made clear his priority is deepening ties with Australia. Just weeks after coming to office, Wale declared he would review the China security pact and negotiate a comprehensive new treaty with Australia. He also announced he wanted to achieve an ambitious regional security pact – a move that would limit China’s ability to pick off individual countries.



When China test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile across the region in July, Wale showed no compunction in criticising the superpower, labelling it “not the act of a friend”. One of his top ministers, Peter Kenilorea Jr, has called for security and policing co-operation with China to be sidelined. This is why, despite no firm proof of meddling, Australian officials were convinced Beijing was helping to orchestrate the move against Wale. “It is just speculation, but I imagine they would have been very active,” says James Batley, a former Australian ambassador in Honiara. “They certainly have the motive.” There was even a chance Sogavare could have returned to power in a nightmare scenario for Canberra and a dream come true for Beijing. The Chinese government, for its part, angrily denies it seeks to interfere in Pacific nations’ internal affairs. The Solomons have long been known for its cycle of “grasshopper politics” in which MPs jump from one side of the aisle to another, driven less by ideology than personal advancement. Wale’s rapid attempts to drive domestic reforms and overhaul foreign relations undoubtedly rankled some of his cabinet colleagues, who found him high-handed and accused him of failing to consult on key decisions. Unlike Kevin Rudd, who faced similar accusations as prime minister, Wale has been given a chance to improve and grow in the job.



Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy China’s policing plans should be sidelined, says top Solomons minister Wale and Albanese will look to lock in their comprehensive treaty, which has largely been completed by officials. Initially slated to be struck by the end of the year, a deal could come ahead of schedule, with an Albanese-Wale meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this month the next opportunity to make progress on the pact. Wale’s proposal for a Pacific-wide security agreement will prove far more difficult, and perhaps impossible, to achieve given the diverging views within the region. Even so, Wale’s willingness to propose bold ideas that challenge Beijing shows why Albanese is delighted the push to oust him failed — at least for now. World.content:
“Found recently in a Work, Health and Safety learning module, which I completed as part of the training for a new job: ‘Laptops must not be put on your lap.’ Oh, modern life! I really had to laugh.” Stay safe, Kerrie Wehbe of Blacktown.

“Harking back to the four-in-hand carriage drivers’ competition thread (C8) and (sort-of) defending Prince Philip, a brief internet search reveals that not only did he play a leading role in creating this competition, but that he actively assisted in writing the rules (including penalties for swearing. Ironically, he was frequently penalised),” writes Shirley Cook of Armidale. “He and other horse-loving royals did participate in the grooming, feeding and general care of their much-loved horses. At times, it was difficult to pick the prince from the groomsmen. Notably, there were two of the prince’s favourite carriage horses, plus an empty carriage, in his funeral procession.”

“Karin Viles (C8), before any fellow readers pun me out of town, know this,” declares Mike Fogarty of Weston (ACT). “Spaghetti bolognaise, lasagne and pizza supplement our national diet. The absence of these magnificent three staples, from any cafe menu or home kitchen, is long pasta joke.”

“Has anyone else noticed an abundance of the most efficient killers of the animal world suddenly swarming?” asks Dermot Perry of Mount Keira. “I’m referring to the dragonflies which have appeared in large numbers here in the Illawarra.”

“One wonders if anybody could have a legitimate reason for wearing camera glasses (C8) but now there’s the camera toothbrush!” observes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Could there be a more useless object and what will come next, the hairbrush camera?”

World.title: Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy Daniel Lo Surdo September 7, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Barnaby Joyce’s latest interview on ABC’s 7.30 program devolved into chaos when he shouted that he was One Nation’s treasury spokesman – “not Jesus Christ” – when pressed on modelling central to his party’s controversial superannuation policy unveiled on Monday. Loading Joyce was facing a grilling on Monday’s edition of 7.30 when host Sarah Ferguson challenged the One Nation MP to model the lifetime losses different Australians would incur from the policy, which would allow renters and mortgage holders to dip into a quarter of their superannuation contributions over three years. Joyce railed against the question, upset that he wasn’t provided the examples before the interview, as Ferguson pushed him for an answer. “Well, here we go folks, I’ll try and answer something which we’ll need an annuity table and will also need a sort of lineal regression, but I’ll do it for you, straight down the barrel,” Joyce said.



Ferguson responded: “Barnaby Joyce, if I may, obviously this is a policy that your party has come up with, so we would expect you as the Treasury spokesman for that party to be across it, just try it.” Joyce: “The Treasury spokesman [yes], not Jesus Christ.” Ferguson continued, listing the forecast superannuation losses for Australians aged 30, 40 and 50, earning a range of incomes. Joyce refused to engage with the question, though did say he was “happy to come back tomorrow” and give informed answers provided Ferguson was “prepared to pay my accountancy fees”. Less than two months ago, Joyce unleashed at his dog, Stella, while being interviewed by Ferguson, creating a video clip that quickly went viral across the country. One Nation capitalised on the attention by selling custom dog leads following the interview, as part of a wider push of products under the “Sit Down! Barnaby’s Dog Leads” merchandise umbrella. Barnaby Joyce yells at his dog, Stella, during a live interview on the ABC current affairs program 7.30 in July. ABC



Joyce announced the superannuation policy alongside party leader Pauline Hanson at a rare Canberra press conference on Monday, dismissing suggestions the proposed reform would raise inflation and discourage real pay rises. One Nation claim that almost two-thirds of workers would be able to access the scheme, and that a median worker would receive an additional $2300 per year under the policy. Related Article Superannuation ‘They’ll lie again’: Barnaby Joyce hits back in superannuation fight with Labor It has been panned by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, with Chalmers saying it was setting the scene for the next election to be a “referendum on super”. Chalmers said One Nation’s policy was a “recipe to make Australian workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off in retirement”, and argued that compound interest losses would negatively outweigh the short-term financial benefit of the new policy. Hanson promptly called Chalmers “hysterical” in a post on social media and blamed him for the state of the economy. “Perhaps if you hadn’t so thoroughly buggered the economy, Jim, they wouldn’t need to [access superannuation],” she wrote.



One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce hold their press conference in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Hanson and Joyce said there would be no threshold of financial difficulty for access to the scheme, meaning all renters and mortgage holders – about two-thirds of the population – could benefit. Joyce said he anticipated that “overwhelmingly” people would only access the scheme if they were in financial hardship, and would need to make applications to their superannuation funds claiming support to make rent and mortgage payments. He acknowledged that “a couple” of people may attempt to flout the system. Later in Monday’s interview, Joyce revealed he hadn’t known about allegations of illicit drug use and “sexual deviance” levelled at One Nation Victorian party leader Warren Pickering, reported in The Australian. World.title: Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: energy healing at police HQ, rethinking the First Nations Health Office, musical chairs at CS Energy, and more. Sometimes after a tough week serving the public, you just need your energy healed. If you work at the Roma Street police headquarters, you might turn to the volunteers at the Zi Zai Dong Zen Association, an organisation based in Brisbane’s south that offers a good cleansing through the ancient Chinese meditation technique of qi gong. Zi Zai Dong Zen Association volunteers at police HQ for a monthly session late last year. Zi Zai Dong Zen Association Inc Facebook ZZDZ gently hover their hands over the bodies of police staff, a process they say improves sleep quality, relieves stress, eliminates negative energy and even boosts immune systems and emotional stability.



Police spinners chose not to respond to direct questions about how the relationship with ZZDZ came about, but a spokesperson said it was a voluntary staff welfare program. Related Article Vale Former police commissioner Steve Gollschewski dies, months after retirement ZZDZ’s public co-ordinator Angela Nee said the not-for-profit had been healing cops’ qi since 2018. “Police officers sacrifice so much and work daily in highly stressful environments to protect our communities. Providing these sessions is our way of returning their kindness and helping them relieve stress,” she said. One participant told Circus the process is quite relaxing, and it sounds like a popular way to spend some time on a Thursday morning.



In a post from June, ZZDZ said 13 volunteers provided healing to 110 QPS staff, “with staff leaving emotionally rejuvenated and experiencing a tangible boost to their physical and mental wellbeing”. Police health coach Jarrod Presland, in a 2024 testimonial on the group’s website, said the monthly healing, chakra initiation and coaching sessions were “extremely popular”. “I would highly recommend ZZDZ energy healing to any QLD Government entity who is looking to provide wellbeing initiatives to their staff and would welcome any queries from anyone considering utilising the association’s services,” Presland wrote in a letter published by ZZDZ. Maybe we could use a session in the tent! We’d certainly like to hear any tips about the wellbeing offerings at your public sector workplace. First Nations Health Office, first downgraded, now under review



The government has denied any coordinated campaign to remove First Nations representation, but it’s been difficult not to see a trend emerging since the 2024 election. So the Circus tent was intrigued to hear of a review of the First Nations Health Office, within director-general David Rosengren’s Department of Health. Queensland’s Chief First Nations Health Officer Samantha Wild and Health Minister Tim Nicholls, announcing her appointment in a Facebook post in July. Tim Nicholls MP / Facebook Readers may recall recent criticism of Rosengren from one hospital and health service insider, who suggested he had misled estimates with remarks about the reason three legally required First Nations board roles were vacant. Neither Rosengren, nor his departmental spinners, have answered our questions about the roles, citing applicant confidentiality. Our approaches this week delivered no update on how recruitment is going, but it’s said to be “nearing an end”.



Another role recently subject to a lengthy hiring process was that of the Chief First Nations Health Officer, after it was vacated by inaugural figure, Yalangi and Tagalaka woman Haylene Grogan. January saw job ads go up for the gig – downgraded from its previous deputy director-general level in July last year, as previously reported by the ABC – with Wakka Wakka and South Sea Islander woman Samantha Wild named as Grogan’s replacement in July. Wild is said to be considering opportunities to improve the operating model of the office, which issued its first report under Grogan last September. That report noted a continued focus by the department on increasing representation and authority of First Nations leadership. In a statement, a Queensland Health spokesperson told Circus the work had been kicked off from inside the unit, which now reports “operationally” to deputy director-general for system policy and planning Peta Bryant – currently filling in as Townsville HHS chief executive – and “strategically” to Rosengren.



“To ensure we continue to deliver healthcare that drives meaningful outcomes for mob and communities across Queensland, an internal strategic review has been initiated from within the First Nations Health Office.” Related Article Public service Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show This was said to be a regular practice, part of good governance and organisational effectiveness, and something which would “help ensure the First Nations Health Office continues to provide strategic leadership and maximise its contribution to better health equity and outcomes”. We reached out to Wild independently of the department, but didn’t hear back. Musical chairs at the top of CS Energy





A check of the CS Energy website confirmed Bellas ended up taking a “temporary leave of absence” from his board duties, with Seeney in the big chair since April 9. Jeff Seeney during his time as deputy premier in the Newman government. Glenn Hunt Why the change of plans? We sought some clarity from Seeney and Bellas’ media team, and were advised by a company spokesperson it was about avoiding “any corporate governance issues that could arise from the combined role of Acting CEO and Executive Chair”. Harty starts on 28 September. A familiar face joins the TEQ board



We’d gone at least a couple of Fridays without news of new appointments on a government board. That was until 2.30pm on the final day of last week, when Tourism Minister Andrew Powell lobbed a media release with changes to the one steering Tourism and Events Queensland. Out of the chair after one term is nature-based and Indigenous tourism leader Grant Hunt AM, replaced with former Tourism Australia managing director John O’Sullivan. Also out, some 12 months ahead of the end of their terms, are Karen Bolinger, Stephanie Parkin, Rob Hudson and Brian Hennessy. Among those replacing them is former Brisbane deputy mayor and still-serving Holland Park ward LNP councillor Krista Adams, who announced last year she won’t contest the next council election.



At the time, she also stepped back from her deputy mayor and civic cabinet role – and the topped-up pay packets that come with them. But not to worry: in the past three months, Adams has picked up not only the TIQ board gig (worth about $15,000 in 2024-25) but also a spot on the Economic Development Queensland board (worth more than $80,000 in 2024-25). Then-deputy mayor Krista Adams with Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner after the re-election of their LNP administration in 2024. Cameron Atfield Others landing on the TIQ board include Jacob Cassidy, Roderic Rees and Damien Massingham – a former Tourism Noosa chief executive and LNP preselection candidate. We might hear more news from Adams before her council term is up – given City Hall’s habit of having outgoing councillors hand over the baton within a year of an election.



No fireworks for you As far as Riverfire views go, 1 William Street has one of the best. So it’s no surprise it was a hot ticket, with public servants offered the opportunity to watch the show from the Tower of Power. Not every public servant was invited. According to an email from acting DPC Deputy Director General Jaime Blackburn, only those who serve from 1 William Street in their 9-to-5 could get access to the spots. Once accepted, they could bring their families (up to four visitors, in some cases) along to the strictly no-booze viewing. Workers were asked to donate $20 to the Starlight Children’s Foundation in exchange for the privilege, and spots on some levels were gobbled up in under an hour.



A government spinner said 1 William Street employees were allowed to attend the floor they work on during Riverfire, as has been the case for years. Another reason for ladder-climbers to try and get up a few rungs before next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: Locals-focused wine bar and op shop lands in brilliant heritage location
World.content:
Eating outFood Locals-focused wine bar and op shop lands in brilliant heritage location One of the city’s cherished small-bar spots rides again, dedicated to funky small-producer wines, approachable eats and vintage threads. Matt Shea September 7, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Louise Marks couldn’t sleep. She and a colleague had gone to inspect the Valley premises previously occupied by Barry Parade Public House. “Shaun [Fugill, co-owner of Teneriffe’s Zero Fox] told me about Barry Parade closing and how beautiful the space is, and I thought, ‘We should go have look just for shits and giggles.’ And it was amazing. I could envisage exactly what it would look like.” Bar Lou Lou has opened in the premises previously occupied by Barry Parade Public House. Markus Ravik “It” would become Bar Lou Lou, a wine bar that Marks opened in the space mid-August. It completes a heady career change who Marks, who just nine months ago was working in media. In between, she’d been pouring beers with Fugill at Zero Fox.



“I literally packed up my career,” she says. “Zero Fox had always been one of my favourite venues in Brisbane, and I said when I started that my goal was to one day have my own venue. It felt like such a pipe dream.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead Bar Lou Lou demonstrates an impressive degree of vision for a first-time owner. It perhaps helps that Marks was working with such good bones with the old Barry Parade Public House. The venue’s 1920s-built heritage facade is just as beautiful as ever, and the terrazzo floors, timber bar and globe pendant lights are all present and correct. Otherwise, Marks has swapped the green paint job for a rich burgundy and filled the bar with mismatched furniture and cushions, giving it a homey and lived-in vibe. At the back, there’s the same timber outdoor area but Marks has converted a side room into a mini op shop. The heritage facade remains much the same. Markus Ravik



“People are literally buying clothes and immediately putting them on and sitting there finishing their drink. It’s so fun,” she says. “Everything in the place is second hand. Even the plates are from the op shop, which was driving chef insane at first but he loves it now.” That same unfussy approach has been applied to the drinks list. Bar Lou Lou is billed as a wine bar first but it drills down on just 12 drops, all available by the glass and bottle. Much of the fitout remains unchanged from its Barry Parade Public House days, but the venue now has a more homey, lived-in vibe. Markus Ravik Marks’ focus is the interesting and unusual. Expect the list to change regularly but you can currently order wines such as a Harrison grenache blanc from McLaren Vale, a Clare Valley Sigurd chenin blanc, and a Barossa Adlib GSM.



“I’ve just tried to pick my favourite wines that I’ve tasted over the past year at Zero Fox and other places, and arranged them from different vendors or direct from the winemakers.” The venue still boasts its winsome courtyard. Markus Ravik Alongside the wines there are three beers on tap – including Guinness – six more available by the stubbie or can, and a handful of cocktails – and that’s pretty much it. For food, chef Adnane Khattabi has created a fun but filling menu of bar eats. There’s fried chicken served with a Sriracha mayonnaise dipping sauce; toasted roti with a red curry satay sauce; banh mi crostinis; and tuna tataki served with house made blood orange ponzu, hazelnut crisp and avocado puree. The food menu is intended to be fun but filling. Markus Ravik



“I really want it to be a neighbourhood local, especially because of where it’s situated,” Marks says. “If you live in the Spring Hill area, it’s a stop before you head into the Valley. And other than The Alliance, there aren’t too many local-focused bars around here.” Open Wed-Sat 12pm-10pm, Sun 12pm-8pm 122 Barry Parade, Fortitude Valley barloulou.com.au

World.title: Maps, icons, symbols and other false flags
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Maps, icons, symbols and other false flags September 7, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. NATIONALISM The Coalition is proposing to make burning the Australian flag a criminal offence. (″⁣Angus Taylor wants to criminalise flag burning″⁣, 6/9). Back in the Vietnam days, people asked why we protestors didn’t burn the Australian flag like our American counterparts. The answer was that ″⁣no one could care less about the Australian flag″⁣. For many of us that is probably still true.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris No limit to politicians’ silliness

Clearly, silliness has no limits in politics. Angus Taylor wants to criminalise the ″⁣desecration″⁣ of the Australian flag. But, what constitutes an Australian flag? If I make a flag that wholly mimics the Australian one, but omit (for example) the tip of one of the rays on the Federation Star, and then publicly burn my creation, have I desecrated the Australian flag, potentially earning a 12-months’ jail sentence?

At the very least, the law would need to specify – in some exact detail – what constitutes an Australian flag. If I publicly burned such a legally defined flag, I need only ask the prosecutor (or prosecution witness) if they can swear with absolute certainty that my flag had no modifications (such as a missing ray point); in other words, that it met the legal description.

And they would need to explain the basis of that certainty. Absent such sworn certainty, and appropriate supporting evidence, the case would necessarily have to be dismissed.

Dennis Dodd, Shepparton



Maybe start with kindness and fairness first

I really struggle to fall for the false flag of Australian nationalism being promoted by One Nation and the Coalition. What is there to celebrate when one in six of us live in poverty?

Neither of the above two parties has suggested that kindness and fairness are Australian values. I would gladly set the Australian flag alight if I thought it might reduce poverty. I am sure stopping poverty is the last thing on their nationalistic agenda.

And, with a pathetic Labor government so full of its self-induced dismality, it wouldn’t try. The Australian flag stays safe in the interim.

John Rome, Mount Lawley, WA In the US, size always matters

It’s no surprise that the USA (alone) has rejected the suggestion that world maps be changed to reflect more realistic comparative sizes of countries with respect to one another (″⁣Australia and Africa expand, North America and Europe shrink: UN adopts new world map″⁣, 6/9). The Trump administration’s negative knee jerk reaction to the attempt by the rest of the world to fix the problem caused in 1569 when cartographer Gerardus Mercator converted the world global spherical map to the familiar rectangular flat version, is driven by the same childish mentality behind the USA’s decision to change the names of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to the Gulf of America and Lake America respectively.

Russell Brims, Bentleigh East An icosahedron shows Earth at its best

In 1954, the inventor Buckminster Fuller produced his Dymaxion Air-Ocean World Map in which the spherical Earth was projected on to a 20 triangular-faced surface (icosahedron), which could be arranged in different ways on a flat surface to give a representation of the Earth with minimal distortion everywhere.

Depending on where the icosahedron is placed with respect to the globe, maps can be made showing all the land surfaces in a connected way or all the oceans.

The map can be folded into an icosahedron, which can be viewed from any direction. Why did the UN (6/9 ) not promote this map for general use, as there can be no politicisation of it, and it would provide a more accurate, unbiased understanding of our world?

Don Jordan, Mount Waverley THE FORUM Unengaged boys

Columnist Sean Kelly suggests it is illogical for the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, to blame Respectful Relationships programs in schools for boys’ lack of interest in pursuing respectful relationships (″⁣As Labor leaves an opening, Coalition takes the wrong path″⁣, 7/9).

However, Kelly reveals little insight into the minds of adolescent boys and young men. He expects them to respond as he, a mature adult man, would on hearing the key messages of Respectful Relationships. He would give credit to those trying very hard to tackle misogyny.

Meanwhile, back in the school program, some boys have stopped listening and are looking out the window, wishing they were outside kicking the footy or are thinking about lunch. But some are more engaged. They have listened to the message delivered by boring, overly earnest people, and decided to think pretty much the opposite to what they are being told. Matt Canavan understands this.

Rod Wise, Surry Hills



Listen, Tim Wilson

I listened to Tim Wilson on community radio yesterday, and while I find One Nation erratic and devoid of substance, his disparaging remarks about Pauline Hanson only adds fuel to the fire of her support base.

It’s this type of elitism that has alienated their own base for many years and has led to this rise in inequality, among many other sociological factors.

Please listen to the frustrations of ordinary Aussies. They are angry and deserve your respect, not a sneering attitude.

Jenny Smith, East Melbourne Jess Wilson’s pledge

Such a relief in the week of the death of feminist icon Gloria Steinem to see Jess Wilson say “abortion law will not change under a Liberal and Nationals government”. This right to free, accessible and shame-free abortion has only ever been threatened by the religious right wing of LNP governments, so it’s a pretty unconvincing ‴⁣⁣promise”.

Hopefully, in her next press puff piece, she will also enshrine the right of women to be educated, vote, get a housing loan, own property, retain their own name and work after marriage.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn Fasten your seatbelts

Years ago, when the road toll was at crisis levels, seatbelts in cars were made compulsory. Each belt is a precaution, in case there is an accident. It is a hedge against a much greater potential cost.

There were objections, outcries of infringements to liberty, but the government held fast. If we could use that approach to today’s climate crisis, imagine what future damage, and cost, we could avoid.

Barbara Darvall, Caulfield North Bottom-line rules

Your correspondent (Letters 5/9) describing $5.50 daily charge for an aged care resident to watch TV in her room, appropriately asks, ″⁣What have we become?” On the next page, Gabriel Sherman’s opinion article about Rupert Murdoch’s profit-driven lies (“How Sun King sold out the planet”) illuminates “how” and “why” we have become this.

For decades, our governments embraced the particularly amoral, rapacious version of capitalism unencumbered by social conscience proudly championed by the US – endless pursuit of infinite profits by a privileged, powerful and insatiable few, regardless of cost to individual, society, natural environment, and future generations’ life quality or survival.

Successive governments’ failure to govern and regulate in public interest abetted widespread corporate exploitation of their citizens. Even now, government is still pussy-footing around effective controls for gambling and toxic social media content/algorithms and their “Tech Bro” masters. Albanese’s concept of “right balance” is wrong when dealing with these societal poisons.

Other exploitation examples include unreasonable surcharges, price gouging, fraudulent charges for little or no service, important services eroded by understaffing or outsourcing, everyday time-wasting frustrations e.g. deliberately obstructing personal communication to force it online etc.

Bottom-line rules! Selfishness, is not how human tribes survived for thousands of years – nor how football teams succeed.

Joe Di Stefano, Geelong Uni is for thinking

The report (“Inside Melbourne universities’ plans to future-proof degrees and jobs”. 7/9) that universities in Melbourne are going to establish their own businesses and train their students within them in order to make them “job-ready” is problematic and undermines the traditional role of university education.

It is true that most Australian universities are run top-down like corporations, but even so, they have managed to retain their role as teaching students to think critically, especially about the world around them and the veracity of the subjects they are being taught.

However, the push to introduce students very early on to working in a business environment and to make considerable use of AI could easily lead to a collapse in the kind of critical thinking universities have traditionally been adept at fostering. We can only hope that this will be maintained even with the greater commercialisation of universities.

Greg Bailey, St Andrews



Pothole quick fix

Re “Victoria’s Deepening Pothole Crisis” 5/9. As an engineer with 40 years’ experience working in road maintenance, construction design and testing, I have seen this pothole situation develop over the past 20 years

The issue not canvassed in the article was “why is it that the roads in the 1990s and 2000s did not suffer the same pothole problem?“

There are two items that are different in the management of the roadways now – privatised maintenance by contract (at the lowest price), and neglect of resealing of aggregate seal pavements as a cost-saving measure.

The lack of rapid response to repair potholes can be squarely laid at the feet of the contractors, and probably poorly written contracts. Large potholes sufficient to damage tyres and wheels do not happen overnight. Rapid response is essential to prevent small holes from becoming wheel busting holes.

The neglect of resealing of bitumen seal pavements over many years has compromised the waterproofness of our sealed roads. What is not apparently appreciated by those who should know, is that bitumen hardens usually within six to 10 years. When the bitumen loses its ductility the surface will crack, water then penetrates the underlying material leading to potholing.

Unfortunately, penny-pinching has been carried out without thought of the cost to the road user. It will be some years before this neglect can be corrected.

Norman Butler, former VicRoads regional manager, Traralgon NGV Gandel protest

Your correspondent (Letters 7/9) in discussing the demonstrations outside the NGV that targeted John and Pauline Gandel is highly disingenuous. He claims they targeted the Gandels’ support for Israel, not their Jewish identity.

But the fact that the Gandels are major Australian philanthropists of the NGV and that’s where these demonstrations took place makes it difficult not to see the demonstrations as focusing on them as wealthy Jews, a classic antisemitic trope.

The Gandels’ philanthropic support for the NGV had nothing to do with events in the Middle East, and demonstrating against them contributes nothing to the pursuit of peace in Gaza or promoting political rights for Palestinians.

The whole point of the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion was to recognise the distinction. Simplistic, reductive arguments about Jewish complicity abroad, and outright attacks on prominent Jewish Australians are themselves threats to social cohesion.

We hope the royal commission will expose them as such.

Rabbi Fred Morgan, Melbourne Finding leaks

The article ″⁣Dozens of military staff subjected to polygraph tests in major leak hunt″⁣ (7/9) reports the US government is testing personnel to determine whether they disclosed classified information.

One wonders why the citizenry of that country doesn’t insist on the same for its politicians. They are public employees too, and rather more prone to leaking than the average staff sergeant.

A regular polygraph regime could perhaps neatly catch any divulgence of ″⁣classified information” — to the press, foreign nationals, business cronies, or family members.

Other democracies may wish to take note.

Martin Hunt, East Malvern Swans’ on-field form

Apropos Jake Niall’s assessment ″⁣Embattled Swan’s produce one of their finest wins″⁣, 7/9), it looks like the Sydney Swans are on a path to redemption.

Their unexpected and convincing win over the Brisbane Lions went some of the way to redeeming the team in the conspicuous absence of the five players who were banned, and also redeemed the aspirations of the club after the disappointments of the recent grand final losses in 2016, 2022 and 2024.

Time will tell in 2026. But the question remains, what to do with the five players in 2027?

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Grown boys are men

Your letter writer (7/9) inadvertently highlights one of the issues in sport, writing “Given the Swans’ emphatic win over the Lions, the club now can dispose of its dropped boys without worrying about the finals or the future”.

The people who play professionally are not boys – they are men. No excuses for their behaviour due to age. The sooner we stop referring to 20 and 30 year olds as boys, the better.

Stephanie Howell, Brunswick



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Flag burning

It is clear that the Coalition and One Nation’s opposition to regulating social media algorithms is not based on free speech. If they truly believed in free speech, they would not, at the same time, be proposing the outlawing of flag burning.

Denny Meadows, Hawthorn It’s embarrassing the bereft federal opposition have flag burning as their current best national issue to tackle.

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon Algorithms

Thankfully, my local librarian is not an algorithm. If so, I’d have to carry home dozens of books instead of one.

Geoff Allen, Parkdale



Do commentators (Letters, 7/9) realise how silly it sounds to talk about ″⁣algorithm-free social media″⁣? An algorithm is just like a cake recipe, so do they want to ban the media recipes? I doubt it.

Barbara Lynch, South Yarra Furthermore

″⁣Australia passes EV tipping point” (7/9) and there’s lots of chat about chargers. Meanwhile, bike riders, the heavy lifters, when it comes to cutting carbon emissions, are waiting for just 5 per cent of the billions spent on transport infrastructure in Victoria each year to be spent on Strategic Cycling Corridors.

Lesley Walker, Northcote Finally, Melbourne Airport is making policy in recognition of the climate crisis (7/9). Making the airport less appealing — now that’s climate action.

Christine Harris, Spotswood It is revealing that Pete Hegseth hasn’t denied reports of US depleted missile stocks during the Iranian war, but instead instituted a witch hunt via polygraph tests to find who spilled the beans.

Alan Inchley, Frankston The irony of the Crown/Salvation Army Red Shield Appeal full page ad (7/9): how many Salvo recipients were former customers of Crown? It’s well past time for more effective gambling legislation.

Steve Earley, Gisborne



Finally

It seems noteworthy that all five mainland states of Australia remain represented in the AFL flag race.

Brian Kidd, Mt Waverley The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Shameful con’: Labor proposes last-minute change to IBAC reform
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll’s promised reforms to give the state’s peak anti-corruption body greater reach and powers are at risk of collapse following a proposed last-minute change that would prevent IBAC from investigating some allegations relating to Victoria’s Big Build sites. Both the Coalition and the Greens have threatened to withdraw their support for Labor’s proposed legislation, which is set to be introduced into parliament on Tuesday, after the government confirmed its law change would declare any allegations IBAC had already dealt with under its old powers off limits. The carve-out includes allegations former premier Jacinta Allan referred to IBAC more than two years ago after a joint investigation by The Age, The Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes revealed organised crime had infiltrated government-funded major building projects. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll. Chris Hopkins The proposed legislation, which gives IBAC follow-the-money powers and a broader definition of corruption to launch investigations, prevents it from applying the broader powers and jurisdiction to matters it has already investigated, decided not to investigate or referred to another integrity agency.



The government believes the new Kourakis royal commission is the primary body for investigating allegations of corruption and misconduct associated with the Big Build, and that the commission will work closely with a special prosecutor, IBAC and Victoria Police to ensure all claims of serious wrongdoing are examined. On Monday night, shadow attorney-general James Newbury described the move as a “shameful con” and an eleventh-hour manoeuvre before parliament is prorogued ahead of November’s state election. “Ben Carroll and Labor are shamefully trying to keep covered up the worst corruption scandal in our state’s history,” Newbury said. “Labor has confirmed their proposed new powers won’t let IBAC revisit old corruption allegations it has dismissed, referred elsewhere or finished investigating. “Victorians deserve to know the extent of corruption on the Big Build. IBAC must not be blocked from that work. What a shameful con from an end of days government.”



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Integrity experts urge royal commission to look beyond crooks to deeper problem Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt rejected the criticism. “The Liberals are lying,” she said. “The royal commission will be able to investigate any allegations of crime, corruption and serious misconduct on Big Build projects. “We’re fast-tracking the new laws, so IBAC has the follow-the-money powers it needs to uncover corruption this year, not in 2027.” An opposition party room meeting scheduled for Tuesday morning is expected to withdraw support for the bill unless it is substantially amended.



Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the legislation needed to provide greater scope for IBAC to conduct public examinations of witnesses, including parliamentarians. “The Greens dragged Labor kicking and screaming to finally strengthen IBAC, but as per usual with Labor, they’ve done it in a way that has big carve-outs to protect themselves and leave Victorians in the dark,” Sandell said. Allan wrote to IBAC in July 2024, a day after the first revelations of the Building Bad investigation were published by this masthead, urging the anti-corruption body to investigate the claims. “I am concerned to ensure that any allegations of serious corruption that are within the remit of IBAC are identified, investigated and appropriate action taken by IBAC,” she wrote. In February this year, it was revealed that IBAC had assessed the premier’s referral and found it to be outside its jurisdiction at the time.



At the time, IBAC was still assessing a separate referral from Newbury about the contents of a report from anti-corruption advocate Geoffrey Watson, SC, which outlined serious misconduct in the CFMEU, the union which under the Andrews and Allan governments established an industrial monopoly over Big Build projects. In July, Newbury made a further referral over allegations that state government officials told builders to cut a deal with the CFMEU following a dispute on a key level crossing removal site. Jacinta Allan faced increasing questions about corruption in the state’s Big Build projects in the lead up to her resignation as premier. Penny Stephens The status of Newbury’s referrals is not known. IBAC does not typically confirm or deny what matters it is investigating. It responded to media requests about Allan’s referral only after the former premier publicly released her letter. The proposed changes to IBAC’s laws would allow the agency to use its new powers and jurisdiction on matters it is currently investigating, as well as any future investigations.



The government legislation would expand IBAC’s working definition of corrupt conduct beyond its current requirement that it must constitute a criminal offence punishable by five years’ jail. This jurisdictional limitation, which has been criticised by successive IBAC commissions, is more narrow than that used by any other peak anti-corruption body in Australia. Related Article Opinion

Kourakis royal commission Courage or a cop-out? Carroll faces defining test in his very first decision Nick McKenzie Investigative reporter The definition of corruption would be broadened to include any offence or serious disciplinary matter. This covers a much wider range of activity – such as misconduct and major breaches of ministerial and local government codes of conduct – and would enable IBAC to investigate what its former commissioner Robert Redlich described as “grey corruption”. Redlich, the Centre for Public Integrity, Transparency International Australia, former ombudsman Deborah Glass and other integrity advocates have repeatedly called for IBAC’s working definition of corruption to be brought into line with the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption and the National Anti-Corruption Commission. IBAC’s proposed follow-the-money powers, would allow it to pursue investigations beyond major government contractors, into subcontractors and labour hire firms who ultimately receive taxpayer funds.



Since replacing Allan, Carroll has staked his nascent premiership on restoring government integrity, promising to bring forward greater powers for IBAC and establish a royal commission into Big Build corruption on the first day of his leadership. Alongside the proposed IBAC legislation, the government will this week introduce into parliament proposed legislation to establish a special prosecutor’s office to work in tandem with the royal commission.
