World.title: MSD blames administration error for denying applications for food help
World.content:
The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) is again in the spotlight for an administration error, this time over a reason for declining Special Needs Grant applications for help with food.

A 1 News investigation has found the ministry told more than 8000 people that food was not an essential need over six years.

The ministry has put that down to selecting the wrong category when processing the application.

MSD group general manager of client service delivery Graham Allpress said applicants being told food was not an essential need was an administrative error.

"Where the code was entered, it does not mean the underlying decision was incorrect, but selecting this category was an administrative error," Allpress said.

The wrong decline code had affected 0.094 percent of applicants, with MSD processing more than 8.5 million applications over that six year time period.

The 1 News story also found the total number of declined applications had increased in the past two years.

Allpress told 1 News the ministry's eligiblity criteria had not changed, and MSD continued to approve the vast majority (94 to 96 percent) of food grant applications.

"Before Covid-19, managers were required to approve some hardship grants. These requirements were temporarily waived during the Covid-19 response, but this was never intended to be permanent," he said.

Documents 1 News received under the Official Information Act also showed 318,930 individuals asked for food grants in 2025 alone. On average, each person asked for help around four times, giving a total of 1.4 million applications.

Overall, 88,000 Special Needs Grant applications were declined.

Reasons for declining grants for food included "you do not have an immediate need" or "you have caused or contributed to your immediate need".

Others were told their "circumstances could have been reasonably foreseen", which was applied to more than 18,000 applications.

While most applications are approved, Labour said the increase in people needing support was a consequence of National making life more expensive.

"No one chooses to go hungry. Food is a basic necessity, and it is shameful that so many Kiwis are being left without enough of it," said Labour's social development spokesperson Willow-Jean Prime.

Social Development Minister Louise Upston said MSD continued to provide Special Needs Grants for food to hundreds of thousands of eligible New Zealanders.

"Through Budget 2026 we have enabled $45 million for community food support to assist those in highest need," she said.

"For the first time ever, I have secured baselined funding to maintain existing community food distribution infrastructure at the current level, and an additional investment of $7 million for community food providers, such as foodbanks, in 2026/27."

Upston said funding for Kick Start Breakfasts had additionally been secured, which currently provided breakfast to 46,000 children.

Upston and MSD have already apologised for two administrative errors, which saw people's Winter Energy Payments and benefits wrongly suspended.

World.title: Barge detained and still awaiting repairs, two years after grounding
World.content:
A barge that ran aground at Carters Beach on the West Coast remains under a detention order at Port Nelson, more than two years after it came ashore during a storm.

The barge's owner WMS (Westland Mineral Sands) Group said the Manahau was still awaiting repair and certification, which was expected to take six months.

Westland Mineral Sands established a sand mine at Cape Foulwind, south of Westport, in 2022. It was granted consent to mine about 500,000 tonnes of heavy mineral concentrate over about seven years across a 25-hectare site.

It was also granted consent to mine at Mananui, south of Hokitika, last year, after an independent panel of commissioners unanimously approved the consent, allowing 300,000 tonnes of minerals to be extracted from the 112-hectare site, every year for 16 years.

It was said the Mananui mine would create 70 jobs and inject $37.9 million to the West Coast economy, but residents and iwi voiced concerns about the impact on the environment, noise, dust, light pollution and truck movements.

In March, WMS Group announced it was pausing mining operations, citing a downturn in global titanium and mineral sands markets, alongside ongoing volatility in shipping and energy costs.

West Coast Bulk Logistics - the logistics and shipping division of the WMS Group - said in late 2025 that a repair plan for the Manahau had been submitted to the international certification body, RINA and the work was expected to take one month while the vessel was in dry dock.

The company had not explained why the repair work had still not been completed, but a spokesperson said once the repairs were complete, the plan was for the barge to return to service, shipping heavy mineral concentrate between Westport and Nelson.

The barge hooked up to a tug arrived in Nelson in 2024. Maritime NZ

The Manahau first arrived on the West Coast in mid-August 2024, to ship concentrated mineral sand mined at Cape Foulwind from Westport to Nelson.

The company said at the time it was also exploring options for use the Manahau to move bulk commodities around New Zealand.

In 2022, the government announced $30 million in funding for four suppliers to enhance coastal shipping services. On of those was Aotearoa Shipping Alliance, of which Westland Mineral Sands is a member, which received $7m to go towards the purchase of the Manahau.

The vessel had only just entered service before the grounding.

An investigation by the company, led by former Transport Accident Investigation Commission chief investigator Tim Burfoot, found it could have been avoided.

He found the vessel was fit for purpose, equipped with the necessary capabilities and properly supported by a shore-based management team.

He said that better decision-making by the crew at several key points during the incident could have prevented the vessel from running aground.

Maritime NZ the Manahau would remain under the detention notice until the required repairs are undertaken to the satisfaction of its classification society and the flag state (Niue).

The regulator also investigated the grounding and a spokesperson said "after careful consideration of the evidence and circumstances" it took regulatory action by issuing a formal warning to Westland Mineral Sands.

World.title: 'Nature's recyclers': Growing coffins from mushrooms
World.content:
The mixture is placed in a coffin-shaped mould and put in a "climate room" to grow for seven days.



They're suitable for traditional burials, natural burials and cremation.



While they're now available in New Zealand, they're currently only grown in the Netherlands.



Hendrikx hopes to gain enough traction to grow them here and cut down on emissions from shipping.



"As a sustainable entrepreneur [it] is of course a big challenge because you have these ambitions and yet there's... also... the financial reality."



Everywhere they ship to, they try and offset their carbon, he said. In New Zealand they are investing in wind.



Hendrikx said the biggest challenge when growing the mushrooms themselves is to ensure they remain only one species.



When the project first launched overseas he was surprised to see support from as far away as Australia and New Zealand, he said.



Australia had its first burial with a mushroom-grown coffin last week and three families showed interest here on launch day.



"I think it makes sense because you guys have a very beautiful relationship with nature."



While the price was dependent on each funeral direction, Hendrikx said they would be sold at a similar price to a traditional coffin.

World.title: Skilled jobs put at risk by cheap aluminium imports - industry
World.content:
Thousands of skilled regional jobs are at risk, unless the Government puts a stop to cheap aluminium imports flooding into the country, according to an industry group.

Aluminium extrusions are shaped components that can be used in windows, door frames and thousands of other construction and everyday times.

The local industry says there has been a 38 percent increase in low cost imports of the products in the past year, with New Zealand becoming a dumping ground.

MBIE launched an investigation in May.

But the Aluminium Extruders Association wants the Government to impose a temporary import duty to stem the flow, or New Zealand risked losing jobs it can not replace.

Cheap aluminium imports putting regional jobs at risk Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Aluminium Extruders Association chair Nick Collins told Checkpoint that New Zealand was out of step with every comparable trading partner, which all acknowledged that the aluminium industry was strategically important to their economies.

"We are sitting there, completely open to imports."

He said it was not a matter of competition, and was not free or fair trade.

"Imports are flooding into the country, and a large proportion of these imports are coming in below the cost of the raw material that is a globally traded commodity that every extruder needs to buy.

"This is not a failing industry in New Zealand, it's not asking to be propped up, it's asking government to act and use what is a legal safeguard that already exists in law."

Collins said without action, the country will gradually see the loss of critically important businesses and jobs.

"Already our members are working fewer shifts, they haven't laid people off because they are largely skilled people, some of whom have worked a very long time for those businesses and we will never recover the workforce if you start to cut it."

New Zealand could not afford to lose any more critical manufacturing after closures of work processing, pulp and canning factories in the past year, said Collins.

"Without local manufacturing, you miss the flexibility, the short lead times, the small order sizes, and the ability to innovate and quickly develop new products."

He said the industry just needed a temporary measure to enable it to respond to the "abnormal situation we find ourselves in".

Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer said after receiving advice about introducing provisional duties he had decided not to impose them at this stage.

World.title: Future governments told to spend more on medicines and reap big savings
World.content:
Spending more money on medicines would pay for itself, report finds Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Future governments are being urged to spend more on medicines and reap big savings.

An economic analysis commissioned by Business NZ has found every additional dollar spent on medicines delivers an almost $2 economic return.

Business NZ chief executive Katherine Rich said the report from Business and Economic Research Limited (BERL) was clear.

"If you spend more money on medicines and treatments as a government you will reap significant economic and fiscal benefits - and society will reap benefits as well."

She said the report showed that New Zealand's spend on medicines - 4.9 percent of the health budget - was "way behind" comparable countries.

The OECD average was 13.3 percent, she said, while Australia put 12.2 percent of its health expenditure into medicine - which showed.

"You can get more drugs, more modern drugs in Australia, which is a 3.5 hour plane ride for many Kiwis."

Rich said New Zealand had spent years debating the cost of medicines.

"The wider question is the cost of not funding them.

"Better access to medicines keeps people healthier, in work for longer, and more productive while they are there. It also reduces avoidable pressure on hospitals and other high-cost services. The economic dividend is substantial."

The BERL report estimated an additional $2.7 billion annual spend on medicine was needed to reach the OECD benchmark and "capture the economic and fiscal gains".

However, it said the economic return built quickly. The report found benefits to Gross Domestic Product would overtake the cost within three years.

Rich said she wasn't arguing for more overall health spend, but for more of the budget to go towards medicines over time.

"We just need to change the proportion to direct more over to medicines to prevent some admissions to hospital and boost quality of life and in many case, cure."

Rich pointed to the now funded cystic fibrosis drug - Trikafta - as an example.

The report states that it received funding from pharmaceutical companies AbbVie, GSK, and Roche. It said while the sponsoring companies contributed high-level subject matter expertise, the analyses, findings, and conclusions expressed in the report are entirely those of the authors.

She said Business NZ had become concerned in recent years about the lack of medicines in New Zealand compared to other modern countries and the length of time to approve new medicines.

She said the report was designed for policymakers and political decision-makers, not to bolster the coffers of pharmaceutical companies.

"The reason Business NZ has looked at this as a topic is that we would argue that health is our biggest asset as a country - personally and for our families - and it is important to look at the evidence in favour of significantly upping the amount that we spend on medicines, particularly those that cure and add to a quality of life."

Business NZ director of advocacy Catherine Beard told Checkpoint it was "appalling" how little New Zealand spent on medicines, with the report showing that more investment would reduce sick days and boost productivity.

"So reduced absenteeism and there's another word, presenteeism, which means when you're at work but you're not firing on all cylinders because you're not 100 percent well."

The report said every dollar invested returned $1.93 to the economy and $1.15 to the Crown.

World.title: Labour leader Chris Hipkins brushes off latest poll result
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins is brushing off a poll result which puts his party in the mid-20s, saying the only poll that matters is the election result.

Labour was down 1.9 points in the latest Taxpayers Union-Curia poll, putting the party on 25.9 percent.

Meanwhile, Opportunity has fallen short of the 5 percent threshold needed for getting into Parliament, dropping from 6.1 percent to 4.5 percent.

With no seats, it means the party is no longer kingmaker in this poll.

National has also fallen to 29 percent, but the government bloc's 64 seats compared to the opposition bloc's 56 would see it returned to power should the result be replicated at the election.

Labour dismisses result

Last month, Hipkins dismissed the previous Taxpayers Union-Curia poll as "rogue", and an outlier.

But this time, he said the poll results bounced around.

"I'm just not going to comment on every individual poll between now and election day. There'll be increasing numbers of them. The one that we are really focused on is the one that happens on election day," he said.

Hipkins would not address questions on Labour's internal polling, nor would he say what might have been responsible for the latest polling slump.

But he accused National of being "desperate" with its tax attacks.

"They can't campaign on the truth. They can't campaign on their own track record. So they're making things up about the Labour Party."

Hipkins said the Labour team was feeling "buoyant," and the party had been deliberately holding back some of its policy announcements so it could announce them on the campaign.

"I'd love to see better numbers. We'll be working hard to achieve that."

Opportunity points to previous polls

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong pointed to the party's positive long-term trend as the true reflection of its position, saying polls tended to bounce around.

"We focus mainly on the overall trend, we've had ten months of moving up across all of the polls that are out there, so we're still feeling very positive," she said.

"We're never taking anything for granted ... we're continuing to get out there and do the hard work, that's what we would have done anyway."

ACT and the Greens could be the beneficiaries of Opportunity's result, Wong said.

"It's hard to say, we do attract support from across the political spectrum and they've certainly been more visible with policy announcements in the last couple of weeks, so it could be down to that."

National and Labour's results showed people were frustrated with a lack of bold policies and strong leadership, she said.

Every possible future on the table - Greens

The Green Party has also been a beneficiary in the latest poll, with a 3.8 point rise to 13.9 percent.

It would give the party a record 18 seats in the House, but with the current opposition bloc only getting 56 in total, it would not have enough to change the government.

But co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the future was not set in stone.

"If anybody is trying to read the tea leaves on this election, good luck, because the polls and the commentary seems to change every other week," she said.

"Now more than ever, it is critical for New Zealanders to understand that they have to be actively involved in and engage with politics and the future of this country, because every possible future is clearly on the table."

With the Greens and ACT rising, and National and Labour falling, Swarbrick said it showed people were looking for different options.

"I think what we're seeing there is a trend that we're seeing across the rest of the Western world, really, which is where people are moving away from the two legacy parties or the two institutional parties and looking for alternatives, because their lives have not got any better over the last 40 years."

'A long way to go' - Seymour

The poll had ACT up 3.2 to 10.5 percent.

Leader David Seymour put the result down to the party's consistency.

"There's a long way to go in this election, we're grateful and we're encouraged but we know we've gotta keep working," he said.

"We may not be the biggest or the loudest or the newest, but we can point to a long line of changes where we've just had our head down and our bum up, and actually make things better one issue at a time."

Seymour said his party's approach was to diagnose problems and be prepared to offer serious solutions, "even if they're not always popular at first".

World.title: Wellington City Council cuts 47 jobs
World.content:
Wellington City Council has cut 47 staff roles in a drive to save over $4 million.

Acting chief executive Anna Calver confirmed today that 141 roles will be disestablished - of which 41 were already vacant, and 94 created.

The cuts are coming from the Creative Capital, Economic and Engagement, Planning and Environment, and Property and Capital Projects team.

Calver said the council passed this year's annual plan which directed executives to find $4,480,000 in savings from the teams.

She said the targets required a reduction of roles and changes to team structures.

"We have concluded our consultation with staff and final decisions have been made. As with all change processes, the most impacted kaimahi will have the opportunity to express their interest in any new roles."

Calver said a new Urban Development Office within the new Planning and Development Unit is being set up.

The Public Service Association national secretary Duane Leo said the changes could drive skilled people from the capital.

"It's a sad waste to cut experienced staff working in areas critical to the short- and long-term wellbeing of the city."

Workers affected include those working in climate change response and resilience, mana whenua engagement, administration and resource consenting.

Leo criticised the use of a Deloitte report which looked at staffing numbers - a report which was later found to have used outdated information, and of which large-chunks were written by AI.

The cuts would affect Wellington communities, Leo said.

"They will also profoundly affect the people who will be cut from the council, who will now have to look for work in the local job market, which has been devastated by government austerity."

World.title: Family seek judicial review of police shooting of unarmed Taranaki man Kaoss Price
World.content:
The family of Kaoss Price is seeking a judicial review of the Independent Police Conduct Authority's (IPCA) investigation into his fatal shooting in April 2022.

The unarmed 22-year-old died on State Highway 3, between New Plymouth and Waitara, after ramming a police car and attempting to steal cars from passers-by.

The IPCA's investigation found the officer who fired the fatal shot used excessive force, but did not recommend prosecuting the officer.

The family is now asking for that recommendation to be ignored, and for prosecution to go ahead.

At the High Court in Wellington on Monday, the family's lawyer Christopher Stevenson KC said when the officer shot Price point blank, the young man was running for his life.

Previously, his lawyers argued police had not provided adequate information to support the decision not to prosecute.

"Given the alarming rate of fatal police shootings, particularly of young Māori men, it is critical that more information is provided so that what happened can be properly understood," they said.

Monday's hearing was attended by more than a dozen members of Price's family and friends - including his grandmother, mother, sister and aunt.

Stevenson told the court Officer A - whose name has been suppressed - shot Price "point blank in the chest" while he attempted to car jack another vehicle after fleeing a routine traffic stop, driving dangerously and ramming a police car.

He said the IPCA's investigation acknowledged, contrary to the officer's testimony, it was unlikely that the officer saw a high risk of harm from Price as he fled police while under fire.

Stevenson pointed out police fired on Price's vehicle and continued to fire at him as he ran, with his back to officers, before he attempted to hijack another vehicle.

Stevenson said a witness in the second vehicle described Price offering $500 if they would drive him away from the scene and quoted the witness's testimony as saying: "He was just scared and wanted to get away. He was terrified."

"Officer A arrives at the driver's side of the vehicle and it's at this point that he shoots the unarmed Mr Price point blank in the chest," Stevenson said.

Stevenson told the court the IPCA investigation into the shooting found Officer A's contention that he believed Price was going for a weapon at that point was "implausible and improbable".

"The essential facts are not in dispute. By the time he was in the vehicle he was not a threat to the officer or to the passengers in the vehicle - who described him as 'terrified' - the only conceivable threat was driving away," Stevenson said.

Another lawyer for Price's family, Max Harris, said the IPCA's investigation had failed in its obligations under the Bill of Rights to be independent, impartial, prompt, thorough and transparent - and the process had undermined the effectiveness and the credibility of the investigation.

Stevenson noted it took two weeks before Officer A was interviewed about the shooting and during the process the officer was allowed to refer to pre-written notes.

He said interview transcripts revealed a troubling familiarity with how the officer was treated - including being referred to as "mate" 14 times during the process.

"[Officer A] was never appropriately pressed on his account and never appropriately challenged," Stevenson said.

He said it was concerning the officer was treated primarily as "a witness rather than a suspect" in their testimony regarding the incident.

He cited concerns over the independence of interviewing officers, noting that interviewers came from the same region and one had been trained on interviewing procedures by Officer A's lawyer.

"There can be inadvertent and unconscious bias which we know from decades of social sciences," Stevenson said.

He said there was also a lack of transparency regarding the explanation for police's decision not to prosecute Officer A and the family had been further traumatised by the 15-month delay in publishing the IPCA's decision which was "provided in a conclusory form - absent of reasons".

Stevenson described the treatment of Price's family in the investigation as "egregious" and said the disregard was further emphasised by the lack of information in support of the decision.

He said the lack of reasoning to reinforce the investigation's decision not to prosecute contradicted police and the authority's obligations under the Bill of Rights.

"The police should be aware they are subject to the Bill of Rights," he said.

"There doesn't appear to be any recognition in relation to the correspondence [during the investigation] that police are aware of these considerations."

On Monday afternoon, Harris told the court there was a gap of 15 months between the IPCA reaching its conclusion and the report being published.

He said the fact that only a single sentence was devoted to the reasoning behind the decision undermined the transparency and credibility of the IPCA's conclusion.

It reads: "Based on an assessment of the circumstance and the law relating [to] self defence and the defence of another (Section 48 of the Crimes Act), police has determined there is insufficient evidence to support criminal prosecution of the officers involved in this incident."

Harris said it was difficult to see how the IPCA could justify their lack of promptness in their handling of the case.

"The information that was supplied was eeked out following delays only after increasingly assertive requests [from the family's lawyers]," Harris said.

Harris said the IPCA failed to follow "obvious lines of inquiry" concerning the officer's decision to use a firearm rather than a taser, which had been available to him and other officers at the scene.

"Why was Officer A so confident about the precision of the use of a firearm in the incident and not about the use of a taser?" he said.

He said questions raised over the independence of interviewing officers, Officers A's choice of lethal force and assessment of the risks posed by Price "were not followed up" in the course of the investigation.

Chance of Price being armed was remote.

The ICPA report into the shooting concluded the chances of Price being armed was "remote".

"With regards to this threat, our view is that it was a remote possibility at best. Officer A had seen Mr Price place both hands on the car, prior to entering the car through the window.

"Further, Mr Price had not fired or presented a firearm at Police while they were chasing him. We therefore conclude that Officer A must have known that the risk of Mr Price having a firearm was remote."

Stevenson said that police had made an "error of law" in concluding that "evidential sufficiency" was not met in a way that could warrant prosecution of Officer A.

"Force must reasonable. i.e. it must be proportionate. The provision of self defence does not provide the person involved with a blank cheque.

"The threat asserted as perceived must be imminent and the force applied to that threat must be the only reasonable option.

"[Officer A] has made a decision to chase Mr Price as he was attempting to flee and has encountered him at the vehicle. At this point he was inside the vehicle and was a threat to the occupants of the vehicle."

Stevenson told the court the presence of an alternative response such as a taser - given police training on de-escalation and alternative options - made the use of lethal force unreasonable.

Stevenson said there was "a plainly valid proposition" to assert that there was not an imminent threat to officers or members of the public.

He said the decision not to prosecute was unlawful "in light of what was known and the legal injunctions on police".

"When a human life has been taken - by the use of force - ordinarily the application of the law is to lay charges and let a fact finder [determine the case]."

He said in cutting off a future prosecution because of an untested assertion of self defence was uncommon move and saw the authority effectively assuming the role that would more typically be a jury's.

The decision not to prosecute was just not open on these facts. One does not speculate on what a jury would do and one does not usurp the jury's role as a fact finder.

"It is inarguable on these facts - shooting a fleeing, unarmed man - that [other] options were simply not available," Stevenson said.

He said the family sought to quash and reconsider the authority's decision not to prosecute Officer A.

History of shootings in Taranaki influence community perception of police

Another lawyer for the family, Julia Spelman said Taranaki's history of five people (four of which were Māori men) being shot dead by police in the time between Stephen Wallace's death in April 2000 and Price's shooting in 2022 had implications for the community's perception of police attitudes to Māori.

She said the fact that Price was unarmed and shot at close range was "aberrant" and underlined the family's need for legal assistance to negotiate the police processes in response to the shooting.

She said ICPA's direction not to prosecute in Price's case contrasted significantly with other previous decisions to step back in instances where lethal force had been used by police.

"It does put the applicant in a difficult position where the respondent [police] is withholding key reasons and saying that without them the case can not proceed. The respondent has resisted at every turn the applicant's efforts to obtain that information.

"Only after the intervention of the Ombudsman the police have disclosed a 30 page memorandum that has been almost entirely redacted.

"The police shot Mr Price and will not give to this family the reasons for the decision why not [to prosecute]."

She said it had taken repeated requests from counsel in order for police to merely state the number of shots fired and Price's cause of death.

"The pattern of behaviour was that no information in our submission was provided willingly. It was only with intervention of counsel ... that information was provided," Spelman said.

She said police were asking the family to accept that they had conducted "an excellent transparent investigation" none of which could be disclosed.

She told the court she hoped tomorrow's testimony by lawyers for the Crown could go so far as to disclose some of the reasoning behind the decision.

She said the ICPA's single sentence explanation of the decision had left the family and counsel "in a vacuum" as to their reasoning.

"A failure to give reasons means that the lawfulness of what was done cannot be assessed by a court."

Spelman said in doing so police had failed to provide protections against wrong or arbitrary decisions which had become all the more crucial in the light of the Jevon McSkimmings' case and the concerns raised over the ability of the IPCA to negotiate "the blindingly obvious" conflict of interest with police investigations of their own conduct.

Spelman said the IPCA's failure to give reasons to back up their decision amounted to a breach of the family's rights under the Victims Rights Act.

She also said "significant periods of silence" interspersed by the "drip feeding" of packages of information in the lead up to the IPCA's report in November 2024 was a pattern of breaches of Natural Justice that had necessitated the family and counsel having to go to the Ombudsman to request information into issues that only became apparent to the family when the ICPA's report was published.

The family sought a declaration that the decision to not charge Officer A was unlawful and that decision should be set aside and reconsidered.

The family also sought awards for damages would require Justice Victoria Heine to assess the seriousness of the rights breached.

She highlighted the difficulty the family had endured not just in relation to Price's loss but the ongoing process of engaging with police and the justice system to address the problems with the investigation.

She said the significant number of whanau who had made the journey to attend the proceedings indicated the impact of the events and the police process on the family.

World.title: V'landys accuses NRL players of 'not telling truth' on rule confusion
World.content:
Peter V'landys has accused players of "not telling the truth" about set-restart confusion, as a survey of finals captains revealed ongoing uncertainty around the ruck.

The topic of set restarts is set to dominate the NRL finals, after Melbourne star Harry Grant claimed widespread frustration from players at the weekend.

The Melbourne captain declared most no longer knew what constituted a fast or slow play-the-ball, and the NRL needed to decide between being rugby league or touch football.

An AAP survey of captains and representatives at Monday's finals launch backed up Grant's claims, with six of the sides indicating they were still not entirely clear on what ruck speed referees wanted.

According to V'landys, Storm skipper Harry Grant (pictured) has 'got it wrong' when it comes to set-restarts. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Also raised by players was the fact there is no chance to ask for clarification, given the game rolls on quickly with a set restart.

But V'landys disagreed, pointing to the fact there are only two reasons for set restarts and players had become more compliant for offside ones.

"I don't buy that," ARL Commission chairman V'landys said.

"The wrestling's got to go. The fans did not like the wrestling, they didn't like people slowing down the ruck speed. And we've accommodated that.

"The players know when they're trying to control the ruck speed.

" I think that they're not telling the truth if they believe when they're giving a six again, they didn't know what it was for. I mean, I think it's pretty obvious. "

Set restarts increased dramatically over the first half of the season, before dropping off through the State of Origin period and rising again in recent weeks.

The rise at the start of the year coincided with the NRL expanding the area in which they can be awarded to from 60 metres of the field to 80.

V'landys indicated they would not be repealed next season, rejecting Grant's claims there was confusion this year.

"I have the ultimate respect for Harry, and Harry's an absolute ornament of the game, but he's got this one wrong," V'landys said.

"When you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. It's around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way.

Sharks co-captain Cameron McInnes (pictured) backed up Grant's viewpoint over the players' confusion. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down … we make no apology that we're going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams.

"The raw numbers don't back up what Harry is saying."

The majority of club representatives surveyed on Monday did not blame referees, but suggested there was still some grey area around ruck interpretation.

"With some of the six agains, who knows what they are for," Cronulla co-captain Cameron McInnes said.

"I just think about a fan watching at home … you just see them and think 'what was that for? It was like the tackle before'.

"That's a problem."

Warriors captain Roger Tuivasa-Sheck (pictured) is concerned that a faster game will lead to more injuries for the players. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if he shared the same confusion, McInnes suggested he did.

"I get the clear as day ones where guys are taking the piss … but then there are flops and re-grips that don't get called as well," he said.

"I don't know what their mindset is, but there will be some at the start of the game that is given a six again, and others that are not."

Some players at the NRL finals launch also raised concerns around whether a faster game had prompted an increased injury toll.

"I feel like it's not a clear understanding [of the interpretation]," injured Warriors veteran Roger Tuivasa-Sheck said.

"As players we understand they want a faster and more entertaining game, but they're risking that with the number of injuries every team has.

"That's what they have to weigh up.

"Yes we're building a very entertaining game and people love the product. But at the same time you lose all these big players out."

AAP

World.title: Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
World.content:
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.

The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.

Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.

Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.

Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.

It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.

Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.

This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.

The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Mills was seen on crutches as his Swans teammates celebrated their win over the Lions on Saturday. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.

Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

AAP

World.title: AFL acts to reduce head trauma at training for men and women
World.content:
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.

All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.

The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.

Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.

AFL hits Geelong with monster fine over concussion waiver scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.

Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.

Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.

Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.

Shane Tuck died in 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with CTE. (AAP: Mal Fairclough)

These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.

The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

AAP

World.title: 'Not value for money': Plans for Tuggeranong ice sports facility scrapped
World.content:
The ACT government has announced a proposed ice sports facility intended for Tuggeranong will not go ahead.

Plans for the facility featured two international-standard ice sheets for figure skating, ice hockey, broom-ball and speed skating.

But the government said today that despite extensive discussions with advocates of the project, it has been unable to reach an agreement on a way forward at the Tuggeranong site.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said an evaluation of an updated proposal to build and manage the facility found the project "did not represent value for money for the territory".

Canberra Brave players have been calling for an upgraded training facility. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

Updated proposal presented 'unacceptable risks'

The multi-purpose ice sports facility, dubbed Canberra Arena, was promised by ACT Labor during its 2016 election campaign, and at one stage of the project's planning, the completion date was even listed as 2025.

In addition to the government investment of $16.265 million, the remaining funds needed to build the estimated arena — estimated at $70 million at one stage — were to come from developers Cruachan Investments and Pelligra Holdings, who would "build, own, operate and maintain it".

"Unfortunately, we haven't been able to find a way forward with the partners Cruachan and Pelligra to build, maintain and operate this facility in Tuggeranong," Mr Steel said.

"The tender evaluation found that unfortunately there were a range of unacceptable risks and the updated proposal that was provided to the ACT government in January did not represent value for money for the ACT government."

Chris Steel says he's disappointed the project will not progress. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Steel said the proponents "were asking for more than double the territory's contribution to the project" in their latest updated proposal.

"That was one of the factors that led to the proposal being deemed not to be value for money," he said.

Cruachan chief executive Stephen Campbell said he supported the government's decision as additional costs associated with developing the site had become "prohibitive".

"We look forward to presenting a new proposal to the government in the coming months that will be more cost-effective, better meet community needs, and create improved access opportunities for all Canberrans," he said.

He said the Tuggeranong site was "too challenging" and the new proposal would include options for different locations.

Money to be spent on other sports facilities

Mr Steel said the $16.265 million that was committed to the facility would instead be spent "dollar for dollar" on upgrades to other sporting infrastructure projects in Tuggeranong.

Sporting clubs in the ACT have been invited to share their sporting and recreation infrastructure needs via a survey, which will inform how the money is spent.

"This investment will not be lost for Tuggeranong. The investment will go back into Tuggeranong to improve sporting infrastructure," he said.

Debate about the future site of a dedicated ice sports facility continues. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

The proposed dedicated arena was to be a new training and competition facility for a variety of ice sports teams who currently use the aging Philip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre.

At one stage it was also to be a new home for the Canberra Brave ice hockey team which has been using a temporary ice rink set up at the Australian Institute of Sport in recent years.

Mr Steel acknowledged that the outcome would be "deeply disappointing" for the ice sports community.

"Now we will need to continue to work with our ice sports community on what the next steps are and what other opportunities there are to improve ice sport facilities in the ACT," he said.

"It's important to note that on the current Phillip site, the requirement for an ice skating facility that meets national competition standards still remains."

'Not the end game'

ACT Ice Sport Federation spokesperson Sandi Logan said they were "profoundly disappointed" but that it was "not unexpected".

"We've not had a great deal of confidence in recent times in the proponents' ideas and the proposals that they put up to amend the original concept of a community facility for the ACT ice sports community," he said.

"The second thing I'd say is that we've moved into overtime, this is not the end of the game.

"There's still a lot of work ahead of us, and we're grateful that Sports Minister Chris Steel and the ACT government continues to support us.

"And we're in a way grateful that we'll have another chance to come up with a better arrangement, a better partnership, and a better opportunity for the community to pursue ice sports in Canberra and the ACT."

The Phillip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre is now being run by Geocon. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

He praised Geocon for how they had been managing the Phillip ice skating facility since taking over as lessees at the site.

"And maybe, just maybe, Geocon is looking at the Philip ice rink with a possibility for something into the future. I have no idea," he said.

"But we know that they have backed the Philip ice rink, maintained it, in fact, improved it to a state where we can now go with regular certainty that there'll be ice, there'll be a game, there'll be a sport to play."

Mr Logan said the foundation was in it "for the long run" until a solution was found.

"The ice may be thin under us, we may be skating on the proverbial thin ice, but we're here for the long haul, and we need to get a new ice rink built for the community."

World.title: Swans AFLW star says club's men's and women's players closer than ever
World.content:
Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".

Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.

The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.

Swans offer timely reminder of what 'Bloods' culture is meant to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.

The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.

In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Errol Gulden (right) has been getting Sydney's men's and women's players together for breathwork sessions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.

"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.

"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.

"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.

" In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before. "

As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.

"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.

"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."

GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.

Sydney's AFLW side has received a mountain of support from both inside and outside the club. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.

Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.

Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.

"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.

"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.

"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

AAP

World.title: Opals remain perfect at World Cup despite 2am fire alarm wake-up call
World.content:
Australia has made it two from two at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup with an 87-71 win over Türkiye in Berlin.

It was an improved performance by the Opals after their opening 70-54 victory over Puerto Rico, leaving Sandy Brondello's side set to progress to the knockout stages.

New captain Ezi Magbegor was instrumental in the second straight victory with 21 points on 10/14 shooting, leading the way with able support from Steph Talbot's 17 points.

It was an impressive performance considering the unceremonious 2am wake-up call the teams received when a fire alarm went off at the team hotel.

Ezi Magbegor led the way with 21 points. (Supplied: FIBA)

The players and coaches all had to evacuate the hotel before going back inside the building about an hour later.

There was no fire, someone had pushed the emergency alarm button in the elevator, according to Brondello.

"That's a what-if situation, isn't it?" Brondello said.

"Now we have that in our toolbox. Never done that before."

The interrupted sleep did not seem to hurt the Opals in the first game of the day that tipped at 11:30am local time.

"It was kind of crazy. Just kind of happened," Australia forward Ezi Magbegor said.

"Knowing that it's out of our control, so just getting back to sleep and waking up. No-one was going to feel sorry for us."

Turkish coach Andrea Masson said he and his players got about three hours of sleep because of the alarm.

"They had a really bad night last night," Masson said.

"That's not an excuse, but that's the reality."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AP

World.title: Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.

There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.

Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.

"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.

Is Marnus Labuschagne running out of luck? After spending years as one of the luckiest Test cricketers in the game, Marnus Labuschagne's fortunes appear to BE turning and, unfortunately for him, so has his form.

"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."

Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.

Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.
